15919-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Harison's weekly paper for boys and girls, number forty-two, dated August 26, 1897. Five cents bought news, science, and stories in words young readers could follow. One new subscriber earned a scientific box kite, patent applied for, billed as the latest thing. The paper's premiums show how it won young readers.

Kite notes explain how to put in the sticks and how to start, beside the week's news. Serial tales and nature items keep the pace brisk. Editors explain treaties and inventions in short, clear paragraphs. Seen now, the issue captures late summer 1897 for American children: kites in the sky, and the world in a weekly paper.
24254-history-of-the-english-people-volu:
John Richard Green wrote this sixth volume of his History of the English People, published by Macmillan in London and New York in 1896, in the Eversley edition. The first edition appeared in 1879. Book Seven covers Puritan England from 1642 to 1660, in chapters on the Civil War, the army and the Parliament, the Commonwealth, and the Protectorate.

Book Eight carries the Revolution from 1660 to 1683, through the Restoration and the Popish Plot. Maps show Marston Moor, the Naseby fight, and Europe as it stood under Louis XIV. Green tells the story of a people, not only of kings, in clear narrative. Readers get a standard Victorian history of England's mid-seventeenth-century crisis.
30502-the-gorgeous-isle-a-romance-scene-:
Gertrude Atherton writes The Gorgeous Isle, a romance set on Nevis in the British West Indies in 1842, illustrated by C. Coles Phillips and published in New York in October 1908. Atherton dedicates the book to Mrs. Spencer Wigley of St. Kitts, quoting Helmholtz: we are all souls of fire and children of the sun.

An illustration asks, but what a joy to see you in colour, and how does it happen, hinting at the romance's visual charm. Atherton sets love, rank, and island life against a Caribbean past, with Nevis as both place and mood. The novel blends historical romance with vivid scene painting, in a handsome illustrated edition.
5945-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2:
Homecoming and farewell fill chapters seventy-three and seventy-four, the close of this Don Quixote portion. Chapter seventy-three treats the omens Quixote had entering his own village, with incidents that embellish and colour this great history, beginning with two boys quarrelling on the threshing floor. Chapter seventy-four tells how Quixote fell sick, made his will, and died, in the history's sober ending.

Readers reach Cervantes's conclusion, where omens, boys' quarrels, and a deathbed will replace adventures. The chapters favor quiet, domestic finality over triumph, letting Sancho mourn and the village witness. This part suits readers finishing volume two, since it delivers the knight's end with gravity, humor, and a will that settles his name.
a-crust-for-the-phrenologists-electronic:
A Crust for the Phrenologists, printed in 1842 and signed by Samuel Read, is an attack on the head-reading science. It presents itself as a vidimus, a summary preview, of lectures shortly to be offered to the public. In those lectures, Read promises, the delusive and unfounded character of that pretended and vaunted science will be demonstrated, in both its departments, physical and metaphysical.

The title throws the phrenologists a crust, a scrap, in mock generosity before the feast of refutation. Read backs the polemic with bibliographical references, marshalling earlier authorities against the doctrine. The pamphlet preserves the case for the prosecution in phrenology's own heyday, proof that the science's critics were lecturing as energetically as its champions.
a-phrenological-chart-giving-a-descripti:
A Phrenological Chart, published in 1842 by P L Buell and Nelson Sizer, gives a description of the phenomena of the human mind in phrenological form. Phrenology mapped the mind into separate faculties, each seated in an organ of the brain and marked on the skull. A chart let a practitioner record a reading: faculty by faculty, the subject's head could be scored and kept.

At eighty-four pages, the book is more than a wall chart; it explains the phenomena the chart records. Sizer became one of America's best-known practical phrenologists, and works like this were his trade's tools. The book preserves how a phrenological examination was documented in the eighteen forties, when the science filled lecture halls.
addison-history-knights-templars-1842:
Charles G. Addison, an English lawyer of the Inner Temple, wrote this history of the Knights Templars in 1842. It was the first full history of the order in the English tongue. Addison knew the Temple Church in London, the order's old seat, at first hand.

He tells of the order's rise in the crusades, its wealth, and its famed rule of life. Then come the shock of its fall: the arrests, the trial, and the fire that ends its tale. Bound with it is the tale of the Temple Church and the Temple grounds in London.
arxiv-2509-00042:
Poyraz Baydemir, working alone, presents ARTPS in 2025, a hybrid AI system that ranks targets for a Mars rover on its own. A rover must pick which rocks and soils merit close study, with no human in the loop. Depth from a single camera, anomaly spotting, and a learnable curiosity score are joined in one system.

The curiosity score weighs known value, anomaly strength, depth spread, and surface roughness. Scores on Mars rover data reach strong levels across three gauges of hit quality. Ablation tests, which drop one part at a time, show each part aids the whole. False alarms fall by near a quarter while sensitivity stays high across terrain types. Smarter picks could raise the science yield of each rover day.
arxiv-2509-00142:
Scott C. Scharlach, working alone, defines academic miscommunication in physics teaching in 2025 and tests its link to exam grades. The term names the gap when a professor's classroom expectations, beliefs, or goals differ from those of students. Scharlach surveyed undergraduates in two introductory physics classes just after their first exam grades arrived.

One class served majors, the other non-majors. Students rated how well the exam matched what they expected in form and content, which yielded a miscommunication score. In both classes, higher scores went with lower exam marks in a clear inverse line. The link was sound for majors and present for non-majors as well. Aligning exam cues with student expectations could lift scores fairly.
arxiv-2509-00542:
Monirul Shaikh leads seven authors in total, with Fengyi Zhou, Sathiyamoorthy Buvaneswaran, Rajan Gowsalya, Trilochan Sahoo, Duo Wang, and Saurabh Ghosh, in predicting new magnetic oxides. Insulating ferro and ferrimagnets, materials that act magnetic yet block current, are uncommon because of Hund's rules for electron filling.

Shaikh and his co-authors use symmetry analysis, first-principles calculations, and Monte Carlo simulations, random sampling methods, on double-double perovskite oxides, crystals with a layered doubled structure. They predict a family with band gaps, energy gaps for electrons, between about one and two electron volts in plain scale, and magnetic change temperatures up to a stated value. They also check stability, for spintronic and optical uses.
arxiv-2509-00642:
Qizheng Yang, with four co-authors, Tung-I Chen, Siyu Zhao, Ramesh K Sitaraman, and Hui Guan, builds HADIS for serving text-to-image diffusion models, systems that generate images by gradual denoising. Query-aware serving routes requests through stages of rising cost, but forcing every query through a light model wastes work on hard queries.

HADIS pairs a pre-generation router, which sends predicted-hard queries straight to the heavy model, with a post-generation discriminator that catches false-easy cases. Routing thresholds, model pairs, and graphics processor allocation are tuned jointly, using an offline table of good configurations and online re-optimization. On a sixteen-processor cluster with real traces, response quality rises and deadline violations fall sharply.
arxiv-2509-01342:
Suicide is a major public health concern worldwide, and Spain has seen rising rates among women while men's rates stayed fairly stable. A. Adin, G. Retegui, A. Sanchez Villegas, and M. D. Ugarte examine suicide mortality across Spanish provinces from 2010 to 2022. Their study splits the data by age and sex to trace both time trends and spatial patterns.

Mixed Poisson models, suited to count data, handled province and year effects while testing links with social and economic factors. Rurality and unemployment stood out as influences on suicide mortality in their results. Adin and the co-authors aim to show where risk concentrates and which conditions travel with it, so prevention efforts in Spain can be aimed with better evidence about place, time, and group.
arxiv-2509-01442:
Digital painting usually imitates physical media, but Joao S. Ferreira, with seven co-authors, built a painting tool powered by quantum computing instead. Quantum Brush is open source, and each of its four brushes turns a user's stroke into a distinct quantum algorithm. Each algorithm lets a different quantum effect shape the artwork's look.

The brushes are designed to run on today's noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices, the limited quantum hardware now available. The team demonstrated them on a real device, IQM's Sirius machine. Ferreira and the co-authors present the tool as a way for artists to work directly with quantum behavior, producing visual effects that classical software cannot copy exactly. The project joins art practice with hands-on access to quantum machines.
arxiv-2509-01542:
Terahertz rays sit between microwaves and infrared light. They are prized for imaging and sensing. Some materials may offer a tunable source of them. Ramaz Khomeriki, Kathrin Dorr, and Jamal Berakdar study rays linked to currents in domain walls. The walls lie inside bismuth ferrite, a ferroelectric material. The rays appear after the material is struck by infrared light.

In their picture, stripes of domain walls act as metal resonators. Charge piles up at the wall edges and swings back and forth. The swing rate is set by the plasma rate inside the wall. That rate fixes both the pitch and the strength of the emitted rays. For certain wall shapes and light angles, the rays carry a handedness. The authors argue domain walls could be tuned as steady terahertz sources.
arxiv-2509-01642:
Estimating how loaded a person's mind is during a task helps tune work and training, but models trained in one setting often fail in another. Maximilian P. Oppelt, Andreas Foltyn, Nadine R. Lang-Richter, and Bjoern M. Eskofier introduce REVELIO, a multimodal data set and evaluation for universal task load estimation. It extends established cognitive load benchmarks with a real-world gaming application, grounded in the classic n-back memory test.

Task load labels come from objective performance, subjective workload ratings on a standard scale, and the task design itself. Leading end-to-end models, including recurrent, convolutional, and transformer designs, were trained and tested across several data types and domains. Multimodal approaches consistently beat single-source baselines, though which sources and designs helped most varied by application. The team aims at load models that travel across real settings.
arxiv-2509-01842:
Qifu Wen leads six co-authors with GradES, a method that stops training parts of a transformer once they settle. Standard early stopping watches overall test loss and halts all updates at once, which costs long test passes. Parts of a transformer, the core model design in modern AI, settle at different speeds. GradES tracks gradient shifts, the size of update signals, inside attention and feed forward matrices.

When a matrix gradient shifts fall below a set line, that matrix stops updating alone. Slow parts keep learning while done parts freeze, with no test passes needed. Training runs several times faster in their tests. Accuracy also rises slightly on language and mixed media tasks, since freezing guards against overfitting.
arxiv-2509-01942:
Alex Leviyev, Francesco Iacovelli, and Aaron Zimmerman speed up Bayesian sampling with a diffusion that can spawn and remove walkers. Bayesian inference weighs hypotheses under uncertainty but needs many samples from complex distributions. Hard cases are skewed, multi peaked, or live on curved spaces. Wave parameter work motivates the design, where signals are noisy and spaces twist.

Their Langevin diffusion, a noise driven drift, gains a birth-death process that adds or drops samples. A simple preconditioner rescales the motion, and the method extends to cube and torus product spaces. It runs in parallel across model calls, suiting modern accelerators. Tests on toy problems succeed, and the sampler recovers the first observed black hole merger parameters.
arxiv-2509-02142:
Yuelin Shao, Hao Shi, and Xi Dai build a small scale theory of how bilayer exciton insulators react to fields. An exciton insulator binds electrons and holes into a dense phase across two sheets. Their frame uses Hartree-Fock counts that feed back on self for the ground state, plus a time form for motion. Charge and exciton paths react to fields that are same or flipped by sheet.

Two gapped plasmon modes rule the long wave charge path in the counts. The exciton path is ruled by a Goldstone phase mode that spreads in a straight line. London type rules for the dense phase come next, with loss free push as a superfluid sign. A cross field bends that mode toward stripes and mixes charge with exciton flow. Dipole Hall effects spring from that mix as clear lab targets.
arxiv-2509-02242:
Martin Bubel, Tobias Seidel, and Michael Bortz bring a machine learned model fluid for flowsheet work in chemical plants. Plant flowsheet work stalls when sound heat and phase data for mixes are thin. Machine learning now calls mix traits at vast scale, which opens fresh design paths. Their model fluid folds those calls straight into flowsheet tools for plant work.

Traits rest on core vapor and liquid phase facts, so they stay clear and smooth. Fit with live plant sims and slope based search is built in from the start. A test case picks a helper fluid for a hard split of a mixed feed. The frame finds best, phase true helpers with high truth next to old models. The path brings large scale calls into day to day plant design.
arxiv-2509-02342:
Ksenia Slepova, Ivan Etoku Oiye, and Martin B. van Gijzen wrote a 2025 medical imaging paper on cleaning and splitting MRI scans that contain heavy noise. Both steps matter before a scan can guide care, and equation-based methods are known to handle them reliably.

Their pipeline runs in stages. First, a raw image is rebuilt from noisy measurements. Next, anisotropic diffusion, which smooths along structures but not across edges, removes noise. Those stages are merged into one optimisation, guided by a rough early segmentation. A final stage then cuts the image into regions using clustering and region growing. Tests cover images with known truth and scans from a cheap experimental scanner.
arxiv-2509-02442:
Chen Sun and six co-authors present a 2025 transport communications paper improving hazard warnings between vehicles and roadside units. Current vehicle-to-everything messages say what to avoid but not why, so drivers may brake too hard or ignore context.

Their SEE-V2X system adds meaning and explanation. Smart cameras at the roadside spot obstructions, and the units then send context-aware messages, so drivers can judge the right response for their own situation. A field demonstration shows a see-through feature that reveals pedestrians hidden behind obstacles. Simulations across traffic conditions compare the design with standard warnings. The enhanced system improved traffic flow and cut needless slowing, suggesting richer messages can make connected roads both safer and smoother.
arxiv-2509-02542:
Avi Wadhwa wrote a 2025 solo theoretical physics paper on soft theorems in Chern-Simons matter theories, working in five spacetime dimensions. Soft theorems describe the universal behaviour of scattering when one particle carries very little energy.

Such theorems usually follow from gauge invariance, the symmetry that defines the theory. Chern-Simons terms complicate the story because they stay invariant only up to a boundary term. Wadhwa shows the subleading soft theorems for quantum electrodynamics and quantum chromodynamics pick up corrections once Chern-Simons terms enter, and derives those corrections. The calculation starts from the gauge argument, builds the needed interaction vertices, then computes each correction. The result tests how far the symmetry explanation of soft behaviour extends.
arxiv-2509-02642:
Bin Feng and four co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on protein motion. It introduces BioMD, a generative model for biomolecular dynamics. Standard molecular dynamics is accurate but slow. Its cost blocks long timescales for many biological processes.

BioMD is, its authors say, the first generative model at all-atom resolution for long protein-ligand dynamics. It works in a hierarchy. First it forecasts coarse motion. Then it interpolates the detail between frames. Tests use a ligand unbinding dataset and the MISATO benchmark. The shapes it made looked physically plausible. Reconstruction errors were low. The model also found full unbinding paths for nearly all test systems within ten tries. The authors pitch it as a tool for drug discovery.
arxiv-2509-03042:
Shad Ali wrote a 2025 paper reviewing ideas about how much space lies inside a black hole and how entropy is counted there. Entropy measures how many hidden arrangements a system can have. A well-known definition by Christodoulou and Rovelli takes a black hole's interior volume as the largest volume of any suitable slice bounded by a given sphere.

Under that definition the interior grows in proportion to advanced time, so a black hole could hold vast amounts of infalling information. The same behavior held when the idea was extended to charged, still black holes. A later study by Zhang counted the entropy of simple quantum modes inside a Schwarzschild black hole. That entropy scaled with surface area, like the famous horizon entropy, but with a smaller constant. The review notes these results assume black holes heavier than the Planck mass.
arxiv-2509-03142:
Luca Barbieri tackled a 2025 plasma physics problem: how the ambipolar electric field in a star-like atmosphere can arise on its own. In a collisionless plasma, meaning particles rarely bump into each other, gravity tends to sort charged species by weight. An electric field then appears that holds the mix together and keeps charge balanced overall.

Textbooks often impose that field from outside using a classical formula. Barbieri instead expands the electric interaction into multiple Fourier modes, a sum of wave patterns, and lets the field emerge self-consistently. Under suitable conditions the method recovers the classical field and restores neutrality without outside help. Tests covered both single-temperature and multi-temperature plasmas. The framework is meant as a base for adding collisions and ionization later.
arxiv-2509-03242:
Gianmarco De Vita, Nargiz Humbatova, and Paolo Tonella introduced TopoMap in 2025, a tool for mapping where a deep learning system struggles. Finding inputs that make a model fail is fairly easy; grouping those inputs by what makes them hard is the open problem. Grouping helps teams spot neglected regions and prioritize labeling work.

TopoMap uses only features of the inputs themselves, not the model's internals. It shrinks those features into embeddings, compact numeric summaries, then clusters them into regions of an input map. A separate neural network judges which embedding and clustering settings separate inputs meaningfully, standing in for a human evaluator. The resulting maps showed distinguishable, sensible regions in tests. Mutation analysis, which seeds artificial faults, confirmed the clusters help select revealing test inputs.
arxiv-2509-03342:
Gabriel Pérez-Angel and 4 co-authors used simulations in 2025 to pull apart depletion forces between large particles in a mixture. Depletion forces arise when small particles crowd around big ones and effectively push the big ones together. Real effective forces bundle pair, triple, and larger group effects into one whole, and separating them is rarely attempted.

Their new simulation approach measures the full effective interaction accurately enough to judge higher-order terms. Earlier work centered on the small particles; this study turns to what the large particles themselves contribute, especially away from dilute mixtures. When the size gap was extreme and the small particles' chemical drive was held fixed, large particle concentration did not affect the entropic force. For milder size gaps that effect became considerable, and the authors compare those cases with theory.
arxiv-2509-03442:
Zhuoyun Qian and 6 co-authors surveyed feature-oriented malware analysis for Internet of Things devices in 2025. Connected devices keep multiplying, and their reliability is increasingly limited by security problems. Malware analysis for such devices leans on extracted features, measurable traits of an app or its behavior, and many extraction styles have appeared.

The survey organizes the field from several angles. Static methods read code without running it, dynamic methods watch execution, and hybrid methods combine both. A further section covers representation strategies based on graph learning, where programs become networks of related parts. Strengths and limits of each family are compared directly. The authors close with open challenges and promising directions, aiming to guide researchers entering a crowded, fast-moving area.
arxiv-2509-03642:
Melissa Butler and four co-authors map how Texans moved during the February 2021 winter storm, broken down by industry sector, in a 2025 research paper. Knowing which trips people keep, cut, or prioritise in a disaster supports emergency planning. Their case study covers the storm that froze much of Texas that month.

Movements between census tracts are organised into time-varying multilayer networks, where each layer holds trips for one sector, such as schools or hospitals. Trips to ambulatory health care, restaurants, and schools fell sharply during the storm. Trips to gas stations and grocery stores were prioritised instead, holding up far better. The authors also test how predictable each tract's incoming and outgoing trip counts are. Inward movement proved harder to predict than outward movement, especially while the storm was underway.
arxiv-2509-04142:
Naonori Sugiyama, writing alone, builds a cleaner way to model how galaxies trace invisible dark matter in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Galaxies do not spread exactly like the dark matter beneath them, and that mismatch is called bias. Older bias formulas needed ad hoc fixes, known as renormalization, to stay meaningful. Sugiyama's framework grows out of a unified theory that follows matter as it moves from its starting positions.

Bias terms come only from the dark matter's own nonlinear growth, written with Galileon-type operators. A handful of adjustable numbers then describes clustering patterns. Fits against a large simulation library matched measured galaxy clustering within about one percent over wide ranges. Fast public software ships with the method for other teams.
arxiv-2509-04242:
Raphaël Maire and one co-author, Ludivine Chaix, show that unusually even spreads of matter arise when conservation laws meet outside driving in a 2025 physics paper. Hyperuniform systems suppress density swings, meaning clumping, far more than plain materials at large scales. The mechanism looks like self-organized criticality, where systems tune themselves to a threshold state. Four new far-from-equilibrium models display the effect again and again.

Systems conserving several kinds of mass moments show stronger, tunable hyperuniform patterns, with strength set by the count of conserved moments. Fragility appears too: one class built from conserved noise loses its evenness under nonlinear effects. Such damping destroys hyperuniformity in special fluids entirely. Conservation laws thus both create and protect the pattern.
arxiv-2509-04442:
Zhiqiu Xu and three co-authors fingerprint fine-tuned language models by how their insides shift in a 2025 research paper. Thousands of adapted open models now crowd public repositories, with messy metadata that hides what each one is for. Their method, Delta Activations, measures changes in internal activations, the activity patterns inside a model, relative to the base model it came from. Those shifts become a vector embedding, a compact numeric portrait of the adapted model.

Portraits cluster neatly by task and domain, revealing structure across the model landscape. The representation stays robust across fine-tuning settings and adds up cleanly when training sets mix. Few-shot fine-tuning can even embed whole tasks this way. Model selection and merging get a practical compass.
arxiv-2509-04742:
Surfaces of two layered compounds host electronic order that the bulk does not dictate. Tongrui Li, lead author with twelve co-authors, investigate strontium and europium tetra-aluminide in a 2025 materials paper. Both materials show well-known charge-density-wave transitions, where electron density forms a repeating pattern.

Using photoemission spectroscopy and scanning tunnelling microscopy, they find linearly dispersing states and replica bands running against the bulk wave direction. That imaging also reveals a rebuilt surface layer tied to ordered missing surface atoms. That surface order vanishes after heating, showing surface and bulk orders are decoupled. The materials become platforms for studying surface-confined electronic phases.
arxiv-2509-04942:
Job titles written freely by employers rarely match official occupational categories. Heinke Hihn, lead author with five co-authors, present an embedding-based alignment process for that problem in a 2025 labour market analytics paper. Hand-built ontologies support reasoning across data sources but cost expert effort to maintain.

Their process links German job titles, however freely written, to two established classifications, one for occupations and one for education. Public employment agency data fine-tune a sentence embedding model to learn the ontology structure. The resulting similarity graph supports fast nearest-neighbour search, framing classification as semantic search. The authors discuss design choices and open challenges for extending the graph.
arxiv-2509-05042:
Inspecting a ship's hull with a mixed fleet of marine robots is risky work that benefits from shared control. Cristiano Caissutti, lead author with five co-authors, study shared autonomy for that setting in a 2025 robotics paper. Their architecture combines three layers for heterogeneous marine robotic fleets.

Large language models let operators specify tasks at a high level in natural language. Human-in-the-loop frameworks support adaptive, intent-aware coordination among agents. A modular mission manager built on behaviour trees gives interpretable, flexible control. Early results in simulation and lake-like settings suggest lower operator load and better alignment with human intent.
arxiv-2509-05142:
Training large foundation models on data that cannot leave hospitals or companies is the promise of federated learning. Cosmin-Andrei Hatfaludi and one co-author survey how the two fields are being combined in a 2025 review paper. No unified survey existed, so they build a taxonomy that follows the development life cycle of such systems.

From an initial pool of thousands of articles, they review a few hundred in depth and compare methods technically. Topics include self-supervised learning, fine-tuning, distillation, and transfer learning. Practical guidance focuses on healthcare as a case study, where private data and large models could combine with significant impact.
arxiv-2509-05242:
Andreas Thom studies free groups and their finite quotients in a solo 2025 paper on the restricted Burnside problem. A group is called anabelian here when none of its basic building blocks are abelian, meaning none are groups where order of operations does not matter.

Thom proves that the relatively free group set by a chosen group law has a largest anabelian finite quotient, and he estimates its size. The bound rests on explicit limits for how long a law must be in finite simple groups, drawn from work with Bradford and recent work by others. The result ties a classic group theory question to new bounds on simple groups.
arxiv-2509-05342:
Editing a generated image without oversmoothing it is the target of Gaspard Beaudouin and four co-authors in a 2025 paper on rectified flow models. These generators move noise toward pictures along learned paths. Earlier editing shortcuts often blur fine detail.

Their method, called DRFS, directly models the gap between the source and target velocity fields that steer generation. A shift term that changes over time pushes noisy states closer to the target path. The authors show older editing methods appear as special cases when parts of their method are switched off. On a widely used editing benchmark, DRFS gave better quality, faithfulness, and control with no change to the model itself.
arxiv-2509-05642:
Particles settling on a flat surface form crystal patches whose shape and jitter obey sharp laws, Manuel Friedrich, Leonard Kreutz, and Ulisse Stefanelli prove in a 2025 mathematical physics paper. Short-range two- and three-body forces favour square lattice arrangements, while an extra coupling ties the particles to the substrate.

Their first result proves crystallisation for every positive coupling strength, giving discrete versions of the Winterbottom shape, the equilibrium crystal shape on a substrate. The second bounds how far distinct minimisers with the same particle count can sit from each other. The scaling of that distance depends sharply on whether the coupling is rational or algebraic irrational, a genuine substrate effect.
arxiv-2509-06442:
Scoring how good a super-resolved image really looks takes a network that mimics human perception, propose Yixiao Li and eight co-authors in a 2025 paper. Full-reference quality metrics for super-resolution are scarce, so algorithms are hard to compare fairly. Their Perception-oriented Bidirectional Attention Network encodes the images, then builds visual attention in both directions, matching how super-resolution images are generated and judged.

Grouped multi-scale deformable convolutions adapt the network to distortions at several scales, and a sub-information excitation step steers attention to sub-pixel and sub-channel detail. A prediction module regresses the final score. Extensive experiments show the network beating leading quality assessment methods on super-resolution benchmarks.
arxiv-2509-06742:
Gas components flowing through one pipeline tend to fall into step, and Martin Gugat proves that tendency in a solo 2025 applied mathematics paper. Each component obeys the isothermal Euler equations, with an added coupling term pulling the components' velocities together. The motivation is blending hydrogen into natural gas pipelines during the energy transition.

With suitable boundary conditions, Gugat shows the velocities synchronize at an exponential rate, as long as the synchronization error stays outside a certain interval set by the interaction terms. Inside that interval the guarantee pauses. The result justifies, in some cases, using a simpler drift-flux model where all components share one velocity, and it bounds the error of that simplification. The proof uses a Lyapunov function built on relative energy, a standard tool for showing that systems settle down.
arxiv-2509-07642:
Sascha Kaltenpoth and 1 co-author view language model alignment through agency theory in a 2025 paper. Firms that adopt large language models can get off-topic, biased, or harmful output. The authors frame the problem as a contract issue. The adopter, the principal, cannot see inside the black-box agent. So errors made during adoption go unnoticed. Alignment research has rarely treated that imbalance of information, or the adoption process itself.

Their framework is called LLM ATLAS, an agency theory-led alignment strategy. It is aimed at the phases of adoption inside an organization. A conceptual review of the literature is organized by adoption phase and by agency concepts. It yields an extended analysis process for alignment methods, and a first map from alignment problems to solutions. The aim is practical. Firms should spot and contract around alignment risks before deployment, not after an incident.
arxiv-2509-08042:
Mario Reig and 1 co-author test whether a loophole saves heterotic string theory from a future axion discovery, in a 2025 particle physics paper. Finding an axion-like particle above the line predicted for the QCD axion would rule out grand unified theories, including the standard heterotic string constructions. The loophole uses a non-standard embedding of the Standard Model into the string's gauge group.

If electromagnetism draws on both E8 factors of the E8-by-E8 string, axions could couple to photons without coupling to QCD. The authors bound how large that coupling can be relative to the particle's mass. Such bounds turn a hypothetical discovery into a sharp verdict on string constructions that are otherwise hard to test.
arxiv-2509-08542:
Running a large language model inside a memory chip is efficient, until the model has billions of weights to store. Wenlun Zhang and 3 co-authors present BitROM in a 2025 research paper. BitROM is a compute-in-memory accelerator designed around a model quantized to about one and a half bits per weight. Earlier chips of this style stored weights permanently, which made huge models physically enormous.

Three innovations shrink the design. A bidirectional memory array stores two ternary weights per transistor. A tri-mode accumulator handles those weights efficiently. An on-chip refreshable memory manages the conversation cache, cutting trips to outside memory nearly in half. Adapters also allow light transfer learning for new tasks. Built in an older chip process, the design still reached strong efficiency. It suggests edge devices could host serious language models without the cloud.
arxiv-2509-08642:
Hang Ruan and 4 co-authors propose a beamforming method for sensing several targets without a direct line of sight in a 2025 paper. Their system combines sensing and communication, known as ISAC, in the near field. A reconfigurable intelligent surface, a panel that steers signals, creates a path around blocks.

Classic measures of beam strength and target separation are extended to use both angle and distance. The design jointly sets base station beams and surface phase shifts while keeping communication rates. An alternating optimization method solves the hard problem step by step. Simulations show clear sensing of targets that share an angle but differ in distance.
arxiv-2509-08742:
Forecasting financial markets from raw charts and text, rather than cleaned numbers, is the ambition behind FinZero. Yanlong Wang and 10 co-authors present it in a 2025 research paper. Earlier forecasters standardized time series before modeling, losing information in the encoding. They also demanded fixed variable counts and window lengths, limiting scale.

The team first built a diverse financial image-text dataset for training. They then fine-tuned a multimodal model with a new reinforcement learning method that adjusts for prediction uncertainty. The model outputs forecasts together with analysis of its own confidence. After fine-tuning, accuracy in the high-confidence group improved clearly over a leading commercial model. FinZero also adapts across tasks without fixed input shapes. Interpretable, uncertainty-aware forecasts matter in finance, where a confident wrong answer costs real money.
arxiv-2509-08942:
Xenia Konti and 6 co-authors propose group robust machine learning under group level uncertainty in a 2025 paper. Models trained on mixed sources can learn spurious patterns that work on average but fail for rare groups. Prior methods optimize worst group performance.

Those methods assume each group's distribution is known well from training data, which often fails in noisy, changing settings. A Wasserstein based robust method, which guards against nearby distributions, accounts for uncertainty within each group. A gradient descent-ascent algorithm solves the problem, with convergence results given. Tests on real data validate the approach. Worst group performance remains the goal throughout.
arxiv-2509-09142:
Minsuk Kim and 6 co-authors study shortest-path percolation on scale-free networks in a 2025 paper. The model consumes network resources: random node pairs are chosen, and if their shortest path fits a budget, its edges are removed. The network eventually breaks into small components.

Large simulations and finite size scaling examine networks with power law degree distributions. Unlike ordinary percolation, the transition matches the one on Erdős-Rényi networks, independent of the degree exponent. Finite and infinite budget cases still form distinct universality classes. The process homogenizes the network's uneven structure before the transition. That homogenization explains why degree details stop mattering.
arxiv-2509-09342:
Recommendation engines remember your history but cannot hear what you want right now; chatbots listen but forget your history. Yifan Wang and 5 co-authors merge the two in a 2025 research paper. Their framework, CESRec, feeds conversational feedback into a sequential recommender. The goal is recommendations shaped by both long-term taste and immediate intent.

The system reads chat feedback and constructs pseudo interactions, synthetic history entries reflecting the conversation. Those entries update the user's sequence seamlessly. A second mechanism masks outlier items in the history that clash with the user's core preferences. The masking uses representations aligning semantic and collaborative signals. Experiments show CESRec lifting strong sequential models to state-of-the-art performance. For streaming and shopping platforms, the blend promises suggestions that respect both who you have been and what you just said.
arxiv-2509-09642:
Entong He and 1 co-author measure the cost of programming shallow quantum circuits in a 2025 paper aimed at today's noisy machines. Such devices are naturally described by low-depth circuits, and running one means sending a program state that encodes the instructions, often through a cloud service. Generic programming methods waste effort in this shallow regime, so a sharper accounting is needed as qubit counts grow.

The authors pin down the program cost for brickwork circuits, meaning the memory size a universal programmer must hold. In the large system limit the worst case grows in step with the qubit count times a modest logarithmic factor, and the bound is tight. They also weigh how layout description costs trade against gate programming costs.
arxiv-2509-09942:
Lei Yu and 5 co-authors train a model that writes smart contracts and can show its security reasoning in a 2025 software paper. Contracts guard serious money on blockchains, and a single flaw can drain it. General language models write such code as black boxes, with no auditable thought process, and the output too often carries critical holes that audits catch late or never.

SmartCoder-R1 starts from a seven-billion-parameter coding model, specialises it with continued pretraining, then studies nearly eight thousand expert-checked samples pairing long reasoning with code. A final reinforcement stage rewards compiling, safe, well-formed output in a weighted mix. Against seventeen rivals on 756 real functions, the system topped five headline measures and set a new best mark.
arxiv-2509-10342:
Approximation with orthogonal polynomials on mirror-symmetric regions is Yuan Xu's subject in this solo 2025 paper. The domain he studies is generated from a triangle in the first quadrant. It has full symmetry. For a family of weight functions on it, he examines the polynomials that are orthogonal there.

A tidy reduction does the heavy lifting. Take the polynomials on this domain that are even in the second variable. They match, exactly, the orthogonal polynomials of the unit disk pulled back through a quadratic map. The same trick extends further. Rotate the region into higher dimensions, and the match survives. Results about approximation and Fourier-style expansions then transfer over at once. The coverage includes shapes such as the double cone and the double hyperboloid.
arxiv-2509-10442:
Ferronematics are liquid crystals seeded with magnetic particles. Shilpa Dutta and three co-authors study them in this 2025 study. The materials are candidates for displays, sensors, and microfluidic devices. The team models a thin ferronematic film in two dimensions. Their tool is a variational energy. It couples the liquid crystal's order parameter to the magnetization.

The energy blends two theories. One is the Landau-de Gennes description of nematics. The other is micromagnetics, with terms for a stray field and an external field. The stray field term is an approximation, and it matters. First, the authors prove a lowest-energy state exists. In some parameter ranges, it is unique. Then they compute stable equilibria by following the energy's gradient flow. The numerics show the stray field at work. It steers where nematic defects and magnetic vortices settle inside the film.
arxiv-2509-10642:
Wheel loaders burn fuel digging, and Armin Abdolmohammadi with three co-authors build an automation framework to dig smarter in this 2025 engineering paper. Their soil modeling rests on the Fundamental Earthmoving Equation, which predicts the forces between bucket and soil. A reduced-order estimation method, guided by a global sensitivity analysis, identifies soil parameters online from the previous digging cycle.

Those parameters feed an optimal control problem that plans the most energy-efficient bucket trajectory for the next scoop. High-fidelity simulations in Algoryx Dynamics confirmed the force predictions and showed energy savings between fifteen and forty percent against standard paths. Crucially, the whole computation takes about as long as one digging cycle, so the planning can keep pace with real work, a step toward wheel loaders that automate themselves economically.
arxiv-2509-10742:
Weizhi Li, Gautam Dasarathy, and Visar Berisha redesign matched-pair experiments in this 2025 paper. The redesign centers on where a treatment works best. Matched pairs compare similar participants who differ only in treatment. They are efficient when effects are broad. When the average effect is tiny, the picture changes. Only some regions of the population respond strongly. The real job is finding those high-effect regions.

Their design enrolls participants actively and sequentially. It steers the experiment toward promising regions. Finding the target region is framed as a classification problem. An active learning method, tailored to matched pairs, drives the search. Theory on label complexity backs the claim. Practical experiments back it, too. The design lowers the cost of proving efficacy. It guarantees the identified region encloses the full high-effect territory. A convenient subset would not do.
arxiv-2509-11042:
The Red Spider nebula spreads its legs in new James Webb images, and Joel Kastner with seven co-authors present them in this 2025 astronomy paper. NGC 6537 is a bipolar planetary nebula, the expelled envelope of a dying star, rich in molecules and highly excited. Near-infrared cameras aboard JWST imaged it in hydrogen, iron, and dust emission lines, joined by ALMA radio maps and archival Hubble pictures.

The infrared hydrogen traces bubble-like lobes over a light-year wide, blown by fast polar outflows, while ALMA reveals a slow, point-symmetric equatorial torus. Ionized iron glows in an S-shape where an active collimated wind rams slower material along the lobe rims. Deep X-ray imaging found nothing, but the central star shows hot dust nearby. The authors propose a close companion star sculpted the whole display: ejecting the torus, forming a shared dust disk, and launching the wandering jets.
arxiv-2509-11442:
Ayhan Can Erdur and 6 co-authors pre-train a brain MRI model that tolerates missing scan types in this 2025 paper. Clinical MRI exams combine several sequences, and in practice some are often absent, which breaks models trained to expect a full set. Their method adapts the masked autoencoder idea to many modalities and many tasks at once.

Each sequence enters as its own modality through a late-fusion transformer, and separate decoders rebuild each one, so the encoder learns both per-sequence detail and cross-sequence reasoning. Tested on segmentation and classification with inputs missing, it beat a standard masked autoencoder baseline by wide margins on both tasks. The authors present the encoder as a flexible base for downstream brain imaging work.
arxiv-2509-11542:
Giorgi Tsintsadze and 3 co-authors simplify the design of via transitions, the plated holes carrying signals between circuit board layers, for very high frequencies in a 2025 electronics paper. Good via design normally demands expensive three-dimensional simulations.

The authors analyze how barrel radius, anti-pad size, and the distance to neighboring ground stitching vias each affect bandwidth, then give selection guidelines. Three-dimensional full-wave simulations were correlated with measurements on a test board for validation. With enough stitching vias, the structure approximates a coaxial transmission line, and the method builds on that approximation while accounting for higher-order modes. Engineers can then optimize parameters intuitively and design high-bandwidth vias without heavy simulation tools.
arxiv-2509-11842:
Erdal Catak and Mustafa Mullahasanoglu find new solutions to the decoration transformation in a 2025 paper in mathematical physics. This transformation is a symmetry act used to build Ising-like integrable lattice spin models. Those models arise through a link between gauge theories and an equation known as the Yang-Baxter equation.

The new solutions are written with special functions. They include the hyperbolic gamma function, the basic hypergeometric function, and the Euler gamma function. The integral identities that form each solution come from three-dimensional partition functions. They also come from the superconformal index for dual supersymmetric gauge theories. Such identities matter because they let builders decorate spin models while keeping them integrable.
arxiv-2509-11942:
Luís F. Gomes and 3 co-authors describe VisDocSketcher in a 2025 paper on making visual documentation for software. Pictures of a system's structure and data flow can help developers grasp unfamiliar code faster than long text. Yet such pictures are slow to draw by hand, and judging their quality is hard to standardize.

VisDocSketcher combines static code analysis, which reads code without running it, with language-model agents that pick out key parts and draw them. The authors call it the first agent-based attempt at this task. They also propose AutoSketchEval, a framework that scores the pictures using code-level measures. Together, the two pieces aim to make visual documentation that can grow with large code bases.
arxiv-2509-12042:
Finding the right passage inside a long company filing is hard. Ying Li and 4 co-authors propose FinGEAR in a 2025 paper to improve retrieval, the search step before a language model answers a question. Filings such as 10-K reports are long, follow a strict section hierarchy, and use specialized financial language.

FinGEAR uses a finance word list to guide search within each numbered section, builds two kinds of hierarchical indexes, and then reranks results in two stages. Tested on full 10-K filings with questions from the FinQA dataset, it raised precision, recall, and related scores over flat, graph-based, and tree-based search. Answer accuracy also rose with the same reader model. The design offers a practical base for high-stakes financial analysis.
arxiv-2509-12142:
Sending meaning, not just bits, over a channel someone else taps is the setting Denis Kozlov and two co-authors analyze in 2025. Their model pairs a semantic source with an observed companion source, correlated with it, and demands fidelity and secrecy for each part separately.

The coding is lossy joint source-channel coding over a wiretap channel, and two cases split on what the encoder can see: only the observed samples, or the underlying semantic samples as well. Single-letter converse and achievability bounds carve out the rate-distortion-equivocation region, using a stochastic superposition scheme with two private parts. Special cases for Gaussian and Bernoulli sources follow, and the results fold several older source and channel coding problems into one frame.
arxiv-2509-12342:
The spectrum of a graph, the eigenvalues of its matrices, fingerprints its structure and drives applications from chemistry to network analysis. Indranil Mukherjee and two co-authors compute spectra in 2025 for two elaborate constructions built from the total graph, which merges a graph's vertices and edges into one object.

They treat the vertex and edge neighborhood corona versions of that construction, pairing a regular graph with any other regular graph. All adjacency and Laplacian eigenvalues are expressed through the spectra of the two ingredients. Applying the formulas, they manufacture pairs of non-regular graphs that share a spectrum despite differing in structure.
arxiv-2509-12442:
Rui-Feng Wang and 5 co-authors present Cott-ADNet in a 2025 paper on detecting cotton bolls and flowers in fields. Cotton is a major natural fiber crop, but harvesting still depends on labor-intensive manual picking, with losses when the best harvest window is missed. Accurate recognition of bolls and their maturity supports automation, yield estimation, and breeding.

Cott-ADNet is a lightweight, real-time detector built on YOLOv11n and tailored to complex field conditions. New modules improve attention to weak, low-contrast features and widen the receptive field for multi-scale context at low cost. The authors curated a labeled dataset of nearly five thousand images and released an external validation set. Experiments reported high precision, recall, and detection scores for the system.
arxiv-2509-12542:
Some conjectures in geometry predict a strong rigidity. A geometry modeled on a flat template must itself be flat. That hope is in the spirit of an old Lichnerowicz result. In a solo 2025 paper, Toby Aldape shows the hope fails. The failing class is wide. It covers parabolic geometries whose model group is simple, of real rank at least three.

The models in question are Yamaguchi nonrigid. That trait is required for curved examples to exist at all. Using techniques developed by Erickson, Aldape builds the counterexamples. They are closed, nonflat, essential, regular, normal Cartan geometries on those models. The examples rule out Lichnerowicz-type statements across this whole rank range.
arxiv-2509-12942:
Michael Senn and Christian Cachin let each process pick its own trust rules in 2025 without breaking joint work. Quorum rules state which groups must agree for a step to count. Classic rules force all to share one view of faults.

New systems let each side hold its own view. The trap is clear: how to agree on fit rules with no shared rules at hand? Grid quorums based on trait groups break the trap. Each side picks the set that fits its view, and all picks fit by design. Uses span cloud hosts and block chains.
arxiv-2509-13442:
Arnab Roy, Hemant Kathania and Paban Sapkota classify dysarthric speech severity in 2025 with DSSCNet under speaker-free protocols. Severity grading guides clinical tracking for motor speech disorders. Generalization to unseen speakers remains the hard bar.

DSSCNet joins folded layers, squeeze-excitation focus, and residual links on mel spectra. Focus blocks lift key traits and cut loss. A cross-corpus tuning frame adapts detection transfer ideas. Two corpora under two strict protocols beat prior best marks. Tuning lifts scores by large shares in both protocols. Fine severity grades transfer across corpora with care.
arxiv-2509-13842:
Iván Martín Vílchez and Carlos F. Sopuerta propose a machine learning route to weighing massive black hole binaries in a 2025 gravitational wave paper. Estimating such a binary's properties from its signal normally means evaluating huge numbers of waveform templates, which is slow for the space-based detectors that will hear these systems.

Their method trains normalizing flows, flexible probability models, on simulated data to approximate the likelihood function directly, a scheme called sequential neural likelihood. Posterior samples then come from standard sampling at much lower cost, and small models can be refined iteratively for individual events. Dimensionality reduction decides whether the scheme is feasible at all. First results cover one binary in Gaussian noise, with messier real-world complications as next steps.
arxiv-2509-13942:
Duc Minh Ha and three co-authors test old software processes on new AI teams in a 2025 paper. Multi-agent systems of language models now write code collaboratively. Classical development processes offer ready-made patterns for coordinating that collaboration. Waterfall, the V-Model, and Agile are the three patterns tested. The team ask what each process does to quality, cost, and speed.

They ran eleven varied software projects under all three process models and four GPT variants. The runs total well over one hundred. Scoring covered output size, run time, and token cost. It also covered code smells and bugs found by AI and human reviewers. Waterfall was most efficient. The V-Model produced the most verbose code. Agile delivered the highest quality at the highest computational cost.
arxiv-2509-14042:
Alessandro Gabbana and five co-authors explain boiling hysteresis in a 2025 fluid dynamics paper. Between efficient nucleate boiling, where bubbles carry heat away, and film boiling, where a vapor blanket insulates the surface, lies the unstable transition regime near the boiling crisis. Systems remember which side they came from, a hysteresis that threatens industrial cooling and reactor safety, and its origin was disputed.

Large three-dimensional simulations of pool boiling on flat, constant-temperature surfaces show hysteresis arises even under idealized conditions, so it comes from the liquid-vapor flow dynamics themselves, not surface defects. The two directions behave differently: heating jumps abruptly with no memory, while cooling lingers in metastable mixed states that delay the return, an asymmetry with direct safety implications.
arxiv-2509-14342:
Bikram Pandit, Aayam Kumar Shrestha and Alan Fern teach teams of legged robots to carry objects together in 2025. Each robot is a quadruped with an arm. The objects cannot be grasped, so robots must pinch, lift and move them by contact alone.

Unlike rigs that bolt robots to the load, these robots share no link, no messages and no central control. A layered policy separates walking from arm control. A constellation reward scores position and orientation together, pushing robots to act as if rigidly attached. Training with a staged curriculum builds the behaviour gradually. Success through reward design alone suggests contact itself can carry enough signal for tight team carrying.
arxiv-2509-14642:
Yuemin Wu and eight co-authors put forward DeCoP in 2025, a pretraining frame for time series that keeps a grip on how time links change. Pretrained time series models often fail when link patterns shift across scales and data spreads. False links learned early then hurt later tasks.

DeCoP fakes shifting links between time patches while it pretrains, so the model learns links as moving, not fixed. A patch noise step at input level, set per instance, adds one more grip on link learning. Short and long term links are both treated as dynamic. The frame aims at features that hold up when data shifts. A strong shared base would serve forecasts, class tasks and anomaly checks at once.
arxiv-2509-14742:
Peng-Zhang He and three co-authors study Krylov complexity in 2025 in Schrödinger field theory with a positive chemical potential, a setting that counts how fast a state spreads in a special basis. Chemical potential biases the system toward more particles. Positive values change the spectrum qualitatively.

The fermionic power spectrum becomes effectively one sided and sharply cut at the chemical potential. Lanczos coefficients, which drive the complexity growth, then show a two stage pattern: slopes change between early and late stages, with a bend in the second coefficient family. Analytic support backs the resulting complexity behaviour. A crossover from bulk dominated to spectral edge dominated dynamics is the physical story behind the numbers, testable in related chaotic systems.
arxiv-2509-14942:
Minh-Khoi Pham and eleven co-authors model the risk of a drug-resistant gut germ in an Irish hospital in a 2025 paper. The germ, known as CPE, is a threat to infection control. How it affects return visits, deaths, and long stays in hospital is still not well mapped with modern deep learning tools.

The team uses health records from one acute hospital. Codes for diagnoses, ward moves, age and sex data, infection flags, and contact links all feed the models. Several Transformer-based models are tested next to classic methods. Tools that explain model choices show why a patient gets flagged. One model, TabTransformer, did best across the outcomes. The work shows how a hospital could aim its checks at the patients most at risk.
arxiv-2509-15342:
Jiuyi Xu and five co-authors accelerate diffusion image generation by starting small in a 2025 computer vision paper. Diffusion models generate superb images slowly, and most speedups shrink the model or cut denoising steps. LowDiff instead exploits resolution: early generation happens cheaply at low resolution, where mistakes cost little, and detail arrives in a cascade.

A single unified model refines images progressively from low to target resolution, so far fewer expensive high-resolution sampling steps are needed. The framework applies to diffusion models in both pixel space and latent space. Across experiments, image quality matches or beats the standard pipeline at a fraction of the high-resolution compute. Resolution scheduling becomes another dial, beside step count, for trading speed against fidelity.
arxiv-2509-15542:
Zhoufan Mu leads a team that simulates how Saturn makes a narrow radio signal. Planets can emit narrowband radio waves when one wave type turns into another at a steep change in density. Past models of this shift used a simple fluid view and skipped fine particle effects. The team wanted a full particle level view of the process at Saturn.

Their simulation follows the whole chain: the first wave grows, travels, bounces, and turns into the escaping wave. They use a method that tracks many charged particles and their fields together. The yield of the shift comes out at about a tenth to a fifth of the energy. This is the first such estimate from this kind of simulation.
arxiv-2509-15642:
Fangyuan Mao leads a large team that unites heat based and normal vision in one model. Seeing in both modes helps machines cope with bad weather and poor light. Models trained on one mode, though, drop sharply on the other. The team blame a shortcut: models lean on sensor surface patterns instead of true meaning.

Their model, UNIV, learns a shared space for both modes. A patch level contrast method pairs patches with like meaning across modes, using a frozen model to pick the pairs. Like pairs are pulled close and unlike pairs pushed apart. They also build the largest paired data set of its kind, with near a hundred thousand aligned pairs. Tests span many scenes.
arxiv-2509-15742:
Yu Chen leads a team that lays out quantum circuits with the controller in mind. Layout tools place a circuit's parts on a device to cut depth. Dynamic circuits add a catch: a classical controller must act mid run, and talk between controllers takes time. Device centered tools ignore that delay.

Their tool, CLASS, aims to cut talk time between controllers in a split control system. It models the circuit as a hypergraph, then splits that graph with a smart heuristic. Tests show talk delay can drop to zero in some cases. The cost is a small rise in extra operations, about two percent on average. The work fits quantum design tool chains.
arxiv-2509-15942:
Graham Clyne leads a team that emulates a climate model with deep learning to explore natural swings. Climate forecasts over years carry doubt from internal variability, the system's own churn. Sorting that churn from forced change takes large ensembles of runs. Full Earth models are costly, so ensembles stay small.

Their emulator, ArchesClimate, trains on past cast runs of a French climate model. It predicts next month's state from the two months before, then feeds its own output forward. Runs stay stable and physical for up to ten years. For key variables, its output can swap with the real model's. The work could cut the cost of probing near term climate swings.
arxiv-2509-16142:
Number races often hide a bias, where one side of a count stays ahead more than chance would suggest. Seewoo Lee studies such a bias for polynomials over finite fields, in a form tied to the Liouville function and a quadratic character. The race compares how often a signed product lands on the plus side versus the minus side.

Under a broad hypothesis about L-functions, Lee proves the count leans toward the plus side. A few cases where that hypothesis fails are also given. The result extends a classic bias first seen for prime numbers into the world of function fields, with clear limits.
arxiv-2509-16342:
Filling a long gap in a music recording is hard for generative models, which tend to wander off style over several seconds. Sean Turland, Eloi Moliner, and Vesa Välimäki guide a diffusion model with look-alike segments pulled from a corpus of music. The retrieved parts steer the filling process toward music that fits the surrounding context.

Listeners judged the guided fills for two-second gaps in piano music as more plausible than unguided diffusion fills. The hybrid also often beat plain look-alike search when fair matches were on hand. Blending search with generation offers a route to longer, more faithful repairs.
arxiv-2509-16442:
Small search models are cheap to run but lack the world knowledge of giant language models. Pranjal A. Chitale and three co-authors test whether text generated by large models can train the small ones up, across more than a hundred setups. They vary how much extra text is made, which model makes it, and how varied it is.

Extra data helped, but gains faded past a certain scale, even with diverse text. Small generator models proved nearly as good as giants for this job. The least pretrained search models gained the most. The map of trade-offs can save teams real money on augmentation.
arxiv-2509-16942:
Bin Wang and co-authors clean noisy labels for satellite image segmentation in a 2025 paper. A model trained in one region must adapt to a new region with no labels and no source data. It labels the new images itself, but those pseudo-labels carry errors. The team denoise them with class prototypes, which summarize each class.

A contrast step pulls features of the same class together. That helps the model learn sharp target features without true labels. Tests show clear gains over prior methods. Cleaner adaptation matters for land mapping, where new regions and sensors arrive faster than labeling teams can follow.
arxiv-2509-17442:
Hideaki Joko, Shakiba Amirshahi, Charles L. A. Clarke, and Faegheh Hasibi study what people really ask chatbots. Their 2025 arXiv paper starts from a shift: language models have turned chat systems into daily tools for millions. Yet research on information access in chat has focused on plain, explicit questions, leaving real-world use largely unexplored.

The team first observed WildChat, a large set of real user chats with ChatGPT. They found that information seeking often hides inside chats whose main aim is not information at all, such as creative writing, in the form of check-worthy factual claims made by the system. To study that pattern, they release WildClaims, a data set of well over a hundred thousand claims drawn from thousands of utterances. Each claim is graded for check-worthiness. Early counts suggest a large share of chats hold such claims, a fact fact-checkers must face.
arxiv-2509-17542:
Xing Chen and six co-authors split language model serving across GPUs from rival vendors. Their 2025 arXiv paper starts from the two stages of inference: prefill, which reads the prompt, and decode, which writes the reply token by token. Run together, the stages interfere. Splitting them onto distinct hardware helps, but past work assumed uniform GPUs.

A mixed fleet can cut costs, raise utilization, and loosen dependence on one vendor, if the data can move smoothly between cards. The team designs a disaggregated system for that fleet, with a transmission module built for cross-vendor traffic. Their design targets real business settings rather than lab clusters. The paper argues that serving stacks should treat mixed hardware as the normal case, since few providers can afford a uniform, top-tier fleet for every model they host.
arxiv-2509-17642:
Roberto Balossi, Paolo Tanga, Marco Delbo, Alberto Cellino, and Federica Spoto uncover an ancient asteroid family in the middle Main Belt. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that asteroid families are usually found by clustering orbits, a method that struggles when families overlap, interlopers sneak in, and old structures fade. Spectra offer an independent check.

Gaia's third data release holds visible spectra for tens of thousands of asteroids, a sample built for family studies. The team focused on a central belt region tied to L-type asteroids, where past clustering studies disagreed on membership. They sorted candidates by a color taxonomy from Gaia data and by spectral likeness to each family's template. The result is an L-type family with the asteroid (460) Scania as its largest member. Its age and spread may rewrite part of the belt's collisional history.
arxiv-2509-18242:
Dainis Dravins and Hans-Gunter Ludwig track tiny shifts in the Sun's light lines to learn how the surface churns. Their 2025 paper deals with a snag in planet hunts: a star's own flicker far outweighs the pull of a small planet on its light. Iron and other lines in sunlight were tracked across years of telescope data.

Line widths moved in step with a known activity signal, but at far smaller size. Blue iron lines shifted most, while some lines moved the other way. Sims of surface boiling give disk-wide wobbles of a few metres per second. Line jitter shares a phase, with size set by line strength.
arxiv-2509-18342:
Vineyard rows all look alike, and that sameness trips up farm robots. Rajitha de Silva and five co-authors present a way for a robot to keep track of its place among the vines. Their 2025 paper adds meaning to a standard tracking method called a particle filter. The robot uses laser scans plus two steady landmarks: vine trunks and support poles.

Found landmarks are placed on a top-down map and merged with the laser data. A trick the team calls semantic walls links nearby landmarks into loose walls, which cuts row confusion. Where landmarks run thin, a noisy GPS signal backs up the filter. In tests in a real vineyard, the robot stayed in the right row and recovered from drifts. A standard method failed the same tests, and camera-based mapping scored worse.
arxiv-2509-18542:
Mixture-of-experts models switch on only part of a large network per task, which saves compute. Qi Wang, Hanyang Peng, and Yue Yu present Symphony-MoE, a way to build such a model from several ready-made models at once. Their 2025 paper notes that older reuse tricks copy one model into all experts. That limits how varied the experts can be.

Models trained apart sit in mismatched regions of the parameter space, so naive merging hurts scores badly. The team first blends the models into a shared backbone with a layer-aware fusion, all without training. An activation-based alignment step then lines up the experts. A final training stage tunes the whole system. Tests show the blended model beat baselines on mixed-domain tasks and on unseen data. The approach turns spare pre-trained models into one stronger whole.
arxiv-2509-18742:
Some graphs change over time and carry text on their nodes and links, from social feeds to citation streams. Yunan Wang, Jianxin Li, and Ziwei Zhang present DyGRASP for reasoning over such dynamic text graphs in this 2025 paper. Older graph networks and language models mostly target static graphs. They miss how recent texts link together and how node meanings drift over the long run.

DyGRASP splits the job. A sliding window with node-centric implicit reasoning captures recent semantics cheaply. An explicit reasoning chain, guided by tailored prompts, tracks each node's long-term meaning. Update and merge layers then join both time scales with the graph structure itself. On benchmark tasks, the method improved destination retrieval scores by up to 34 percent. It also generalized across varied temporal graph backbones and language models. Efficiency, the authors note, is what makes language models usable here.
arxiv-2509-19142:
Robots often need two hands to lift large or awkward objects, yet most grasp planners think one arm at a time. Kangmin Kim and five co-authors present BiGraspFormer, a single transformer system that plans both hands' grasps together from a 3D point cloud of the object. Older two-stage pipelines plan grasps first and judge pairs later, which invites collisions and lopsided forces.

Their strategy starts from many single-hand candidates made by a transformer decoder. Special attention layers then reuse what those candidates learned to predict paired poses and quality scores jointly. Working from singles first shrinks the huge twelve-degree search space and keeps the two hands coordinated. In simulations and real-world trials the system beat existing methods while answering in a fraction of a second. Code and extra material are posted online.
arxiv-2509-19342:
Network operators building digital twins of their radio networks need local channel models, and Xinyu Qin and five co-authors supply one from cheap data. The classic method learns the angular spread of signals from drive-test measurements, which are costly and cover little ground. Measurement reports, routinely sent by phones, are plentiful but lack location tags. Their framework starts by recovering those locations with a semi-supervised hypergraph neural network that exploits several kinds of information at once.

Modeling then works on a grid, but grid layout and channel estimation are optimized together rather than separately. Alternating between clustering for the grid and sparse recovery for the channels makes the method robust where data are unevenly spread. Experiments on a real measurement-report dataset show better localization and channel modeling than prior approaches. The work targets digital-twin-assisted network optimization.
arxiv-2509-19542:
Algebraic topology builds elaborate spectra whose products can hide simpler pieces. Jackson Morris, Sarah Petersen, and Elizabeth Tatum split one such product into clean parts. Their object is a truncated motivic Brown-Peterson spectrum, smashed with itself. Classically, the matching split was found through Brown-Gitler spectra and later retold with Adams covers.

The authors lift that split into the motivic world, where geometry over fields enters the picture. The lift works over complex numbers, real numbers, and finite fields away from the prime in play. With the split in hand, they compute the first page of a key spectral sequence as a module. A simpler companion split is recorded as well. Such computations feed the long project of charting stable homotopy groups.
arxiv-2509-20242:
Kwang-Hyun Uhm and three co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on medical imaging. CT scans are usually taken with thick slices to save storage and time. The result is a volume that is sharp within each slice but coarse between slices. That mismatch can hinder diagnosis.

Their method fills in missing slices by borrowing texture from the sharp in-plane images. A multi-reference attention module gathers useful detail from several in-plane views at once. Those details guide the reconstruction of high-frequency structure in the through-plane direction. The design leans on the anisotropy of the scan instead of fighting it. On public CT datasets, including a real paired benchmark, the method beat competing approaches clearly. The authors released the source code as well.
arxiv-2509-20442:
Sterile neutrinos, hypothetical particles that ignore most known forces, could hide in data from Antarctic ice. Emilse Cabrera and three co-authors assess that hunt in a 2025 arXiv paper. The IceCube-Upgrade detector will record huge numbers of atmospheric neutrinos at low energies. Very light sterile neutrinos would subtly change how those neutrinos oscillate.

The authors compute the upgrade's sensitivity to sterile states below one electronvolt in mass splitting. The lowest-energy window does most of the work. Mixing angles as small as about five degrees could be probed across the whole mass range studied. They also check how a sterile state would blur the standard atmospheric mixing parameters. The study helps set expectations before the upgraded detector's data arrives.
arxiv-2509-20542:
Proteins that change shape when they bind defeat rigid docking tools. Rujie Yin and Yang Shen propose a hierarchical diffusion model for flexible protein docking in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their framework separates two kinds of motion. Global rigid-body movement between the proteins diffuses on one track. Local bending inside each protein diffuses on another.

Separate noise schedules mimic the induced-fit effect, where binding itself reshapes the partners. The local schedule adapts to the predicted size of the shape change, flexing faster when more change is expected. A shared scoring network, fed with sequence, evolution, structure, and dynamics features, couples the two tracks. Pretraining used a new dataset of nearly thirty-nine thousand examples. On an independent benchmark, the model beat two strong rivals, with the largest gains on the most flexible cases.
arxiv-2509-20642:
Atomic nuclei have been computed on a trapped-ion quantum computer by Sota Yoshida and three co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their targets are the ground states of oxygen, calcium, and nickel isotopes, systems with strong correlations among nucleons. The nuclear shell model is rewritten using hard-core bosons. A paired unitary coupled-cluster ansatz then prepares the states on the RIKEN-Quantinuum Reimei machine.

Symmetry-aware preparation and particle-number post-selection help capture the pairing correlations that dominate these nuclei. Ground-state energies landed within under one percent of exact noise-free simulation values. That fidelity on real hardware is the headline. The authors present the run as a foundation for scaling quantum simulation toward heavier, more complex nuclei. It also marks a working bridge between quantum computing and nuclear structure theory.
arxiv-2509-20842:
Alzheimer's disease leaves traces across genes, proteins, and other molecular layers, but patient datasets often miss whole layers. Sungjoon Park and ten co-authors present MOIRA in a 2025 paper on multi-omics integration. The method is built to learn robustly even when some data types are absent.

MOIRA projects each omics dataset into a shared embedding space. A learnable weighting system then fuses the available layers for each sample, so samples with missing modalities still count. The authors test the method on the ROSMAP dataset, a major Alzheimer's study cohort. They report better disease prediction than existing approaches. Robust integration could help researchers use every patient record instead of discarding incomplete ones.
arxiv-2509-20942:
Transformers rule language and vision tasks, yet at forecasting time series they often lose to simple linear models. Zida Liang, Jiayi Zhu, and Weiqiang Sun ask why attention fails there in a 2025 paper. They slowly strip a transformer down into a plain multilayer perceptron and watch what changes.

To their surprise, the blocks in many forecasting models had already decayed into perceptron-like parts, with attention adding little. The team built a small, clear dataset to find the cause. Attention mixes facts across time points, and that mixing can blur the local patterns that forecasting rests on. Their tests show where attention helps and where it hurts. Model builders get a clearer guide to when attention earns its cost.
arxiv-2509-21142:
Gamma-ray bursts may launch magnetically dominated jets, and a flash of coherent radio waves would betray that composition. A Hennessy and nine co-authors searched for such flashes with the LOFAR radio array in a 2025 paper accepted by Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society. Four long gamma-ray bursts were followed up.

LOFAR's rapid response mode began observing within a few hundred seconds of each Swift satellite trigger. The team modeled the high-energy pulses from Swift alongside the radio data. Under a magnetic wind model, prompt engine activity should produce low-frequency coherent emission riding with the burst. The paper reports what the observations found and what limits they place. Pinning down jet composition matters for understanding how these extreme explosions channel their energy.
arxiv-2509-21642:
Virtual synchronous generators let inverters mimic rotating machines, but fleets of them can swing against each other. Junjie Xiao and 4 co-authors explain those active power swings through impedance in a 2025 paper. Past fixes need system settings in advance or lack actual clarity. An RLC matching circuit model gives a plain account first. Inertia, damping, and feeder impedance map to capacitive, resistive, and inductive elements.

Mismatches among converters then appear as LC resonance between units. That explains swings in both standalone and grid connected modes. Two mode specific mitigation strategies build on the insight. The authors aim for damping performance without complex models. Actual interpretability is a stated priority for useful use in inverter dominated grids.
arxiv-2509-21742:
Brain graphs map regions of the brain and the links between them, and they can help spot disease. Learning from them is costly, though, when models keep every detail.
