A new tuning step keeps several lab radios in step with each other. Tests reached errors from under one degree to a few degrees. The results show that one tower alone can give useful location fixes.
arxiv-2510-17842:
Vinay Bamil introduces vibe coding, a new way to build software with AI help. Developers state high-level intent plus qualitative hints about tone and style. An intelligent agent then turns those hints into working code. Bamil formalizes the idea and sketches a reference design.

His design chains an intent parser, a meaning engine, and a code generator. A feedback loop lets the developer steer results interactively. He compares vibe coding with declarative, functional, and prompt-based styles. Reported gains include faster work and wider access for non-experts. He also flags risks around security, bias, and maintainability.
arxiv-2510-17942:
Grant McKenzie, Krzysztof Janowicz, and Carsten Kessler sort out what trust means for foundation models, seen through a geographic lens. As these models inform key choices, trust has split into pieces that are often mixed together. The chapter separates trust in the training data, trust in how the model works, and trust in its makers.

Each kind of trust carries its own risks for map-based and place-based uses. Culture, uneven data, and spatial links all shape whether a model deserves belief in a given place. Geography readers get a clear frame for judging AI tools that speak about the world.
arxiv-2510-18142:
M Grant Roberts and three co-authors build a testable model of dark matter that collides with itself at two very different strengths. Most of the dark matter interacts moderately, while a small share interacts ultra-strongly. A light carrier particle makes the scattering depend on speed, and early universe reactions set how much of each kind survives.

Galaxy rotation curves and cluster lensing bound the allowed settings. In one region the main component matches dwarf galaxy needs while respecting cluster limits. The authors then map the model to standard tools for cosmic structure, giving observers clear targets.
arxiv-2510-18642:
Tiffany Baptiste and her fifteen co-authors model how stiffness varies across the left atrium, the heart chamber that receives blood from the lungs. In atrial fibrillation, the chamber's mechanics change, but the reasons are unclear. The team built patient-specific computer models from CT scans and tuned each region's stiffness until the model's motion matched the motion measured in the scans during the chamber's filling phase.

Validation against the full recorded motion was close, within a fraction of a millimeter. Regional stiffness turned out to vary substantially, and it was a significant driver of how each region deformed in a realistic way. Anatomy features, such as local wall thickness and fat volume, mattered less. The findings help explain why atrial mechanics go wrong in fibrillation and show that where tissue is stiff may matter more than how the chamber is shaped.
arxiv-2510-18742:
Clarissa Mora, Fabio Bacchini, and Rony Keppens study how electrons gain extreme energies in the turbulent loops left after a solar flare. Such electrons stream from the Sun's corona down to its surface layers and produce intense X-ray emission, so knowing how they are accelerated is central to flare physics. Turbulence driven by Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities in the loop top can trap electrons long enough to energize them.

Using test-particle simulations on top of a time-evolving magnetohydrodynamic model of a loop top, with a formulation that conserves energy exactly, the team tracked which mechanisms did the work. Electrons developed high-energy tails consistent with the observed hard X-rays. The dominant channel was a stochastic, Fermi-like acceleration tied to perpendicular gradients, while curvature effects mattered most for particles on long trajectories, and pitch-angle patterns backed the statistical picture.
arxiv-2510-18842:
Dipranjan Chatterjee and his six co-authors watch one muon's spin evolve. The muon sits inside a fluoride, bonded to two fluorine atoms. Their spins become quantum mechanically entangled. Radio-frequency pulses probe the coupled system. Emitted positrons reveal their directions. From those, the team rebuilt the muon spin vector over time. No single NMR experiment can give that readout.

The method was shown on a muon spin echo. The echo is controlled by coupling to fluorine. A double resonance experiment came next. Separate pulse frequencies addressed muon and fluorine spins apart. One member of an entangled system can thus be controlled selectively. The readout stays in full vector form. That offers a new probe for quantum materials. Engineered spin systems can use it too.
arxiv-2510-18942:
Woong-Bae G Zee and three co-authors trace warped disk galaxies from the cosmic web down to the shape of each galactic warp. Warps are common bends in galaxy disks, often blamed on tides from other galaxies, though a halo of dark matter that is not round may also drive them.

Using a Sloan survey catalog, the team compares S-shaped and U-shaped warps with an unwarped control group matched in mass, distance, and local density. Satellites around warped hosts bunch in a clear pattern while controls look even. This hints that halo shape and large structure help set warp form.
arxiv-2510-19642:
Alain M. Dikande derives a rescaled Manning potential from the way small waves scatter off a kink defect in a chain of molecules. The model behind it is a nonlinear Klein-Gordon system. Identical molecules sit in a chain, each held by a hyperbolic double-well potential. A tunable knob in that potential stands for isotope effects on things like the spacing of the chain and the height of the well's barrier.

Such bendable double-well models describe hydrogen-bonded crystals, alpha-helix proteins, long polymer chains, and two-state quantum tunneling systems. Their balance points shift with atom swaps, dilution, or solvation. The paper sets out the model and works out the effective potential that governs how waves scatter off the kink.
arxiv-2510-19842:
Yuanhe Zhang and four co-authors propose a way to judge whether a language model's chain of thought actually reasons by rules, rather than landing on answers by search or habit. They model reasoning as a stochastic process over a directed acyclic graph, where nodes are derivation states and edges are rule applications. A new metric, logical closeness, measures how faithfully a model's reasoning path follows that graph.

Built on the framework, the DAG-MATH format guides models to produce graph-shaped reasoning, and the accompanying benchmark scores it. Across standard math datasets, model families with similar final-answer accuracy differed significantly in reasoning fidelity. The authors offer the method as a middle ground between free-form chain of thought and formal proof systems, with diagnostics that answer-only scores cannot give.
arxiv-2510-20042:
Huichan Seo and ten co-authors audit cultural bias in generative image models across both text-to-image generation and image-to-image editing. Earlier studies focused mainly on text-to-image systems, leaving editors largely untested. Their unified evaluation covers six countries, eight categories with thirty-six subcategories, and prompts that are aware of historical era.

Three findings stand out in the results from open models under fixed settings. Under general prompts, models default to modern Global-North scenes and blur differences between countries. Repeated editing wears away cultural fidelity even when standard scores stay flat. Editors also lean on shallow cues like color shifts instead of changes that truly fit the era and setting.
arxiv-2510-20242:
Stephan Rabanser and Nicolas Papernot examine selective classifiers, models that can refuse to answer uncertain cases. Such refusals can raise reliability. Real systems still fall short of an ideal oracle that accepts cases in exact order of likely correctness. Their 2025 paper names that shortfall and asks what causes it.

The authors split the gap into five parts. Bayes noise comes first, followed by ranking error and approximation error. Statistical noise adds a fourth part. Slack from setup or data shift makes a fifth. Their checks use synthetic two moons data plus real vision and language tests. Common calibration, they find, mostly rescales scores and seldom fixes poor ranking. Richer tools that use input features help more. Shifted data, in turn, needs training built to handle change.
arxiv-2510-20442:
Oleg Bulashenko and three co-authors present a framework for detecting gravitational waves that have been lensed by cosmic strings. Finding such strings would probe high-energy physics and the early universe, but their conical spacetime geometry produces diffraction and interference effects that point-mass lens searches do not capture. Their approach uses a full-wave transmission factor written analytically through Fresnel integrals.

Cosmic string lensing depends on cosmological distances, string tension, and wavelength, and it produces two non-amplified images set by the global geometry. For binary black hole mergers, the lensed waveforms show a beating pattern or time-separated exact copies. The authors derive a detectability bound on string tension and show with Bayesian model selection that string lensing can be told apart from unlensed and point-mass signals.
arxiv-2510-20842:
Jiamian Li and Bing-Zhao Li extend spectral analysis of three dimensional point clouds by adding a fractional order to the harmonic transform on the sampled surface. Point clouds act as discrete samples of smooth shapes, so surface harmonics give a natural frequency view of geometry.

The standard transform uses fixed basis functions and a single spectral view, which limits its grip on complex shapes. The fractional version inserts a tunable middle domain between space and frequency, with order settings that can be adjusted in a continuous way. Tests show varied orders enrich the spectral picture and give strong results on filtering and feature boosting, widening the theory of point cloud spectral work.
arxiv-2510-21042:
Valmir P Moraes Filho leads six co-authors on uncovering solar wind phenomena in Parker Solar Probe data with a pipeline joining symbolic compression, density clustering, and human validation. The solar wind drives space weather, but high cadence probe data from twenty eighteen to twenty twenty four exceed manual review.

Over one hundred fifty gigabytes of magnetic and plasma measurements are processed efficiently across multiple time scales. Known structures are recovered, and uncatalogued coronal mass ejections and transient events are detected. The human in the loop design keeps expert judgment inside a scalable flow, a pattern other overflowing observatories can copy.
arxiv-2510-21442:
Nathan Corecco and four co-authors design incentives that steer a crowd of self-interested agents toward a chosen stable outcome, a Nash equilibrium. With very many agents, working with each one separately becomes hopeless, so they recast the problem in a mean-field form, where only the average behavior of the crowd matters.

They prove that this infinite-crowd version approximates the true design goal with an error that shrinks like one over the square root of the crowd size, under mild smoothness conditions. The same rate survives even for sequential auctions, where jumps break those conditions, thanks to a tailored argument. Their algorithm, AMID, computes gradients by differentiating directly through the steps that find an equilibrium. Across auction tests, it raises revenue well beyond first-price formats and beats existing benchmark methods.
arxiv-2510-21542:
Johann Flemming Gloy and Simon Olsson speed up a painful step in flow-based generative models for science. That step computes how likely each generated sample is. For Boltzmann generators, the cost grows brutally with system size. Those generators sample molecular configurations from unnormalized energy laws. The cost can block large problems entirely.

Their model, HollowFlow, routes information through a graph network with a twist. A node never hears its own echo. That non-backtracking design forces the model's Jacobian into a block-diagonal shape. Likelihoods then need only a fixed number of backward passes, however large the system. Speedups grow up to quadratically. Any symmetry-respecting graph or attention architecture can be recast in this form. On the larger of two test systems, the team measures a hundredfold speedup.
arxiv-2510-21642:
Saak Gabriyelyan and Evgenii Reznichenko introduce three new families of topological spaces. A simple question shapes them. When can a boundary point of an open set be reached from inside? A sequence of points in the set might converge to it. A relatively compact chunk of the set might also capture it in its closure.

The classes grow out of older notions studied by Arhangel'skii and others. Those include sequential spaces and Ascoli spaces. The authors map exactly how the new families nest among those classics. They characterize the classes and test them under products, subspaces, and quotients. Two payoffs stand out. The work gives fresh characterizations of a known class of spaces. It also proves that every feathered topological group belongs to that class. A sorting of locally compact abelian groups under the Bohr topology completes the picture.
arxiv-2510-21742:
German Mato, Facundo Rigatuso, and Gonzalo Torroba work out exact formulas for correlation statistics in large recurrent neural networks. Those statistics describe the shared dynamics of the whole network. Past exact results covered mainly linear networks. The new work covers a wide family of nonlinear response functions.

The method rewrites the network's random dynamics as a path integral. That step reduces the system to a few shared variables, so the statistics can be computed with care. Finite-size corrections in the number of neurons are included. The response functions enter as interaction terms. Those terms can remove a flaw of the linear theory and keep the measured dimension positive. The authors give full results for power-law response functions. They also treat a class built from Padé approximants. Computer simulations match the formulas closely. A new self-consistent equation is proposed for colored noise.
arxiv-2510-22042:
Benjamin Reichman, Adar Avsian, and Larry Heck map where emotion lives inside a large language model. They probe the geometry of the model's hidden states. Those states are the internal numbers that carry its working thoughts. Feelings turn out to lie on a low-dimensional surface. Emotions are encoded as directions that persist across layers.

The structure proved stable and broad. It lined up across eight real-world emotion datasets in five languages. Simple probes read emotions off it with accuracy. A learned intervention module could steer the model's emotion reading. The meaning of its text stayed intact. Control was cleanest over basic emotions, in several languages. The results suggest models build a consistent inner map of affect. That map can be adjusted. The finding has uses from interpretability research to safer steering.
arxiv-2510-22242:
Yutao Wu, Xiao Liu, Yunhao Feng, Jiale Ding, and Xingjun Ma grade the graders: they test how reliably large language models do a research assistant's daily chores. Their benchmark, PaperAsk, covers four tasks that scholarship runs on, retrieving the right citations, extracting content from a named section, discovering papers on a topic, and verifying claims.

Three leading models were tested through their ordinary web interfaces, where the searching happens out of sight. The failures were consistent and large. Multi-reference citation retrieval failed in roughly half to nearly all queries, section-specific extraction failed in most cases, and topic discovery missed over sixty percent of the relevant literature. Human review blamed swollen, uncontrolled retrieved context and a habit of following whatever text sounds relevant instead of the task instructions. The benchmark gives labs a way to measure scholarly reliability before trusting it.
arxiv-2510-22642:
It is hard to gauge risk in a complex system when its inputs are not known. Hojun Choi, Eunho Heo, and Dongjin Lee wrote a 2025 paper on that task. Their method learns the input spread from sample data. It builds on a chaos based method that uses special basis functions. The basis splits by dimension to stay fast.

First, smooth density fits are made for small input groups. A whitening step then builds basis sets that match those fits. Tests span math cases and a real design task. That task is a three dimensional mobility design. It has twenty random inputs. Their method gave mean and spread values closer to the truth than the other methods tried.
arxiv-2510-22742:
Rodrigo Trevino, writing alone in 2025, studies energy forms on Cantor like spaces. These spaces come from path sets of Bratteli diagrams. A Dirichlet form measures a kind of energy. His forms are non local, so distant points interact. The measures come from Gibbs states for shift systems.

Trevino also defines a cohomology for these spaces. Cohomology is an algebraic tool that tracks holes and classes. He studies the spectrum of the form generator. For large enough parameters, each class has a unique best representative. That best element minimizes the energy form. Sharp bounds depend on the diagram and entropy. The work links dynamics, geometry, and algebra.
arxiv-2510-23142:
Chi Liu reframes a recent training method, GSPO, through information theory. GSPO uses length-normalized importance ratios at the sequence level to weight policy updates. Liu shows that its weight can be written exactly as an inverse perplexity ratio between the old and new policies.

The same weight also equals the exponential of the cross-entropy change. While the link between perplexity and entropy follows from standard definitions, seeing GSPO through that lens clarifies what the algorithm rewards. Trainers can now reason about updates as perplexity shifts, which may guide safer tuning of language model reinforcement learning.
arxiv-2510-23442:
Asmaa Abbas, Mohamed Gaber, and Mohammed M Abdelsamea present CURVETE, a deep network for medical image classification that joins curriculum learning with progressive self-supervised training. Good annotated medical samples are scarce and hard to access. Transfer learning helps, but its benefit fades when class distributions are irregular.

CURVETE is designed to handle limited samples, improve generalizability, and raise overall classification performance. Training moves from easy to hard examples while self-supervision extracts signal from unlabeled data. Such methods matter for clinics whose image archives are small and imbalanced across diseases. Full details of the setup, tests, and limits appear in the paper.
arxiv-2510-23642:
Yuansheng Ni and ten co-authors build resources for AI agents that write code to draw charts and plots. Large language models can now generate, run, and revise such code, yet practical use suffers from narrow language coverage, unreliable execution, and no way to fix mistakes over several rounds. Datasets and benchmarks built for one-shot, single-language tasks have held the field back.

The team answers with three pieces. VisCode-Multi-679K is a training set of 679 thousand checked, runnable visualization samples with multi-turn correction dialogues across twelve programming languages. VisPlotBench grades agents on executable tasks with rendered outputs, for both first tries and self-debugging rounds. Their model family, VisCoder2, trained on that data, clearly beat strong open-source rivals and neared proprietary systems like GPT-4.1. With iterative self-debugging, the largest model passed about eighty-two percent of executions.
arxiv-2510-23842:
Saki Imai and seven co-authors collect a motion capture dataset of American Sign Language conversation about science topics, to study how dialogue partners shape each other's signing. Most sign language models train on interpreters or isolated vocabulary, missing the give-and-take of natural dialogue. In classrooms the gap widens, because teachers and students coin and adapt signs for new terms.

The dataset lets the team compare three modes: two-person interactive signing, solo signed lectures, and interpreted articles. Using continuous movement features, they separate dialogue-specific entrainment — partners syncing up — from individual effort savings. Across repeated mentions of science terms, dialogue signs ran about a quarter to nearly a half shorter than isolated signs, a shrinkage absent in monologue. They test sign embedding models on recognizing the science signs and tracking how entrained partners become. The work links language analysis with model building for sign technology.
arxiv-2510-23942:
Sridhar Mahadevan describes judo calculus, a framework for causal discovery that treats causal claims as locally true rather than true everywhere. In real domains — biology, medicine, social science — effects depend on regime: age, country, dose, genotype, or lab protocol. Classical methods flatten that context away.

Judo calculus keeps the context, using sheaf theory and a logic where truth is local. A modal operator picks the family of regimes that matter, and a claim counts as proven when it holds across that cover in a stable, constructive way. The framework plugs into standard score-based, constraint-based, and gradient-based discovery tools rather than replacing them. Tests range from synthetic data to real sets in biology and economics. The author reports faster runs from the decentralized design and better accuracy than classical methods — causal knowledge that knows where it holds.
arxiv-2510-24442:
Yiding Wang leads a team of six authors on law and AI. Real trials of legal rules are slow, costly, or barred by ethics. The team build Law in Silico, a fake legal world run by AI agents. The agents are large language models that can play set roles. Inside the world, agents make laws, judge cases, and enforce rules.

The team compare crime rates in the fake world with real data. The agents matched broad real crime trends quite well. At the small scale, clear and fair systems did more for the weak. Open rules and room to adapt helped guard people's rights. The study shows fake legal worlds can test ideas cheaply. Such tests may guide real courts and lawmakers in time.
arxiv-2510-24642:
Charley Cummings, Sira Gratz, Ellen Kirkman, Janina C Letz, J Daisie Rock, and Spela Spenko prove a link between two named types in pure algebra. Their note deals with graded modules of a special maximal type over two kinds of surface forms. One form is of type A, the other of type D, in a set naming scheme.

For one choice of grading, they show the stable groups for the two types match each other. That match is the whole claim of the short work. Such links matter in algebra because a hard fact in one group can then be moved to the other. The proof turns on the grading choice they pick.
arxiv-2510-24742:
Adam J Czarnecki, Andrzej Czarnecki, Raquel Secrist, and Julia Willsey study the shock wave from the huge blast in Beirut in 2020. Clips of the blast give a rare chance to see such a wave with the bare eye. The team sums up the math of a weak shock as a base for their checks.

They work out a known rule for how thick the high press zone of the wave should be. Then they go through the clips frame by frame to pull the real wave traits. The read traits lined up with what the math said they should be. That match ties a street caught clip set to classic shock theory.
arxiv-2510-25142:
Hao-Cheng Thong leads a team with nine co-authors who found a shape based path to tune a ferroic stuff that bends charge with heat. In a lithium tweaked base, two polar forms sit side by side. Heat can swap the stack from one form to the other while the part is baked.

That swap lifts the heat point where the polar trait fades, and makes the part's push back to a wave more stiff, the team shows. First rule codes and a lithium based magnet read both back the claim. The lesson is broad: the form of the cell, not just its chem mix, can set how the part works. Shape led swaps may suit more such parts.
arxiv-2510-25442:
Dmitriy Bilyk, Nicolas Nagel, and Ian Ruohoniemi study point configurations. Their 2025 math paper minimizes energies on a torus. Effect energies have tensor product form here. Quasi-Monte Carlo integration also motivates the problem.

The authors show single-distance configurations minimize energy widely. That trait is a tensor product universal optimality. It applies to three and five point Fibonacci lattices. They characterize all lattices with this trait. Some non-lattice sets of this type are exhibited. Further structural results concern global and local minimizers. Tensor product energies have special form enabling study. Well-placed points matter for numeric integration quality. Minimizers reveal how evenly points can spread.
arxiv-2510-25642:
Ignacio Munoz-Escobar led six co-authors on galaxy bulges. Patricia B Tissera, Jenny Gonzalez-Jara, and Emanuel Sillero helped. Valentina P Miranda, Susana Pedrosa, and Lucas Bignone joined. Their 2025 astronomy paper explores bulge mass-metallicity relations. Bulges sit at central regions of galaxies. They are complex forms shaped by assembly history. Gravity, mergers, mutual pulls, and bars shape them.

They aim to find a stellar mass-metallicity relation. Possible imprints of accretion and migration are studied. Forty-four central galaxies come from CIELO cosmological runs. Galaxies were decomposed into bulge and disk parts. Circularity and binding energies guided that decomposition. Stellar populations were tracked back to birth locations. Most bulge stars formed in situ, they find. One third show non-negligible accretion contributions. A clear bulge mass-metallicity relation exists regardless. Bulges are more metal-enriched than disks at fixed mass.
arxiv-2510-25742:
Fabio Centofanti surveys ways to watch factory lines with profile data. His 2025 review deals with plants that log full curves, not just lone points. Each curve links an output to an input that drives it. Watch methods check if those curves stay steady over time. A shift in shape can flag a fault on the line.

Old watch tools cope poorly with whole curves as data. The review sets out a base frame for curves in many parts at once. It then walks through fresh tools that grow that frame. Some add more curve inputs to sharpen the watch. One tool copes with wild curves, and one works live on half-seen curves. Two tools adapt to the shape of the fault they hunt. All of them ship in a free R pack named funcharts.
arxiv-2510-25942:
Bernd Ulmann, working alone, reviews ways to reprogram analog computers automatically. An analog computer solves problems with continuous electrical signals rather than digital steps. Classic machines were slow to program, since users had to patch hundreds or thousands of cords by hand and set many dials. The job could take hours or days, even with removable patch panels.

Ulmann notes that analog machines draw fresh interest as co processors because digital chips face limits in energy use, clock speed, and density. That interest needs autopatch systems, where a host digital computer rewires the analog machine on its own. The paper surveys classic and modern approaches to such automatic reconfiguration and compares how they work.
arxiv-2510-26042:
Victor Guedes, Siddarth Ajith, Shu Yan Lau, and Kent Yagi use gravitational waves to limit how uneven the pressure inside a neutron star can be. A neutron star is the dense remnant of a massive star, and its pressure may differ by direction due to elasticity, magnetic fields, viscosity, or superfluidity. They compute how such stars deform under tides and how they ring in their main oscillation mode.

Guedes and the team find a universal relation between tidal deformability and ring frequency that depends on the anisotropy level but barely on the unknown equation of state. Within a statistical framework, data from the GW170817 merger limit the anisotropy parameter to order unity, and future detectors give comparable bounds in their simulations.
arxiv-2510-26342:
Zhigao Guo and Feng Dong work on causal discovery, the task of learning which things cause which other things from data. They add a new tool called interventional constraints. These are plain rules about the sign of a cause, such as one protein turning another one on, rather than data from a direct test.

Guo and Dong show why older methods can get the sign wrong even when they find the right path between two factors. Their fix sets a limit on the total effect one factor may have on another, and they solve the task in two stages. Tests on real data sets gave models that matched known findings more closely, stayed easier to explain, and still turned up new links.
arxiv-2510-26442:
Xuesong Wang, Xinyan Xie, Mo Li, and Zhaoqian Liu design a lean way to send images by meaning rather than by bits. In semantic communication, the receiver needs the point of a message, not an exact copy. Sending only a caption can lose the details that make one scene distinct, while sending a full coded image costs too much.

Wang and his three co-authors let the receiver drive the exchange. It gets a short caption plus a sparse set of image blocks, rebuilds the scene with a diffusion tool, then checks its own caption of the rebuild against the sent one. If the match is weak, it asks for a few more blocks, and stops once the match is good enough. On a photo data set over noisy channels, this adaptive loop gave the best match and fewest failures for its size.
arxiv-2510-26642:
Yongjiang Wu, Yongtao Li, Zhiyi Liu, and Lihua Feng settle counting questions about families of sets that overlap heavily. Two families are cross t-intersecting when any set from one shares at least t elements with any set from the other. The team studies product measures, which weigh families by a bias toward larger or smaller sets.

Wu and his three co-authors prove a sharp cap on the product of the two families' measures for a stated range of biases, building on a recent result by others. A second result caps the sizes of two such families built from sequences. Together these confirm two classical conjectures of Tokushige. As a bonus, they strengthen a recent theorem that generalises a well-known result in the area, and they recover an old Ahlswede-Katona result about a named family.
arxiv-2510-26942:
Asghar Ullah, with four co-authors, shows that a driven quantum system can act as a selective sensor. Periodically driven, or Floquet, systems can filter parameters, responding strongly to one and weakly to another. Their test system is a three-qubit transverse-field Floquet Ising model.

Ullah and the team identify a period-doubling phase, born of pi-pairing in the Floquet eigenstates. It has a stark asymmetry: it sharpens estimates of the interaction strength between qubits while suppressing sensitivity to the transverse magnetic field. Other regimes do the reverse and suit field sensing. Quantum Fisher information analysis quantifies the effect, and the filtering survives in larger systems. It can be read out through accessible observables such as magnetization and two-qubit correlations, via classical Fisher information.
arxiv-2510-27142:
Hidetoshi Awata leads six co-authors in generalizing a non-stationary difference equation tied to conformal blocks and affine Laumon spaces. The equation first appeared for deformed Virasoro conformal blocks and, with tuned mass parameters, becomes a quantum KZ equation for a small algebra. The team extends it to a larger symmetry family indexed by a rank parameter.

Their Hamiltonian uses q-commuting variables, meaning variables that commute up to a factor q, and admits both factorized and normal-ordered forms. With special parameter choices it matches an R-matrix from a three-dimensional tetrahedron construction. The authors conjecture that an affine Laumon partition function solves the equation, and they check the claim in a four-dimensional limit where the system reduces to the known Fuji-Suzuki-Tsuda system.
arxiv-2510-27242:
Miguel Lagos offers a fresh model of how metals bend for good in this 2025 paper. Most metals are polycrystalline, built from many small crystal grains packed tight. When stressed past a point, the metal keeps its new shape instead of springing back. Old accounts blame cracks and holes inside the metal. Lagos instead pictures grains that slide past each other.

In his model, each grain is a rough block that fills space with no gaps. Neighbors slide when the shear force, a sideways push, passes a set level. The math can be solved in full, giving two regimes: normal bending and a softer superplastic one. For nickel alloys and stainless steels, the model's numbers match lab tests closely.
arxiv-2510-27342:
Alireza Gharahighehi, Felipe Nakano, Xuehua Yang, Wenhan Cui, and Celine Vens improve how recommender systems question brand-new users. With no interaction history, cold-start users cannot receive personalized suggestions, so rating elicitation asks targeted questions to learn tastes quickly. Decision tree elicitation personalizes the questioning, asking item ratings node by node until enough is known.

Their extension for music recommendation adds two enhancements. Nodes ask about item pairs instead of single items, extracting sharper preference contrasts. Questions also cover attributes such as genres, helping cluster users with similar profiles sooner. Experiments show both enhancements improve performance, particularly when only a few queries are allowed. The approach helps platforms onboard new users with less questioning fatigue and faster personalization.
arxiv-2510-27442:
Aon Safdar and Mohamed Saadeldin shrink a vision model for medical scans in this 2025 paper. Vision Transformers read images in patches and do well on scans, but they are heavy and can overfit small data sets. Clinics with modest computers need something lighter. Their model, CoMViT, keeps the patch idea and trims the rest.

A convolutional tokenizer, a front end that turns images into patch tokens, starts the pipeline. Diagonal masking, dynamic temperature scaling, and pooling steps follow, each tuned by trial. The result runs with only about four and a half million parameters, far fewer than rivals. Across twelve MedMNIST data sets it matched or beat deeper networks. Heat maps show it looks at the same regions a clinician would, despite its small size.
arxiv-2510-27642:
Nikhil Krishna, Mariola Klusek-Gawenda, and Antoni Szczurek model how pairs of charged kaons form in nuclear collisions in 2025. Kaons are short-lived particles with a strange quark. In glancing heavy-ion hits, pairs can form when light beams fuse or when a light beam strikes a nucleus and makes a short-lived meson that then decays.

The study gives one account that fits both the basic light-fusion case and lead-on-lead hits. Fusion rates are checked against past data from three prior experiments. The authors also compare with data at mid-rapidity and forecast rates for lead hits at a set collision energy. Such forecasts guide detectors that hunt rare meson decays.
arxiv-2511-00142:
Saeed Hashemi Sababe presents a full approach for map-valued positive fixed kernels, driven by useful uses in map theory and random processes. Operator-valued kernels extend scalar kernels to settings where outputs are vectors or maps. Two use paths are developed: dilation buildings in map theory, and broad classes of random processes.

Results from the kernel theory are used to build new Hilbert space-valued Gaussian processes and to study the structure of their covariance setups. Probability and map theory readers get a unified treatment linking kernels, dilations, and Gaussian processes. Such methods support multi-factor time series and functional data analysis, where correlations live between whole functions.
arxiv-2511-00342:
Hendrio Braganca, Diego Kreutz, Vanderson Rocha, Joner Assolin, and Eduardo Feitosa present MH-1M, a large public dataset for Android malware research. It holds well over a million apps, about one point three million in total, with rich features and metadata for each. Labels come from the VirusTotal service, which pools many detection engines for a more reliable verdict on each app.

The processed data, feature extraction outputs, and detection reports are openly shared through GitHub, Figshare, and Harvard Dataverse, totaling more than four hundred gigabytes. The authors argue the set's scale and freshness make it valuable for machine learning, deep learning, language model, and threat intelligence studies of how Android malware evolves. For defenders, it offers a shared test bed in a fast-moving field.
arxiv-2511-00842:
David Amaro-Alcala works on cheaper ways to benchmark passive bosonic devices, hardware such as optical systems whose behavior is tested by randomized benchmarking. The existing proposal for such devices is costly, partly because it relies on Clebsch-Gordan coefficients from group theory.

He introduces two filter functions that use the same measurement data but avoid those coefficients. One filter is built from immanants, the other from characters of the special unitary group, and both yield simple formulas for the variance of the estimate. The character filter is cheap to compute and keeps a constant, low variance. A test case with photon loss and gain suggests estimates stay close to the ideal values, which could simplify device characterization.
arxiv-2511-00942:
Simona Diaconu studies a central quantity in the theory of Gaussian random processes, Talagrand's gamma two functional. For a centered Gaussian process, the expected size of its largest value is comparable to this functional, which depends only on the geometry of the index space under a natural distance.

The functional is defined as an infimum over admissible sequences, chains of ever finer approximations to the space. In practice it is mostly used to compare one process with another. Diaconu instead constructs admissible sequences that come close to optimal, treating the functional as an object worth computing in its own right. The aim is a more direct route to understanding expected suprema of Gaussian processes.
arxiv-2511-01042:
Tobias Dijkhuis and colleagues ask which uncertain inputs astrochemical models of interstellar ice should worry about most. Ices on dust grains in cold clouds host rich chemistry, but the models need many parameters, from binding energies to reaction barriers, and most are poorly measured.

Using the UCLCHEM code, they sample binding energies, diffusion barriers, prefactors, and reaction barriers in Monte Carlo fashion across a grid of temperatures, densities, radiation fields, and cosmic ray rates. The abundances of the main ice species prove most sensitive, under all conditions, to the diffusion barriers of small, mobile reactive species such as atomic hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen. Those are the parameters laboratory and theory work should pin down first.
arxiv-2511-01442:
Benedikt Reible, Nils Liebreich, Carsten Hartmann, and Luigi Delle Site build a fast, exact tool for spotting when a molecular simulation box is too small. Splitting a modeled system into independent subsystems changes its free energy, and the two sided Bogoliubov inequality bounds that cost exactly, for both classical and quantum many body systems.

That theorem yields a quality factor measuring how consistent a given box size is. For systems with two body interactions and a known radial distribution function, the factor needs only two six dimensional integrals. The authors present an algorithm for computing it. Its results agree with published findings from simulations run at different box sizes. That gives simulators a solid check for length scale errors.
arxiv-2511-01742:
Muhammad Gaffar and Wei Ku present computer evidence for a hidden actor in strongly linked materials. The actor is a boson made of two electrons bound tightly, each one carrying charge 2e. Such pairs could explain the odd non-Fermi liquid behavior seen in many working materials. Yet the idea is often dropped when tests show clean electronic bands.

The authors use the attractive Hubbard model. With determinant quantum Monte Carlo, they compute how the pairs and the leftover electrons each move. The pairs emerge in force, and can even lead in number. Still, the electronic spectrum shows sharp quasiparticles with barely raised mass. So the pairs dodge the spectrum. Only above the superfluid point does a pseudogap in the spectrum give them away. A clean band, the moral runs, is no proof that strong links are absent.
arxiv-2511-01842:
Haniyeh Tajer and five colleagues run planet-formation simulations to explain Mercury's oversized iron heart. Mercury's core makes up about 70 percent of its mass, more than double the share in the other rocky planets, and dense exo-Mercuries are now turning up too. Two explanations compete: giant impacts late in formation stripped the mantle away, or the raw material near the Sun was iron-rich from the start.

Their N-body simulations test both, starting either from a uniform core fraction or from a step pattern enriched in the inner region. Under the uniform start, erosive impacts do create iron-rich debris, but without a mechanism to remove the stripped mantle material, the debris merges back into lower-fraction bodies, diluting the enrichment. The framework is built to extend to high-core-fraction exoplanets.
arxiv-2511-02042:
M. Z. Haider, M. U. Ghouri, Tayyaba Noreen, and M. Salman aim a hybrid quantum-classical generative model at the events that matter most and occur least: financial crashes, climate extremes, and biological anomalies. Classic generative models often botch these rare cases. They collapse the rare modes entirely, or get their uncertainty wrong. Scarce heavy-tailed data gives them little to learn from.

Their Quantum-Enhanced Generative Model couples a deep latent-variable model with variational quantum circuits. Two ideas carry it. One is a hybrid loss, jointly tuning reconstruction fidelity and a tail-aware likelihood. The other is quantum randomness-driven noise injection. It varies samples and fights mode collapse. Training alternates classical backpropagation with parameter-shift updates. Tests cover synthetic mixtures and real finance, climate, and protein datasets. The model cut tail divergence by up to 50 percent, against GAN, VAE, and diffusion baselines. Recall and calibration improved too.
arxiv-2511-02942:
Ekaterina Kubyshkina, Marcio Kleos Pereira, and Mattia Petrolo ask when not knowing something can excuse a wrong act, and they treat the question as logicians. Philosophers debate which kinds of ignorance excuse. One strong case is a fact the agent never thought about at all. Their 2025 paper gives the first formal analysis of ignorance as an excuse, using epistemic logic.

They introduce a complete and sound logic where excusable ignorance is a basic operator, not a derived one. Its semantics uses Kripke models whose worlds may be incomplete, so a fact can fail to be considered rather than simply false. They then extend the system with public announcements and a new update rule, so the logic can track how learning or disclosure changes what an agent can be excused for not knowing.
arxiv-2511-03542:
Roberta Di Marino and colleagues assemble SOLVE-Med, a team of small specialist models that answer medical questions together. Single models answering across all of medicine face hallucinations, bias, heavy compute, and privacy strain. SOLVE-Med routes each query to the right specialist among ten small models, each tuned on one medical field.

An orchestrator then blends the chosen specialists' answers into one reply. On Italian medical forum data across ten specialties, scores beat standalone models many times larger. All parts run locally, which protects patient privacy and cuts cost. The design trades one giant generalist for a panel that mirrors how real care splits by specialty.
arxiv-2511-03842:
Niels Bottner, Roman Schnabel, and Mikhail Korobko propose a readout scheme to clean back-scatter noise out of gravitational-wave detectors. Stray laser light bouncing back into the signal path creates loud, uneven disturbances, and the noise also appears in the normally unmeasured orthogonal quadrature of the light.

Measuring that second quadrature at the same time gives a witness channel. From it, the disturbance in the signal channel can be reconstructed and subtracted. The scheme stays compatible with frequency-dependent squeezing, already used to cut both shot noise and radiation pressure noise. If it works as designed in a real detector, loud back-scatter events would do less damage to sensitivity.
arxiv-2511-03942:
Shih-Lun Wu, Dave Carlton, Ryan Miyakawa, Yoon Kim, Chris Donahue, and Cheng-Zhi Anna Huang present MIDI-LLM, a recipe for text-to-MIDI music generation built by adapting a large language model. Catalog evidence credited a different author set; the arXiv record governs, and it adds MIDI tokens to the model's vocabulary with a two-stage training pipeline.

Stage one continues pretraining on music-adjacent text and standalone MIDI files; stage two fine-tunes on text-MIDI pairs. Built on a one-billion-parameter Llama model, it beat a recent text-to-MIDI baseline on control and musical quality. A blind study with fifty-eight Hookpad Aria users over four thousand outputs gave it the highest acceptance rate for lead sheet generation.
arxiv-2511-04142:
Sai Praneeth Donthu, Souvik Roy, Soumyarup Sadhukhan, and Gogulapati Sreedurga pin down strategy-proof probabilistic assignment rules. In this setting, indivisible objects are shared among equally many agents by lottery, and each agent starts with an endowment and strict preferences. The deterministic version is well known through the Top Trading Cycles rule.

A weakened incentive demand is introduced: no trick may raise the chance of getting one's top-ranked object. On broad preference domains, Top Trading Cycles is the unique rule meeting that demand together with efficiency and individual rationality conditions in dominance terms. A weaker pairwise efficiency still is enough on a slightly stronger domain, and extensions to ex post notions follow.
arxiv-2511-04342:
Kaiwen Guo and Yanjun Liu investigate extremal functions for anisotropic Trudinger-Moser inequalities, which mark the borderline where exponential integrals in two planes stay finite. Whether the supremum is attained by an actual function, and what symmetry that function must have, are the central questions for several anisotropic variants.

Convex symmetrization does much of the work, joined by continuity of the key function. A link between subcritical and critical suprema moves attainment from the easier regime to the critical one. Existence and Wulff symmetry results follow for the extremal functions across the cases studied. Sharp constants in such bounds anchor limits of many variational arguments in analysis.
arxiv-2511-04542:
Nicolas Moens leads seven authors simulating the atmospheres and winds of O-type stars. These massive stars have turbulent outer layers driven by radiation near an iron opacity bump. The turbulence shapes both the atmosphere and the spectral lines observers use.

Their two-dimensional radiation-hydrodynamic runs cover a grid of O stars at solar composition. They vary basic parameters to see how the subsurface turbulent zone responds. They also trace how that motion shows up in photospheric absorption lines. Replacing ad hoc guesses with direct simulation could sharpen how stellar spectra are read across the whole O-star range.
arxiv-2511-04642:
Jazmin Ordonez-Toro and two colleagues weigh young stars in tight multiple systems with the VLBA. Very long baseline radio images resolve pairs separated by mere milliarcseconds. Gaia cannot split systems that close, so radio astrometry is essential.

The DYNAMO-VLBA project tracks pre-main-sequence binaries with detectable radio emission. Here the team reports dynamical masses for single stars in two systems. S1 in Ophiuchus is that region's brightest and most massive young member. EC 95 in Serpens is the second target. Direct masses for young stars test the models used to age and weigh whole star-forming regions.
arxiv-2511-04842:
Hongyu Zhang and his co-author test whether split compilation truly protects quantum circuit designs. Quantum circuits are valuable intellectual property, and split compilation hides their wiring. The circuit is cut into two parts, each visible, while the links between them stay secret.

Their oracle-guided attack tries to recover those hidden connections systematically. Candidate links are proposed, checked against an oracle, and refined step by step. A full security evaluation framework wraps the attack for repeatable testing. The work warns compiler designers that splitting alone may leak more than assumed, so obfuscation claims need adversarial proof.
arxiv-2511-04942:
Nikita Guseynov and co-authors give a quantum method to price options when asset prices follow a local volatility model. Pricing can be hard when payoffs are complex, many assets are linked, or price rules are detailed.

Their full method solves the forward Kolmogorov equation, also called the Fokker-Planck equation, by mapping it to a quantum evolution task. They spell out state prep, the main run, and price read-out by a swap test. Read-out gains are a key plus of solving the forward form rather than the backward pricing form used in most past work.
arxiv-2511-05342:
D. Kynoch and co-authors report three months of dense X-ray, ultraviolet, and optical watching of the Seyfert galaxy MCG+08-11-11, with the Swift satellite plus ground telescopes. Light echoes between bands show how the hot core's glow is reprocessed by nearby matter.

The twelve light curves track each other closely. The X-ray to ultraviolet link is the strongest yet seen in a Seyfert galaxy, by the authors' count. Lags grow with wavelength, as reprocessing predicts, but the lag spectrum is far flatter than a past one, which poses a puzzle for disk models.
arxiv-2511-05442:
Frauke Andersen and co-authors present APP, a faster form of path patching for finding circuits inside a language model. Circuit discovery is a key step in mechanistic interpretability, but path patching is slow and has seen little deep use on small models.

APP first prunes the search space with a contrastive attention head method. That method, built on causal mediation ideas, scores heads by how task-bound they are and cuts the rest. With far fewer heads to test, patching runs much faster. Tests check that the found circuits still match the slow method's finds.
arxiv-2511-05542:
Jeff Brown, Andrew Kirjner, Annika Vivekananthan, and Ed Boyden ask whether large language models can proofread brain wiring maps. Making such a map, called a connectome, takes huge human effort. People must check data from imaging and machine segmentation by hand, fixing wrong splits and merges.

Their test, ConnectomeBench, grades models on three proofreading jobs. It uses expert-marked data from mouse visual cortex and the full fruit fly brain. Top models did well on naming segment types and fixing split errors, scoring far above chance. They still lagged experts and struggled to spot merge errors, so human proofreaders remain needed for now.
arxiv-2511-05642:
Justin Williams, Kishor Datta Gupta, Roy George, and Mrinmoy Sarkar show a small robot that sees, reasons, and moves at the same time using only its own hardware. Robots working where GPS fails need local, frugal intelligence. Past systems often split perception from motion or lean on cloud computing.

Their framework runs a compact vision-language model on the robot itself. The model reads the scene and reasons about it while the robot keeps moving through changing surroundings. Trials on a mobile robot checked the trade-off between compute cost, task accuracy, and response speed. The authors present the run as an early proof that small models can guide edge robots in service, disaster, and defense work.
arxiv-2511-05942:
Vladimir Kozlov and Oleg Motygin analyze when a family of water waves trades stability with the smooth flow it branches from. They study steady waves in a two-dimensional channel with a flat bottom and free surface, ignoring surface tension. The flow rotates with constant vorticity, and a branch of Stokes waves grows out of a laminar flow as the wave period varies.

The first eigenvalue along the branch stays negative. The second, small eigenvalue decides whether the exchange-of-stability principle holds, and whether the period grows or shrinks near the critical point. The authors show a critical depth splits the two signs for each vorticity. They compare that depth with the depth where a stagnation point forms, and find the order flips at a specific vorticity value.
arxiv-2511-06142:
Sizhe Tang, Jiayu Chen, and Tian Lan target a weakness of Monte Carlo Tree Search when many agents must plan together. The joint action space grows explosively as agents are added, so the search tree branches too fast to explore well. Their system, MALinZero, compresses that space before searching.

MALinZero projects joint-action returns into a low-dimensional form modeled as a contextual linear bandit problem. A new tree search rule built on linear confidence bounds then balances trying new actions against using known good ones. The authors bound the method's regret and give an approximation algorithm for picking joint actions. Tests on matrix games and the SMAC benchmarks beat model-based and model-free rivals.
arxiv-2511-06542:
Chaegeun Song, Zhong Zheng, Bing Li, and Lingzhou Xue tame categorical predictors that splinter regression data into too many tiny groups. Categories are everywhere in applied regression, and modern datasets keep adding more. Each extra category fragments the available information and drags accuracy down, so merging look-alike categories is attractive if done carefully.

Their method uses a pairwise vector fused lasso, a penalty that automatically fuses categories whose relationship with the response looks the same. The approach fits a broad family of models with general loss functions, and the authors prove it merges the right categories consistently. A practical gradient algorithm, tested on simulations and Spotify music data, improved prediction while simplifying the categories.
arxiv-2511-06642:
Renato Castro, Rodrigo Paredes, and Douglas Kahn predict which shops will actually grow after receiving a free commercial beverage cooler. In fast-moving consumer goods, placing coolers is a costly bet on future sales, and machine learning rarely guides that placement. Churn and demand models are common, but asset allocation decisions stay mostly manual.

The study follows more than three thousand traditional trade clients of a Central American brewer, with a year of sales before and after installation. Gradient boosting models, explained through SHAP values, forecast which clients clear ten, thirty, or fifty percent growth targets. The best model scored strongly at every threshold, and simulations suggest better returns plus savings from skipping clients unlikely to grow.
arxiv-2511-06742:
Adam Piaseczny, Eric Ruzomberka, Rohit Parasnis, and Christopher Brinton probe how attackers should position themselves inside decentralized federated learning. Removing the central server speeds training through device-to-device links but opens new attack surfaces. Where malicious nodes sit in the network, rather than just how many there are, had gone largely unstudied.

The authors adapt span-based and centrality-based placement strategies to this setting and propose a hybrid, MaxSpAN-FL, that randomizes where nodes sit using topology cues. across network shapes and attacker counts, the hybrid attack degraded model training more than baseline schemes. Theory explains why eigenvector centrality attacks underperform here. The results map a weakness that future defenses must close.
arxiv-2511-06842:
Lionel Levine, Haniyeh Ehsani Oskouie, Sajjad Ghiasvand, and Majid Sarrafzadeh present a method for shrinking neural networks without losing accuracy. Their approach, M2M-DC, ranks building blocks of a network by how much label-relevant information they carry and prunes the least informative ones. It then alternates short knowledge distillation phases with careful channel slicing inside each stage.

The slicing respects the shape constraints of residual connections, so pruned networks stay valid. On the CIFAR-100 image benchmark, compressed ResNet-18 and ResNet-34 models kept accuracy near their teachers while using far fewer parameters and operations. A compressed MobileNetV2 even beat its teacher by about two and a half points of accuracy, showing the recipe works across network classes.
arxiv-2511-06942:
Fangqi Dai, Xingjian Jiang, and Zizhuang Deng build a detector for text that machines have revised rather than written outright. Detectors excel at spotting fully machine-generated text but struggle with polished human drafts that a model has reworked, especially when the generating model is unknown. Their idea starts from the hypothesis that human writing has distinctive stylistic patterns a model can be tuned to prefer.

The detector, HLPD, uses a reward-based alignment process that shifts a scoring model's token distribution toward human-like writing, making it more sensitive to departures from human style. It is tested in an adversarial system where a five-dimensional prompt generator and several advanced language models create varied revision cases. Against GPT-revised text it improved detection scores greatly over the ImBD and Fast-DetectGPT baselines.
arxiv-2511-07042:
Arjo Dasgupta and five co-authors explore dipoles arranged in triangular optical ladders, a lab platform where geometric frustration amplifies long-range dipolar interactions. For mobile polarized dipolar bosons, frustration can drive a transition between a chiral superfluid, whose flow breaks mirror symmetry, and an plain two-part superfluid. The authors show this transition should be reachable at temperatures today's tests already achieve, even with the weak interactions of magnetic atoms.

They also treat pinned spin-half dipoles, realized by polar molecules in two rotational states, which emulate frustrated dipolar XXZ spin models. Tuning the strength and orientation of an outside electric field moves these systems through a rich landscape of ground states, including chiral and nematic phases, and yields striking chiral dynamics worth probing.
arxiv-2511-07342:
Lorenzo Baldi, Rainer Sinn, Máté L Telek, and Julian Weigert extend Pólya's classic theorem for certifying that a polynomial is positive. Pólya's method multiplies a homogeneous polynomial that is strictly positive on the nonnegative orthant by a high power of the sum of variables. It then simply checks that all coefficients come out positive, an easy certificate. But the method can fail when the polynomial misses certain monomials of its degree, as sparse polynomials do.

Using tools from positive toric geometry, the authors present extensions and converses of Pólya's theorem adapted to sparse polynomials, so the missing-monomial cases gain certificates of their own. They also explore an application outside pure algebra. They use these positivity certificates to study the convergence of Feynman integrals in particle physics, where knowing an integral's integrand has a definite sign matters.
arxiv-2511-07542:
Hakim Atek and a large collaboration introduce GLIMPSE, among the deepest sky surveys yet taken with the James Webb Space Telescope. The program images one lensing field for twenty to forty hours per filter across nine near-infrared bands. Gravity from a foreground cluster magnifies faint early galaxies behind it.

Depths reach fainter than magnitude thirty, exposing galaxies from the era when the universe was first lit up. Hubble imaging, ground spectroscopy, and Webb spectra support the survey. Early results already probe galaxy birth and cosmic reionization. The overview lays out design, lens models, and goals for astronomers planning follow-up work.
arxiv-2511-07642:
Rafael Pereira, Túlio Vales, and Cássio Morais extend dynamics theory to maps that return sets instead of single points. For open set-valued maps, each point maps to an open connected region. Earlier work described the combinatorial shape of the final recurrent set where motion returns.

Adding transitivity and mixing brings that framework closer to Smale spectral decomposition for ordinary maps. Such maps turn out to carry infinite topological entropy, meaning their complexity grows without bound. Transitive examples also connect to transitive Anosov diffeomorphisms, the classic chaotic systems. The results give set-valued dynamics, used in economics and control, a firmer theoretical footing.
arxiv-2511-07742:
Luan Lazzari and Kleinner Farias built a checker that catches clashes between software diagrams as modelers draw them. UML class diagrams and sequence diagrams must agree, yet students and engineers routinely let them drift apart. Teaching consistency is notoriously hard when feedback arrives late.

Harmony Validator plugs into the Papyrus modeling environment and watches editing events live. Inconsistencies are flagged and reported at the moment they appear. Event-driven checking turns consistency from an exam topic into a habit formed while drawing. Modeling courses and professional teams both gain earlier, cheaper correction of design mistakes.
arxiv-2511-07942:
Rishabh Agrawal, Yusuf Alvi, Rahul Jain, and Ashutosh Nayyar tackle imitation learning when conditions change after training. Robots often learn from expert examples because writing reward rules by hand is hard. Standard methods assume the world stays fixed, yet real shifts in dynamics can badly hurt performance.

Their balance equation approach learns only from demonstrations gathered under normal conditions, with no new interaction. It seeks a policy that does well even under the worst likely change in dynamics. Tests on continuous control tasks show stronger robustness and generalization than leading offline imitation methods, especially in disturbed settings.
arxiv-2511-08042:
J V Roig presents KAMI, a benchmark meant to judge agentic AI systems on work that resembles enterprise use. Ordinary language model tests suffer from training data contamination and ignore multi step tool use under uncertainty. Companies need rankings that predict real deployment value, not just exam style scores.

The index runs one hundred seventy thousand test items, over five and a half billion tokens, across thirty five model setups. Traditional rankings poorly predicted practical agentic results, and newer models did not always beat their predecessors. The report also examines cost against performance, model behavior patterns, and how reasoning affects token efficiency.
arxiv-2511-08242:
Waseem AlShikh and co-authors argue that AI agents should be judged by outcomes rather than by infrastructure measures such as latency or token speed. A white paper framework offers eleven task agnostic, outcome based metrics covering decision quality, autonomy, adaptability, and business value. Named examples include goal completion rate, an autonomy index, multi step task resilience, and business impact efficiency.

A large simulation compares four agent designs, from ReAct to a hybrid, across health care, finance, marketing, legal, and customer service domains. Clear trade offs emerge between designs. The hybrid agent performs most consistently, with the highest average goal completion rate in their tests.
arxiv-2511-08642:
Jingwen Fu and four co-authors design a communication system that sends only what a task needs from text, audio, and video traveling together. Bandwidth is tight and channels are noisy, so the system must squeeze out overlap between the streams without losing the details the receiving task depends on.

A two-stage variational information bottleneck does the squeezing. Each stream is first compressed alone, keeping its task-specific features, while an adversarial module trims cross-stream dependence so the streams complement rather than repeat each other. A second stage compresses the fused result and hardens it against channel distortion. On multi-modal emotion recognition tests the framework beats existing baselines on accuracy and reliability. The gains grow largest when the signal-to-noise ratio is low.
arxiv-2511-08942:
Mobin Habibpour and Fatemeh Afghah hand the strategy of household navigation to a vision-language model instead of letting it merely label what the robot sees. In object-goal navigation the robot must find a named target in an unfamiliar home, and frontier-based exploration alone wanders without a plan.

Three techniques make the model an active strategist. Structured chain-of-thought prompting draws out step-by-step reasoning about where the target likely sits. The robot's recent action history is fed back in, which keeps the agent from looping over the same ground. The model also reads top-down obstacle maps beside its first-person camera views, sharpening its spatial sense. On the HM3D, Gibson, and MP3D benchmarks the resulting paths are notably more direct and logical than earlier approaches.
arxiv-2511-09542:
Jingyang Li and Yang Chen forecast matrix and tensor time series by using the fact that most interactions are local. Each entry in such data depends mainly on a small neighborhood, like nearby grid cells in an ionosphere map. Modeling only those local interactions shrinks the model a lot.

Their Local Interaction Autoregressive approach includes a separable variant sharing row and column parts. Fitting runs through parallel least squares, with a BIC-type selector choosing each entry's neighborhood. Theory ensures consistent neighborhood recovery and bounds the fitting errors. Simulated runs confirm sharp selection and forecasts beating matrix time-series baselines. A total electron content case study recovers localized space-time patterns with improved prediction.
arxiv-2511-09942:
Mustafa Munir, Md Mostafijur Rahman, and Radu Marculescu present AdaptViG, a vision graph neural network designed to be both accurate and cheap to run. Vision graph networks are powerful, but building their graphs costs heavily. AdaptViG constructs its graph on an efficient static axial scaffold and adds a dynamic gating rule that weighs long-range connections by feature similarity, with weights decaying exponentially.

Early stages use the light gating, while the final stage uses a full global attention block for maximum feature gathering. The mid-size model reached about eighty-three percent top-one accuracy, beating a larger vision graph baseline while using eighty percent fewer parameters and far fewer operations. It also surpassed a much larger efficient transformer on segmentation and detection tasks.
arxiv-2511-10342:
Christos Charalambous, writing alone, models vaccine choices in an epidemic as driven by regret, doubt, and social norms, not by cold math alone. Agents in his model weigh payoffs, fear, and peer approval. They look ahead to regret, let trust shift with doubt, and react to three norm types: their own norms, signs of peer approval, and what peers are seen to do. A standard disease spread model runs while these choices play out.

Group results were best at a mid level of rationality: keen enough to heed risk, loose enough to adapt. Mild regret aided self-correction, while strong regret or greed shook choices loose. Mild doubt bred care, but deep doubt broke joint action. Norms filled the gaps left by thin facts, with approval signs counting most when facts were weakest.
arxiv-2511-10442:
Aarush Agarwal and four co-authors present FastGraph, a graphics-processor algorithm for quickly building nearest-neighbor graphs in low dimensions. Such graphs underpin graph neural networks, but building them can dominate the cost of a project. FastGraph targets spaces of two to ten dimensions and keeps its data resident on the graphics processor.

The method splits space into bins, tunes its own parameters, and supports gradient flow, which learning pipelines need. Benchmarks show speedups of twenty to forty times over well-known libraries such as FAISS, ANNOY, and SCANN, with almost no extra memory. The gains matter most for heavy low-dimensional jobs like particle clustering in physics, object tracking in video, and graph clustering.
arxiv-2511-10842:
Jugal Gajjar, Kaustik Ranaware, Kamalasankari Subramaniakuppusamy, and Vaibhav Gandhi present HyperComplEx, a knowledge graph embedding method built to handle many kinds of relations at once. Single-space embeddings each fail somewhere: Euclidean models flatten hierarchies, hyperbolic models mishandle symmetric relations, and plain vector models miss asymmetry.

Their framework combines hyperbolic, complex, and Euclidean spaces in one model. A learned attention mechanism chooses, for each relation type, how much each space counts, and a consistency loss keeps the spaces' predictions coherent. Tested on research knowledge graphs growing from about a thousand papers to ten million, plus standard tests, it beat strong baselines including TransE, RotatE, and ComplEx throughout. On the largest graph it led the best baseline by a clear margin while keeping inference fast.
arxiv-2511-11042:
Michael Farber, Stefan Kurz, and Mathias Pillin develop math tools for robots and other systems that must move while their surroundings keep changing. A fixed setting is easier to plan for, but real settings shift during motion. The authors use layered space maps, called fibrations, to model how a system's options sit inside a changing world.

They treat two cases. When future changes are known ahead, planning costs no more than in a fixed setting. When changes cannot be foreseen, the system must react from live measures of state and speed. For that case they define a reaction mechanism, a local lifting rule that generalizes a classic connection idea, with examples.
arxiv-2511-11442:
Martin Gray, Celine Guervilly, and Graeme Sarson simulate fingering convection in rotating planetary cores, where layered liquid metal sits at the top of the core. Their setup has a stable temperature gradient but an unstable composition gradient, a case tied to Mercury. Because heat and composition diffuse at very unlike rates, narrow fingers of sinking and rising fluid form and stir the layer.

In a rotating spherical shell, the main finger mode forms narrow, elongated structures that tilt from the rotation axis toward gravity as stratification strengthens. Fingers stay laminar, with widths set by thermal stratification, not rotation. Secondary large-scale flows, from zonal winds to gyres, arise across most settings.
arxiv-2511-11642:
Matheus Duzi, Paul Szeptycki, and Walter Tholen bring Fraïssé theory, the model-theoretic machinery for building universal homogeneous structures, into the study of abstract two-player games. Recent generalizations of the theory to category-theoretic settings make the move possible.

For the class of finite games considered, an infinitely countable game exists that is both universal for the class and ultrahomogeneous, meaning its symmetries are as rich as possible. Odd features of the game categories clash with the usual framework, so weaker categorical properties are formulated that still produce a Fraïssé limit. The result extends a classic construction technique to games, where universal objects were far from obvious.
arxiv-2511-11742:
Desmond J. Higham, Francesco Hrobat, and Francesco Tudisco extend the friendship paradox, the fact that your friends have more friends than you do on average, to arbitrary attributes measured through network centrality. Such paradoxes shape social science and epidemic modeling, where sampling friends biases what you observe.

Using linear algebra, the authors find when a generalized paradox must occur, comparing two averaging styles that go back to Feld's 1991 work: global and local. For global averaging, walk-based centralities such as Katz centrality always produce the paradox, and nonbacktracking eigenvector centrality does too. Counterexamples for other centralities mark the boundary, showing the paradox is common but not automatic.
arxiv-2511-11842:
Lucas Fenaux, Christopher Srinivasa, and Florian Kerschbaum study a tension inside responsible AI: transparency helps users trust a system, but it may also help attackers fool it. Their test bed is transferable adversarial examples, where an attacker crafts inputs on a surrogate model to deceive a defender's model.

Nine attacks across one hundred eighty-one models show attackers succeed more when they match the defender's choice of defended or undefended model, meaning secrecy about defenses carries real value. Game theory then formalizes when openness pays and when obscurity protects. The result complicates any simple claim that more transparency is always safer, and gives deployers a strategic frame for disclosure decisions.
arxiv-2511-12042:
Soham Bhattacharyya and Omkar Sridhar derive formulas for gravitational waves from pairs of compact objects on eccentric orbits whose spins are tilted. Tilted spins make the orbital plane and the spins precess, or wobble, over time. Closed formulas that include both eccentricity and precessing spins at once had been missing.

The authors use the fact that orbit, precession and energy loss run on different timescales, and average over the precession to remove direct time terms. From that they obtain analytic phase formulas through the second post-Newtonian order, with eccentricity treated as a small quantity. They also extend a standard waveform model to include spin precession.
arxiv-2511-12142:
Seokwon Song, Minsu Park and Gunhee Kim present MAVIS, a benchmark for judging whether AI answers to visual questions cite their sources well. Good attribution lets users check each claim, but past work focused on text alone. MAVIS tests systems that must grasp the intent behind a visual question, find multimodal evidence, and answer at length with citations.

The dataset holds a large set of visual question cases, each answer tagged with fact-level links to text or image documents. New measures score how informative, grounded and fluent answers are, and they match human judgments well. Findings show multimodal search helps fluency, but image sources are grounded more weakly than text.
arxiv-2511-12342:
Sajjad Pakdamansavoji, Kumar Vaibhav Jha, Baher Abdulhai and James H Elder test whether traffic at intersections is better analyzed on the ground plane than in the camera image. Turning movement counts guide signal timing, traffic management and city planning. Vision systems usually track vehicles in image coordinates, which distort distance and direction.

The authors project detected vehicles from roadside cameras down onto the ground plane, giving real-world coordinates. For a single camera, that change improves both trajectory classification and turning counts. Weak fusion of projections from several cameras improves accuracy further. Their conclusion is plain: analyze traffic where it actually moves, on the ground.
arxiv-2511-12542:
Caixing Gu, Meng Li and Pan Ma characterize when products of block Hankel and Toeplitz operators are compact, a question rooted in the Sarason problem for operators on analytic function spaces. Hankel and Toeplitz operators are structured maps tied to a symbol function, and their block versions act on vector-valued functions on the unit disk. Compactness of a product is a subtle property of the symbols.

The authors describe it through harmonic extensions of the symbols and through Douglas algebras generated by them. They also answer completely when the product of a block Hankel operator with a block Toeplitz operator is itself a block Hankel operator, a structural question that complements the compactness result.
arxiv-2511-12742:
Zhongteng Cai, Yaxuan Wang, Yang Liu, and Xueru Zhang study what happens when diffusion models train on their own output. As synthetic images flood the internet, later models learn from earlier models' work, and this self-consuming loop can destabilize training or collapse the model's variety. The usual fixes, hoarding old real data or adding fresh human-labeled data, are costly. The authors instead examine the geometry of the model's latent space across generations of this recycling.

They find the structure of latent representations from synthetic data steadily degrades. Their fix, Latent Space Filtering, removes the least realistic synthetic examples from mixed training sets before reuse. Across several real-world datasets, filtering beat existing baselines and held off model collapse without extra training cost or human annotation. A supporting theory links the observed latent-space decay to the collapse itself. A cheap hygiene rule for training on web data follows.
arxiv-2511-12942:
Aritro Pathak proves that the elliptic measure doubles nicely for operators whose drift blows up near the boundary in an averaged sense. The elliptic measure tracks how boundary values influence solutions of an elliptic equation. A doubling property, where enlarging a boundary ball at most multiplies the measure by a controlled factor, is basic to its analysis. Earlier results assumed the drift was pointwise small. Pathak only needs smallness on average over Whitney cubes, a Carleson-type condition on the drift's size.

The results hold in one-sided chord-arc domains and are new even for the half-space. Along the way he proves Hardy inequalities in domains whose boundaries are Ahlfors-David regular, using a stopping time argument. The work connects to recent results on Dirichlet problems in rough domains.
arxiv-2511-13342:
Avadhut V. Purohit and Udaysinh T. Bhosale study exact quantum recurrences in the double kicked top, a driven spin model. The model extends the quantum kicked top with an extra kick that breaks time-reversal symmetry. Recurrences, where the system returns exactly to its start, matter for control and for information tasks.

Rewriting the dynamics with two effective parameters, they prove the Floquet operator is exactly periodic at special parameter values, with periods that depend on spin size. Entanglement and fidelity measures show dynamical phase transitions at time-symmetric settings. Level statistics reveal a smooth shift from regular to chaotic behavior as parameters move, so order can be tuned at any size.
arxiv-2511-13642:
Fawzi Aly and Dejan Stojkovic extend the study of coupled gravitational and electromagnetic ripples to rotating black holes. Earlier work used the non-rotating Schwarzschild case; here the arena is Kerr spacetime, handled in a curvature-based Newman-Penrose and Teukolsky framework. Within a minimally coupled Einstein-Maxwell system, they derive the quadratic source terms that feed the spin-weighted Teukolsky equation.

Order-of-magnitude estimates suggest the coupled quadratic modes can matter for charged and magnetized settings found in nature. A brief dilaton example shows the mode spectrum reacts to how gravity couples to electromagnetism.
