Shubhankar Sahai studies how derived algebras, a modern algebraic tool, behave on formal derived stacks, the geometric spaces behind prismatization theory. The paper classifies derived algebras living in quasi-coherent sheaves on a class of filtered formal stacks, including those whose sheaves form prismatic gauges over a perfectoid ring. As it goes, it tracks derived algebras across schematic quasi-affine maps.

One clean result: algebras on the source correspond exactly to algebras on the target that receive a map from the pushed-forward structure sheaf. Extensions to classifying stacks of diagonalizable groups are sketched, plus side classifications for sheaves that were missing from the literature. The work supports the author's forthcoming research and aims to be broadly useful.
arxiv-2602-09842:
Fabian Schaipp and two co-authors present a theory analysis of random tuning methods in terms of step-size feel in their 2026 paper. A key number is found that, for each method, tells how scores fall as the step size grows too large. For convex problems, this number straight impacts the gap bound of the method. Most key, the analysis gives straight theory evidence that tuned step-size methods, such as SPS or NGN, are more robust than random gradient descent.

The edge of tuned methods is thus sized beyond observed tests. Tests show the theory bound mirrors actual scores in shape as a function of step size, even for non-convex problems. Step-size staying power gains a theory footing: a single number captures fall, favors tuned methods on convex problems, and tracks real ways beyond them.
arxiv-2602-10342:
Normal cones to sublevel sets of suprema describe optimality geometry, but sharp formulas in terms of data functions have been partial. A 2026 paper led by Stephanie Caro, with two co-authors, provides sharp and detailed formulas for normal cones to sublevel sets of suprema of any functions. They use only data-function subdifferentials. In the convex case, formulas use the approximate subdifferential of single data functions at the nominal point. The quasi-convex framework needs the Fréchet subdifferential of those functions taken at nearby points.

These results yield optimality rules for infinite convex and quasi-convex optimization work, giving users precise cone formulas from data subdifferentials alone.
arxiv-2602-10442:
Hao Zhou and Mahanth Gowda infer full-body muscle activity from shoe insoles in a 2026 paper. Muscle activation drives movement and matters for injury prevention and rehabilitation, yet standard sensing needs skin electrodes that few people will wear all day. The new system, Press2Muscle, reads activation from pressure patterns under the feet instead.

Foot pressure shifts as muscles across the body fire during movement, and the system learns to decode those shifts. A data-driven design adjusts how much weight it gives each foot region, adapting to differences in gait, weight, and movement style. The result is an unobtrusive, everyday sensing route: ordinary footwear becomes a window onto muscle activity without electrodes or clinic visits.
arxiv-2602-10542:
Ozgur Ercetin and Mohaned Chraiti rethink message flow for an age of strong guessers in a 2026 paper. Older Shannon theory treats message flow as moving symbol strings well. When both endpoints run strong forward models, however, much of the message is already guessable, and literal transport wastes the channel.

Their plan, PSC, keeps a stated shared forward state at both ends. The channel then carries mainly fixes: new bits that match the receiver's draft path with the transmitter's real one. The paper swaps entropy-rate counting for cross-entropy counting under model mismatch, and derives fit limits that join room, delay, and sense flow into one picture.
arxiv-2602-10842:
Norifumi Ojiro studies rational curves on a special algebra surface in a 2026 paper. A smooth Hermitian surface is a projective surface isomorphic to the Fermat surface of degree one more than a prime power, in positive characteristic. The paper examines incidence relations among rational curves of that degree contained in the surface.

Those curves produce a family of strongly regular graphs and association schemes, linking algebra shape to combinatorics. The incidence structure encodes how curves meet and arrange on the surface, and the resulting graphs carry the balance of the configuration. The work gives geometers and combinatorialists a concrete bridge: curves on a Hermitian surface become highly ordered graphs.
arxiv-2602-11242:
What does it mean to be human among machines that also move? Yitong Wang and Yue Yao present ReTracing, a multi-agent embodied results that treats AI archaeologically through body, machine, and generative systems. Sentences about human-machine contact are drawn from science-fiction novels.

Language models turn each excerpt into paired prompts for what to do and what not to do. A diffusion video model converts those prompts into choreography for a human performer and motor commands for a quadruped robot. Both perform on a mirrored floor, tracked by cameras and rebuilt as point clouds and motion trails. The archive reveals how generative systems encode social and cultural bias through movement.
arxiv-2602-11342:
Theory of mind in AI is usually benchmarked, rarely designed for. Qiaosi Wang and five co-authors ran thirteen co-design sessions with twenty-six industry practitioners to envision theory-of-mind-enabled everyday AI. Sessions asked how inferring user intentions could shape products, grounded in real design practice.

Three recommendations emerged: such AI should sit in the social context shaping mental states, respond to their changing nature, and respect subjective individual differences. Each recommendation carries tensions between envisioned futures and current practice. The authors argue for moving beyond static, inference-driven theory of mind toward a pervasive capability supporting continuous human-AI contact loops.
arxiv-2602-11542:
Warming at the poles is shrinking the temperature gap between the equator and the poles, and that change may matter as much as freshwater input for the great Atlantic overturning flow. Jasmine Noory reworks a simple box model of that circulation, long used to study tipping points, so that heat forcing can vary instead of staying fixed as a background setting. The model is then tested under heat and salt forcing acting together.

Inside the model, the work maps where steady circulation holds and where it breaks down. It identifies a cusp point where two kinds of tipping boundary meet, marking the edge of the stable range. The key result is that heat-driven erosion alone can push the system past a threshold, even with no extra freshwater forcing, giving researchers a second distinct route to destabilization.
arxiv-2602-11642:
Recovering a 3D surface from scattered points often means estimating a signed distance field, a job usually framed through the Eikonal equation and learned approximations. Diego Patiño and three co-authors reframe the task through a different equation: Poisson equation, the same mathematics that describes electrostatic potential from a charge distribution. Using Green functions they obtain a closed-form expression for the solution and exploit linearity to build the target shape field as a superposition of solutions.

The electrostatics analogy is more than decoration, since it yields a parametric form that can be evaluated directly rather than fitted blindly. In tests the method captures high-frequency surface detail better than rivals, even when given only a small number of shape priors. Physics, in this telling, supplies structure that pure learning must otherwise discover from data alone.
arxiv-2602-11842:
Power system security assessments often use operating set-points from optimal power flow dispatch, an idealized clearing that ignores how market participants actually behave. Driven by cost minimization, that dispatch can overstate security. Andrej Stankovski and three co-authors introduce a social-welfare-based day-ahead market-clearing model and analyze its security implications with Cascades, a model for cascading failure analysis. They apply it to the IEEE-118 bus system with three independent control zones.

Market dispatch leads to demand not served up to 80 percent higher than optimal power flow, revealing significant security overestimation. The effect is strongest in large cascading events with unserved demand above 100 megawatts. Increased dispatch of storage and gas units drives the gap, placing the system in critical operating conditions. Operators can use these findings to estimate market impacts on security more honestly and plan expansion strategies accordingly.
arxiv-2602-11942:
Late gadolinium enhancement imaging is the standard for heart scar checks, but scarce labeled data slows automated masking. Soufiane Ben Haddou and six co-authors propose a framework that synthesizes both enhancement images and their masks using neural maps combined with denoising diffusion models. First, neural maps learn smooth spatial layouts of scan data with muscle and fibrosis masks.

Those maps are then compressed into compact latent codes that keep key anatomy. A spread model works in that latent space to create new representations, decoded into synthetic images with body-consistent masks. On 133 cardiac MRI scans, adding 200 made volumes to training lifts scar segmentation, with the Dice score rising slightly. The method needs no new annotations, offering a practical answer to data shortage.
arxiv-2602-12042:
Preparing arbitrary quantum states costs exponential resources, but matrix product states admit cheaper constructions when accuracy trades against circuit complexity. Tomasz Szołdra and two co-authors present an end-to-end build framework combining rule-of-thumb circuits with variational optimization in one pipeline. Staircase-like and brick-wall circuits warm-start the tuning, enabling high-quality builds for large systems.

Target states come as physical quantum states or from classical data via amplitude codes, using singular value splits or tensor cross interpolation. Entanglement-based qubit reordering, cast as a quadratic assignment problem, plus low-level optimizations cut depths by up to half and CNOT counts by a third. Tested on systems of 19 to 50 qubits, tuned brick-wall circuits give the lowest depths while staircase circuits minimize gate counts, offering principled, scalable recipes for near-term devices.
arxiv-2602-12342:
Agents that must act over long horizons face a credit problem: which middle steps actually helped? Ilze Amanda Auzina led this work with five co-authors, proposing DeltaBelief-RL, which rewards intermediate progress using the language model's own beliefs. Credit follows the change in probability the agent assigns to the target solution, rather than waiting for a final outcome alone.

Training on synthetic interaction data teaches information-seeking skills that beat purely outcome-based rewards, and gains carry to out-of-distribution uses from customer service to personalisation. Performance keeps improving as test-time interactions run beyond the training horizon, with interaction efficiency rising even on Pass at k measures. The method offers a scalable way to teach agents to navigate uncertainty step by step.
arxiv-2602-12442:
Muons helped establish the Standard Model, and they remain sharp probes for new physics. Bertrand Echenard led this work with one co-author, Alexey A. Petrov, reviewing a decade of theoretical and experimental advances in precision muon physics. A global program is now pushing sensitivity across a wide range of muon probes, with large gains expected over the next decade.

The review covers recent work on muon decays, measurements of muon magnetic and electric dipole moments, and searches for charged lepton flavour violation. It explores what those results mean for physics beyond the Standard Model, focusing on models with light new particles such as axions and hidden sectors. Novel experimental concepts and proposals for new muon facilities close the picture, pointing toward the next discovery frontier.
arxiv-2602-12642:
Reward-maximising RL methods can boost thinking scores of language models, but often cut output variety. Dohyung Kim led this work with five co-authors, noting that recent works address this by adopting GFlowNets, training models to match a target spread while jointly learning its partition function. Prior works treat that partition function solely as a normaliser.

This paper re-reads it as a per-prompt expected-reward signal, that is, online hit rate, using unused info to improve sample use. A theory link between the partition function and per-prompt hit rate estimates is first shown. Building on that insight, Partition-aware scheduling prioritises prompts by hardness, improving thinking tests and variety over strong RL rivals for verifiable rewards.
arxiv-2602-12742:
Old paintings often carry craquelure, fine networks of cracks that are hard to restore digitally without damaging the brushwork, and labelled examples are scarce. Jana Cuch-Guillén and two co-authors avoid labels altogether: they first generate synthetic cracks with realistic branching shapes, then train a model to find real ones. A classical detector maps candidate cracks, and a SegFormer model refined with a lightweight adaptation sharpens those maps.

A masked loss and a spatial prior keep training focused on crack regions, and the refined masks then guide an inpainting step that rebuilds missing paint. In zero-shot tests the pipeline beat leading photo restoration models while keeping original brushstrokes intact. For heritage work, the appeal is a non-invasive route to restoration that needs no hand-labelled crack maps.
arxiv-2602-12942:
Future wireless networks need site-specific channel predictions, but ray tracing demands detailed 3D models with material properties, and building them by hand takes weeks. Mingjun Ying and five co-authors present HoRAMA, a system that builds ray-tracing-ready models from ordinary phone video. It combines dense point-cloud reconstruction with vision-language-model material assignment, automating what experts did manually.

Tested in a 700-square-metre factory at 6.75 and 16.95 gigahertz across 12 transmitter-receiver pairs, HoRAMA predictions matched field measurements with 2.28 decibels root-mean-square error on multipath power, close to the hand-built model's 2.18. Reconstruction time fell from two months to 16 hours. For 5G and 6G planning, the system makes scalable digital twins practical, with beam management and edge deployment as longer-term goals.
arxiv-2602-13242:
University courses on AI often lean on code first, leaving students to grasp ideas only through syntax. This paper tries the reverse order, with hands-on, screen-free games. Students act out search methods, Markov decision processes, Q-learning, and hidden Markov models before they meet the math or the code. The activities borrow the spirit of CS Unplugged, a school-level approach, and adapt it for a college introduction to AI.

Four activities are described in full, along with ways to bridge from play to coding tasks and honest notes on what proved hard to run. The authors argue that acting out a choice process first builds gut feel for how AI systems decide, which then makes formal steps easier to follow. Jennifer M. Reddig leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13342:
Prime numbers leave traces in the sums of their factors, and this paper turns those traces into geometry. Let sopfr(n) be the sum of the prime factors of n, counted with multiplicity, and let B(x) add those values up to x. A known estimate says B(x) grows like pi squared times x squared over twelve log x, and the paper proves an exact split of B(n) over primes using valuations of factorials.

That identity motivates a sparse prime-indexed Fourier series, studied here from analytic and geometric angles, with norm identities and links to polygon transforms whose eigen-shapes are discrete Fourier modes. The geometric claims are flagged as experimental, while the arithmetic base is rigorous. Dimitris Vartziotis is the sole author.
arxiv-2602-13742:
GPM 1839-10 is a long-period radio transient active for at least three decades, with unusual emission features including orthogonal polarization mode switches, down-drifting sub-structures, and distinct linear-to-circular polarization shifts. Follow-up observations with the FAST telescope at L-band detected seven radio pulses. A steady link between mode switches and a drop in polarized intensity strongly supports the idea that the switches arise from incoherent summing of the modes.

Measured rotation measures match earlier observations, indicating a stable magneto-ionic environment, which, if the source is binary, suggests a weakly magnetized companion. Crucially, one pulse shows clear evidence of a cyclotron absorption feature, rarely seen in radio sources. It implies a magnetic field of at least tens of Gauss at the absorption site, consistent with a weakly magnetized companion star. Yunpeng Men leads the work with ten co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13842:
Severe aortic stenosis is a common life-threatening condition in elderly patients, often treated with transcatheter valve implants. Yet paravalvular regurgitation remains one of the most frequent post-procedure complications, with proven impact on long-term outlook. This work investigates deep learning to predict regurgitation from pre-op cardiac CT, training 3D convolutional neural networks on even CT volumes from a collected data set of pre-op patients.

Results suggest volumetric deep learning can capture subtle anatomical features from pre-procedure imaging, opening new views for personalized risk assessment and procedural tuning. Predicting which patients face regurgitation risk before the procedure could let clinicians tailor device choice and implant strategy to individual anatomy. Michele Cannito leads the work with eleven co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14142:
Hiroaki Ito and two co-authors study a 2026 arXiv method for multi-dim continued fractions. The Reverse method is not unimodular, yet the paper shows it is ergodic. Proving its second Lyapunov exponent is below zero gives almost-everywhere fast convergence, a strong form of calm.

The authors tie swaps to the method and study the S-adic language built from them. A below-zero second exponent means almost all of those language are even. A close study of the swaps then yields a concrete broad family of even language, marked by a simple rule on the base swap sequence. The work links dynamics, exponents, and word combinatorics.
arxiv-2602-14242:
Barry F. Madore and five co-authors propose a 2026 arXiv new standard candle for cosmic distances. In I-band color-magnitude diagrams of nearby galaxies, the reddest asymptotic giant branch stars form a distinct, high-luminosity population, dubbed I-band AGB stars. Their luminosity functions look like single-peaked Gaussians in three calibrator galaxies.

Zero points for modal I-band absolute magnitude are minus 4.49 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, minus 4.67 in the Small Magellanic Cloud, and minus 4.78 in NGC 4258, with dispersions near 0.22 to 0.25 magnitudes. All three galaxies have independent geometric distances, so a weighted global average calibrates the candle. The tight peaks make IAGB stars a promising distance tool.
arxiv-2602-15242:
He and colleagues propose lean adjoint-based design optimization with optimal control. Multidisciplinary design usually moves step by step from system motion to design variables and control, yet that path is wasteful and may yield weak designs. The team frames optimal control and design optimization as one problem with linear quadratic regulator control. They use the coupled adjoint method to compute design slopes, key for gradient-based tuning.

Slope work cost with the adjoint method is free of design count, suiting large problems. The coupled adjoint can be solved in stages and more cheaply through three smaller adjoint equations using the forward shape. The team shows the approach on two tests: a classic cart-pole problem and the airflow shape of a quadrotor blade. For that blade, control cost falls by 10 percent by tuning it for a control task, with a slight penalty in steady hover power use.
arxiv-2602-15442:
Čoko and colleagues offer a grain-based fake sound device using a new softened leaky grain motion version with a hidden push fixer and a minus-push balance plan. It is needed to copy sound travel across MHz-GHz tones. Sound-matter clashes support many medical and soft-matter uses, yet faking these events is hard due to the large gap of sticky and sound sizes. Smooth tools catch large-scale wave travel but cannot see tiny clashes, while grain-based routes offer tiny detail but falter with thrift and calm at bigger sizes.

They show its powers by aping the sound herding of coated bubbles, a key trick in sound-led drop-off. Past this use, the method sets a broad base for faking wave-matter clashes in soft and living stuff, sparking new paths for machine work on sound-driven events in study and building.
arxiv-2602-15542:
Kusiński and Plewik reduce questions about compact sets of real numbers to questions about countable orders. That reduction sets up a variant of homogeneity for such compact sets, with close attention to a family the authors call t-sets. Homogeneity here concerns how alike a set looks from each of its points, and the t-set family gives the variant a concrete test ground.

The paper closes with a counting result: there are exactly aleph-one many non-homeomorphic t-sets. The proof path, from orders to homogeneity to count, is compact, and the result pins down the size of this family in sharp terms. Set theorists and topologists will find a neat bridge between order structure and the shape of compact real sets.
arxiv-2602-15842:
Kohita and Yoshioka introduce the Meme Reply Selection task and the MaMe-Re benchmark, or Manga Meme Reply Benchmark, for funny manga panel replies. Memes are popular in modern web talk, used not only as static artifacts but as live replies within conversations. The benchmark holds 100,000 pairs labelled by people, with 500,000 labels from 2,325 distinct raters, built from openly licensed Japanese manga panels plus social media posts.

Analysis reveals three key insights. Large language models give early signs of grasping social cues like exaggeration, going past matching only on the surface. Adding visual information brings no performance gain, and reveals a gap between grasping visual content and putting it to use for contextual fun. While language models can match human calls in fixed settings, they struggle to distinguish subtle gaps in wit among similar in meaning candidates. Picking replies that are humorous in context stays an open challenge for models today.
arxiv-2602-15942:
Masot-Llima and colleagues ask how far Clifford circuits can simplify tensor network states. Tensor networks work well when entanglement stays limited, while Clifford circuits handle highly entangled stabilizer states with little magic. Joining the two promises cheaper classical simulation, since Clifford steps can strip entanglement from the network form of a state.

The paper maps the regimes where exact and heuristic Clifford disentanglers succeed, and shows how the two styles of disentangling connect. It then traces their failure as non-Clifford resources pile up. A sharp result closes the door on a universal fix: outside stabilizer settings, no Clifford operation can peel even one qubit away from an arbitrary non-Clifford rotation. The limits found here mark where Clifford based simulation stops helping.
arxiv-2602-16142:
Spencer Compton leads a team of five math researchers who study density estimation under Kullback-Leibler divergence. Given samples from an unknown density, the goal is an estimate that stays close to the truth with high odds. Two settings matter. In model aggregation, the truth sits in a finite set of densities. In mixture estimation, the truth blends densities from that set. The authors assume nothing about the base densities. Ratios may be unbounded and supports may differ.

For both problems they pin down the best possible high-odds guarantees, which depend on set size, sample size, and confidence level. For mixtures they match known lower bounds for discrete cases. The mixture case hinges on two new covering results: a sharp bound on local Hellinger entropy for mixtures, and an optimal ratio covering theorem for convex sets. The latter also yields new estimates for approximate Pareto sets.
arxiv-2602-16442:
Kamil Jeziorek leads eight coauthors on graph neural networks for neuromorphic audio and keyword spotting on FPGAs. Edge sensors record ever more data, so hardware-aware architectures are needed locally. The team implements event-graph neural networks for audio with an artificial cochlea turning signals into sparse events.

Built on a system-on-chip FPGA, the baseline model reaches nearly ninety-three percent accuracy on SHD. That is about two percent below the state of the art, with far fewer parameters. SSC accuracy is about sixty-seven to seventy-one percent. Against FPGA-based spiking neural networks, the quantised model reaches about ninety-two percent accuracy, beating them by nineteen percent. The paper also reports the first hardware-accelerated SSC evaluation and first end-to-end FPGA event-audio keyword spotting. That system reaches ninety-five percent word-end detection accuracy.
arxiv-2602-16542:
A large team led by J. W. D. Halliday reports a laboratory measurement of collective behavior in a relativistic electron-positron pair plasma. On CERN's Fireball platform at the HiRadMat facility, high-energy protons generated an ultra-relativistic, charge-neutral pair beam that passed through an ambient discharge plasma. A sensitive Faraday-rotation probe measured magnetic-field growth from a beam-plasma instability, with careful checks on the probe's response.

The measured path-integrated magnetic field matches particle-in-cell simulation predictions in quantitative terms. The result gives a firm benchmark for models of relativistic beam-plasma interaction in space settings such as blazar jets and pulsar-wind nebulae. Readers in plasma and high-energy astrophysics get rare lab evidence for processes usually seen only in distant cosmic sources.
arxiv-2602-16642:
Jim Zhao and co-authors show that optimizer choice shapes Neural Collapse, the highly symmetric geometry that appears in deep nets late in training. Past theory largely ignored the optimizer, hinting the effect was universal. The authors challenge that view. Neural Collapse scores are hard to track in theory, so they bring in a new diagnostic, NC0, whose fall to zero is needed for collapse.

With NC0, they give theory that collapse cannot arise under decoupled weight decay in adaptive optimizers as in AdamW. Stochastic gradient descent, SignGD with coupled decay, and SignGD with decoupled decay show plainly varied NC0 paths. Momentum is also shown to speed collapse under SGD, a first result of its kind. Deep learning theorists get proof that training rules, not just data, drive collapse.
arxiv-2602-16942:
Hexi Jin and co-authors present SourceBench, a benchmark for the quality of web sources cited by AI answers. Language models increasingly answer queries by citing web sources, yet existing evaluations stress answer correctness over evidence quality. SourceBench measures cited source quality across one hundred real-world queries spanning informational, factual, argumentative, social, and shopping intents.

An eight-metric frame covers content quality, relevance, factual accuracy, and objectivity, plus page-level signals such as freshness, authority, accountability, and clarity. It includes a human-labeled dataset with a calibrated language-model-based evaluator matching expert judgments closely. Eight language models, Google Search, and three AI search tools are tested over nearly four thousand cited sources, yielding four key insights to guide future research in generative AI and web search.
arxiv-2602-17342:
Luzhi Wang led a six-author team lifting graph out-of-distribution detection at test time. Such checks flag test graphs that deviate from the training mix, a safeguard for graph neural networks deployed in open-world settings. Recent test-time training methods avoid supervisory data but run one-pass inference, so they cannot progressively correct errors to amplify out-of-distribution signals. The paper proposes SIGOOD, an unsupervised framework joining continuous self-learning with test-time training.

SIGOOD generates a prompt to build a prompt-enhanced graph that amplifies potential OOD cues. An Energy Preference Optimization loss tunes the prompt using energy variations between the original and boosted graphs, and iterative tuning folds the prompt into the detection model in a self-lifting loop. The final boosted graph drives the verdict. Evaluations on twenty-one real-world datasets confirm the method's effectiveness and outperformance.
arxiv-2602-17442:
Marco Avolio led a twelve-author team presenting WarpRec, a framework for recommender systems that unites academic rigor with industrial scale. Progress in the field is blocked by a fractured scene, where researchers must choose between in-memory experiments and costly rewriting for industrial engines at scale. WarpRec removes that trade-off with a backend-free architecture holding over fifty top algorithms, forty metrics, and nineteen filtering and splitting plans, moving from local runs to scale training and tuning.

The system tracks eco responsibility by using CodeCarbon for live energy tracking, showing that scale need not cost science integrity or green goals. WarpRec also looks ahead to agentic AI, leading ranking engines from static ones toward interactive tools inside the generative AI world. In short, it bridges schools and industry and can serve as the backbone for the next generation of sustainable, agent-ready ranking engines. Code is available.
arxiv-2602-17542:
Zhangqi Duan led a four-author team behind a 2026 arXiv paper on grading student code by single skill. Fine-grained skill units, called knowledge components, anchor much of student modeling. Yet labels for whether each skill was used correctly are scarce, above all for open-ended programming, where one solution draws on several skills. Copying a whole-problem verdict onto every skill hides partial mastery and bends learning curves out of shape.

The team proposes a framework that uses large language models to label knowledge component correctness from student-written code, judging whether each skill was applied correctly. A context-aware mapping step ties each skill to the code, sharpening the alignment between skill and evidence. Judged by learning curve fit and prediction quality, the new labels fit cognitive theory better and predict better than baselines. Human checks add weight, showing agreement between model labels and expert judgment.
arxiv-2602-17642:
Dhruv Talwar and team present A.R.I.S., a low-cost, portable sorter for shredded electronic waste. Standard e-waste recycling loses much value because material separation and identification fall short, limiting recovery. The system aims to close that gap with deep learning plus established sorting methods.

A YOLOx model classifies metals, plastics and circuit boards in real time, with low latency and high detection accuracy. Evaluation reports strong overall precision, mean average precision and sortation purity, all at high levels. Better sorting lifts material recovery and lowers barriers to advanced recycling. The work supports longer product life cycles, trade-in and recycling programs, and lower environmental impact across the supply chain.
arxiv-2602-17942:
Marco Carmosino and team advance gate elimination, the only known method for complexity lower bounds for explicit functions against Boolean circuits. They formalize circuit simplification as a convergent term graph rewriting system, and give a constructive proof of a classical lower bound with it.

First, circuit simplification is a convergent system over DeMorgan and AND-OR-XOR bases, with local rules from Boolean identities, so every trimming sequence ends in an identical result. Convergence lets researchers reason about trimmed circuits regardless of order. No similar convergent formalization exists over the U2 and B2 bases. Then they use the system for a constructive bound stretching Schnorr's result that XOR needs three times n minus one gates in the DeMorgan basis. A constructive bound supplies a refuter algorithm that efficiently finds counter-cases for every circuit for the function. Until this work, no constructive bound had been proved via gate elimination.
arxiv-2602-18042:
Karkulali Pugalenthi and team present PINEAPPLE, a framework for reading internal battery values harmlessly. Exact, real-time, non-destructive tracking of internal states in lithium-ion batteries aids early degradation spotting, better use, and longer life. PINEAPPLE joins physics-based neural networks with an evolutionary search algorithm, for rapid, scalable, and interpretable parameter inference.

A meta-learned network predicts unseen electrode behavior from basic physics. Its test errors fall below one tenth of one percent, at roughly ten times standard solver speed. From voltage-time discharge curves alone, across several CALCE batteries, it tracks key internal values such as lithium-ion diffusion coefficients over usage cycles. Those trends agree across the set without any custom wear heuristic, showing physics steadying the fit. The result points toward real-time, physics-based pictures of spread within and between cells, for cell-scale state-of-health diagnostics in future battery management systems.
arxiv-2602-18242:
Craig Alexander and two co-authors reflect on how statistics teaching must keep up with fast-moving technology. Their 2026 paper argues that students need workplace-ready skills, so teachers should weave current tools into the curriculum wherever they fit. University statistics has already shifted heavily, with statistical programming now central and R widely used alongside growing Python.

Coding habits, database handling, and machine learning now appear in some programs. The authors expect artificial intelligence to press harder next, above all the teaching questions raised by generative tools like ChatGPT. The article surveys these shifts and lays out strategies for folding them into modern statistics courses. It speaks to teachers weighing what to adopt, what to drop, and how to keep the subject honest in an AI era.
arxiv-2602-18942:
Ecologists have long equated persistence with stability at a fixed equilibrium point. Cagatay Eskin, with two co-authors, argues in 2026 that the real threat may be different. The stable equilibrium itself can escape to a negative orthant, where abundances cannot live. Fluctuations in species interactions do not merely disturb abundances around an equilibrium. They can displace the equilibrium point itself.

Theory shows that even tiny, light-tailed fluctuations lead to a heavy-tailed power law for equilibrium abundance. Remarkably, the exponent takes a universal value, independent of species, community size, and interaction structure. Empirical analysis of thirty-four species finds a power law signal for many, with a higher median exponent. A formula for critical noise shows larger communities are much more fragile when noise threatens feasibility. Metrics for global and species-specific escape rates predict fragility in dynamic simulations of nearly a hundred real networks.
arxiv-2602-19042:
Quantum memory needs protection, but combining two shields can backfire. Victor Kasatkin, with three co-authors, asks in 2026 whether quantum error correction and dynamical decoupling help each other or clash. Physical decoupling can fight the encoded subspace. Correction also depends on errors that survive decoding, not just those decoupling removes.

The authors study a hybrid cycle. Logical decoupling runs first, using normalizer elements of a stabilizer code. A round of syndrome measurement and recovery follows. Closed-form fidelity formulas cover correction-only, detection-only, decoupling-only, physical decoupling, and the hybrid. A small set of code-dependent polynomials makes the decoder role explicit. For ideal recovery, the hybrid wins exactly when uncorrectable errors cluster in the suppressed sector. A simple design rule guarantees an edge at low noise. Tests on the Steane code and a larger code map where the hybrid pays off.
arxiv-2602-19142:
Learned optimizers promise much but generalise poorly. Abhinav Moudgil, with two co-authors, makes them practical in 2026 with Celo2. Hand-designed rules like Adam still dominate. Learned alternatives often fail beyond their training distribution and cost dearly to meta-train. One prior system burned enormous compute yet stalled below six hundred million parameters.

A simple normalised architecture plus augmented meta-training changes the picture. A performant general-purpose learned rule emerges from a tiny fraction of that compute, in just hours. It scales stably to a billion-scale pretraining task, vastly larger than its meta-training distribution. Strong performance holds across diverse out-of-distribution tasks. Compatibility covers modern harnesses, including orthogonalisation, distinct input-output and hidden rules, and decoupled weight decay. Learnable optimisation thus becomes practically explorable.
arxiv-2602-19342:
André Leroy and Huda Merdach describe the basic structure of multivariable Ore extensions, algebraic objects introduced by Martínez-Peñas and Kschischang. These extensions generalize polynomial rings by letting variables interact with coefficients through twisted rules, and they arise in coding and related areas. The paper sets out their structure in a self-contained way, so readers can see how the pieces fit.

Central to the account are pseudo multilinear transformations, which correspond to modules over the extension ring. These maps tie closely to evaluating polynomials in the ring, and a general product formula is obtained. They also help organize the roots of a polynomial in the extension, giving structure to a root set that would otherwise look scattered.
arxiv-2602-19542:
Text-guided 3D editing should change one part of a 3D asset from a natural-language instruction while leaving the rest intact. Yankuan Chi and three co-authors note that current methods struggle to understand complex prompts jointly, localize edits in 3D automatically, and preserve unedited content. Their framework, Vinedresser3D, works inside a native 3D generative model's latent space.

Given an asset and a prompt, a multimodal large language model infers rich descriptions of the original. It identifies the edit region and type (addition, modification, deletion), and generates decomposed structural and appearance guidance. The agent picks an informative view, then applies an image editing model for visual guidance. It then runs an inversion-based rectified-flow inpainting pipeline using interleaved sampling to perform the edit in 3D latent space.
arxiv-2602-19742:
Spotting wildfires early needs drones that gather data fast and processing close to the action, but route plans, fleet size, and edge computing all pull against each other. A 2026 arXiv paper by Yulun Huang and two co-authors proposes one framework that plans all three together for wildfire monitoring.

The design weights patrol clustering by fire history so risky areas get priority. It assigns edge tasks by balancing distance against computing load. It tunes routes and fleet size jointly, with a rerouting mechanism for emergencies. Tests report large cuts in average response time, energy use, and fleet size against standard baselines. The emergency mechanism answers well inside its deadline, with little effect on routine patrols.
arxiv-2602-20042:
Alignment work has improved average helpfulness and safety, but it still rewards confident single-turn answers and hides failures at the margins. A 2026 arXiv paper by Han Bao and seven co-authors argues, as a position paper, that alignment must take edge cases seriously.

Models do fail on edge cases. Worse, current evaluation hides many of those failures from view. Scalar rewards flatten diverse values into one number. Data and evaluation setups collapse, filter, or miss the hardest cases. Governance often lacks ways to adjudicate contested cases. The result is value flattening, representation loss, and uncertainty blindness. The authors call Edge alignment a detection, evaluation, and governance agenda. It surfaces such failures and links them to interventions. A pilot diagnostic set of edge cases across several contemporary models shows ordinary helpfulness and safety readings missing process failures that edge-aware evaluation exposes.
arxiv-2602-20342:
Christos Maikos and two co-authors build an end-to-end pipeline turning drone video into photorealistic outdoor 3D scenes with minimal delay. Drones already serve real-time aerial perception, and 3D Gaussian Splatting has shown strong potential for real-time neural rendering. Yet the two had rarely been combined into a complete UAV reconstruction and visualization system. The new architecture joins live video acquisition, sensor fusion, camera pose estimation, and splatting optimization.

Continuous model updates and low-latency deployment support immersive augmented and virtual reality viewing. Experiments show competitive visual fidelity with much higher rendering performance and far lower end-to-end latency than NeRF-based approaches. Reconstruction quality stays within four to seven percent of high-fidelity offline references. The system thus suits real-time, scalable aerial perception where waiting for offline processing is not an option.
arxiv-2602-20442:
Electronic health records promise much for medicine, but they are sparse and often incomplete, and most imputation methods handle only known unknowns, such as missing lab values. Jun Han and five co-authors tackle unknown unknowns: cases where it is unclear anything is missing at all. A missing diagnosis code, for instance, may mean the patient lacks the condition or that a provider made the diagnosis but never shared it.

The authors build a general-purpose denoising algorithm for binary health records, using a transformer-based denoising neural network whose output is thresholded adaptively to recover values predicted missing. On a real health-record dataset, it denoises medical codes more accurately than existing imputation approaches and improves downstream tasks. Applied to predicting hospital readmission, it beats all existing baselines by a statistically significant margin.
arxiv-2602-20742:
Pat Lank, the sole author, studies t-structures on Noetherian algebraic spaces that admit dualizing complexes. The work focuses on how they behave in the étale topology, asking how such structures pass to local maps and what survives the passage.

As a result, the paper lists all tensor ones on the bounded derived category of coherent sheaves. That list links local and global pictures, giving a full account of tensor-compatible structures in this setting. Readers get a complete map of these structures for spaces with dualizing complexes, stated in terms of the derived category.
arxiv-2602-20942:
Relativistic fluids threaded by magnetic fields behave very differently from ordinary fluids, and their equations are usually derived case by case. Khwahish Kushwah and Gabriel Denicol derive relativistic dissipative magnetohydrodynamics from the Boltzmann equation in this 2026 arXiv paper, using the method of moments. Their system is locally neutral, built from two oppositely charged species with no magnetization or polarization.

In a magnetic field, the shear stress tensor no longer obeys one equation: it splits into three distinct components, each with its own dynamics. In a Bjorken flow test, strong magnetic fields produce oscillations that an Israel-Stewart-like theory cannot capture. Readers get a first-principles fluid theory that shows where simpler models break down.
arxiv-2602-21142:
Scan readers read chest X-rays over time, tracking shifts that matter for finding and outlook, but manual over-time review is slow. Zhifan Jiang and nine co-authors build a training setup for that task in this 2026 arXiv paper: LUMEN, an over-time multi-modal X-ray model. Multi-image and multi-task prompt tuning targets outlook and finding scores at once.

Trials on public chest X-ray data and a linked visual Q&A set show clear gains over base cases on finding questions, with hopeful outlook skill. A new prompt set with over-time studies backs an outlook Q&A task. The work shows well-built prompt tuning can make vision-language models useful in clinics for time-based X-ray work.
arxiv-2602-21442:
Jesse He and six co-authors introduce MINAR, a toolbox for mechanistic interpretability in neural algorithmic reasoning. That young field studies how graph neural networks emulate classical algorithms like Bellman-Ford, a match called algorithmic alignment. Meanwhile, mechanistic interpretability seeks the small circuits inside models that perform specific computations.

MINAR adapts attribution patching methods from language-model interpretability to the graph-network setting for efficient circuit discovery. Two case studies show it recovers faithful neuron-level circuits from networks trained on algorithmic tasks. The study also shows how circuits form and prune during training, and how networks trained on several tasks at once reuse circuit parts for related tasks. Code is public.
arxiv-2602-21842:
Surojit Ghosh applies RO(G)-graded Bredon cohomology to mass assignment problems, extending classical mass partition methods. Within this setup, he reproves a recent result of Lessure and Soberón from earlier work. For n plus 1 given mass assignments on k-dimensional affine subspaces of n-dimensional space, there exists a k-subspace containing a sphere that simultaneously bisects all measures.

The Bredon cohomology setup thus recovers the old-style bisection result through new topological tools, and its flexibility suggests further mass partition problems may yield to the same new approach.
arxiv-2602-22142:
Video language models handle clips well, but live streams break them: frames arrive one by one, and the future is not yet visible. Yulin Zhang and two co-authors diagnose a core flaw they call time-agnosticism, treating video as an unordered bag of evidence. That flaw yields two failures: muddled chronological order, and blindness to what is present versus what is history.

Their framework, WeaveTime, first teaches order and then uses it, adding a lightweight temporal reconstruction objective that builds order-aware representations with minimal extra tuning. The approach is simple, efficient, and model-agnostic, fitting streams where order is the whole game. For builders of live video AI, it offers a principled fix for models that forget time.
arxiv-2602-22242:
Language models are now embedded in real systems, where prompt-injection and jailbreak attacks can hijack their behavior. Piyush Jaiswal and four co-authors evaluate that vulnerability across several open-source models, using a large manually curated attack dataset. They also test lightweight inference-time defenses that filter attacks without retraining or heavy fine-tuning.

Models vary widely in behavior, from refusals to complete silent non-responsiveness triggered by internal safety mechanisms. The lightweight defenses blunt straightforward attacks, the authors find, but longer attacks consistently slip past them. The study gives deployers a sober map of which defenses hold and where they fail.
arxiv-2602-22342:
Can any well-behaved random vector be built as a sum of a universal number of standard Gaussian vectors? Antoine Song proves that question, Talagrand's convexity problem, is equivalent to the subgaussian vector problem. Using elementary arguments, he settles it for one-dimensional subgaussian variables and for vectors with good norm and covariance bounds.

Those results already confirm the permutation-invariant case of the convexity problem, and yield optimal estimates for the largest ellipsoid inside a sum of large sets in Gaussian spaces. Song also proposes a Riemannian version for spaces with nonnegative Ricci curvature. The paper thus turns a convexity puzzle into a concrete vector problem, and solves its first major cases.
arxiv-2602-22442:
Agent-based AutoML systems make multi-stage choices across data processing, model choice, and scoring, but scoring usually judges only final results. Gaoyuan Du and three co-authors survey prior systems and find none report structured, choice-level metrics for post-hoc review of in-between choices. They propose an Evaluation Agent that watches choices without getting in the way.

The watcher agent scores in-between choices on four fronts: validity, reasoning consistency, model-quality risks beyond accuracy, and counterfactual impact. Across four proof-of-concept trials, it spots faulty choices with a high F1 score and flags reasoning gaps. AutoML builders gain a way to audit the trip, not just the arrival.
arxiv-2602-22542:
Timothy Bickmore and two co-authors test a strange idea: a robot that lives in the refrigerator and talks people toward healthier snacks. Kitchens are where food choices happen, yet appliances have rarely been used as health coaches. The team frames such devices as relational appliances, everyday machines that act as social partners through steady, personal contact.

In a home-lab apartment, volunteers fetched snacks during fake TV commercial breaks while chatting with a human-sized robotic head inside the fridge. Half heard healthy snack tips; half got plain social chat. People found the robot persuasive, engaging, and more natural over time, often calling it helpful and companionable. Most said they noticed their snack choices more and would welcome such a robot at home.
arxiv-2602-22642:
Qin-Wen Luo and six co-authors tame a failure mode in efficient reasoning. Chain-of-thought prompting strengthens language models, but long explicit reasoning is slow and costly. Compression methods that reward brevity often trigger rapid entropy collapse, shrinking exploration too early and hiding valid reasoning paths, especially for hard questions.

Their method, CEEH, compresses easy questions while letting hard ones explore. It judges instance difficulty on the fly, preserving a diverse search space where questions are currently hard and allowing aggressive shortening where paths are well established. A dynamic length penalty anchored to the shortest past correct response counters length inflation and steadies rewards. Across six reasoning benchmarks, CEEH shortened answers while holding accuracy and beating length-only optimization on pass rates.
arxiv-2602-22742:
Akihisa Watanabe and three co-authors give animators exact spatial control over generated human motion without retraining. Past methods need task-specific training or slow optimization, and hard constraints often wreck naturalness. Noting that many animation tasks form a linear inverse problem, the team built ProjFlow, a training-free sampler.

A kinematics-aware metric encodes skeletal topology, so corrections spread coherently across the whole skeleton instead of warping single joints. For sparse inputs like long gaps between keyframes, a time-varying form uses pseudo-observations that fade during sampling. Tests on motion inpainting and 2D-to-3D lifting show exact constraint satisfaction with realism matching or beating zero-shot rivals, rivalling trained controllers.
arxiv-2602-22942:
Hongchao Du and six co-authors rethink phone-native agent systems. Phones combine tight running limits, splintered control panels, and fast-changing app states, a harsher home than cloud or desktop for action-aimed agents. As language models shift from chat to action, reliable phone self-rule demands a rethink of how thinking and control compose.

ClawMobile splits high-level language thinking from ordered, fixed control pathways in a layered design, lifting running steadiness and reruns on real devices. As a case study, it distils rules for mobile language-model engines and names key hurdles in speed, flex, and steadiness. The lesson is careful teamwork between chance-based planning and fixed system panels, with open-source build to seed further work.
arxiv-2602-23142:
Zeno Romero and three co-authors guess spread values in mixes with tensor filling. Guessing spread values matters widely, yet lab data remain scarce, and machine learning offers hopeful options to semi-lab models. Matrix filling methods work well for heat properties, including spread values in binary mixes, but are limited to single-heat guesses, with scores resting on high-quality lab data supply.

The team offers a tensor filling method for heat-dependent spread values at endless thinness in binary mixes, using a Tucker split trained on lab data. SEGWE predictions act as prior knowledge in a Bayes setup, and the method extends in a line to any heat between 268 and 378 kelvin with improved scores. The database was grown by active learning picks and pulsed gradient NMR readings, with spread values in 19 systems measured at 298, 313, and 333 kelvin. Adding these results yields a gain in scores.
arxiv-2602-23242:
Yegon Kim and one co-author introduce AIQI, the first model-free universal agent proven asymptotically epsilon-optimal in general reinforcement learning. Established optimal agents, including AIXI, are model-based: they explicitly maintain and use models of the environment. AIQI instead performs universal induction over distributional action-value functions, rather than over policies or environments as prior work does.

Under a grain-of-truth condition, the authors prove AIQI is strongly asymptotically epsilon-optimal and asymptotically epsilon-Bayes-optimal. They also apply their new proof techniques to show asymptotic epsilon-optimality for Self-AIXI without ad-hoc assumptions. The results widen the known family of universal agents, showing that model-free methods can reach the same strong optimality guarantees long associated with model-based designs.
arxiv-2602-23342:
Weijian Chen and five co-authors present AlayaLaser, an on-disk graph index system for large-scale, high-dimensional vector similarity search. Such search is essential for big vector retrieval, yet on-disk graph systems are widely seen as limited by I/O costs. The authors find the opposite as dimensionality rises into the hundreds or thousands: performance becomes compute-bound, not I/O-bound.

That insight opens a neglected optimization space, since existing on-disk systems target I/O reduction and largely ignore compute overhead. AlayaLaser starts from a roofline-model analysis, then introduces a novel on-disk data layout that eases the compute bound by exploiting SIMD instructions on modern CPUs. Added techniques include a degree-based node cache, cluster-based entry point selection, and early dispatch. Tests across many large high-dimensional data sets show AlayaLaser beating on-disk rivals and matching or beating in-memory systems.
arxiv-2602-23542:
Harufumi Tsuchiya models secondary cosmic rays in sky electric fields to explain long-lasting gamma-ray bursts from storm clouds. Using the PHITS particle transport code with true-to-life spectra of gamma rays, electrons, positrons, and muons, the study pins down what field region can speed up matter to seen energies.

Gamma rays supply the main seed particles for long bursts no matter the field shape or strength. The runs reveal the field structure and strength needed to produce gamma rays above several tens of MeV, so far seen only from high sites. Matching estimated burst fluxes with measured fluxes, including readings at Yangbajing at four point three km height, narrows the possible range of field strengths and setups.
arxiv-2602-24242:
Takato Yoshimura and three co-authors derive the exact distribution of typical spin-current fluctuations in the quantum XXZ spin chain, in the easy-axis anisotropy regime. The 2026 paper uses ballistic macroscopic fluctuation theory to tackle a hydrodynamic problem.

The resulting nested Gaussian distribution is fully characterized by its variance, which the authors relate analytically to the spin diffusion constant and the static spin susceptibility. They check it against numerical simulations. The same mechanism that produces anomalous charge current fluctuations in single-file systems appears in the XXZ chain. That link establishes a universal hydrodynamic origin for the observed anomalies. The result connects quantum spin transport to a broader class of anomalous fluctuation phenomena. In short, one rule links two worlds. The link is deep. The link holds.
arxiv-2603-00142: Kostka and Chudziak study how Theory of Mind and internal beliefs shape teamwork in LLM-based multi-agent systems. Simply adding Theory of Mind or belief machinery does not automatically improve coordination, and performance across such worlds varies wildly. The authors build an architecture joining Theory of Mind, BDI-style beliefs and symbolic solvers that check logic. Tested on a resource-allocation problem across various language models, it reveals an intricate interplay between model capability, cognitive machinery and performance.
arxiv-2603-00342: Fu, Wang, and Chandrasekaran examine why scoring the worth of each training sample clashes with strict privacy rules. Privacy rules demand that one record barely move the result, yet value scores exist to measure one record's pull. Simple privacy fixes thus blur the fine gaps that rank samples, most of all for rare cases. The team maps which shared building blocks cause this clash, sets out design rules for gentler methods, and measures how privacy erodes ranking quality across methods and data sets.
arxiv-2603-00442: Ishii, Sasabe, and Yamasaki show altermagnetic X-ray magnetic circular dichroism in hematite, a compensated collinear magnet with no net magnetism that still breaks time reversal symmetry. A symmetry chosen setup places X-ray travel at right angles to the weak ferromagnetic moment, leaving a signal no plain weak ferromagnetism can explain. Distinct states switch back and forth under an in plane field. Theory traces the signal to an anisotropic dipole in excited states, making dichroism a direct probe of that order.
arxiv-2603-00742: Dragutinović, Zhang, and Ranganath probe a downside of the Muon optimizer, whose speed comes at the cost of gradient descent's simplicity bias. Theory on deep linear networks and linear attention shows Muon dodges saddle points but sacrifices the sequential growth of solution complexity that marks gradient descent learning. Experiments show Muon struggles to find shared structure across tasks and may fit spurious features instead. Faster optimisation, the paper warns, is rarely free: gains can reshape the inductive biases that govern generalisation.
arxiv-2603-00842: Zhang and twelve colleagues introduce MedGPT-oss, an open weight 20B parameter generalist vision language model for biomedicine, closing a deployment gap. Top systems are closed or too costly to run, blocking on premises use for patient privacy. MedGPT-oss pairs the GPT-oss language backbone with a front end via three stage training, bridging the capacity gap. It beats bigger open medical models on out of distribution multimodal reasoning and text only clinical tasks on commodity GPUs. The team releases its training recipe, open weight checkpoints, and evaluation harness.
arxiv-2603-01042: Lin and five colleagues bridge language models and time series with Thoth, the first family of mid-trained models for general time-series understanding. Mid-training aligns time series with language in a task-agnostic way. It is powered by Book-of-Thoth, a corpus supporting generation in both directions between time series and text. A new KnoTS benchmark tests combined reasoning about time patterns and field knowledge, and Thoth beats its base model and advanced rivals, even when fine-tuning data is scarce.
arxiv-2603-01142: Wang and six colleagues generate articulated 3D assets directly from complete meshes with ArtLLM, a 3D language model trained on a large articulation dataset. The dataset mixes curated and procedurally made objects. ArtLLM autoregressively decides how many parts and joints to predict, inferring kinematic structure from point clouds, then conditions a generative model to synthesize detailed part shapes. On PartNet-Mobility it beats leading methods on layout and joint prediction, generalizes to real objects, and helps build digital twins for robot learning.
arxiv-2603-01642:
Katarina Karlova and Jozef Strecka map the states of a quantum magnet on a decorated honeycomb lattice in this 2026 work. The lattice mixes paired spins and lone spins on a warped honeycomb frame, all pulling against each other. Such clashes can breed odd quantum phases that plain magnets never show.

The pair combine four tools: large-scale numeric methods, exact checks on small cases, and a gas-like model. Their map shows many phases, from ferrimagnetic and spin-canted states to mixed dimer and tetramer patterns. Flat steps in magnetization appear at zero and at quarter, half, and three-quarter levels of full strength. Heat slowly smears those steps, while the gas-like model still tracks the cold behavior well. The map guides hunts for real materials with like traits.
arxiv-2603-01742:
Yi-Nan Wang, Wenbin Yan, and Peihe Yang study the Higgs branch of four-dimensional superconformal field theories. Their 2026 work builds those theories by geometric engineering, placing type IIB string theory on singular threefold spaces. The Higgs branch records one family of vacuum states, and a linked algebra encodes its protected data.

For terminal singularities, they explain how to derive the Higgs branch from a small resolution of the space. Cases with compact four-cycles in the resolution get several computation methods. A symplectic duality argument yields first examples whose Higgs branches are E-type Kleinian singularities. The linked algebras are conjectured to be affine E-type W-algebras, with many new cases lacking known descriptions. Index calculations and quiver predictions round out the picture for two named families.
arxiv-2603-01942:
Huw Day, Adrianna Jezierska, and Jessica Woodgate reframe jailbreaking chatbots as a peaceful way to defuse online conflict. Their 2026 work studies social media, where language-model bots now steer political talk at scale and stir escalation. Most research backs platform moderation as the main counterweight to that manipulation.

The authors propose a user-centric view instead, centered on ordinary people who engage suspected bot accounts. By prompting around model safeguards, users can expose automated behavior in public view. That exposure disrupts the spread of misleading narratives without threats or abuse. Jailbreaking here is presented as an emergent, non-violent de-escalation practice, not as an attack. The lens shifts defense from platform control rooms to the everyday tactics of users themselves.
arxiv-2603-02142:
Kwame Mbobda-Kuate and Gabriel Kasmi question a common belief in this 2026 vision paper: bigger models are not always better. They test small object finding under tight limits on power and data. Their case is rooftop solar panels in Madagascar, seen from above. They vary model size, data size, and image detail across many setups.

Judged by score per unit of model size, the smallest model won by a wide margin. That tiny model also earned the highest raw score of all. Sharper images helped far more than extra training data. In fact, small models with sharp images beat all rivals in both speed and score. For scarce-data field work, the lesson is to spend on image detail first.
arxiv-2603-02342:
Daniel Humphrey, Cristian Vega, Stanislav Boldyrev, and Vadim Roytershteyn study particle angles in turbulent plasma in this 2026 paper. Jets and nebulae shine by synchrotron light, which depends on electron energies and angles. Relativistic turbulence speeds electrons up well in these magnetized flows. Energy spectra are now fairly well mapped by simulations, but angle patterns are not.

The pitch angle describes the tilt of an electron's path against the field. The team runs a detailed case with a strong steady field and high magnetization. Even tiny numerical noise scatters pitch angles a lot, they find. They show methods to tame that noise and track very small angles faithfully. Final angle patterns match an earlier phenomenological model. Better angle data sharpens how astronomers read synchrotron spectra.
arxiv-2603-02642:
Jiawei Wang, Arshiya Taj Abdul, and Evangelos Theodorou speed up safe path planning for machines that face uncertainty. Their 2026 framework, cuNRTO, computes control plans that respect limits under any bounded disturbance. The catch is cost: the safety math creates huge cone-shaped constraint problems that solve slowly.

The team built two designs that run these problems on graphics processors. One splits the work with the Douglas-Rachford method, the other with a tailored alternating-direction method. Custom chip code handles the repeated projection and matrix steps in parallel. Tests on a wheeled robot model, a quadcopter, and a robot arm reached speedups up to about one hundred forty times. Faster safety checks make robust planning far more practical.
arxiv-2603-02842:
Rosanna Milner, Michael Foster, Twin Karmakharm, and colleagues built a browser tool that helps journalists check suspect content fast. Their 2026 paper presents the Verification Assistant, part of a widely used plugin with well over one hundred thousand users. Fact-checkers face floods of false and AI-made media, yet expert detection models often sit outside their daily tools.

A user pastes a link or uploads a file, and the assistant pulls the content and routes it to a suite of language classifiers. It returns clear signals about credibility, persuasion tricks, and possible machine generation, plus practical next steps. By packaging many models in one plain interface, the tool brings research-grade checks into everyday newsroom work.
arxiv-2603-02942:
Juan Manuel Pacheco-Arias, Philippe Amram, Benoît Epinat, and Wilfried Mercier draw the first maps of how spin is spread inside spiral galaxies. A galaxy's specific angular momentum measures how much rotation each unit of star mass carries. Its map across the disk had never been analyzed before this 2026 study.

Combining infrared brightness maps with gas velocity fields and rotation curves, they built spin density maps for thirty nearby spiral and irregular galaxies. Standard shape measures, plus two new scores for disk likeness and paired structure, sorted the galaxies into five classes named for rings, spirals, bars, clumps, or irregular patterns. For nearly half, the spin class disagreed with the visible shape class. Spin also tracked galaxy mass and star formation as expected.
arxiv-2603-03242:
Patrick Gerard and Svitlana Volkova align language models to online communities by reading what those communities already accept. Standard alignment needs explicit preference labels or fixed principles, which most communities cannot supply, especially around sensitive topics. Yet members constantly signal taste by engaging with some posts and letting others die.

The authors show accepted replies cluster in dense, coherent regions of the model's representation space, while rejected ones scatter. Their method, DGRO, turns that local density into a training signal with no preference labels at all. Recovery tests confirm density mirrors real pairwise judgments. Across platforms, topics, and languages, DGRO-aligned models produced replies that human annotators, experts, and model judges preferred over baselines.
arxiv-2603-03542:
ChunJun Cao and Brad Lackey design quantum error-correcting codes by gluing small ones together, like Lego. Transversal gates, applied qubit-by-qubit across a code, are the simplest fault-tolerant operations, yet codes supporting useful ones, especially non-Clifford or individually addressable gates, are hard to build with standard methods. Their 2026 paper uses the quantum lego framework, where such gates appear naturally as symmetries of the pieces.

Small codes carrying desirable symmetries are glued into larger ones, and operator-flow rules track how the logical symmetries survive the gluing. The method systematically builds codes with addressable transversal gates aimed at specific logical qubits, Clifford or not. New finite-rate families support several prized gates at once. Holographic and fractal-like codes gain addressable gates within and between blocks, and a holographic black-hole-inspired code inherits fully addressable controlled gates as a corollary.
arxiv-2603-04142: Gabrielli and others present a multi-agent method for time series. Their system Vivaldi explains physiological time series, tested in a pilot with experts because regulation bars deployment. Experiments show agentic pipelines help non-thinking and medically fine-tuned models. For thinking models, orchestration worsens explanations, including a 14-point relevance drop, while improving sharpness.
arxiv-2603-04342: Bommireddy and colleagues hunt optical light from gravitational wave mergers with public alerts. Zwicky Transient Facility alerts flow through the ALeRCE broker for LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA O4a and O4b. The pipeline queries alerts in sky regions, then classifies, matches host galaxies, and cuts by time within 200 days after merger. It finds one O4a candidate and four O4b candidates, several like supernovae or tidal disruption events. One proves to be a Bowen flare in a discarded active galactic nucleus, showing brokers can ground systematic searches.
arxiv-2603-04442: Mohsin and colleagues propose an AI mesh for green wireless networks. Macro cells waste most power on empty areas, below 5 percent efficiency. Hajj crowds need about 7,000 diesel towers yearly, yet fail near 40 percent at peak. Their mesh puts low power nodes near users, reuses spectrum across zones, and forecasts traffic seconds ahead to cut congestion. Evaluations show far better energy delivery, much lower cost, and solar power ending diesel use.
arxiv-2603-04542: Omer Katz presents Beyond21, an open source package for cosmic dawn and reionization. Observations of early galaxies improve steadily, needing consistent interpretation across probes. Beyond21 implements flexible Pop II and Pop III star formation recipes, computing radiation backgrounds and intergalactic medium effects in one self consistent pipeline. It predicts ionization history, UV luminosity functions, the global 21-cm signal, and cosmic X-ray background contribution. A full run takes about 0.1 seconds on one core, opening wide parameter searches. A millicharged dark matter example shows baryon cooling through elastic interactions.
arxiv-2603-04742: Gao and colleagues present the first framework joining HE with sparse matrix-vector math. SpMV drives lab work and machine learning, yet privacy matters when data are private. HE enables math on locked data, but its use for SpMV stayed open. The paper adds Compressed Sparse Sorted Column, a compressed matrix format designed for locked sparse matrix math. By keeping gaps and fast locked text packing, CSSC cuts storage and compute cost sharply. Tests on real-world data show big gains in run time and memory use, aiding shared learning.
arxiv-2603-04942: Ian Gabalski and team present a fast algorithm for particle coincidence finding in a TimePix3 speed map imaging instrument. The TimePix3 camera localizes many simultaneous hits in space and time, but its sparse stream makes grouping pixels into hits hard. Their centroiding method exploits data thinness to localize hits within a single pixel, and it runs on a GPU. Processing runs about 25 times faster than acquisition at 1 kHz, and the detector beats delay-line anode detectors at separating simultaneous hits.
arxiv-2603-05042: Zhaonian Kuang and team revisit multi-camera 3D object finding, where models struggle on unseen platforms with new camera setups. Meta-camera ways unify form but ignore spatial prior discrepancies like intrinsics, extrinsics, and array layouts. CoIn3D folds all spatial priors into embedding and observation via spatial-aware modulation and camera-aware augmentation. Spatial-aware modulation integrates ground depth, ground gradient, focal length, and Plücker coordinate; camera-aware augmentation uses novel-view synthesis. Tests show cross-setup results on NuScenes, Waymo, and Lyft across BEVDepth, BEVFormer, and PETR.
arxiv-2603-05242: Jakub Holobrádek and team use focused ion beam irradiation to transform metastable iron-nickel thin films on copper substrates. The films start paramagnetic and face-centered-cubic, and the beam turns them ferromagnetic and body-centered-cubic. The beam scanning plan controls the easy-axis, and it yields eight domains with distinct traits. Local orientations from electron backscatter diffraction, set next to local magnetometry, show anisotropy follows residual lattice strain after the shape change. The results open a way to pattern high-quality nanostructures with precise magnetization landscapes.
arxiv-2603-05342: F. Robinet and team present SVOM Microchannel X-ray Telescope on-board studies. The telescope detects and localizes burst X-ray afterglows. One year after launch, it reviews 15 afterglows detected between October 2024 and August 2025. Localization uncertainty stays below 2 arcmin for bursts. Positions sit 40 arcsec from better-detail tests on average. On-board analysis gives a precise location only seconds after observation begins. An lean antenna network quickly collects and disseminates this information, key for SVOM's multi-wavelength follow-up program.
arxiv-2603-05542: Fekete and team look at human-data interaction, search, and visuals as AI transforms human-centered systems. Work more and more covers large, mixed, multimodal, mostly loose data, plus base models that add doubt to thinking. Lasting problems include latency that feels off, growth limits, and limits of current dealings and search styles. Doubt covers AI-made insights, their trust, and their clarity. Meeting them needs more than speed and growth gauges. It needs new roles for humans and machines, and thinking, seeing, and design rules woven through the stack.
arxiv-2603-05742: Kandybo and Świątkowski show edges of endlessly ended groups take dense amalgam form under finite-subgroup splittings. The dense amalgam, from arXiv:1410.4989, links to any set of finite metric compact sets a new highly broken compact metric space. Placed copies of the initial spaces sit evenly apart within it. Working in the EZ-boundaries framework joining Gromov, CAT(0), and systolic boundaries, they study edges of endlessly ended groups. Any edge Z of such a group with a fitting splitting takes dense amalgam form of its factor subgroups' limit sets.
arxiv-2603-05942: Pham and team propose a skew finding method pulling the main skew angle of a paper image via Tuned Radial Cast on the Fourier Size spectrum. Skew finding is vital in paper handling, above all for scanned images, since its scores straight impacts later steps. The authors also give DISE-2021, a high-quality skew finding data set for testing other finders. Finally, they provide full studies of several Fourier-based gain aspects. Results show the proposed method robust, steady, and ahead of all compared methods.
arxiv-2603-06542: Bertolino and team bring RAMoEA-QA, the first respiratory audio question-answering model with focus across mixed recordings and query types in a two-stage plan. Such audio offers screening, yet tapes vary by device and protocol, and queries vary in intent, format, and objective. The design is studied across clinical and self-recorded settings, formats, and targets, beating single baselines and controls in-domain and under shifts. It reaches 0.72 in-domain accuracy on tasks, with the best regression performance and transfer under dataset, type, and task shifts.
arxiv-2603-06642: V P revisits SR-TTT, routing high-surprisal tokens to a Residual Cache, credited with Needle-in-a-Haystack gains. Those gains were artifacts: the metric read logits at answer positions rather than one position earlier. The cache attended non-causally over tokens including the answer. Correction refutes the SR-TTT hypothesis. Failure splits into storage and addressing: biased surprisal gating stores early needles at minimal rates, while addressing cannot resolve ordered slots with near-interchangeable contents. Exact match stays 0% in all 2,250 trials, and v1 claims are retracted.
arxiv-2603-06742: Liang and colleagues tackle constrained generation, where samples must land inside feasible regions like road maps while still looking realistic. Such regions rarely reduce to simple linear inequalities, so they tune a ready-made generator so its outputs stay inside the region and still look real. Experiments show their method differs from both tuned and tune-free constrained rivals, revealing a fresh trade-off between meeting constraints and keeping sample quality high.
arxiv-2603-06842: Kim and colleagues add expert motion critics to LLM-based robot coding for users. Novices struggle to re-task robots without specialist skill, and generated code is opaque code, hard to verify or debug, with real safety and trust risks. Critics encode robotics know-how and check motion traces for fast joints, collisions, and unsafe end-effector poses. When a problem appears, critics show clear feedback and offer one-click fixes that send clear messages back to the model. The loop refines code steadily while keeping users in charge.
arxiv-2603-06942: Hwang and colleagues run a meta-evaluation case study for long-form question answering benchmarks. Report-generating systems are now common, judged by judge models and claim checks, while meta-evaluation seeks to validate those methods. Many meta-evaluations rate quality against human pairwise preferences. Prior work warns pairwise preference can be too simple and miss expert nuance. Using ScholarQA-CS2, a benchmark for retrieval-augmented deep-research QA in science, they validate the benchmark through human pairwise judgments and probe the approach, finding pairwise rankings best for system evaluation.
arxiv-2603-07042: Wu and Zhang study how whole flows behave over long times for fourth-order parabolic and hyperbolic models with Dirichlet edge rules. The models describe micro-machine systems and depend on one power setting. They prove whole flows settle to an equilibrium, and give rates for how fast they settle. Number models back up the results.
arxiv-2603-07142: Lu and colleagues improve medical image anomaly detection with PDD, a distillation framework built on manifold priors. Standard activation maps that work on industrial images fail on subtle, varied medical anomalies. So the team unifies two frozen teacher encoders, one for global context and one for local structure, into a shared high-dimensional manifold.
