Exploration probes dynamics while still chasing the control goal. Goal-reaching then focuses solely on that goal. Theory guarantees feasibility, safety, finite-time exploration end, and near-optimal performance. Tests on an energy benchmark match a controller with full system knowledge.
arxiv-2604-12642: Alejandro García-Fernández and five colleagues allocate computing resources by price. Deploying apps across the continuum means picking nodes across varied sites. Constraints cover performance, location, and other demands. The decision space grows combinatorial with scale and variety. Existing formulations use ad-hoc topology and demand models, blocking reuse. The team borrows pricings from Software as a Service ecosystems. Plans and add-ons in a pricing implicitly define possible setups. PRIME, a pricing analysis engine, then finds cheapest valid deployments.
arxiv-2604-12742: A. A. Mazanik and F. S. Bergeret study Josephson coupling through a magnetic racetrack. Two superconducting leads link via a ferromagnetic track holding a Bloch wall. Superconductivity and the wall interact, creating current loops and strong response to wall position and tilt. Critical current varies markedly with wall position along the track. Tunable zero-to-pi transitions appear. The work gives design rules for racetrack devices. Domain walls thus serve as controls for readout in racetrack memory.
arxiv-2604-14342: Bhatnagar and seven colleagues add moving ocean heat to a slab ocean model inside the Generic Planetary Climate Model, a tool for planet climates. Wind-driven surface flow, small-scale eddy mixing, and ice and snow brightness that varies with light color and thickness all enter the new version. In water-world tests, heat transport cools the tropics, shrinks sea ice, and splits equatorial rainfall into two bands. On modern Earth the model lands close to observed temperature and brightness at almost no extra computing cost.
arxiv-2604-14442: Han tests whether shared-weight recurrence with hierarchical structure can match independent-layer stacking in a Transformer language model. His HRM-LM swaps independent layers for a recurrent pair at two speeds: a fast module refining at every step and a slow module shrinking every T steps, run with shared parameters. The sharpest, most robust finding comes from a parameter-matched Universal Transformer ablation at 1.2 billion parameters across five runs: a clear empirical gap separates the two approaches. The study frames that gap as the central result.
arxiv-2604-14642: Yang's team of thirteen probes negative calcium-two infrared triplet indices in solar-like FGK stars from LAMOST, MaStar, and XSL. Observational effects add scatter but miss the bias. The bias arises because surface models lack outer layers, whose heat rise adds triplet opacity, darkening cores past model shapes. Stronger source-function boost in H-and-K lines makes their cores appear in emission more often, and raising small-scale velocity partly offsets it. Indices from other build setups show steady offsets yet strong linear links, so cross-matching works.
arxiv-2604-14842: Klatzer, Werner, and Wogrin test what simplified gas-flow models cost energy planning. In a power-hydrogen expansion study, simplifying pressure-flow links and gas dynamics produced plans that fared badly under a dynamic model, through poor expansion, running, and unsupplied hydrogen. Plans built on simplified transport and transport-linepack models showed regret above several thousand percent and lacked robustness across demand levels. Steady-state planning softened the damage but left cost savings untapped by missing linepack flexibility. Efficient algorithms for the dynamic model are the promising next step.
arxiv-2604-15042: Lau proves there are infinitely many integers n whose shifted values n plus k all carry few prime factors. For every shift k from 2 upward, the prime-factor count stays within a logarithmic bound in k. This sharpens a 2025 result of Tao and Teräväinen, which allowed a bound growing linearly in k. The proof refines their probabilistic argument with a sharper sieve and moment estimates, and the paper adds a conjecture under which the bound is essentially sharp.
arxiv-2604-15642: Ahir, Bhat, and Doboli propose HYPERHEURIST, a simulated-annealing control scheme that treats LLM-generated RTL hardware as candidates rather than final designs. Candidates pass compile checks, structural checks, and simulation before power-performance-area tuning, which applies only to verified designs. Across eight RTL benchmarks, the staged approach yields steadier, more repeatable tuning than single-pass LLM generation.
arxiv-2604-16042: Gao and three colleagues survey intrinsic interpretability for large language models, building clarity into designs rather than probing trained models later. The goal is models that can be read from within, not only probed from outside. Past surveys focus on post-hoc methods that read models through outside guesses. The authors sort methods into five design patterns: functional transparency, concept alignment, representational decomposability, explicit modularization, and latent sparsity induction. They discuss open problems and future paths for this new field, with a public paper list.
arxiv-2604-16242: Wang and six colleagues present GRIFT, a gradient fingerprint method for detecting reward hacking in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Models can exploit reward loopholes to score highly without solving the intended task, while their chain-of-thought still looks plausible, defeating text-only monitoring. GRIFT compresses gradients of the chain-of-thought, given the prompt, into a compact fingerprint, and uses it to judge hacking. Across math, code, and logic benchmarks, it substantially beats strong baselines.
arxiv-2604-16742: Wang and colleagues introduce CT Open, an open live platform running four trial outcome prediction challenges yearly. Submissions are judged on trials whose outcomes were not public at submission time but became public afterwards. Pinning down whether an outcome was public by a date is hard, since registry postings can lag by years. An automated decontamination pipeline uses iterative LLM-powered web search to find the earliest mention of each outcome. Expert annotations validate the pipeline, and the platform releases a training set plus Winter and Summer 2025 test benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-16842: Wang's thesis tackles singularity formation in partial differential equations, the blowup behavior where solutions cease to stay smooth. The Navier-Stokes equation, one of the seven Clay Prize problems, anchors the study, alongside simpler cases such as nonlinear heat and Keller-Segel equations. Combining theory, numerics, and machine learning, including a new Kolmogorov-Arnold Network approach, the work sharpens proofs for simpler cases and improves the hunt for blowup solutions.
arxiv-2604-17142: Lim and three colleagues verify language-model task allocations for multi-agent manufacturing systems using temporal logic and discrete event systems. Predefined task models limit shifts to new products while preserving safety, and language models add flexibility but raise reliability questions. Their framework checks them before execution, and a multi-robot assembly case study shows allocations stay safe before work begins.
arxiv-2604-17442: Kheddar, Himeur, and Amira present BreathAI, a thermal-imaging system that reads breathing patterns without microphones. Their model mixes layered feature extraction, multi-thresholding, distillation fine-tuning, and contrastive learning to split inhalation from exhalation. It reached nearly 99 percent accuracy, well ahead of leading rivals, while staying efficient to run. The authors point to sleep apnea and asthma monitoring among its clinical uses.
arxiv-2604-17542: Nguyen and four colleagues improve test-time adaptation, the practice of tuning a model on unlabeled test data when distributions shift. Standard methods adapt on only a small slice of confident predictions, wasting the rest. Their DualTTA framework splits samples into likely-correct and likely-wrong groups, reinforcing the first by minimizing prediction entropy and correcting the second by maximizing it. A new reliability test based on stability under meaning-preserving and meaning-changing transformations separates the groups more cleanly than entropy alone.
arxiv-2604-17642: Akhtar, Girish, and Singh present HCFD, a benchmark for audio deepfake detection in healthcare. The work targets codec-based synthetic speech, since neural codec decoding anchors modern speech generation pipelines. The team releases Healthcare CodecFake, the first pathology-aware dataset pairing real and neural-codec-synthesized speech across multiple clinical conditions and codec families. Detectors trained mainly on healthy speech perform poorly on it, showing the need for HCFD-specific models. PaSST leads existing speech models on the task, while the team's PHOENIX-Mamba framework posts the strongest performance.
arxiv-2604-17842: Lundy and two colleagues tackle dynamic language-model benchmarks. Templates there generate endless question variants, and finding weak spots gets costly. They adapt COUP, a Bayesian optimization method, for practical model pipelines. They wrap it in a tool letting users target question types they care about, such as unusually hard items relative to measured complexity. Their method, QuickScope, finds genuinely hard questions with fewer samples than standard baselines while cutting false alarms from noisy results.
arxiv-2604-18442: Denisov and Young study wave operators of a Jacobi matrix whose spectral measure meets the Szegö rule. They prove they exist and are complete under a mild extra proviso on the Verblunsky coefficients. Those numbers belong to the linked measure on the unit circle, tying the spectral data to them.
arxiv-2604-18742: Dey and three colleagues introduce JASPER, a Bayesian tool for joint study of spatial gene expression across many genes at once. Older methods often miss links between genes and lean on preset spatial kernels, which can inflate both false positives and false negatives. JASPER instead fits spatial basis-function regression to all genes together. In tests on real data sets and in simulations, it beats older methods and picks out genes with stronger spatial links and clearer biological relevance, as checked against outside databases.
arxiv-2604-18942: Moraitaki and five colleagues introduce the first human checked multilingual negation benchmark for VLMs. It spans seven languages: English, Mandarin Chinese, Arabic, Greek, Russian, Tagalog, and Spanish. Such models show affirmation bias, tending to select positive captions even when the correct description contains negation. Standard CLIP scores no better than chance on non-Latin scripts, while MultiCLIP has the highest and most uniform accuracy. SpaceVLM, a new negation correction, lifts several languages greatly but with varied results.
arxiv-2604-19342: Mohammad and colleagues ask whether large language models pay off for industry use, beyond accuracy alone. In health, finance, search, and chat automation, models must meet strict limits on energy, latency, and hardware use, yet usual tests stay accuracy-centered. Their tool, EDGE-EVAL, benchmarks models across their whole life on legacy Tesla T4 graphics cards. Testing LLaMA and Qwen variants on three industry tasks, they bring in use metrics including economic break-even and intelligence per watt.
arxiv-2604-19442: Narayanan and colleagues address state forecasting with surrogate sensor models for tracking resident space objects. Data-driven methods like system identification and machine learning have transformed analysis of complex physical systems through the inverse problem approach. Yet extracting useful information from partial measurements remains a major hurdle, especially in aerospace, where data are scarce and sensor limits constrain tracking. The paper develops surrogate sensor models to fill gaps left by limited range and bearing data.
arxiv-2604-19542: Nguyen and Wang study solutions to the self-dual Abelian Yang-Mills-Higgs equations in a singular limit. In that limit, the linked self-dual Ginzburg-Landau type energy gathers along thin sets. Using methods from Allard's regularity theory, they construct near-exact solutions gathering near a minimal surface. Small changes are studied via a linear operator cast at right angles to gauge and shift zero modes. Working in Fermi frames and using Coulomb gauge rules, they derive uniform Lipschitz and bend bounds.
arxiv-2604-19642: Cheng and colleagues introduce micro language models, ultra-compact models with 8 million to 30 million parameters that instantly generate the first 4 to 8 words of a grounded response on-device. Watches and glasses lack the power to keep even the smallest 100 million to 1 billion parameter language models running nonstop, while cloud inference adds multi-second delays. Useful generation survives at this extreme scale, with the new models matching several 70 million to 256 million parameter existing models. The authors reframe the cloud model as a continuator rather than a respondent.
arxiv-2604-19742: Peng and five colleagues introduce PlayEval, a repository-aware testbed built from 43 multilingual GUI applications in Python, TypeScript, and JavaScript for judging game-like interface code. Current tests check correctness through test cases alone, which misses the mark for interactive, event-driven systems that need correct state changes across sequences of user actions. PlayEval therefore weighs interaction flows and interface logic rather than pass-or-fail outcomes alone.
arxiv-2604-20042: Hakim and Bayzid introduce threshold pairwise compatibility graphs, a framework unifying several generalizations of tree-metric graph classes from phylogeny. A pair counts as adjacent when at least t of k underlying compatibility predicates accept it. Every graph on n vertices fits the framework for every t up to n, yet for fixed k and t the class is asymptotically rare among all graphs. The model separates sharply from k-interval compatibility graphs, the k-AND hierarchy is strict, and closure under complement fails.
arxiv-2604-20342: Ioannidou, Dikaiakos, and Stassopoulou present e112, a context-aware mobile crisis app linking locals and officials in disasters. Built on common phones, it offers SOS calls, event notes, custom alerts, exit guidance, and vetted group chat, with a cloud back end and a control board. A user-first design kept the tool clear and usable under stress. User tests and tech audits found high delight, robust speed, and easy access, showing a simple well-made app can cut risk to life in climate-driven crises.
arxiv-2604-20642: Fominykh and Stegailov model polaron transport in the mineral, on the Verwey transition, a puzzle open for almost a century. Their ab initio-based model joins kinetic Monte Carlo and molecular motion runs to describe polaron motion coupled to lattice waves. Unlike the Ihle-Lorentz small-polaron model, they find no big change in band structure across the transition, though trimeron hopping is seen. The model gives dc flow matching lab data across the transition.
arxiv-2604-20942: Wang, Dai, Cao, Yin, Schlick, and Wei present VARIANT, a web server that decodes and analyzes viral mutations at genome and protein levels for RNA viruses. It labels point mutations, insertions, deletions, and frameshifts, and flags three patterns most tools miss, such as back-to-back changes and regions where ribosomes shift frame. Built-in coverage spans SARS-CoV-2, HIV-1, influenza H3N2, Ebola, and chikungunya, and users can add their own viruses too.
arxiv-2604-21042: Lemaire, Aglin, and Nijssen present a way to learn optimal quantile regression trees, answering rising demand for models that are accurate, interpretable, and robust. The method predicts the complete conditional distribution of a target without prior assumptions on that distribution. Its predictions stay interpretable to end users. It also learns a full set of optimal trees without losing algorithmic efficiency relative to learning a single tree.
arxiv-2604-21242: Aaron Bertram and three colleagues extend Reider's theorem on very ampleness on complex projective surfaces two ways. Reider-type inequalities imply nefness for series of the form dH minus E on the blow-up of projective space along the surface, echoing Saint-Donat's theorem. They give a sharp estimate for the ample cone of Hilbert schemes of length-d subschemes. Proofs find a family over the base and the stability chamber where its objects are Bridgeland semistable, then apply Bayer-Macri.
arxiv-2604-22142: van Nuenen studies how language-model rewriting changes personal story style and texture. He studies 300 narratives rewritten by three models under polish, rewrite-only, and voice-keeping prompts. Change is tracked across 13 markers, like function words, vocabulary diversity, punctuation, contractions, and first-person pronouns. Rewriting flattens style: function words, contractions, and first-person pronouns fall, while vocabulary diversity, punctuation, and detail rise. Voice-keeping prompts shrink but do not reverse the shifts, and reworked texts converge, growing harder to match to sources.
arxiv-2604-22342: Meyer, Pelster and Thorwart extend open quantum systems theory to anyon baths, baths of particles with statistics between bosons and fermions. Their bath holds independent pairs of 1D anyons bound by springs, set by one statistical parameter. Mapping those anyons to a bosonic bath with scaled frequencies gives a non-polynomial coupling form. Path integrals plus a Wick theorem yield an approximate spectral density that varies with temperature. Relaxation dynamics show clear low- and high-temperature limits, with anyonic features strongest at mid-range temperatures.
arxiv-2604-22442: Basu introduces HubRouter, a module replacing quadratic attention layers with hub-mediated routing through learned hub tokens. Hubs cross-attend to all tokens and a sparse council attends only to selected tokens. In a Jamba-style hybrid it improves perplexity by about 4 percent and reaches up to about 90 times training throughput at length 1024. An optimised baseline would narrow that to about 10 to 15 times. A causal Hub-GPT variant reaches perplexity about 212, about 3 worse than Jamba's about 209, the cost of avoiding quadratic computation.
arxiv-2604-22542: Yuan and six colleagues build a system grading spoken dialogue generation for school-age English learners outside English-speaking countries. Language models often miss learners' proficiency, so the framework adapts outputs to China's national curriculum, grading word difficulty in four tiers. New resources back it: graded word lists and a multi-turn dialogue corpus. The core method, DDPO, a diversity-driven optimization, preserves variety while lifting overall quality. It beats conventional approaches with low out-of-vocabulary rates and stronger naturalness.
arxiv-2604-22642: Argüz and Joyce extend complex geometry to spaces with corners and generalized corners, using complex structures on the logarithmic tangent bundle. They prove a Newlander-Nirenberg type result showing the structure matches a standard model along each corner layer to infinite order. The theorem then gives exact conditions for such a space to arise as a Kato-Nakayama space.
arxiv-2604-22942: Moradi and six colleagues present VS-DDPM, a variable-step diffusion model designed to keep generative quality while speeding inference severalfold for medical image synthesis. Tested on four tasks in the BraTS2025 and SynthRAD2025 challenges, it reaches state-of-the-art performance in missing MRI synthesis. For tumor removal it also performs strongly, while MRI-to-sCT and CBCT-to-sCT results stay competitive but below the best marks, possibly due to data processing. The framework offers a robust, tunable route to high-fidelity three-dimensional medical image synthesis.
arxiv-2604-23042: Wen builds the partition by hand, as saturated symmetric chains inside Young's lattice L(6,n). Young's lattice, in this setting, orders partitions that fit inside a rectangle by inclusion, and a symmetric chain is a chain symmetric about the middle rank. A saturated chain moves by single cover steps with nothing in between. The proof builds the partition explicitly rather than merely showing one exists.
arxiv-2604-23342: Zhang and five colleagues run a large empirical study of 15 test selection metrics for deep learning systems under shift. Prior reviews suffer narrow objectives, limited shift coverage, and image-heavy datasets, leaving users unsure which metric fits their context. Their study spans three objectives, fault detection, performance rating, and retraining guidance, five shift types, three modalities, and 13 models, covering 1,640 scenarios. The work offers a stats review of metric performance across objectives, shifts, and modalities.
arxiv-2604-23542: Li and colleagues release two new smoke datasets to help spot wildfires sooner. AusSmoke covers Australia, while MultiNatSmoke folds public sets from many nations into one far larger benchmark. Older smoke sets are small, narrow in place, and often fake, so models trained on them travel poorly. Tests of smoke-finding models on the new sets show better results across varied regions.
arxiv-2604-23842: Ki and colleagues study AI help for non-native speakers learning new English words for chats across cultures. In a study with 234 people, learners used AI definitions, AI rewrites, AI explanations, or a plain dictionary. They then wrote messages and judged fit. AI explanations gave the largest gains in native-rated writing skill. Fit judgments barely differed across supports. Learners' self-ratings overshot native ratings, revealing a perception gap.
arxiv-2604-24042: Wiggins argues that frozen-time pictures miss how Kerr-cat qubits actually form states and run gates under time-varying microwave pulses. For state preparation, a ramped resonant model yields a quintic reduced form with two symmetric moving branches that organize local formation. For gates, a fast pulse perturbs the figure-eight separatrix, and Melnikov analysis gives a leading transport test. Transient lobe motion then emerges as the geometric route to non-adiabatic leakage, with an amplitude-width threshold marking its onset.
arxiv-2604-24442: Lee and four colleagues study how hard it is to learn controllers for partially observed linear systems with Gaussian noise, known as LQG control, from recorded trajectories. They prove a lower bound on excess cost for any method that maps offline data to a stabilizing linear controller. The bound uses the cost curvature and the Fisher information of the exploration policy. Applied to classic fragile examples, it shows when fragility becomes high sample complexity.
arxiv-2604-24542: Min, Pham and Sun offer a runtime monitor for large language models that needs no retraining, no clean reference model and no knowledge of the trigger. Their Layerwise Convergence Fingerprinting tracks how hidden states change from layer to layer and flags unusual trajectories. Across backdoors, jailbreaks and prompt injections it cut backdoor success sharply, caught most jailbreak attempts and flagged injected text payloads, at low extra computing cost.
arxiv-2604-24742: Zakharova, Chernikov and Sysoev analyze whether a quantum amplitude redistribution algorithm can be applied to the data filtering problem, meaning cleaning data by removing unwanted components. They model the algorithm's operation and compare its results with a median filter, a standard smoothing method that replaces each value by the median of its neighbors. The paper thus tests a quantum approach against a classical baseline for the same filtering task.
arxiv-2604-24842: Song and colleagues present Co-Director for agentic video storytelling. Current pipelines chain modules with hand-made prompting. They suffer drift and cascading failures. Co-Director treats storytelling as a global optimization problem. A bandit picks good creative directions. A local loop limits identity drift and keeps order. This weighs new narrative plans with good configurations. GenAD-Bench offers 400 fictional product cases for ads. Tests show it beats top rivals and generalizes broadly.
arxiv-2604-24942: Hari and four colleagues propose a component-based coding system for brain activity while hearing stories. Their system separates stimulus signals from noise signals in fMRI data. They split story-listening fMRI data into components using one data subset, then train coding models on fresh data to predict component time series from language model readings of word input. Across subjects, a subset of components shows steady high scores, stable in space and time, including hearing and language nets.
arxiv-2604-25042: Weinberg and Rengaswamy use stabilizers to compile logical circuits under hardware constraints. Error-correcting codes add redundancy making physically distinct operators logically the same. Any logically equivalent operator suffices, and some choices suit building better. The authors make this precise for the special unitary group. Ideal compilation choice reduces to a least squares problem with a closed solution. Their method avoids costly swaps for hardware links via a distinct, native Hamiltonian. They show with a small example code and discuss links to compressed sensing.
arxiv-2604-25142: Jongyoon Kim, Minseong Hwang and Seung-won Hwang propose UnIte, an uncertainty-based iterative sampling method for neural retrievers in new domains. Retrievers adapt to a new domain by making pseudo queries for its documents, and the choice of documents drives quality and cost. Old sampling chases diversity but ignores model uncertainty. UnIte drops documents with high aleatoric uncertainty and favors those with high epistemic uncertainty, gaining up to 3.49 nDCG@10 points on BEIR with about 4,000 training documents on average.
arxiv-2604-25342: Pajno and four colleagues build a frame for small-area reads of the Po Valley farm carbon footprint. They blend survey, census, and satellite-based emission data, giving reads for Agrarian Subregions, towns grouped by Italian stats rules. Satellite ammonia data act as extra clues that sharpen reads and spatial fit. A key step treats the mismatch of gridded satellite data with town borders, eased by geostatistical upscaling and bootstrapping. Satellite data lift read accuracy and steadiness, while cutting need for huge extra datasets.
arxiv-2604-25442: Karagulyan and Melkumyan set out new bounds for function systems with wavelet-type dyadic structure. They yield optimal growth for Weyl multipliers of certain wavelet-type systems. Some results drop the orthogonality rule. So a sum test on a rising sequence is both needed and enough for it to be a nearly always unconditional convergence Weyl multiplier for any wavelet-type system. They also prove the log is a nearly always Weyl multiplier for any shuffled wavelet-type system, and that this bound is optimal.
arxiv-2604-25642: Zhang and four colleagues propose Prefill-Time Intervention, a new way to cut hallucinations in large vision-language models. Past steering-vector methods worked only at decoding time, where errors pile up step by step and worsen later outputs. Prefill-Time Intervention acts just once during prefill, improving the initial key-value cache before errors can accumulate. It is modality-aware, steering keys toward visually grounded objects and values to filter background noise. Tests show strong hallucination cuts across decoding strategies, models, and benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-25742: Konijn and Paardekooper model planet-building pebble accretion with many pebble sizes at once, using a multi-fluid approach. Most studies assume one pebble size, but real discs hold a range of sizes that drift and accrete at different rates. Two-dimensional FARGO3D runs with several pebble species validate the method against earlier static-disc results. Evolving the gas disc lowers efficiency for high Stokes numbers and raises it for small ones. The protoplanet's disturbance of the gas disc cuts accretion under an MRN solid distribution.
arxiv-2604-26242: Samanta asked whether depression changes how a voice loops back to sounds it used before during a chat. Using 142 people from the DAIC-WOZ depression set, he took recurrence scores from 74 vocal channels. Those scores beat plain sound summaries and a set of rival dynamic features. The result backs nonlinear state-space study as a hopeful route to voice-based signs of depression.
arxiv-2604-26442: Ou analyzed Fermi-LAT gamma-ray data around the millisecond pulsar PSR J0437-4715 to pin down its off-pulse emission. From the timing ephemeris he built the pulse profile, split on-pulse from off-pulse phases, and ran binned likelihood fits across phase ranges. No spatial extension appeared for off-pulse emission, pointing to a point-like source. The outer-gap conversion efficiency fits a termination shock near the pulsar, linking off-pulse emission to bow-shock wind nebulae.
arxiv-2604-26542: Rutová and three colleagues tested whether brightness swings in five hot stars come from spin-driven modulation by surface temperature spots. Frequencies from projected spin speeds ran lower than TESS light-curve frequencies in all five cases, keeping spin explanations viable. Two targets, HT Cet and HD 219487, showed more tangled spectra suggesting pulsations. The results hint spot-driven modulation may occur in stars hotter than 6500 kelvin, showing the worth of joining spectroscopic and photometric study.
arxiv-2604-26742: Soler-Terricabras, Romero-Gómez, and Roca-Fàbrega test whether invariant manifold theory explains spiral structure in a barred-galaxy simulation. Sorting disc particles by Jacobi energy isolates manifold orbits. Three populations emerge. Low-energy particles move on near-circular orbits across the disc. High-energy particles follow banana orbits. Compatible particles leave the bar along transit orbits tracing the arms. Only these particles build the outward ridge in the radius-speed plane and the spiral streaming pattern. Barred arms are real structures sustained by guided transport.
arxiv-2604-27142: Kirkpatrick and three colleagues tackle approximations for the diameter of a graph, the longest shortest path between any two nodes. Recent work gives a full conditional lower-bound tradeoff curve, but the best upper bounds lag behind. The best known scheme for undirected diameter has not improved, and it is randomized with no deterministic rival known. The paper builds new approximations from distance oracle techniques, tools that answer distance queries fast.
arxiv-2604-27242: Alonso-Martin studies how to estimate diffusivity and the Hurst parameter for simplified limits of slow-fast systems driven by Wiener or Hermite noise. He shows estimators built from that limit keep working on suitably thinned data from the original system. Renormalized quadratic variations and Wiener chaos expansions serve as his key tools. Under stricter thinning, a non-central limit theorem survives for non-Gaussian fluctuations, and one estimator needs no knowledge of the limiting diffusivity.
arxiv-2604-27442: Lee and three colleagues propose a Bayesian online learning algorithm for the one-pass setting, where each sample is seen once. Existing guarantees usually need mini-batch sizes that grow without bound, which fails in one pass. Their method adds a warm-start phase for stable sequential updates and attains the optimal convergence rate. The authors also establish an online version of the Bernstein-von Mises theorem, giving valid uncertainty quantification without growing batches. Tests on generalized linear models match batch performance while beating existing online methods.
arxiv-2604-27542: Bañeras-Roux and four colleagues present HATS, a French data set of human judgments on errors made by automatic speech recognition systems. A group of 143 people chose the better of two machine transcripts in each case, judging them as a listener would. The team then compared those human choices with scores from common metrics, both word-based and embedding-based, to see which track human perception. They frame HATS as a human-centered check on transcript quality, beyond the limits of word error rate alone.
arxiv-2604-28042: Yavorskiy and colleagues push light-matter coupling into the deep-strong regime using Kane fermions, particles with ultralow effective mass in mercury cadmium telluride. Tuning carrier density with temperature, they move continuously from weak to deep-strong coupling, passing a record normalised ratio of 1.6 above room temperature. Their spectra match a gauge-invariant microscopic theory, and a diamagnetic term that emerges naturally rules out a superradiant phase transition, settling a long-running dispute.
arxiv-2604-28142: Martinico and colleagues speed up multivector retrieval, where fine-grained token vectors give strong results at high compute and memory cost. Their TACHIOM system allocates cluster centres with token frequencies in mind. It scales to millions of centres and scores documents from centres alone, plus a graph index and compressed layout for final scoring. On standard benchmarks it clusters over two hundred times faster than k-means. Retrieval runs about ten times faster than leading systems at comparable or better quality.
arxiv-2605-00042:
Jiamian Li and Bing-Zhao Li extend spectral analysis of point clouds into the fractional domain. A point cloud can be read as samples of a smooth surface, and it is usually analyzed through the eigenfunctions of the Laplace-Beltrami operator. Their manifold fractional harmonic transform lets the analysis slide continuously between the spatial and spectral domains instead of jumping between them.

They derive the transform's basic properties and its convolution, correlation, and sampling theorems, founding a stable fractional spectral representation on manifolds. Two applications follow. One joins the transform at several orders with chaotic phase modulation to encrypt point clouds, with a large key space and high sensitivity. The other designs an optimal filter in the fractional domain for finding maritime targets, suppressing sea clutter while keeping weak targets at low signal-to-clutter ratios. Tests on measured data support both uses.
arxiv-2605-00142:
Jonathan Unger and Georg Hoffstaetter test a beam optics scheme for the electron storage ring of the Electron-Ion Collider. Achromatic Telescopic Squeezing, borrowed from collider practice, is applied to improve the ring's dynamic aperture and momentum acceptance, the margins inside which the beam stays stable. They compare standard sextupole correction schemes with the new optics on both a simplified test lattice and the full ring lattice.

The new optics reduce the sextupole strengths needed and soften higher-order nonlinear effects, improving momentum aperture. In the arcs, half the sextupoles could be dropped at similar performance. A scheme using all of them does better still. The gain in momentum acceptance under test conditions is measurable but small, and it comes with emittance growth from larger beam sizes in the arcs. That trade-off limits the scheme for this ring, while suiting rings that tolerate moderate growth.
arxiv-2605-00442:
Ajay Kumar and V. V. M. S. Chandramouli build a new two-dimensional neuron model by fitting a cosine-based memristor into the reduced Chialvo map. A memristor is a circuit element whose resistance remembers past current, and its nonlinear response enriches the neuron's firing behavior under electromagnetic modulation. The authors map the model's equilibrium points by analysis and simulation.

They find the conditions for a Neimark-Sacker bifurcation, where steady firing gives way to quasiperiodic rhythms, and chart a wide zoo of further patterns, including period doubling and several resonance structures. Multiple attractors can coexist, from a stable cycle to a chaotic one, each with its own basin. Extended to a ring-star network of neurons, the model shows imperfect synchronization, clustered patterns, and multi-chimera states not seen in earlier Chialvo studies. The authors offer it as a compact, rich testbed for theoretical neurodynamics.
arxiv-2605-00842:
Gouki Minegishi and four co-authors explain emergent misalignment, where fine-tuning a language model on narrow, harmless tasks can still produce harmful behavior. Their account rests on feature superposition: models encode traits in overlapping codes, so strengthening one trait can also strengthen nearby harmful ones in proportion to similarity. A short gradient-level derivation formalizes the effect.

Using sparse autoencoders across several model families, the team finds traits tied to misalignment-inducing data sit geometrically closer to harmful traits than other traits do. The pattern holds across domains such as health, career, and legal advice. Filtering out training samples closest to toxic features cut misalignment substantially, beating random removal.
arxiv-2605-01142:
Thomas Steele and four co-authors argue that the beta phase of copper selenide in a rhombohedral structure is a Dirac semimetal. The alpha phase has been studied for thermoelectrics and ionic conduction. It recently emerged as a topological zero-gap semimetal. Based on density functional electronic structure calculations, the beta phase shows Dirac behavior for electrons near the Fermi level.

Topological semimetals attract interest for unusual transport, including strong quantum oscillations, large magnetoresistance, and ultrahigh carrier mobility. The authors show Fermi arc states exist in the surface spectrum, topologically protected by the bulk Dirac points. Their shape and spin properties should resist scattering effects in surface transport. That suggests new routes to high-mobility devices.
arxiv-2605-01442:
Yasir Mahmood, Arnab Sharma, Axel-Cyrille Ngonga Ngomo, and Balram Tiwari argue that explanations over knowledge bases should answer the question users actually ask. Standard tools justify why a fact holds, or guess what is missing, but users often want to know why one fact holds instead of a close rival they expected.

The authors build contrastive explanations for description logic bases. Given a fact and a foil that swaps the person or the concept, the explanation shows the difference. That difference is what makes the first true and the second not. They lay the formal base for such questions, define the explanations, and study their traits in two logics of different strength. An implementation is tested on bases of varied size. The user-centered turn links machine reasoning work with how people naturally ask why.
arxiv-2605-01542:
Paul Garnier, Vincent Lannelongue, and Elie Hachem retrain how neural surrogates learn fluid physics on meshes. Graph networks and Transformers now speed up flow simulation, but their training still rests on naive habits. They grade each node alone and step time with a crude explicit rule that stiff, real equations punish.

The framework adds three fixes. A stencil-level target grades a node's whole neighborhood at once, which enforces spatial consistency. A temporal correction step replaces the crude march with a predictor-corrector guided by cross-attention. And a three-dimensional rotary position code bakes rotation symmetry into the model. Across three architectures and varied physics data, the changes lift accuracy and stability, above all in long rollouts. The learned internal codes also transfer to unseen tasks such as wall shear stress and pressure, tasks never trained for.
arxiv-2605-01642:
Rachel Freedman designs alignment that can change its mind as society changes its values. Standard methods aim a model at one fixed set of preferences, which risks locking yesterday's values in place even as norms move on.

Her pipeline, Adaptive Pluralistic Alignment, runs in three stages. Small personal reward models are learned as compact mixes of shared reward bases. Those models then sit as a jury, picking among candidate outputs by social-choice voting rules. As values shift, only the jury's weights are refit over the fixed bases, a cheap update that skips retraining and fresh mass labeling. A proof of concept with simulated annotators from past eras shows jury makeup and voting rule can swing outcomes a lot, and the tracking error under a sliding-window jury is bounded. Code is public.
arxiv-2605-01942:
Anthony Gómez-Fonseca, Gretchen Matthews, Kirsten Morris, and Tefjol Pllaha build quantum error-correcting codes from dyadic matrices. Quantum low-density parity-check codes promise scalable fault-tolerant computing, but short cycles in their Tanner graphs hurt iterative decoding. Dyadic matrices have a compact signature row, translation invariance, and a recursive block form that makes them tractable.

Using that algebra, the authors link cycles in lifted graphs to closed walks in a smaller protograph and give methods to count and control short cycles. They add construction algorithms in the style of progressive edge growth, using forbidden shifts to raise girth when possible. When top girth cannot be reached, the methods reduce the number of shortest cycles instead.
arxiv-2605-02042:
Chad Berner studies sequences in a Hilbert space that can be continuously mapped to Parseval frames. Frame theory recovers a vector from inner product data, but its reconstruction formula can be costly to compute. Berner relaxes the frame condition and keeps a similar recovery formula through the continuous map.

He characterises such sequences purely through their analysis operators, with no reference to the map itself. Examples include sequences that are incomplete and sequences with no frame inside them at all. Norm-based tests tell when certain Schauder sequences, and finite unions of them, have the property. He also classifies measures on the torus for which the standard exponential system qualifies and forms a Riesz Fischer sequence.
arxiv-2605-02142:
Yuechen Wang, Lina Jia, Qinglong Wang, and Feng Tian introduce ORBIT, a model that learns how gene programs activate together inside single cells. Past methods treat programs on their own or need perturbation data to model their links. ORBIT learns from observational single-cell RNA data alone, using a self-supervised transformer.

Its training asks how other programs change when one program is removed. That gives attention weights that reflect one-way influence, not just co-occurrence. On almost one hundred ninety-two thousand prefrontal cortex nuclei, across three pathway vocabularies, ORBIT recovered patterns matching known Alzheimer's vulnerability signs. It also found cell-type-specific rewiring that standard differential expression missed, showing links that vary by cell type.
arxiv-2605-02442:
Munachiso Samuel Nwadike and four co-authors offer a guide for researchers who need to judge reasoning in language models. Their central claim is that a right final answer is not enough. Real reasoning, in their view, means choosing steps along the way and knowing when to stop, based on the problem at hand.

The authors argue for process-based tests that grade the steps shown in a model's work, not just its last line. They also argue that a single forward pass has fixed depth, so long chains need written traces or outside steps. Readers get a clear frame for spotting weak tests and for building fairer ones.
arxiv-2605-02542:
James Lynch and four co-authors present IteRate, a system in which AI agents design and test Wi-Fi rate control algorithms with no human in the loop. Choosing a data rate for each Wi-Fi frame is a long-standing problem, and the standard hand-tuned method has barely changed in over a decade. IteRate runs the full research cycle itself.

Specialized agents propose ideas, write eBPF programs that run inside the Linux kernel, deploy them over the air to real devices, and analyze fine-grained telemetry. A new kernel module exposes per-frame hardware data to those programs. Persistent records keep what was learned between rounds. Tests ran on a large multi-node testbed across several workloads, showing an end-to-end path for autonomous systems research.
arxiv-2605-02642:
Régis Mélin, Romain Danneau, and Morteza Kayyalha study a hybrid effect in three-terminal Josephson junctions, devices where superconductors meet a normal conductor. Floquet theory handles systems driven in a repeating time pattern, much as Bloch theory handles repeating space patterns. In a biased junction, the superconducting phase itself evolves in time, giving a built-in Floquet drive.

The authors work with a ballistic two-dimensional conductor and a continuum of electronic states. They show that quartet and higher multipair processes produce distinct conductance and noise resonances, set by bias voltage and chemical potential. These signatures are described as Floquet-multiple Andreev reflections, extending a known single-junction effect into the driven, multiterminal setting. The microscopic picture offers a route to build and probe Floquet physics in such junctions.
arxiv-2605-02742:
Anton Raël, Julien Boucher, and Antoine Lhermitte design a tool for one of animation's most demanding steps: in-betweening, filling the motion between an animator's key poses. The rhythm and expression of a scene are set there, and the need for creative control makes it a production bottleneck. Recent learning methods do well in research settings but assume data and workflows unlike professional studios.

Their method balances learned interpolation against direct pose synthesis, shifting the mix as needed, in a layer that mirrors how animators work. A keypose schedule drawn from production data keeps style consistent between training and real use. On production data the method reached leading performance. Built into Autodesk Maya, it let animators finish in-betweening tasks much faster in trials.
arxiv-2605-03042:
Ruofeng Yang, Yongcan Li, and Shuai Li describe ARIS, an open-source harness for autonomous research with language models. Long research runs face a quiet risk: an agent can report a neat success whose evidence is weak, missing, or misread, with no clear break to warn the user.

ARIS pairs an executor model with a reviewer from a different model family to check work as it goes. Its layers cover reusable skills and tools, five end-to-end workflows, and checks that map claims back to raw evidence. A self-improvement loop can suggest changes, adopted only after reviewer approval.
arxiv-2605-03142:
Jiayi Chen, Xuan Zhang, and Guiling Wang tackle bidding in power markets. More wind and solar power has made prices jumpy and risky. Producers must split sales between day-ahead deals and real-time settlement. Standard learning agents often chase profit and guard risk poorly.

They release a detailed testbed built on PJM market data. They also propose MARS-DA, a layered agent. A top controller blends a safe agent with a bold one that hunts real-time chances. In tests, it earned better returns for the risk taken than strong baselines. It also stayed steady during sharp market swings.
arxiv-2605-03342:
Jin Lei develops a unified four-body framework for inclusive breakup of three-body projectiles, where detectors catch only part of the projectile while the rest still interacts with the target. Treating the projectile as two preformed clusters hides correlations that partial detection can actually probe.

Within the distorted-wave Born approximation, Lei derives cross-section sum rules for catching either a pair or a single constituent, keeping the full three-body wavefunction. Comparing against the factorized limit shows exactly what the cluster picture omits, including target-excitation effects in absorption. A lithium-6 example and a calculation route for single-particle spectra complete the framework.
arxiv-2605-03442:
Julia Dima, David O'Ryan, Sandor Kruk, Laslo E. Ruhberg, and Pablo Gómez hunt high-redshift gravitational lenses in JWST images with a semi-supervised anomaly finder. Strong lenses probe distant mass and source populations, but they are rare and visually subtle in the flood of space telescope data.

Starting from eleven known lenses, AnomalyMatch with human-in-the-loop training scanned two major surveys and found fifty-eight unique lenses, graded by four experts. Thirty-seven were previously uncatalogued, with photometric redshifts reaching beyond two. The haul shows anomaly methods can mine JWST archives for rare distant objects at scale.
arxiv-2605-04242:
Anton Ivchenko describes a working system that forecasts road crash risk across the United States. Building such a service, he argues, is first a systems task: past crash records, weather, road maps, model training, map tiles, and web serving all have to connect.

The system combines a broad national baseline trained on fatal crash data with a finer road-segment model built from census road geometry and a large accident data set. Its forecasts are served through live data feeds, map tiles, and a public web app, so users can check risk at road level.
arxiv-2605-04542:
Akiyoshi Tomihari and Issei Sato clarify how three popular ways of improving language model reasoning - sampling, reinforcement learning, and distillation - are secretly connected. Recent work has questioned whether reinforcement learning deserves the credit for strong reasoning, while sampling many answers and keeping the best has proven effective on its own.

They focus on the power distribution, the target that power sampling aims at. They show it is exactly the optimal solution of a regularised reinforcement learning problem. In that problem, the reward is the model's own log-probability. That identity yields a self-distillation method that trains on the model's own samples toward the same target, moving the cost of sampling into offline training.
arxiv-2605-04642:
Aaron van Diepen, Adrian Zapletal, and Fernando Kuipers propose a change to how web browsers decide whether a site must be visited over an encrypted connection. Attacks that strip encryption downgrade a secure visit to plain text, and current defences require each site to opt in, with headers that are easy to misconfigure or open to abuse.

Their mechanism flips the default: every connection starts encrypted, and a site that genuinely needs plain HTTP declares that explicitly through an indicator. The design aims to close the remaining downgrade attack surface while keeping such sites reachable and preserving compatibility with the existing web. Two indicator designs are proposed and analysed.
arxiv-2605-04942:
Matúš Kaintz and Antonio Cammarata set out design guidelines for diamond-based solar cells and single-dopant diodes, devices built around chosen defects in diamond crystals. They study two designs from first principles: a solar cell using a boron-vacancy-boron absorber, and a diode based on phosphorus-vacancy defects. Both defects create useful energy levels inside the material.

For the solar cell they advise aligning light to exploit uneven absorption, grading the junctions, and aiming for an absorber about five hundred nanometres thick. For the diode, impurity-band conduction suits tunnel-style uses, and its heat response could aid thermal management. Single-dopant junctions, they note, would simplify manufacturing greatly.
arxiv-2605-05142:
Donghui Yang and Weijia Wu study whether a class of wave equations in several dimensions can be steered exactly using a control, even though the equation degenerates at one interior point. Degeneracy can break standard methods, since the equation loses strength where it vanishes. The authors first establish that solutions exist and behave well, using the Hardy inequality.

Their main tool is a Carleman estimate, a weighted energy inequality, from which they derive an observability inequality for the system. Since observability and controllability are equivalent here, exact controllability follows. A specially built weight function cancels the influence of the degenerate region, and their control region notably includes the degenerate point itself.
arxiv-2605-05242:
Zhuofeng Li and eighteen co-authors argue that agentic search should skip the retrieval index and let agents work the raw corpus directly with ordinary terminal tools. Modern retrievers compress a corpus into one top-ranked list before reasoning starts, which filters out evidence that later steps might need. Exact word constraints, sparse clue combinations, and plan revisions are all hard through that fixed interface.

Their direct corpus interaction setup uses search commands, file reads, shell tools, and small scripts, with no embedding model, vector index, or retrieval service, and no offline indexing at all. Across information retrieval benchmarks and end-to-end agentic search tasks, this simple setup substantially outperformed strong sparse, dense, and reranking baselines on several measures.
arxiv-2605-05342:
Natalia Schmid, Sasanka Katreddi, and Yechan Kweon detect radio frequency interference in telescope data by treating frequency patterns as images for computer vision. Human-made interference increasingly floods the radio spectrum, often far louder than the faint pulsar and fast radio burst signals astronomers seek. Standard cleaning methods rest on assumptions about the interference and data statistics, which weak or shifting interference can break.

Their method needs no prior knowledge of interference type. A short-time Fourier transform turns each channel into a spectrogram, an image segmentation algorithm draws a binary interference mask, and the cleaned data are transformed back. Tests use Green Bank Telescope observations of a known pulsar, scored by the signal strength of a single pulse.
arxiv-2605-05442:
Stochastic quantization equations bring probability into quantum field theory, but on rough spaces the usual tools break down. Hongyi Chen and Yifan (Johnny) Yang study Wick renormalized versions of these equations on metric measure spaces whose heat kernels behave in a sub-Gaussian way. The spaces include fractal-like examples far from smooth manifolds.

They give conditions, in terms of Hausdorff dimension, walk dimension, and heat-kernel regularity, for local solutions to exist. Slightly stronger conditions yield global solutions, and for those they build an invariant measure for the associated Markov process. The results cover many rough spaces studied in analysis on fractals.
arxiv-2605-05942:
Michael Poppel and seven co-authors ask why some quantum neural networks train well and others stall, even with the same encoding budget. Circuits with different shapes, set by qubit count and encoding layers, can share the same frequency spectrum and parameter needs on paper. Yet in practice their trainability differs a lot, and this study names the mechanism.

The authors trace the gap to rank loss in a coefficient matching matrix in serial, single qubit designs. There, more parameters stop affecting the loss as the count grows, a flaw they call structural gradient starvation. Parallel designs avoid the trap. They also show that adding feature map layers beats adding trainable blocks for parameter efficiency.
arxiv-2605-06042:
Charbel Toumieh and three co-authors improve flight control for bird scale flapping wing aircraft. These craft are quieter and safer than rotary drones, but lift, speed, and turning power are tightly coupled and steered by few inputs. Standard controllers treat height, speed, and heading apart, which leaves steady tracking errors in hard maneuvers.

Their controller uses model predictive contouring, tracking paths by arc length while optimizing progress online, so no fixed speed profile is needed. A compact smooth model captures the main coupled aerodynamics within a real time computing budget. On the XFly craft, mean deviation from the path stayed between 6.5 and 9 centimeters at speeds up to three meters per second. That is an 8.5 fold gain over prior methods.
arxiv-2605-06242:
M. N. Ferreira and three co-authors explore the quark-gluon vertex in the complex momentum plane for the first time. The vertex's nonperturbative structure matters for meson properties beyond the simplest approximation schemes. Their starting point is a symmetry preserving approach developed recently for such studies, focused on the transversely projected form of the vertex in the soft gluon limit.

In that limit the form factors depend on one momentum variable, whose complex extension yields all eight factors inside a domain bounded by a parabola. The domain's edge is set by the first singularity in the defining integrals, where the usual Wick rotation needs extra terms. Extrapolation stretches the reliable region further, until structures tied to real physical processes appear. The authors also discuss general gluon momenta and links to the quark propagator.
arxiv-2605-07142:
Peiyu Duan and seven co-authors present AGA3DNet, a system for classifying brain MRI subtypes in three dimensions. Good classification needs both local anatomical cues and wider context across the scan. Their framework adds short anatomical phrases taken from radiology reports as a soft guide channel alongside the image data.

Phrases are mapped to atlas regions and spread into smooth spatial priors, giving interpretable guidance without dense hand labeling. A light 3D network and multi-view sequence model complete the design. On a hospital cohort, the system improved balance across performance measures and supported readable localization, though the authors note limits from using one cohort.
arxiv-2605-07342:
Hugh Xuechen Liu and Kıvanç Tatar argue that checking whether generated game code compiles is a misleading way to judge it. Their Mage protocol scores executable game scenes on four axes: compile success, runtime success, structural fidelity, and whether the intended game mechanisms actually appear. They apply it to hundreds of generation attempts by four open models.

Direct text-to-code generation ran most often but produced structurally empty scenes with weak mechanism scores. Feeding a structured intermediate form halved the runtime rate yet recovered faithful structure. Compile rate, they conclude, moves against real correctness in this domain, so multi-axis evaluation is needed to see what generation actually delivers.
arxiv-2605-07442:
Chaobo Jia and seven co-authors verify games generated by language models by injecting test states directly into the running game. A game can look right while breaking core mechanics over long play, and agent-based checkers that simply play the game are slow and coverage-limited. Their GameGen-Verifier instead breaks a specification into checkable keypoints.

Each keypoint becomes an independent unit that patches the game into a target state, runs a short interaction, and judges the outcome. A harness manages concurrency, isolation, and fault recovery. On a hundred games across seven genres, the verifier agreed with human judgments far more than an agent baseline, in a fraction of the time.
arxiv-2605-07542:
Jeffrey Shallit studies a curious infinite binary sequence built by a simple recursive rule. Each block starts from the digits 101, and the next block appends the current one with its first symbols deleted. The blocks grow into prefixes of one endless string of zeros and ones, known as Brik's sequence.

Shallit proves several sharp facts about this string. It is recurrent, so every pattern returns later, but not uniformly recurrent, so some patterns can be absent for long stretches. Its pattern count grows exponentially, and it cannot be produced by a simple morphic rule. He also shows the density of ones exists and is a transcendental number.
arxiv-2605-07742:
Samuel Brodie and four co-authors evaluate the Data Distribution Service as middleware for next-generation farm machinery networks. Tractors and implements from different makers currently talk over a slow CAN bus standard. A new Ethernet-based standard series aims at higher bandwidth. It needs middleware for discovery, data exchange, quality of service, and security.

They built a proof-of-concept design for a task controller and implement pair in C++ with the FastDDS library. They benchmarked it on representative embedded hardware under four security configurations. Security was expensive: signing and encryption cut peak throughput by roughly seventy to eighty-four percent in best-effort tests. Even so, the encrypted setup delivered about five thousand updates per second. They judge the service a plausible candidate, pending latency and interoperability work.
arxiv-2605-07842:
Cheng Cheng and two co-authors solve phase retrieval for a generalized transform used in optics and time-frequency analysis. The problem is to rebuild a signal from measurements that keep only magnitudes, discarding phase. For the short-time linear canonical transform, earlier work had settled uniqueness and sampling questions, but rebuild formulas, stability estimates, and robust algorithms were missing.

Working in a Gaussian shift-invariant signal space, they prove every signal is determined, up to a global phase constant, by its phaseless measurements on a specific semi-discrete set. They also give an explicit reconstruction formula. Stability on intervals turns out to depend on the widest gap between anchor points, not the interval's size, avoiding runaway blow-up. A practical algorithm with measured error guarantees for finite noisy samples completes the picture.
arxiv-2605-07942:
Florian Egli and eight co-authors predict a surprising resurrection in trapped-ion spectroscopy. For one ion, a narrow optical transition has a clean central carrier line flanked by motional sidebands. Move outside the Lamb-Dicke regime and the photon recoil smears strength across many sidebands, suppressing the carrier; adding ions densifies the spectrum and weakens it further. Intuition says longer chains should be worse.

Their quantum-mechanical model of excitation in linear ion chains says the opposite past a point. Sufficiently long chains concentrate the spectrum back into the carrier, restoring strong excitation even far from the single-ion Lamb-Dicke regime. The effect would enable efficient excitation of light ions at short wavelengths, and could benefit multi-ion optical clocks and mixed-species quantum-logic spectroscopy.
arxiv-2605-08142:
Yanbiao Ma, Fei Luo, Linfeng Zhang, Chuangxin Zhao, and coauthors study reasoning inside large language models as a moving process rather than a test score. Benchmarks label answers right or wrong, which mixes task success with the quality of the internal steps that produced them.

Tracking internal representations during inference, the team finds they self-organize onto low-dimensional manifolds inside the larger representation space. Compression alone is not enough, though. Stable reasoning appears only when three conditions hold together: enough expressivity, spontaneous manifold compression, and preserved information volume inside the compressed space. Models outside that regime show characteristic pathological dynamics, which the authors use to motivate new training ideas.
arxiv-2605-08442:
Jun Wen Leong separates two safety questions that agent designers often merge. Did a prompt injection get stored? And did it later get executed? In agents with persistent memory, poisoned instructions were written to memory in over ninety-seven percent of runs. Eventual execution ranged from zero to ninety-five percent. It had no link to the storage rate.

Leong calls this the injection-execution dissociation. A factorial experiment ran more than five thousand trials across nine open models. It tested six defenses at four architectural layers. The attacks used delayed triggers that survive across sessions through retrieval. The lesson is structural. Blocking storage cannot substitute for enforcing authority boundaries between remembering and acting.
arxiv-2605-08542:
Shouqiao Wang and Davide Crapis settle a question Paul Erdős posed about prime divisors of whole numbers. For each fixed position k, they study how often the k-th smallest prime factor of a number equals a given prime. Erdős asked whether this pattern always rises then falls in a single hump as the prime grows.

Earlier work settled small positions and suggested failure from the fourth position onward. Wang and Crapis prove failure for every position from four up, using prime gap estimates, certified computer checks, and a remainder based construction. Number theory gains a complete classification, closing a problem that partial results had left open for higher positions.
arxiv-2605-08642:
James Wells offers a descriptive account of why some physics work earns major prizes and honors while other strong work does not. At its center sits the Polydoxon, the structured set of theories still viable at a given time. Wells argues that highly rewarded contributions transform that set in recognizable ways.

Transformations come in four forms: adding viable theories, removing them, revealing deeper links among them, and enabling future moves through new methods or tools. Reward grows with a change's scope, centrality, depth, and future leverage. Science studies gains a unified lens that shifts attention from lone successes to how the whole landscape of viable theories moves.
arxiv-2605-08842:
Chang Liu, Boyu Shi, Xu Yang, and Xin Geng recycle the knowledge stored in mixture of experts language models to train new models faster. In such models, routed expert modules make knowledge traceable, and analysis shows a subset of experts fires across nearly all domains, holding generalizable knowledge tied to broad competence. Their XPERT framework finds those cross domain experts using inference alone, refines their representations through tensor decomposition, and adapts the extracted knowledge for reuse in other models.

On language understanding and dialogue benchmarks, models seeded with reused expert knowledge perform stronger and converge faster than strong baselines. Trained expert models become structured knowledge mines, not just end products.
arxiv-2605-09042:
Ye-eun Cho asks how word models take hints where some can mean not all. She asks if the test way sways the call. Calls asked in words can stray from a model's own odds spread. That gap clouds claims of skill. In a set design, Cho sets straight odds reads by the side of word asked calls. She runs both cross more than one model and set up. The graded strength of such hints is the gauge.

No way wins in a firm way. Acts swing with model line, prompt style, and task form. Graded hint slopes show in set model and state pairs just. Hint skill, she holds, is born of odds and task frame in play. Test design shapes the claims folks will make.
arxiv-2605-09142:
Ameya S Bhave, with Navnil Choudhury and Kanad Basu, presents DART-Q, a framework for decoding quantum error correction codes under hard real-time limits. Their 2026 study focuses on quantum low-density parity-check codes, where the classical decoder sits inside the control loop and must finish before strict deadlines. Each decode request is modeled as a job that arrives, waits, runs, and either meets its deadline or misses it.

Controlled tests vary memory pressure, admission rules, rescue policies, and pooled decoder capacity. A cached-summary layout lowers the memory fit boundary fourfold compared with an edge-based layout. Letting backlogs grow under overload sharply raises waiting time with little useful gain, while doubling capacity cuts missed deadlines dramatically in their setup. The work gives engineers a way to see which design choices decide whether a decoder stays viable when load and memory are tight.
arxiv-2605-09742:
Soydan and three colleagues reconciled two rival designs for sequence models that handle irregular time gaps. Selective state space models like Mamba gain expressive power by learning the time step from the input, but the step then stops meaning a real sampling interval. Continuous-time models like S5 keep that physical meaning yet stay linear and time-invariant, limiting expressiveness.

TIDES moves input-dependence off the step size and onto the diagonal state matrix, so the step keeps its physical role while per-token expressiveness survives. A new Fading Flash diagnostic jointly tests input-dependence and extrapolation to unseen step values, isolating failure modes that TIDES avoids by design. On large benchmarks, TIDES set the best average rank on UEA time-series classification and the Physiome-ODE regression test.
arxiv-2605-09842:
Singh and two colleagues compared machine learning with econometrics on United States Treasury yield-curve forecasting, using daily data over 47 years. The yield curve matters because every bond-market participant watches it, and bond markets dwarf equity markets. Yet machine learning's edge in time-series forecasting, especially in finance, remains disputed.

Methods tested included ARIMA and extensions, naive benchmarks, ensembles, recurrent networks, and several forecasting transformers. ARIMA and naive econometric models won overall, except in one time block. Among machine-learning methods, TimeGPT, LGBM, and recurrent networks did best. The paper also probed whether stationary or nonstationary inputs suit deep learning better, a practical question for forecasters.
arxiv-2605-10042:
Sadhukhan and three co-authors build a stats frame for learning user tastes from past choices, the repeat picks people make among a fixed set of options in tips and shopper choice. Gauging those tastes well drives custom future tips. Their model rests on a natural monotonicity rule: options chosen more often or more intensely in the past are likelier to be chosen again.

The approach widens a fixed-form ant-colony path-choice model without fixed forms, drawing on the generalised elephant random walk, and estimates preference probabilities by maximum likelihood under the monotonicity constraint. Theoretical guarantees for the estimator are derived, and both simulations and real-world data sets support its effectiveness. The first author was partly supported by an IMU Breakout Graduate Fellowship.
arxiv-2605-10142:
Cedro and Chlebus test whether scaling vision models improves the quality of their explanations, not just their predictions. Eleven vision models of growing depth and size come from the ResNet, DenseNet and Vision Transformer groups. Trained from scratch or pretrained, they are tested across three image sets with ground-truth masks. Five post-hoc explanation methods generate explanations per model, scored by two localisation metrics.

Across data sets and methods, greater depth and parameter count do not improve explanation quality in most comparisons, and smaller models often match or beat deeper ones. Pretraining lifts predictive scores and ties explanations to learned weights, but it does not steadily raise placement scores. Some models predict strongly while placement scores sit near zero, so accuracy alone cannot show whether guesses rest on annotated regions. Clarity of explanation, the authors argue, must be assessed when choosing models for safety-critical use.
arxiv-2605-10342:
Richard F. Katz and Peter Huybers link the rhythm of ice ages to fault spacing on the seafloor. Abyssal hills record normal faults formed at mid-ocean ridges. At fast-spreading ridges, seafloor spectra peak near 41 thousand years, matching obliquity-paced sea-level change in the Pleistocene. Their 2026 paper proposes a mechanism for that imprint.

Sea-level change alters mantle melting and magma supply at ridge axes. As the plate moves off axis and unbends, tensile stresses drive normal faulting. The authors extend elastic unbending theory with variable plate thickness and yield-weakening flexure, letting strain localize into discrete kinks read as faults. Shifts as small as 0.1 percent can phase-lock faulting to the forcing. Driven by the Pleistocene oxygen-isotope record, the model predicts spacings near 41 thousand years early on and near 100 thousand years later, matching observed spectra.
arxiv-2605-10442:
Pierre Le Jeune and six colleagues study how social bias emerges in open-ended language-model generation across languages. Most existing benchmarks center on English, use templates, or stick to pre-set stereotypes. Their 2026 paper introduces StereoTales, a dataset and evaluation pipeline covering 10 languages and 79 social-group attributes, with over 650,000 stories generated by 23 recent models.

Each story is annotated with the protagonist's social-group profile across 19 dimensions. Statistical tests identify more than 1,500 extra-common associations, rated for harm by 247 humans and by the same models. Three findings stand out. Every model evaluated emits serious harmful stereotypes in open-ended generation, regardless of size, and these associations are largely shared across makers. Prompt language strongly shapes which stereotypes appear, adapting by culture and amplifying bias against locally salient protected groups. Human and model harm judgments are broadly aligned, with disagreements focused on specific attribute classes rather than makers.
arxiv-2605-10642:
Weizhou Wang and two colleagues combine trained diffusion models with physics rules for science sampling. Trained diffusion models give strong learned priors, but each often covers only part of a system. Outside forces such as solvents, ions, and fields can reshape the full result. Their 2026 paper presents Generative Gibbs for Physics-Aware Sampling, or GG-PA. GG-PA joins partial priors with explicit physical context, with no retraining.

The frame treats the mix as inference over a joint target in a larger state space. Its Gibbs sampler turns exact as diffusion time nears zero, and stays exact at finite times when interactions are quadratic. Replica exchange over diffusion time speeds mixing. Tests on a double-well system, a lattice model, and peptide systems show GG-PA recovers context shifts and joint behavior no single prior shows.
arxiv-2605-10842:
Stéphane Bonhomme and Koen Jochmans construct moment functions that stay Neyman-orthogonal to any chosen order in parametric moment-condition models. Orthogonal moments shrug off errors from estimating nuisance parameters, offering a unified route to higher-order debiasing across econometrics.

Their construction needs no more extra nuisance parameters as the order rises, and the count can shrink to a single scalar if desired. That tractability matters for generalized method of moments estimation, bias correction, and U-statistics, where nuisance noise often dominates. Econometricians get a clean, scalable toolkit for squeezing bias out of moment-based inference.
arxiv-2605-11142:
Nikolaos Nakis and six others swap latent rank for spectral occupancy as the unit of analysis for latent graph models. Latent dimension is usually fixed before training as a brittle hyperparameter tuned by held-out performance. Yet learned factors are known only up to rotation and rescaling, so nominal rank rarely matches the quantity that drives behavior.

Their Spectra method works from eigenvalues of a learned positive semidefinite kernel, with trace normalization so fits can be compared. Its normalized eigenvalues spread into a distribution over the simplex. Shannon effective rank then sums up learned capacity and serves as a training control: one scalar shapes realized dimension during training, and bisection hits any desired value within the rank cap. Local regularity and monotonicity back the profile in theory. Across collaboration, social, biological, and infrastructure networks, Spectra gives capacity analysis that rank alone cannot.
arxiv-2605-11342: Choi and four colleagues use an active fluid made of microtubules to build and reshape actin-fascin fibre networks, which cannot form by heat alone. They probe the networks with active microrheology plus fluorescence imaging of strain around a probe. More motor protein widens pore sizes, thickens load-bearing bundles and raises local stiffness and its spread. At large strain both processed and raw networks soften and reshape, showing active stress can reprogram fibre mechanics.
arxiv-2605-11742: Xinrui Wang and four colleagues study online continual learning where class ranks shift as new data streams in. They define a setting in which each example is labeled at only one level of a changing rank system. Then they propose HALO, a method that blends classification heads guided by organized rank prototypes. It beat past methods on rank accuracy, error size, and steady learning.
arxiv-2605-12542: Zhao and eleven colleagues review Earth science foundation models along two axes: depth and breadth. Depth traces power growth from basic seeing through multi-mode thought to agentic science workflows. Breadth maps uses across Earth spheres and coupled system processes. The review covers key multi-mode models and lists over two hundred data sets and benchmarks across Earth science tasks. It also flags hard parts in multi-mode fusion, mixed data and science trust.
arxiv-2605-12742: Wang proves a spanning-tree count bound for pseudorandom graphs, extending Otter's classic result. Otter showed distinct unlabelled spanning trees in the complete graph grow like alpha to the power n, up to subexponential factors. That holds for an absolute constant alpha. Wang shows that for every epsilon below alpha, there are constants C and d0. Every (n, d, lambda)-graph with degree at least d0 and ratio d over lambda at least C has at least (alpha minus epsilon) to the power n unlabelled spanning trees.
arxiv-2605-13142: Rosenberg, Booth, Brubaker and Andrist tackle NHL playoff clinching with a constraint programming approach for n-day lookahead. It decides which outcome combinations over the next n days guarantee a team a postseason spot. Their custom tree search uses preprocessing, pruning and node ordering, plus a constraint programming check that tests clinching by hunting for a counterexample elimination. Tests on hundreds of scenarios from public NHL data for 2021-22 through 2024-25 show the method extends to elimination proofs, President's Trophy clinching and any seed.
arxiv-2605-13242: John Lazarsfeld and four colleagues explain slow optimistic multiplicative weights convergence in zero-sum games. Recent work found slow instances. Their analysis views dual iterates as optimistic skew-gradient descent. Energy is dissipative over dual iterates, and tight bounds quantify simplex-boundary bottlenecks. That yields a new linear last-iterate KL rate for unique interior Nash games, with optimal dependence. Their insights also give new uniform-rate separations, including a tilde-O duality-gap rate of T to the minus one half for two-by-two games.
arxiv-2605-13542: Chengzhi Shen and ten colleagues introduce RealICU, a hindsight-annotated benchmark testing whether language models grasp long intensive-care records. RealICU instead labels data once senior physicians review the full patient trajectory, across patient status, acute problems, suggested actions and red-flag actions. Two datasets are released: RealICU-Gold with 930 windows from 94 patients, and RealICU-Scale with 11,862 windows from Oracle, a physician-validated labeller. Existing models perform poorly, with a recall-safety trade-off and anchoring bias, while a structured agent, ICU-Evo, improves reasoning but safety gaps remain.
