arxiv-2605-13842: Hareesh Thuruthipilly and 21 colleagues explore domain adaptation for cross-survey detection of low-surface-brightness galaxies. They train models on the Dark Energy Survey and search for such galaxies in the Kilo-Degree Survey Data Release 5. An ensemble of one convolutional neural network and two transformer models fitted on DES cutouts is applied to KiDS DR5 imaging. They identify 20,180 low-surface-brightness galaxies and 434 ultra-diffuse galaxies in KiDS DR5.
arxiv-2605-14142: Belhadji, Sharp and Marzouk introduce mean shift particle systems for Bayesian inference. Adding up a distribution known only through its unnormalized density is a central Bayesian task. Their methods guess such means with a few weighted samples, a quadrature rule, built by a particle system that shrinks mean discrepancy to the target. The approach extends the old mean shift algorithm and recent optimal quantization methods to smooth distributions. Its motion ignores the unknown normalizing constant and comes in gradient-free and gradient-informed versions.
arxiv-2605-14642: Recke and Hudoba de Badyn present a distributionally robust model predictive control framework for virtual power plants under electricity price uncertainty. One model links buildings, battery storage and renewable generation under weather and market signals. Data-driven forecasts feed quantile-based uncertainty sets that adapt to forecast spread, yielding a tractable controller. On Nordic weather and market data, gains up to about eight tenths of a percent over standard predictive control are claimed for small ambiguity radii.
arxiv-2605-14842: Ventura, Hirsch, Bitton, Cohen and Reichart formalise abstract image editing, where people communicate through concepts like mood rather than literal commands. Current benchmarks focus on explicit instructions, leaving abstract instructions underexplored. The authors introduce Entity-Rubrics, a framework splitting abstract edits into entity-level assessments that correlate strongly with human judgement. Alongside it comes AbstractEdit, the first benchmark for abstract image editing across diverse real scenes. Eleven leading models struggle to balance intent and preservation, defaulting to under-editing or over-editing.
arxiv-2605-15042: Wuyang Li and six colleagues present EverAnimate, a light post-training method for minute-scale human animation. Chunk-by-chunk generation drifts in two ways: backgrounds degrade, and character identity slips. EverAnimate anchors generation to a persistent latent memory that carries identity and motion across chunks, plus a restorative flow objective that corrects drift within each chunk. With only lightweight tuning it beats long-animation rivals at both 10 seconds and 90 seconds, with gains growing at longer horizons.
arxiv-2605-15342: Arsha Nagrani and eight colleagues introduce Minerva-Ego, a benchmark for complex egocentric video reasoning. Standard benchmarks score only final answers, ignoring intermediate reasoning, and usually stay in text. Minerva-Ego adds multi-step multimodal questions with spatiotemporally dense human-annotated reasoning traces from egocentric video. State-of-the-art models still trail humans by a large margin, but prompting frontier models with hints about where and when to look yields substantial gains, pinpointing the gap.
arxiv-2605-15442: Alexander Polok and five others study how synthetic conversational data shapes multi-talker speech recognition and speaker diarization. Fake data makes up for scarce chat tapes, but simulation choices matter. Their FastMSS simulator lets them vary turn-taking, source domain, acoustic augmentation, and mixing for leading systems. Optimal recipes prove task-linked: more speech overlap helps ID but harms speaker splits, while broad source diversity beats exact domain matching. Fake-only training nears real-data baselines, and joint training a lot beats real-only training.
arxiv-2605-15542: Yichao Liu, Huawen Shen, Liu Yu, Shiyu Liu, Zeyu Chen, and Yu Zhou present DRS-GUI, a no-train frame that helps multimodal models find screen items. Busy high-resolution screens hide the right items amid clutter. A light perceptor probes with three human-like moves: focus, shift, and scatter. A tree-search planner times those moves. A quality score then picks the most apt region. It lifts grounding on ScreenSpot-Pro by 14 percent for both broad and GUI-tuned models.
arxiv-2605-15742: Federico Butori and Yassine Tahraoui study stretching of FENE polymers in random turbulent flow. Under a scaling with main space scale near N-inverse, main time scale tau and white-in-time noise, the stochastic Fokker-Planck density equation converges weakly as N grows to a deterministic limit. A new second-order operator in the limit expresses average flow stretching. Unusually, the limit is obtained pathwise, with no averaging over flow realizations. Taking tau to zero then identifies the stationary distribution of polymer length.
arxiv-2605-15942: Chenhao Wang and three colleagues propose Decomposed Vision-Language Alignment for fine-grained open-vocab segmentation. Open-vocab models struggle with new category-attribute mixes, since descriptions arrive as whole sentences mixing several meaning units. The framework splits textual prompts into a concept token plus attribute tokens, allowing separate cross-modal links per unit. A Feature-Gated Cross-Attention module builds attribute gating maps to fuse information by products, keeping compositional meaning. Per-token scores combine in log-space for stable, clear matching, lifting generalization to unseen attribute-category pairs.
arxiv-2605-16342: Karimi Monsefi and six others propose DACA-GRPO, a denoising-aware credit boost for RL in diffusion language models. Current methods treat all denoising steps as equal and rely on biased, high-variance odds guesses. Denoising Progress Scores pull per-token weights from midway guesses at no extra forward cost. Stratified Masking Likelihood splits token spots into strata so each token is guessed with most of the sequence as context. Applied atop three GRPO base methods, it gains up to 36.3 points on constraint tasks and 7.4 points on code writing.
arxiv-2605-17042: Qian's team proposes the first thermal-only system for private crowd counting, dropping RGB at inference. RGB-thermal counting works, but RGB capture raises privacy concerns, and misalignment weakens fusion. Depth-to-RGB diffusion serves as a bridge, yielding signals that boost thermal views. Single-step LCM denoising gives signals faithful to depth structure, while multi-step denoising decouples signals from control input and adds errors that hurt accuracy. Tests on two sets match leading RGB-T methods while needing only thermal input at run time, cutting RGB capture.
arxiv-2605-17142: Xodarev proves four linked results for signature volatility models, which price assets from iterated path integrals. First, strong solutions exist for all time and are unique. Second, he splits the no-arbitrage rule from the risk that finite transforms blow up. Third, he pins down when a market is complete, via a depth number tied to the price path. Fourth, he splits hedging error into a hedge part plus a bounded leftover. One design rule ties all four results into a single frame.
arxiv-2605-17342: Huang and colleagues split human preferences into transitive and cyclic parts to fix a flaw in alignment models that tangle the two. Their Hybrid Reward-Cyclic model separates scalar hierarchy from vector cycles with game theory, while Dynamic Self-Play Preference Optimization treats alignment as a shifting game heading for Nash equilibrium. Tests show faster convergence, higher accuracy in mixed settings, and gains on RewardBench 2 and downstream chat benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-17642: Alishahi and colleagues describe tabular data using copula transforms and kernel density models. Tabular generation considers numeric, grouped, or ordinal columns, aiming for new rows matching the original distribution. Recent progress mostly used expensive methods employing one-hot encoding, VAEs, and diffusion. Modeling the distribution with a kernel density estimate nearly matches previous methods, yet with almost no training time. The method is scalable, running on much larger datasets than prior methods. Kernel estimates let the model be stored as a coreset, the first for generative modeling.
arxiv-2605-18542: Lee Ricketson and Jingwei Hu extend, in a 2026 paper, an explicit, energy-conserving PIC scheme to the relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell system. The method rests on a solvable optimization problem, local to each particle, enforcing exact energy conservation. Although answers are not always real, such cases stay rare enough for practical settings to allow big conservation gains over old explicit schemes. The scheme works with Yee/FDTD and PSATD field solvers and is checked on standard relativistic tests.
arxiv-2605-18642: Tingwei Chen and two co-authors benchmark, in a 2026 paper, three language models on Gauss-Seidel AC power flow computation for a three-bus system across four prompt formats. Gemini 2 point 5 Pro with the simplest narrative prompt achieves the lowest error, zero point two five seven MW/MVar mean absolute error. Its JSON-structured prompt raises error about threefold. GPT-3 point 5 Turbo fails on at least 90 percent of cases under all formats. A 100-case replication confirms the ordering, yet no configuration proves reliable enough as a direct numerical solver.
arxiv-2605-19042: Ying-Hua Huang and three colleagues tackle machine unlearning for models sharing one backbone, where erasing one task can damage the others. They cover two settings: erasing an instance from every task, or only from selected tasks. Their method pairs task-specific gradient projection, which confines updates to task subspaces, with gradient orthogonalisation separating forget signals from retain signals. On two vision benchmarks spanning five tasks, it cuts interference by about 30 percent for full-task removal and about 53 percent for partial-task removal, beating the strongest baseline.
arxiv-2605-19342: Tianrun Xu and colleagues enrich latent visual reasoning, where models reason over compact image codes instead of explicit pictures. Current latent codes lean on visual supervision alone and lack the semantic detail needed for varied region-level tasks. Their SLVR framework first learns region codes under fine-grained attribute supervision, then aligns them across multiple queries about the same region with a grouped policy optimizer. Built on roughly 400 thousand attribute labels and 800 thousand question samples, it proves more robust and semantically consistent than prior latent methods.
arxiv-2605-19442: Duda and team solve exactly the dynamics of a single-photon emitter in a waveguide closed by a partly transparent mirror. Using a local-photon approach to the Schrodinger equation, they find the decay is generally non-Markovian, with a non-exponential profile. The decay looks exponential only long after the emitter-mirror round trip, and turns truly exponential in the Markovian limit where that trip is neglected. They also derive the spatial and spectral shape of the emitted photon wave packet and show how the environment reshapes it.
arxiv-2605-19742: Nakamura derives a bid-ask spread and welfare split for the Glosten-Milgrom trading model when the market maker sees trade direction through a binary flip channel. Under a committed Bayesian rule the equilibrium spread equals the informed-trader fraction times one minus twice flip probability times range. The welfare split finds a per-trade transfer from liquidity pools to traders, the privacy subsidy, mirroring the Gaussian-Kyle analog. The result extends the privacy-subsidy concept from Gaussian to discrete two-state markets for MPC matching engines using private disclosure.
arxiv-2605-20342: Zuhao Yang and nine co-workers present ParaVT, the first multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for video tool calling. It sends time crops in one turn. They let one bad crop spread errors and cost grow with turns. Reinforcement learning hits the Tool Prior Paradox: tool priors shake format and open the skip-tool shortcut. PARA-GRPO adds a format reward at spots and frame-budget randomization favoring tool calls over skipping. On six benchmarks, ParaVT beats Qwen3-VL by 7.9%, and PARA-GRPO lifts compliance from 0.13 to 0.64.
arxiv-2605-20442: Hasan and Shahid map emotional dynamics among AI agents on Moltbook, a social network for agentic systems. They build an emotion-aware framework that sorts agent text into fine-grained emotion classes, yielding profiles across agents and contexts. A Persona-Stimulus-Reaction test then checks whether emotional replies line up across similar contexts. Agents show distinct emotional signatures, with stability varying by interaction context.
arxiv-2605-20542: Luis Medina-Dozal and three colleagues model a two-level atom coupled to two quantized light modes, off resonance. The single-mode version is exactly solvable, but the two-mode version has infinite-dimensional invariant subspaces despite conserved total excitation. Their scheme splits off an exactly solvable semiclassical part, the atom meeting the mean fields of both modes. Remaining quantum fluctuations are handled by unitary transforms, and the results match numerical solutions closely.
arxiv-2605-21142: Yorgo Chamoun builds a general way to form categories of combinatorial manifolds. These are objects that meet a local rule at each point. He places them inside larger categories of relational presheaves, using unique factorization systems. The result is a model category whose cofibrant objects are exactly the manifolds. He tests the method on grid-like precubical sets and on a new abstract proof of Kleene's theorem.
arxiv-2605-21242: Haechan Mark Bong and colleagues tackle robot skill prediction. The task is to match a plain-language task to the body skills it needs, such as flying, wheels, legs, water, or hands. No labeled task-to-skill data existed, so they built a synthetic set with language-model help and label checks. A small ensemble of two tuned sentence encoders, about one hundred thirty-three million parameters, hit eighty-three point five percent on a two-hundred-task test. That beat far larger general models tested with no tuning.
arxiv-2605-21342: A. U. Kapoor and co-authors identify boxy and peanut-shaped dwarf galaxies in the Perseus cluster with Euclid Early Release Observations. Dwarfs in dense clusters face tidal interactions that alter shape and motion, yet boxy isophotes remain poorly understood in dwarfs. With a cumulative light fraction method for the shape parameter c-four, suited to low surface brightness, they select about one hundred ninety early-type systems from about eleven hundred dwarfs. Thirteen dwarfs show significantly boxy isophotes, interpreted via mock observations of tidally transformed dwarfs.
arxiv-2605-21442: Mark Obozov and co-authors introduce torchtune, a PyTorch-native library for post-training large language models. Post-training is the main way to adapt open-weight models, yet many fine-tuning tools trade openness and extensibility for ease of use or hardware speed. Torchtune streamlines fine-tuning, tests, and deployment workflows. It emphasizes modular design, hackability, and direct access to PyTorch parts.
arxiv-2605-21542: Andi Xu presents a lag-gated neural audit framework for entity-conditioned lag heterogeneity in time panels. Country time panels are widely used in empirical work. Researchers check how entities respond to past signals over varied horizons. Current tools usually lack directly checkable entity lag summaries. He proposes AC-GATE, making effective lags structural outputs rather than after-the-fact notes. It builds on Moderated Distributed Lag, using observable entity proxies to set lag-weight spreads over past observations.
arxiv-2605-21742: Samuel McDowell, Nathan Stromberg, and Lalitha Sankar tackle class imbalance in prior-data fitted networks, which classify tables from context instead of weight updates. Rare classes suffer most when classes are uneven, yet loss-based fixes do not fit these models' in-context learning. The authors adapt several classical remedies and test them on tabular tasks. Thresholding works exceptionally well, thanks to the models' calibration, while downsampling matches it and cuts inference cost. The findings give practitioners two proven, cheap remedies for skewed tabular data.
arxiv-2605-21842: Athanasios Zeris presents Energy-Gated Attention, which gates value aggregation by the spectral energy of key token embeddings. Standard attention treats all tokens as equally salient. In turbulent fluids, high-energy coherent structures carry most energy and govern transport. The author argues tokens behave in the same way. A learned linear projection finds the main spectral mode of the embedding field. On TinyShakespeare the method cuts validation loss by zero point one zero three with twelve thousand four hundred eighty added parameters, and Penn Treebank confirms dataset independence.
arxiv-2605-21942: Sheng Zhao and Peng-Bo Li introduce a new photon blockade mechanism that uses three-body interactions between one photonic mode and two qubits. Standard blockade schemes suffer a purity-brightness trade-off that blocks high-performance single-photon sources. Their mechanism breaks that trade-off, reaching extreme purity and high brightness at once, well beyond prior schemes. It also stands up to thermal noise, and it avoids unwanted oscillations in the delayed correlation function. The work thus points toward single-photon sources that stay robust, a key quantum resource.
arxiv-2605-22042: Papathanasiou and co-authors develop a method for hydroelastic flexure of arbitrarily shaped ice shelves forced by long ocean waves. Flexure under long waves stresses Antarctic ice shelves, amplifying fractures and contributing to calving. Their model follows Kirchhoff-Love plate theory for a plate floating on shallow water under linearized conditions, extended to varied shelf shapes. A Dirichlet-to-Neumann map bounds the open-ocean domain. After verification, the method studies how deflection responds to shelf shape, wave direction, and grounded fraction, identifying resonant responses across a frequency range.
arxiv-2605-22142: Kim and co-authors study short-term to long-term memory transfer for graphs under partial observability. Learning under partial observability requires deciding what to retain, yet most memory approaches ignore symbolic transfer from short-term to long-term memory. They cast transfer as a value-based decision task: for each observed triple, the agent keeps or drops it before long-term insertion. Their methods beat baselines, and a lightweight short-term-only variant performs best, keeping navigation- and query-relevant facts.
arxiv-2605-22542: Cho and Erk offer Scene Abstraction, shaped maps of word scenes across usage contexts. Coffee and tea share many properties, yet evoke different scenes. These placed sides of word meaning are real, but hidden in most maps. Each scene pairs a Contextual Scene with an Expression set, built via few-shot prompting. The team offers a shaped framework and COCA-Scenes (520 instances, 26 keywords). Two experiments show scenes are reliably identifiable (82.4% accuracy, +11.8 pp over text-only embeddings), and scene profiles beat ATOMIC-based alternatives (86.4% preference).
arxiv-2605-22642: Chi and others train spreadsheet agents by reinforcement learning inside a realistic Excel setting, replacing prompt only agents that falter on long multi step workflows. Their Spreadsheet-RL system gathers paired start and goal sheets from online forums and adds a finance and supply chain benchmark. Training runs inside a Spreadsheet Gym exposing Excel tools through a Python sandbox. Tests lift a Qwen3 4B model from 12.0 percent to 23.4 percent on SpreadsheetBench and from 8.4 percent to 17.2 percent on the new domain set.
arxiv-2605-22942: Carrillo-Perez improves vision-to-chart buoy association for the MaCVi 2026 challenge with a small change to a DETR-based fusion baseline. The baseline forced the transformer to learn the world-to-image projection implicitly from distance and bearing queries. Instead, a dedicated QueryMLP network predicts each buoy's waterline contact point in the picture from chart data and IMU orientation. The added spatial prior lifted the entry to second place, with an overall score of 0.7386.
arxiv-2605-23242: Farooque and five coauthors present Cogniscope, an open testbed for early-risk AI over time. It faces drift, sparse notes, and delayed evidence. It combines a fake engine making traces tied to risk paths, and a Chrome add-on recording use logs and answers on YouTube. The benchmark holds 200,000 fake records from 200 users, 200 days, a 504-session set across nine, an 18-table schema, and metrics. Cogniscope is not medical and claims no medical proof. Tests show fit signals split fake risk states, while rule-based sorting stays hard.
arxiv-2605-23542: Garnero and colleagues advance the gaseous photomultiplier, a photon detector pairing a cathode with a chamber avalanche for Cherenkov particle ID at a future Belle II upgrade. The device hit 25-picosecond timing in 2022, but a 2023 test with a window and cathode fell to 70 picoseconds. The team traces the loss to photon feedback, ultraviolet light from de-exciting gas molecules that overlaps the main signal. A new 10-gigasample digitizer plus beam and cosmic tests split the feedback signal from the true one and probe a hardier lanthanum hexaboride photocathode.
arxiv-2605-23642: Waqar and colleagues revisit fast fluid antenna access, which fights interference by moving the receiver antenna port by port. Standard studies assume each terminal probes all ports and knows the split everywhere. They ask whether a terminal can act as if it knew per-port interference while observing few ports. Their copula framework learns the joint dependence of signal, channel, and interference across ports, then infers them. An attention-copula model trained under partial masks reaches error near ten to the minus four once observed ports exceed spatial freedom.
arxiv-2605-23842: Emilio Torrente-Lujan builds a dissipative colored fluid in lower dimensions. He gets it by squeezing a viscous conformal fluid on a group manifold. Off diagonal pieces of its stress tensor turn into non-Abelian color currents. Its shear tensor seeds shear, bulk-like and vector dissipation. The paper maps the equation of state, sound speed, color and entropy currents and first order transport coefficients. It untangles reduction's frame ambiguity and traces how the second law survives descent. It is a toy model for quark gluon plasma.
arxiv-2605-23942: Cattani and Motta Monte-Serrat model the mind as a feedback loop in which states evolve through internal change, interpretation, and a check for same meaning. Their update rule sends each state through inner change, an interpretive mapping, and a projection that enforces semantic equivalence, with fixed-point and contraction arguments securing stability. A categorical version captures how the pieces compose. A language example shows context-dependent reading settling into a stable meaning class, tying dynamical systems, category theory, and cognitive modelling into one frame.
arxiv-2605-24042: Bell tests whether hidden-state privacy has a middle ground and finds none in the Gaussian class. Of 1536 Gaussian releases tried, zero give both middling utility and middling privacy against an adaptive attacker. A Fisher-ball lower bound proves the gap: every full-rank Gaussian release at order-one utility leaks a direction whose signal grows with width. One diagonal inverse-Fisher release is minimax-optimal and uniquely safe on a 32-layer grid. Yet it sits on a privacy-utility edge, pushing the field toward co-design.
arxiv-2605-24242: Yu develops unified exact answer rules for optimal trading through stepwise limit-order placement. Rather than steering only a big order's trading speed, the paper sets how single limit orders should be quoted. The model covers signal drift, price impact, stock risk, and trading risk. Four rules are set: mean final wealth and CARA payoff, each with and without a running stock penalty. For general impact and penalty functions, all four reduce to a three-way structure solved exactly, giving exact value functions and optimal quotes.
arxiv-2605-24442: Psomas and eight co-authors benchmark mixed image search for Earth viewing, pairing a source image with a text note. How modern methods transfer to Earth viewing pictures remains little known. The team adapts and tests sample methods with six vision-language bases on PatternCom. They also add xView2-CIR, a change-centric set for harm watch. Training-free methods give strong marks, while change-centric search poses new hurdles because scene look must be preserved. The study sets a handy benchmark for mixed search in archive browsing.
arxiv-2605-24742: Emanuele Guidotti and Sara Puglioli align molecular graph explanations with chemical identity through InChIfied Invariants. Drawings of one compound can yield other representations, scrambling predictions. Their traits rest on the InChI standard and stay stable under such changes. On one million PubChem graphs, they give same results for equivalent graphs in 99.62 percent of cases, against under one percent for standard Daylight ones. Across MoleculeNet tasks they preserve performance while making attributions match by design.
arxiv-2605-24842: Masaru Yamada studies how translator labor became core data capital for AI. Translation memories and parallel corpora link source and target text one to one, making them prized training data for machine translation. Yet translators sold renditions as contract goods, cut into technical objects and treated as analysis data under copyright law, losing attribution. The paper names appropriation without consumption: mining works for stats without reading them. It also names the invisible teacherisation of translators, who taught AI through memories, post-editing, and quality checks with no credit.
arxiv-2605-24942: Narmeen Oozeer recasts language-model steering as Riemannian geodesic computation. Steering tweaks internal activations to shift later behavior. Recent nonlinear steering defines transforms without learning an explicit geometry. Newer geometry-aware methods learn one, but demand labeled centroids plus cyclic or sequential structure. Oozeer's framework recovers linear and labeled-spline steering as geodesics under particular metrics. A Hellinger-distance metric, learned by an encoder over a small concept schema, needs no per-prompt labels or topology prior. It reliably steers models onto target classes in arithmetic tests.
arxiv-2605-25042: Weimin Bai and colleagues propose Principled Posterior Matching, a way to invert diffusion models without rough KL loss. Score-based inverse methods rely on that rough step, causing mode collapse and shaky uncertainty guesses. Exact KL tuning uses the Fisher divergence integral, with a usable gradient form. It joins variational inference with wide divergences for variety and uncertainty, and one-shot inference for rapid single-step rebuilds. Tested on filling in, high-detail fluorescence microscopy, and radio black-hole imaging, it shows varied posterior capture and sound uncertainty.
arxiv-2605-25142: Leonardo Teodoro, Kemuel L. Vieira, and Saulo Queiroz study the Brazilian e-Voting interface under TEMPEST attacks. In an attack, an eavesdropper with software-defined radios recovers information from emanations. The authors emulate the machine with a VGA monitor using available specifications. High image contrast, minimal information, and a ban on other electronics in polling stations yield a simple signature observable through a wall. No actual voting hardware was used; the results raise susceptibility concerns.
arxiv-2605-25242: Cameron Dufault, Scott Xu, and Alan Moses train a model that pairs bacterial gene switches with the proteins they control. It works in the style of systems that link pictures to captions. Their method, called C3P, learns from 88 million promoter-protein pairs instead of rebuilding DNA sequences from scratch. Tested on curated labels for gene control, its learned switch patterns beat leading genome models by several fold. It also finds genes switched together with no lab data, at a fraction of the usual training cost.
arxiv-2605-25442: Nitish Shukla and Arun Ross recover the two faces hidden inside a morphed face image, beyond merely detecting morphs. Their reference-free framework uses multimodal language models to guide coupled diffusion reconstruction, drawing embeddings from intermediate model layers. Those embeddings supply reasoning about attributes and identity that complements pixel detail. Both constituent faces are synthesized jointly in RGB space, preserving consistency and fine detail without lossy text cycles. Tests show middle layers carry the most identity information, and RGB demorphing beats latent-space methods by 30 to 40 percent at strict points.
arxiv-2605-25642: Barbato, Sabina de Lis and Segura de León study the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of the weighted 1-Laplacian operator. They prove it equals the weighted Cheeger constant. The proof follows the weighted p-Laplacian's first Dirichlet eigenvalue as p approaches 1. When the weight is Lipschitz-continuous, the limit of eigenvalues exists and equals the weighted Cheeger constant, and normalized eigenfunctions converge to a bounded limit function. For general weights, they identify the first eigenvalue with the same constant and prove its eigenfunction is bounded.
arxiv-2605-25742: Boudabra gives a systematic study of p-Brownian convergence, the notion he introduced to study planar Skorokhod embedding stability. The first part shows shape aspects of it. The second part turns the notion into a metric between domains, placed within optimal transport theory. Results include long-run trends for scaled domains, with computed cases. The paper thus turns it from a stability tool into a full metric scheme for domains.
arxiv-2605-25842: Dutta and Aditya present MuCRASP, a structured pruning framework for vision language models preserving step-by-step thought. Pruning ignores thought: pivot tokens decide consistency, and unimodal methods ignore cross-modal differences. MuCRASP targets critical parts, preserving cross modal alignment under a budget. On four models across three tests, it preserves thought under compression. At 30 percent pruning it scores 8.87 against 7.32 on physical tasks. It holds consistency up to 50 percent pruning.
arxiv-2605-25942: Peterson and seven colleagues release a large dataset for spotting drones at long range. Shared airspace is growing busier, so distant detection matters for safety. The set holds over one hundred thousand high-resolution colour images from 128 flight videos. Range labels cover the whole set, and nearly thirty thousand infrared images pair with colour frames. The authors call it one of the first drone sets to combine very high resolution with paired infrared images.
arxiv-2605-26142: Rogers and twenty-two colleagues make the case for white dwarf exoplanet science from Hubble to the future Habitable Worlds Observatory. White dwarfs, the end state of 97 percent of Milky Way stars, reveal the bulk makeup of rocky bodies they accrete. Up to half of single white dwarfs show metal lines from such polluted material. High-resolution ultraviolet spectra are essential for volatile elements needed for habitability studies and rock-forming elements that constrain interiors. Hubble's COS and STIS spectrographs remain the only facility able to do this science soon.
arxiv-2605-26242: Shashwat Singh, Tal Linzen, and Shauli Ravfogel's 2026 paper asks whether large language models can truly report their own internal states. A test must need privileged access beyond input cues. It must also need second-order reasoning about first-order representations, where the two accounts predict different outcomes. Re-examining two popular paradigms, they find input-only classifiers match the models' predictions in one case. Models fail to separate internal tampering from input meddling in the other, leaving current evidence insufficient.
arxiv-2605-26342: Adrien Kachkachi uses affine surfaces to fully describe the real-time paths of a homogeneous vector field in two complex dimensions. He proves a continuous rotation number exists in the same space and stays constant along real-time paths. The paper then describes paths sorted by their rotation number. The build gives a full path picture from a single conserved value, in a 2026 paper.
arxiv-2605-26642: Hyunchul Bae and Heejin Ahn tackle team perception when new partners with unknown sensors join after deployment. Shared sight boosts 3D detection, yet most methods assume known partner encoders and fail on fresh LiDAR counts or architectures. Their ALF frame lifts tiny box messages into ego-compatible features by blending object cues with scene context. On V2X-Real, across 64 zero-shot cases, it beats the best prior baseline by 35.91 percent in relative mAP at 0.7 while sending just 120 bytes per agent per frame.
arxiv-2605-26842: Li and seven colleagues present MONA, an optimizer that adds Nesterov-style acceleration to the Muon optimizer for large language model training. The acceleration term, drawn from a moving average of gradient changes, adds curvature-aware corrections while keeping Muon's spectral-norm regularization. Across mixture-of-experts pretraining from 1B to 68B parameters, MONA beats both Muon and AdamW. Fine-tuned on the 68B model, it reaches top scores on capability, math, and coding benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-26942: Sigloch and Benzmüller build a hybrid check system for language-model outputs in data-sensitive domains, pairing formal symbolic checks with neural semantic analysis. Logic checks structured inputs with decidable guarantees, while embedding similarity catches hallucinations that formal methods miss. A parallel actor-based pipeline runs both tracks, dodging the biases of prompt-based self-checks. Tested on a medical device damage reporting system, it detects over 83 percent of entity hallucinations and 72 percent of semantic fabrications, while cutting report time by 30 percent.
arxiv-2605-27042: Eykholt and five co-authors report penetration tests on large-scale agent systems, asking whether proprietary products resist better than open-source ones. Many agent flaws, they find, are not novel but recurring weakness classes long seen in prior computing systems. Execution-capable agents act as unbounded, self-modifying programs touching many stack layers, imposing a heavy security burden. The paper presents findings from two 2025 tests of proprietary products and assesses whether agent security posture has improved.
arxiv-2605-27242: Fathi and Gómez study lensing by black holes wrapped in dark matter halos of self-interacting scalar fields, with NFW-type halos for comparison. They rebuild the spacetime numerically through the Einstein cluster method. Then they compute photon sphere radii, critical impact parameters, Einstein rings, image positions, separations, magnifications, and time delays, with attention to M87 star and Sagittarius A star. Halo effects shift most observables only slightly from the Schwarzschild case, so models stay nearly degenerate, but time delays between relativistic images amplify the halo signal most clearly.
arxiv-2605-27342: Ovidiu-Zeno Lipan and colleagues classify memristor hysteresis loops by counting their self-crossings. They treat the crossing count as a stable integer invariant, splitting a six-dimensional parameter space into regions divided by computable catastrophe surfaces. The count changes only at self-tangencies or cusp points, giving a complete classification of multi-lobed loop shapes.
arxiv-2605-27542: Castillo rethinks classical orthogonal polynomials from a broader functional viewpoint. The theory runs on subsets of the complex plane stable under half-step shifts, with both notions read in the dual of a locally convex polynomial space. The framework separates truly new families from fake ones, and for plain quadratic and non-torsion q-exponential cases the regularity tests hold as full if-and-only-if statements.
arxiv-2605-27642: Pitipat Kongsomjit, Suryansh Goyal, and Jacob Whitehill train a model to translate soft prompt embeddings into plain language. Their translator verbalizes what a soft prompt learned, and those wordings used as standalone prompts beat baselines, showing they carry genuine task information. On average the wordings retain 32 percent of the original soft prompt's performance.
arxiv-2605-27842: Sun and colleagues solve a hard wave problem: finding the vibration patterns of materials whose structure repeats almost, but not quite, regularly. Their spectral method lifts the one- and two-dimensional problems into higher-dimensional periodic spaces, then maps answers back with a check based on weighted averages. Tests on continuous media show accurate, sturdy, scalable results.
arxiv-2605-28042: Liu O. Martin, Lucas Bandarkar, and Nanyun Peng shrink translation models by pruning experts a generalist language model does not need for translation. Because multilingual skills separate cleanly, half the experts can go with negligible loss and no retraining. A brief fine-tune then recovers baseline quality with three-quarters pruned, and nearly nine-tenths pruned stays usable.
arxiv-2605-28142: Aleksei Arzhantsev, Otmane Sakhi, and Nicolas Chopin rethink self-consistency for language-model reasoning. Instead of sharpening whole outputs, which entangle reasoning traces with final answers, they target the sharpened answer marginal: answers backed by many plausible paths. A simple parallel sampling scheme approximates that target, beating standard power sampling on math and coding tests while running far faster.
arxiv-2605-28342: Kishony and colleagues mitigate quantum errors cheaply by checking auxiliary qubits that should return to zero. Measuring these qubits at chosen circuit points flags corrupted shots for discard, with corruption likelihood judged from each measurement's backward light cone. Simulations cut the false-negative rate by about ten percent while discarding only about one percent of valid shots.
arxiv-2605-28642: Yexing Du and seven colleagues build ESRT, an edge-cloud framework for speech-to-text translation that keeps raw voice on the device. Pure on-device models strain under resource limits, while cloud systems waste bandwidth and risk privacy by sending raw audio. ESRT trains compact models with multi-task curriculum learning and sends only a compressed tensor to the cloud. On the FLEURS benchmark it leads speech-translation performance across 45 languages, cutting transmitted size roughly fivefold and tenfold for its two variants while keeping speech on-device.
arxiv-2605-28742: Linas Nasvytis and five colleagues present CORE, Contrastive Reflection, a non-parametric learning method that improves reasoning from verifiable rewards. CORE compares past reasoning traces to yield insights, short natural-language notes on strategies and constraints separating successful from unsuccessful attempts. Across four reasoning tasks, CORE gains faster than weight-based and prompt-based rivals while using fewer rollouts. With as few as five training samples under fixed rollout budgets, it posts top performance in most task-data regimes, and it needs fewer prompt tokens than prompt-based baselines.
arxiv-2605-29042: Aarav Sane, Karthik Sivachandran, and Rohan Paleja propose Differentiable Belief-based Opponent Shaping, treating each observer's belief as the shaped opponent state. It works through k-step softmax-Bayes belief dynamics, rather than rewarding tricks or teamwork outright, letting the optimal strategy grow from the environment's reward structure. The belief-space formulation extends to multiple observers by pooling gradients over their guessed belief trajectories. In hidden-role games, it outperforms PPO and BBM, with the largest gains in mixed-goal settings.
arxiv-2605-29342: Vishal Muthuvel constructs Whittaker functions for SL(m,Z) induced from those for SL(n,Z). Starting from Jacquet's function on the generalized upper half-plane, he restricts it to a block-diagonal embedding. This yields a Whittaker function for the smaller group when Langlands parameters meet a sum. Under that rule, the new function carries shifted parameters and keeps the first entries of the old character tuple. This complements Ishii and Stade's step-down formulas, while the new build jumps from n to m in one step.
arxiv-2605-29442: Ningzhi Tang studies coding-agent failures in developer sessions. Benchmark analyses miss developer experience. The study covers over twenty thousand sessions from over sixteen hundred repositories across IDE and CLI workflows. Misalignment means a breakdown visible through developer pushback, tagged by form, cause, cost, and resolution. Seven recurring forms emerge: reading projects, interpreting intent, following rules, bounding actions, coding, and reporting progress. About nine tenths of episodes cost effort and trust rather than irreversible damage, yet over nine tenths of resolutions still need explicit user correction.
arxiv-2605-29742: Yeong-Joon Ju and Seong-Whan Lee tackle question answering for regulatory compliance, where every claim needs a full citation trail across layered rules. Standard retrieval tools falter here, they argue, because flat citation links, split retrieval, and shaky after-the-fact attribution break the chain. Their frame, RefWalk, walks cross-document citations from a shared topic anchor, merges views by max-based pooling, and ties each rule to its own sources. They also build RegOps-Bench from complex national research rules, with gains in recall and citation hit rate.
arxiv-2605-29842: Matteo Milani, Joshua D. McGraw, Anke Lindner, and Stefano Aime review microfluidic oscillatory rheology for soft particles in transit. Tiny channels offer fine control over dynamic forcing on microscale objects, as met in emulsions, biological flows, and soft matter at large. Tailored channel shapes enable precise surface and bulk rheology across wide forcing timescales. After surveying recent experiments, the team sketches future directions, from lubrication films in squeezed droplets to fast relaxation of complex interfaces. High-throughput rheology from single macromolecules to cells rounds out the research agenda.
arxiv-2605-30042: Geremy Loachamín-Suntaxi and four colleagues build a multi-agent system for scientific computing that picks its own methods without losing track of what it chose. Small slips between what agents intend and what they run can warp later results, a drift their design fights with explicit semantic checkpoints. The system blends contextual bandits, structured agent messages, language-model agents, grounded code writing and self-repair loops. On sensitivity and uncertainty workflows, unchecked drift harms learning, while their guarded system converges better and adapts to new problems.
arxiv-2605-30242: J. Eduardo Vera-Valdes shows the airborne fraction of carbon dioxide has risen over six decades, using multi-model land-use emissions. It is the share of human emissions staying in the air, not entering land and ocean sinks. It rose from between a third and two fifths in 1959 to just under a half by 2024. For IPCC assessments, the rise cuts the remaining budget by tens of gigatonnes. Post-Pinatubo years and collapsing varied land-use series into one had hidden the trend.
arxiv-2605-30542: Thorpe and colleagues argue that world models for robots must be physically viable, built to answer what an action would do, not merely to predict the next camera frame. Models that only forecast observations can look convincing while recommending impossible moves or certifying unsafe ones, since different hidden physics can produce identical scenes. The paper proposes models built around the simplest physical abstraction that answers a given query, assembled per query from modular parts by an orchestrator. That keeps parts checkable and outputs auditable against the question asked.
arxiv-2605-30642: Aparicio and colleagues ask whether diffusion models memorize rare samples first, and answer no. Training diffusion models on strings from a Random Hierarchy Model, they find samples built from common substrings are memorized first, even when every training sample is unique. Deduplication at the sample level therefore gives no privacy guarantee. They predict and then observe delayed memorization for fat-tailed data, amplified when fat tails enter high-level rules. In between, common substrings are learned first and then overproduced, yielding the bland reversion to the mean derided as slop.
arxiv-2605-30842: Zhang and colleagues present CoMem, splitting memory management from the agent workflow so the two can run together. Context handling lets agentic models solve long-horizon tasks through past recaps. But this incurs large reading overhead for extra summary tokens. CoMem uses a k-step-off pipeline overlapping memory recaps with agent inference, effectively masking context-processing latency. A reward-driven training strategy aligns the memory model to capture statistics for agent decisions. On SWE-Bench-Verified, CoMem provides 1.4 times latency improvements while preserving performance.
arxiv-2605-30942: Wang, Han, and Zhang propose PRISM, a vision system that reasons over images by iterative refinement, not a single feed-forward pass. Single passes cannot recover missing evidence or refine uncertain views under incomplete observations. PRISM groups visual features into object-centered views, recalls relevant patterns from a learned memory, and refines the representation across multiple scales. Across classification, detection, and segmentation, it matches strong rivals while proving more robust under occlusion and other incomplete observations.
arxiv-2605-31142: Gjorgjevikj and colleagues ask whether multilingual embedding rankings survive changes in datasets and scoring rules. Studying a major benchmark across five languages and nine tasks, with results for about 230 more languages, they introduce two stability measures for dataset mix and aggregation choice. Large language-model-based systems often lead, they find, but only a small set stays strong across tasks, scoring schemes and data samples.
arxiv-2605-31342: Peihong Zhang and colleagues tune together spin coherence and valley splitting in silicon-germanium heterostructures. Single electron spins promise quantum information work. Small valley splittings and hyperfine coupling to nuclear spins hinder progress, though. Density functional theory shows thin silicon wells raise valley splitting. Yet they push more of the wave into buffer layers, raising hyperfine coupling. Wells 3 to 4 nm wide with 50 ppm isotope levels should support valley splittings above 500 micro-eV and dephasing times beyond 15 microseconds. Sharper edges help further.
arxiv-2605-31442: Chu and colleagues look past the symmetric subspace, seeking quantum measurement gains across vast state manifolds. They shape random unitaries by their first-moment pattern. They find thick families of built random states where top precision scaling shows up as the norm, not the exception. Because the gain is so widespread, these states resist parameter disorder on their own. A trapped-ion test backs the idea, beating the standard quantum limit by 6.98 dB. The same approach could serve superconducting circuits, waveguide QED, solid-state spins and polar molecules.
arxiv-2606-00242:
Dardia and co-authors report the first lab sight of a state that grows more stable in stronger fields. Strong waves should rip bound states apart with ease. Some math said the tale can flip past a point. The state splits in two and gains strength as the field grows.

That call, strong field stabilization, stood untested for years. Huge field needs and doubts in the math blocked tests. The team mimics electron acts with cold atoms held in a trap. They film the split of the wave pack in plain view. Break rates fall, then rise, in a non-flat curve. The calm zone is mapped across pulse traits. It holds down to low drive rates that past views missed.
arxiv-2606-00442:
Artemev and co-authors use weight-space sameness to guess the bend of a loss view in big nets. Bend guesses drive many tools, from step plans to doubt marks. At net scale, those guesses are hard to build and store. Past work left one rich source of bounds untapped till now.

Weight swaps that leave loss the same bind how bend can look. Mean over those swaps builds a framed bend guess from one slope. The guess can be stored, flipped, and used at fair cost. Which swap group a user picks sets the cost-truth trade. One pick gives back known tools like Shampoo and Muon marks. Tests span net types and a small chat model run.
arxiv-2606-00542:
Bing Liu, Zhou, and Zhao rethink how gap gauges shape split-form step tools in net training. Shampoo-style tools guess slope spread with a split grid form. Past work read those guesses as casts under Bregman gap gauges. Which gauge to pick, when the true spread is not split, was not clear.

The team read the split through the spread's own wave range. Three gauges spread the forced split miss in split ways across that range. Their split parts track gauge-weighted scraps, not the raw miss. Top range traits line up well with true bend traits. Tail traits prove noisy and weak in their tests. A new tool treats top and tail ranges in split ways on that base.
arxiv-2606-00842:
You, Luna, and Summers plan robot paths under rules about order in this 2026 paper. Their worlds hold obstacles, keys, and doors. Picking up a key opens its door, and open doors can yield shorter routes. The plan must dodge obstacles and honor the order rules, stated in a fragment of signal temporal logic.

Their method starts with an exact convex split of the free space. The split marks how convex regions, keys, and doors connect. On it they build an augmented graph of convex sets. Its layered form encodes the key-door logic in full. A shortest path through that graph does two jobs at once. It picks the best key order and draws the best smooth path, as a Bézier curve. The solution is exact up to that curve form. The frame suits games, warehouses, and any task where access must be earned in sequence.
arxiv-2606-00942:
Farahbakhsh and co-authors give a causal account of metastable failures in this 2026 systems paper. A metastable failure is a bad state a system sustains on its own. No attacker or harsh input is needed to keep it going. Past work tracked symptoms and cast such failures as self-sustaining overload. Causes stayed unknown, and not all cases look like overload.

The team traces these failures to metastable faults. A fault is a cycle of interactions among parts that destabilizes the whole. Each part alone tends to stabilize. Scheduling choices decide which tendency wins. When the destabilizing cycle gains the upper hand, the failure locks in. From this account they derive a method to predict such failures. They also sketch how to build systems that tolerate the faults. Three case studies test the method's reach. The paper reframes a feared outage class as a structure that design can hunt early.
arxiv-2606-01042:
Yuan and co-authors show that fluent cell stories from AI can still fail as forecasts in this 2026 paper. Perturbation tests reveal how cells work, but they are costly and sparse. Language models have been cast as virtual cells. They reason step by step from known biology to guess how genes will respond. The stories sound right, which is the trap.

Tested hard, the guesses miss the specific effect of each perturbation. They overstate differential expression as a rule. In bulk scores they often lose to a plain gene frequency baseline. Per gene, they sink to chance level. The models lean on each gene's general habits, not on true perturbation logic. The team traces the flaw to how proof is shown: pairs judged alone, with no contrast. Their fix, CORE, groups proof into positive and negative sets for the same gene. Prediction becomes comparison.
arxiv-2606-01142:
Charalampopoulos, Fotakis, and Tolias design online auctions that respect a hard budget in this 2026 paper. A buyer hires agents who hold private service costs. The buyer wants to maximize a public submodular value over the hired set, without overspending. Agents arrive in random order, like a secretary problem. Each gets one take it or leave it offer, and the choice cannot be undone.

Their framework, Repeated Descent, posts prices on an adaptive linear ladder. It tunes each price level against how many agents it sees, which keeps the budget safe by construction. Built on it, their mechanism is 1046 competitive for the online problem. That beats the best known ratio from 2025 by orders of magnitude. With random subsampling added, they give the first constant competitive posted price mechanism for non monotone values. The work speaks to ad buys, cloud hiring, and any spend capped procurement run online.
arxiv-2606-01642:
Williams and co-authors model how Gram-negative bacteria build their outer membrane. That membrane is the cell's interface with its environment. E. coli and several deadly pathogens carry this membrane type. Two decades of work found the parts that mediate its growth. Structure and function of those parts are now characterized. Yet neither lab methods nor molecular dynamics can follow the machinery over a cell cycle. Key questions about membrane growth thus stay unanswered. Their semi-quantitative agent-based model explores growth at molecular scale.

Simulations span a broad region of parameter space. Protein insertion by the BAM complex seems prone to stalling. It may happen only in short bursts, they find. BAM complexes may also cooperate with each other and with the Lpt complex.
arxiv-2606-02142:
Campos and co-authors present a foundational time-series system built for data streams. Digitization has multiplied time-series streams across processes. Valuable insights may be drawn from those streams. Language models raise the question of foundational time-series models. Such models should handle many tasks at once. They must also stay light enough for real-time use.

Existing foundational models are often large in size. They suit offline settings without strict time limits. Repeated calibration is rarely needed in those settings. On live streams, size and no continual calibration hurt them. Accurate real-time responses become hard to deliver. Their TimeBlocks system targets that gap directly. It is designed as a continual blockbase for streams. Lightweight, multi-task handling is the design aim.
arxiv-2606-02342:
Sismeiro and co-authors test whether video can track a pen while it lifts off the page. Such in-air motion matters for spotting writing disorders like dysgraphia. Tablets track pen lifts, but only near the surface. High lifts escape them. A top-view camera could fill that gap.

The team builds a pipeline that can be read step by step. A YOLO detector tracks the pen tip. Motion features then feed a machine learning classifier. They label a pilot set of varied writing videos frame by frame. Testing leaves one whole video out at a time. The method finds pen-up segments well, with an F2 score up to 0.805. The authors see video as a cheap, gentle partner to tablets. Larger studies can build on this proof of concept.
arxiv-2606-02742:
Bhat and Yamasaki show that vision-language models can be consistent and still wrong. Spatial reasoning underpins robotics and embodied AI. Metric distance questions expose model weakness. A common belief holds that stable answers across views signal grounding. The team tests that belief and finds the reverse. Leading models give view-invariant answers when the answers are incorrect. Predictions barely couple to viewpoint-specific evidence.

Their protocol, ViewDiag, controls the test. It is built from Hypersim, ScanNet, and KITTI360 data. One hundred seventy-six object-pair tracks span 80 scenes, with 2 to 10 views each. Three axes are scored: metric accuracy, distributional concentration, and internal collapse. A latent feature probe measures the collapse axis. Across models, high stability pairs with large error. The pattern suggests prior-driven collapse, not evidence-based reasoning. Cross-view consistency should not proxy for geometric understanding. ViewDiag gives a diagnostic frame for evidence-sensitive spatial models.
arxiv-2606-02842:
Shen and co-authors present SpecFlow, a light framework for multimodal spatial reasoning. Such reasoning often builds long chains of text and image steps. Those chains pile up visual tokens and attention cost. SpecFlow instead stores each visual step in a fixed-size discrete cosine space.

The cosine form keeps the broad layout and links between objects. Fine detail is added only when a task needs sharper spatial precision. Text steps then steer updates of the visual state through classifier-free guidance. The visual workspace stays bounded, so memory and delay do not grow with reasoning depth. The authors report results that match or beat rival methods. They also report cuts in compute and key-value cache cost of up to 2.1 times.
arxiv-2606-03042:
Wakamatsu reviews the chiral quark soliton model as a tool for predicting what happens inside the nucleon. The model is an effective quark model of baryons. It builds on spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking in the QCD vacuum and the pions that come with it. Like the Skyrme model, it views baryons as rotating hedgehog objects.

The soliton model gives more realistic predictions for most baryon observables. Its decisive advantage is handling non-local quark-quark correlations. Effective meson theories cannot do that at all. This matters for parton distribution functions, which are defined through quark operators with light-cone separation. Wakamatsu explains why and how the model succeeds for many such distributions. Special attention goes to the flavor asymmetry of unpolarized and polarized sea-quark distributions. The review should interest nuclear theorists who model nucleon structure. It shows where an effective model can beat a purely mesonic picture.
arxiv-2606-03342:
Callejas and co-authors test the caustic method for weighing galaxy clusters with data from a future survey. The caustic technique uses galaxy positions and line-of-sight speeds to rebuild a cluster's mass profile. The team works with The Three Hundred Project simulations. They measure the systematic errors that come from premises about velocity anisotropy.

An iterative correction method cuts those errors down. The team also tests how survey magnitude limits bias mass estimates under unlike observing plans. Their own survey, CATARSIS, will take redshifts for all galaxies brighter than a set limit near 16 clusters. A new spectrograph on the Calar Alto telescope will do the work. Such data should let the team tame the systematic errors in density profiles. The survey aims to sharpen mass profile estimates and to clarify the dynamical states of clusters. The study maps what precision to expect before the data arrive.
arxiv-2606-03442:
Barbour, Fischer, and Reinert survey how Stein's method is used in network analysis. Stein's method is a tool for judging how close a count is to a known distribution. Networks raise hard versions of that task. Graph-based statistics often have tangled dependence between their parts. The survey gathers the main lines of work in one place.

Topics include normal approximation for graph-based statistics. Poisson approximation for such counts is covered as well. One strand asks how well an exponential random graph can be matched by a simple Bernoulli model. Another compares distinct random geometric graph models with each other. The brief format suits readers who want a map of the field. Specialists can trace each topic to its source results from here. The survey also shows where Stein's method still has open room to grow in network science.
arxiv-2606-04142:
Sebastian Buhai asks in 2026 when social discounting favors the young. Social discounting weighs future welfare less than present welfare, and the young have more future ahead of them.

The puzzle is a gap between two kinds of comparison. Local comparisons, which ask who should get the next small benefit, always favor the young. But whole-plan comparisons can flip, favoring the old. Buhai traces the flip to how plans are scaled and normalized before comparing them. The gap comes from the aggregate component, not from the discounting itself. His clean characterization shows the two views can point in opposite directions. Policy readers should note which comparison a welfare claim rests on.
arxiv-2606-04342:
Riku Green, Zahraa Abdallah, and Telmo Silva Filho expose in 2026 a structural flaw in how multi-step forecasting is usually judged: by mean squared error alone. That metric rewards predicting the conditional average, but at long horizons the average path looks like nothing that ever actually happens.

They define a conditional uncertainty gap and prove that whenever it is nonzero, no single deterministic forecast can both minimize squared error and match the distribution of realized futures. Controlled systems and nine real benchmarks map the resulting trade-off frontier. Giving up at most five percent in squared error often bought realism gains above seventeen percent. Different forecasting strategies occupy predictably different spots on the frontier, so model selection becomes an explicit choice, not an accident.
arxiv-2606-04442:
Xie and colleagues build a benchmark that tests two hard skills at once, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Existing benchmarks test each skill alone. Their dataset, MemoryDocDataSet, has 50 synthetic micro-worlds and 1,000 questions. Each world mixes several personas and a timeline spanning months. It also holds three to five legal documents and multi-session conversations grounded in them. Twenty questions per world span five reasoning types.

A hybrid question type is the key feature. The system must first search the conversation to learn which document matters. Then it finds the answer inside that document. Hybrid questions make up three quarters of the set. Six baseline setups were tested, from truncated context to retrieval and memory systems. The best setup, a combined retrieval system, scored an F1 of 0.358 overall. Document-only retrieval collapsed on hybrid questions, though it did well on document-only ones.
arxiv-2606-04842:
Pampili and colleagues diagnose and fix a growth problem that destroys the conducting channel in aluminium-rich transistors, in a 2026 arXiv paper. High electron mobility transistors based on AlGaN rely on a two-dimensional electron gas at the barrier-channel interface. Growing aluminium-rich crystals needs high temperatures, but heat lets the barrier and channel alloys intermix.

The authors show that X-ray diffraction can assess sharpness, and that growth schemes in metal-organic vapour phase epitaxy achieve a high-quality electron gas. In particular, they demonstrate sheet resistivities around 2,500 ohms per square for an AlN over AlGaN structure. The strategy matters because aluminium-rich channels promise higher voltage and power than gallium nitride, but only if the interface survives the growth temperatures the crystal quality demands.
arxiv-2606-05342:
Matheus Kunzler Maldaner and colleagues introduce SentinelBench in this 2026 arXiv paper, a benchmark for agents that monitor over long stretches. Agents are increasingly handed work spanning hours, yet their default behavior is continuous action: polling, refreshing, and pushing for progress. Many long-running tasks instead reward attention, waiting until an event makes progress possible, then reacting promptly without wasting resources in between.

SentinelBench contains 100 tasks across ten web environments, including email, calendars, finance, professional networking, and entertainment. Each environment exposes a web interface and replays a sequence of events, so the pages an agent watches change state underfoot while it works. The benchmark measures task completion, reaction time, and resource use, exposing the trade-off between responsiveness and cost. Reporting results for three models under two browser-agent harnesses, the authors establish baselines. Agent design choices, such as how an agent waits, can dramatically change the metrics.
arxiv-2606-05542:
Geiko and Gerenraich prove when a quantum lattice must settle to equilibrium in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their systems are grids of bosonic sites, particles that can pile up without limit. The dynamics come from Gaussian quantum cellular automata, rules that update each site from its neighbors in discrete steps. The question is whether every starting state drifts to the hottest, most mixed state. The authors give two separate sets of conditions that force that outcome.

Each condition set covers states that look normal up close and keep particle counts bounded. The key step is a many-body version of a classic lemma about fading averages. It bounds what local probes can read, based on probe size and particle density. Under either condition set, those readings wash out over time. The result adds a rigorous case to the long effort to ground heat behavior in quantum rules.
arxiv-2606-05742:
Runheng Liu and colleagues speed up text generation by reusing what the model already produced in a 2026 arXiv paper. Speculative decoding drafts several tokens, then verifies them in one pass of the big model. Model-free versions draft by copying earlier text, with no helper model to train. Copying by exact wording misses matches when phrasing shifts, though. A single copied span also breaks when several continuations fit.

AdaPLD keeps exact reuse where it is safe and adds meaning-based search when wording fails. It branches its draft guesses to cover rival continuations instead of betting on one. No training is involved at any stage. Across varied benchmarks the method cut the big model's forward passes sharply. Decoding ran up to about three times faster at the best settings. The gains show careful reuse can rival learned drafters. Adaptive retrieval, not a bigger draft model, does the work here.
arxiv-2606-05942:
Asanuma insists a causal graph should come with its equations attached in a 2026 arXiv paper. Neural causal discovery finds which variables drive which, but each mechanism stays a black box. Extracting formulas from network weights is provably ill-posed. EML-CD sidesteps the network: each edge is a small binary tree built from one composable operator. The tree itself is the closed-form equation.

Because the output is symbolic, exact effect derivatives come free. On the Sachs protein signaling data the method's graph distance matched PC and GES baselines. Every detected edge carried a readable equation, with solid precision. In a two-variable test it recovered ten of eleven known function families exactly. A light-tunnel dataset showed clear gains over a linear baseline. Structure scores on synthetic data merely tied a dictionary method, which the author reports. Interpretability, not raw graph score, is the contribution.
arxiv-2606-06342:
Yan Wang and Tianyang Hu build better rulers for comparing neural network representations in this 2026 arXiv paper. Topological data analysis compares the shape of the data cloud inside two networks, which can reveal whether they learned the same structure. Existing paired measures were asymmetric, scoring A against B differently from B against A, and their values grew with sample size. Both flaws block fair comparison across studies.

They complete the framework with Symmetric Representation Topology Divergence, which merges both directions into one cross barcode signature. That single signature pinpoints where two representations differ structurally, and a lite variant cuts the cost. For benchmarking, their Normalized Topological Similarity compares the rank order in which clusters merge as scale grows. The score is bounded between minus one and one and ignores sample size. It equals one exactly when the two merge orders agree, giving studies a shared yardstick.
arxiv-2606-06642:
Guido Sanchez and co-authors compare three ways to make predictive control computable in this 2026 arXiv review paper. Model predictive control steers a system by repeatedly solving an optimization over its future behavior. The dynamics are continuous time equations, though, and the controller works in discrete steps. Something must discretize them, and the choice shapes speed and reliability. The review covers direct multiple shooting, direct collocation, and successive linearization.

Each method is explained, then benchmarked on two simulated test cases. The verdict is encouraging: current solvers meet real time demands for small and medium nonlinear systems. Successive linearization matched its rivals in quality and speed. It adds two bonuses: analysts can study the controller's stability with standard tools, and quadratic programming solvers guarantee a solution at every step.
arxiv-2606-06742:
Kernel machines are veteran prediction tools that judge new cases by comparing them with past ones. Yikai Zhang, Jia, Ding, and Wang package them for modern graphics hardware in this 2026 arXiv paper introducing TorchKM, an open source software library. It covers support vector machines and kernel versions of logistic and quantile regression, all with a familiar interface modeled on scikit-learn.

The library is built to reuse matrix work across training and model selection, the costly search for good settings, so graphics processors are not fed the same numbers twice. Benchmarks in the paper show prediction quality on par with standard tools, paired with large speed gains over the usual baselines. The authors pitch the package as a kernel learning part for wider AI workflows. They distribute it through PyPI. Code and documentation sit on GitHub for anyone to install.
arxiv-2606-06842:
Tables hide their answers across rows and columns, and language models often reason too narrowly over them. Pan and a large team propose CRAFT in this 2026 arXiv paper. The framework answers table questions and checks table claims. Its core move is counterfactual reasoning, testing what follows if a claim were false.

For each task, the system builds a plain statement and its counterfactual twin. It then gathers evidence along both reasoning paths. A weighted step merges the two sides into a final answer. Tests on the WikiTQ and TabFact benchmarks beat representative baselines. Gains were largest on complex questions needing several steps. The method also narrowed the gap between stronger and weaker backbone models. The authors argue that arguing both sides makes models more discerning. It turns one way inference into a small internal debate.
arxiv-2606-06942:
Defence officials hunt for new capabilities across a maze of reports, papers, and policy files. Bodhankar and co-authors built Didact to search that maze in this 2026 arXiv paper. The prototype focuses on the Australian defence context. Its sources mix public defence reports with a knowledge graph built from research publications.

Users ask questions in plain language. A composite retrieval pipeline gathers evidence from documents and the graph together. Access controls stay in force during retrieval. An interactive Evidence Rail shows the sources behind each answer. It also maps how those sources relate. The team evaluated output quality and running time across task types. Different defence user personas were part of the trials. Results supported the tool's utility for capability discovery. The design should adapt to other fields with fragmented knowledge.
arxiv-2606-07342:
Sviridov and co-authors evolve medical decision software instead of fine-tuning it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Fitting language models to clinical work usually means expensive training or hand-crafted prompts. Their route uses LLM-guided MAP-Elites evolution, an evolutionary search that keeps high-performing candidates, to discover decision programs at inference time. Three clinical tasks serve as test beds: urgency triage, interactive consultation, and medical image classification, each scored by a fitness function.

Evolution improved over hand-designed baselines in all three settings under practical constraints. In triage, one accuracy measure rose from about 77 to 87 percent, while emergency recall jumped sharply from 0.60 toward near-complete detection in their reported results. Policies improved the quality-versus-cost balance across three model families and transferred to held-out data. Prompt-only runs even improved a frozen medical vision model on pneumonia cases while keeping outputs in strict machine-readable format.
arxiv-2606-07642:
Wang and co-authors ask whether vision-language models can judge wheelchair accessibility from street imagery as well as wheelchairs reveal it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Barriers are distributed, context-dependent, and temporary, so auditing cities by hand does not scale. Their framework pairs Google Street View images with accessibility guidance and rubrics, retrieved for the model's ratings. Ground truth is behavior: a campus dataset links hundreds of locations to wheelchair dwell time measured by sensors, treating lingering as a signal.

Model ratings correlated negatively with dwell time and matched its distribution, indicating alignment with the behavioral proxy. Analysis showed features like curb ramps and crosswalks associated with model scores, while alignment stayed weak for surface conditions, transient obstructions, and viewpoint-dependent barriers. The authors conclude expert-guided models can support first-pass assessment, complementing rather than replacing on-the-ground auditing, where the evidence is faint in a photograph.
arxiv-2606-07842:
Gass, Peccati, and Stecconi uncover a shared law behind filament patterns in random waves, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Berry's random wave model superposes waves from all directions and models chaotic wave fields, from quantum billiards to optics. On large domains its geometric observables, such as counts of critical points, fluctuate in ways that resisted classification.

The team proves that any observable whose fluctuations are fully tied to its second-order chaotic component falls into one universality class. It is governed by a fractional Gaussian field with a dimension-dependent index. The same class contains the Poisson line process, a random scatter of straight lines. In practical terms, large-scale observables behave statistically like objects built from random lines. That gives the filamentary scar patterns seen in simulations since the nineteen eighties a natural probabilistic interpretation. A second part pins down the scaling limit of quadratic transforms of the Fourier coefficients.
arxiv-2606-08042:
Naseem Bouchhar overviews the next inner tracker for the ALICE experiment at CERN, in this 2026 arXiv paper. During the LHC's third long shutdown, ALICE will replace its three innermost tracking layers with ITS3, the first fully cylindrical, wafer-scale silicon vertex detector. Its sensors are monolithic active pixel sensors, thinned to fifty micrometres and bent into half-cylinders with radii as small as nineteen millimetres.

Bending the silicon itself removes most support material, and wafer-scale stitching produces seamless sensors twenty-seven centimetres long with power and signalling built in. Together with a switch from water to air cooling, the material budget drops below nine hundredths of a percent of a radiation length per layer, so particles cross almost undisturbed. Full-scale prototypes demonstrated the stitching, yield, and radiation hardness. Engineering models confirmed air cooling keeps the structure stable.
arxiv-2606-08142:
Utsav Atta, Tathagata Ghosh, and Sudip Manna propose a new way for the early universe to rid itself of domain walls, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Domain walls are defects that form when a symmetry breaks to a discrete remnant. Here a global U(1) symmetry is cut down by gravitational effects at the Planck scale, leaving cosmic strings with walls attached. Walls are cosmologically dangerous: they dilute slowly and can dominate the universe's energy density, conflicting with nucleosynthesis.

The new mechanism needs one ingredient: a fermion coupled to the symmetry-breaking field with a small bare mass. Radiative corrections then generate a temperature-dependent bias, an energy preference for one side of the wall, which grows as the universe cools and triggers collapse. The worked example is a majoron framework with right-handed neutrinos carrying small bare masses. The mechanism turns a liability, quantum corrections, into the cleanup crew.
arxiv-2606-08542:
Haizhou Ge and colleagues teach robots to learn from their own failed attempts, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In exploratory manipulation, an apparent failure is often the key evidence for what to do next. A robot pulls a locked cabinet drawer, fails, and succeeds only after opening the lock. The failed pull reveals a latent precondition, the lock, which determines the minimal-success action chain. Reading such a trace correctly is the prerequisite for recovering that chain, and the authors formalize the task as question answering over manipulation traces.

Given synchronized video and proprioception, the body's own sense signals, from an exploratory trace, the system must predict the minimal-success chain under the precondition the probe revealed. Even state-of-the-art vision-language models misread this evidence, failing to recover the chain from raw video, raw proprioception, or both. The authors' approach distills reading heuristics in a closed loop.
arxiv-2606-08842:
Simon investigates the endpoints of simple geodesics on surfaces built from the modular group, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A geodesic is the straightest possible path across a curved surface, and a simple geodesic never crosses itself. The modular group is a symmetry group of the hyperbolic plane, the saddle-shaped geometry where parallel lines spread apart. Each simple geodesic on such a cover lifts to a path whose endpoint is a single real number.

Simon conjectures that this endpoint can only be rational, quadratic, or transcendental, meaning it is either a simple fraction, the root of a quadratic equation, or outside algebra entirely. He proves the conjecture for geodesics that belong to minimal laminations, families of paths that fill a surface region as tightly as possible. The result was already known for the modular torus cover, where simple geodesics correspond to numbers whose Lagrange constant exceeds three.
arxiv-2606-09142:
Li and colleagues predict whether a pedestrian will cross the street, from the pedestrian's viewpoint, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Most prediction uses external cameras. Egocentric vision, from head-mounted devices, captures what the pedestrian sees and where their gaze falls, but its traffic-safety value was underexplored. The team framed the task as closed-ended question answering over short clips, and benchmarked three vision-language-model families zero-shot.
