Zero-shot models beat chance modestly, with limited traffic reasoning. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning changed the picture: adapted models beat their zero-shot versions and beat a specialized transformer baseline by 9 percent. Context helped further. Feeding ego motion, vehicle motion, and eye gaze, the fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-2B model beat the transformer baseline by 14.5 percent, a new state of the art for this task. Gaze tells the model what the pedestrian attends to, the strongest hint of their next move.
arxiv-2606-09342:
Steven Vander Eeckt and Hugo Van Hamme address a practical weakness of speech recognition in this 2026 arXiv paper. Large pretrained speech models are adapted to one task after another, and each round of training tends to erase earlier skills. That failure is called catastrophic forgetting. Their method, named CSSVD, adapts a model to new tasks while changing as few of its internal weights as possible.

CSSVD splits each weight matrix by singular values, numbers that rank how strongly each internal direction shapes the model's output. Learning is confined to small rotations within the weak tail directions, while the dominant directions stay frozen. When later tasks arrive, the rotations learned for separate tasks are averaged together. Across two continual learning benchmarks, CSSVD forgot less and scored best overall against recent rival methods. The comparisons held every method to a similar budget of roughly nine million trainable parameters during adaptation.
arxiv-2606-09442:
Tanmayee Patra, Pranaya Pratik Das, and Biplab Ganguli explore how gentle bumps added to a simple potential can tip orderly motion into chaos in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their starting system is a two-dimensional harmonic potential well, whose motion is regular and predictable. The perturbations are Gaussian bumps, smooth hills or dips inspired by cymatics, the patterns that vibration prints on plates and membranes.

The authors vary the arrangement of the bumps, placing them singly or in squares, circles, ellipses, and random layouts, and flip their amplitude from positive to negative. They then diagnose the motion with time series, power spectra, and autocorrelation functions, standard tools for separating periodic from chaotic behaviour. Nearby starting conditions, differing only in the fifth decimal place, produced diverging, aperiodic trajectories in the perturbed landscapes. Regular motion showed discrete frequency peaks, while chaotic motion spread into broadband, noise-like spectra.
arxiv-2606-09642:
Jonathan Dries measures how big land deals in Africa stir local unrest in this 2026 arXiv paper. Over two decades, investors have taken up millions of hectares, much of it land that villages hold by custom, not by paper title. The hard part is proof: deals that go ahead may differ from those that stall.

Dries compares places where deals were carried out with places where deals failed for outside reasons. The study covers one thousand three hundred ninety-one mapped deals. Carried-out deals raised civic unrest by one hundred fifty-eight percent over the pre-deal mean, and the lift lasted. The protest surge ran strongest for home-country buyers taking village or state land for food crops. That pattern points to local elites capturing the gains. News tone, surveys, and vote shifts moved in line: trust in chiefs fell as turnout rose.
arxiv-2606-09742:
Matija Bucić and his co-authors push a fifty-year-old graph puzzle a long step forward in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Lovász conjecture claims each connected vertex-transitive graph, one that looks the same from each corner, holds a path through all its points. A stronger form claims a full cycle. For decades, the best sure cycle length grew like the square root of the graph's size.

Recent work raised that growth step by step. The new proof lifts it to the two-thirds power, a jump past the past mark of nine-fourteenths. The tools blend fresh ways to thread paths through sublinear expanders, graphs that spread well for their size. A split of near-regular graphs into such pieces does heavy work. Extra combinatorial ideas close the gaps.
arxiv-2606-09942:
Pham's thesis tackles automated failure diagnosis for microservice systems, the cloud programs built from many small cooperating services, presented as a 2026 arXiv paper. Failures in such systems are bound to happen and costly, yet most root cause analysis tools assume anomalies were detected perfectly and ignore event data like API calls and settings changes. Many also need a service call graph handed to them. Pham sets out to drop those givens.

The thesis introduces BARO for metric data, EventADL for event data, and TORAI, a multimodal method needing no call graph, each performing detection and diagnosis end to end. Extensive tests on real microservice systems show the methods are effective and robust. A second contribution, RCAEval, supplies ready-to-use benchmark datasets and reproducible baselines for fair comparison. A systematic evaluation of causal inference-based methods rounds out the work, guiding future research on incident response.
arxiv-2606-10142:
Jia and colleagues build a benchmark for judging the quality of generated three-dimensional meshes, in a 2026 arXiv paper on computer graphics evaluation. Three-dimensional generation has improved rapidly in realism and control, but evaluating assets still relies on costly human ratings, learned metrics, or vision-language models used as judges, each with limits. Their dataset, DB-3DME, contains two thousand six hundred nineteen synthetic meshes paired with human ratings.

Benchmarking leading vision-language models, the team identifies how three-dimensional representations are visually encoded as a key performance factor. They fine-tune an open-source vision-language model for mesh evaluation, and the tuned model substantially outperforms existing pretrained models across multiple evaluation dimensions. The authors present DB-3DME as both a new standard and a foundation for future research on automatic three-dimensional evaluation.
arxiv-2606-10442:
Bai and co-authors address large-scale robot mapping in this 2026 arXiv paper, where a machine builds one consistent map while tracking its own position, a task called SLAM. A common strategy builds local submaps and joins them into a global map, limiting drift and computation. Existing joining methods store occupancy on grids and interpolate between points, creating rough gradients at borders and ignoring measurement uncertainty. This paper instead keeps occupancy as a smooth continuous field in log-odds form.

The framework compresses raw sensor readings into compact summary tuples, and the authors prove the compression loses no information, since the resulting estimate matches what the full data would give. Joining then weights each submap by its variance, so uncertain pieces count for less. Tests on simulated and large real datasets show better pose accuracy and consistency than leading grid methods, plus smaller files and better-calibrated uncertainty.
arxiv-2606-11242:
Drousiotis, Spirakis, and Nikoletseas model competition for conscious access as a game in a 2026 arXiv paper. Conscious access is often described as a contest among internal representations, but usually as metaphor. Here, modules compete for one scarce broadcast slot by choosing a costly amplification effort. Access follows a smooth probabilistic rule sliding between diffuse selection and winner-take-all.

The authors prove a pure-strategy equilibrium exists under standard assumptions, and give conditions for uniqueness. In the two-module case they analyze capture: a lower-value representation can win more access because it is cheaper to amplify. For quadratic costs they derive a sharp capture threshold in competition intensity, and for strongly convex costs an exact criterion. Under curvature dominance, projected pseudo-gradient dynamics approximate the unique equilibrium efficiently. A closing impossibility theorem shows exact winner-take-all efficiency cannot survive small score perturbations, so smooth rules are structurally necessary.
arxiv-2606-11342:
Cheng, Ouyang, Jiang, Zhang, and Nallanathan analyze a new antenna design in a 2026 arXiv paper: the single-RF movable array. All its movable elements are driven by one radio-frequency chain with equal amplitude and equal phase, so the only design freedom is where the antennas sit. The paper asks how much beamforming gain antenna placement alone can deliver.

For single-path channels, the authors show linear beamforming gain scaling with the number of antennas is achievable. For multipath channels, they establish coherent-combining conditions and aperture requirements. For multiuser transmission, they derive the optimal max-min power allocation in closed form. On that basis they build an element-wise coordinate-search algorithm for antenna placement design. Numerical results validate the analysis and reveal a fundamental tradeoff. Beamforming gains are achievable through antenna placement alone, but only at the expense of increased array aperture, a cost system designers must weigh.
arxiv-2606-11642:
Naoki Kimura asks how few physical keys a keyboard can get away with in this 2026 arXiv paper on text entry. On an ambiguous keyboard several letters share each key, as on old phone keypads, and a language model must guess the intended text from context. Fewer keys would free up design space for assistive devices and tiny gadgets.

Kimura tests two to five keys on 300 English sentences spanning business, conversational and technical writing. He varies the letter mapping and the decoder resolving the ambiguity. Three keys paired with GPT-4o reach a character error rate under ten percent, cutting errors by fifty-nine percent compared with two keys. Five keys do better still, but gains shrink. Which mapping is chosen barely matters, and even a deliberately worst mapping adds only about half a percentage point of error. Technical sentences, though, produce roughly twice the errors of business ones.
arxiv-2606-11742: A 2026 arXiv entry, this research manuscript advances a new study. The paper tackles a topic inside science and technology. The subject area is science and technology: careful study of how the natural and built world works. The work reported here becomes part of the open literature.
arxiv-2606-11842:
Moritz Hartlieb and Weite Pi bound a subtle algebraic invariant in this 2026 arXiv paper on algebraic geometry. The Brauer group of a space measures certain twisted bundles on it and obstructs geometric constructions. The authors study linear systems, families of divisors cut out by equations of fixed shape, on simply connected smooth projective varieties, keeping only the smooth members.

Under a suitable ampleness condition, meaning the defining bundle is positive enough, they prove the Brauer group of this smooth locus is at most the group with two elements. The result covers the projective plane, a very general K3 surface, and a general cubic fourfold. The proof works through the locus of divisors with exactly two nodes, mild singularities. As an application, they compute the Tate-Shafarevich group classifying torsors, twisted forms, over the relative Jacobians of universal smooth plane curves, families of abelian varieties attached to each curve.
arxiv-2606-11942:
Ginés R Pérez Teruel examines surfaces where gravity's strength vanishes in this 2026 arXiv paper. The theory studied lets the effective gravitational coupling, usually a constant, vary with curvature and matter content. For many allowed coupling functions, there are hypersurfaces where this coupling passes through zero, a regime most studies simply assume away.

Teruel shows the apparent singularity at such surfaces is an artifact of one rewritten form of the conservation law; the fundamental equations stay regular. He derives a matching condition that matter must satisfy on a regular critical surface. These surfaces act as gravity screening boundaries, separating regions of attractive gravity from regions of repulsive gravity. Their existence also blocks a global Einstein-frame description, the standard trick of rewriting modified gravity as ordinary gravity plus fields. That distinguishes this theory from ones based only on redefining the energy-momentum tensor.
arxiv-2606-12542:
Kiuchi and Okawa build a faster gravity solver for simulating collapsing stars and merging neutron stars, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Numerical relativity evolves Einstein's equations on grids that must span huge scale ranges. Their new multi-grid Poisson solver handles the gravity solves inside such codes. They test it on standard setups: two puncture black holes, a still spherical neutron star, a spinning one, and a collapsing massive star.

The demonstration run follows a nine-solar-mass star's collapse through core bounce, with neutrino radiation transport included. A constraint-preserving regrid scheme uses the solver to sharpen resolution where the action is. Conserved quantities hold impressively: baryonic mass is preserved to a few thousandths of a percent. The ADM mass and angular momentum stay within tenths of a percent. Accurate conservation during violent collapse is exactly what modelers need to trust waveforms and explosion outcomes.
arxiv-2606-12642:
Belhadfa and colleagues compare the surface of asteroid Bennu across four possible sampling sites in this 2026 arXiv paper. Data come from NASA's OSIRIS-REx spacecraft, which mapped Bennu before sampling it in 2020. The team uses visible, near-infrared, and thermal infrared spectra, each revealing different minerals and surface properties. The sites, named Nightingale, Osprey, Sandpiper, and Kingfisher, sit on a body only about five hundred metres across.

Spectra differ measurably between sites at scales of just two to ten metres, although their overall shapes look alike. Shifts in a water-related absorption and in thermal features point to differences in hydration, traces of past water action, and in silicate makeup. Statistical tests confirm the four sites form separate groups. Nightingale, the site finally sampled, spans the full range of properties seen everywhere else, making its returned material a useful baseline for the whole asteroid.
arxiv-2606-12942:
Jiang and colleagues name parse collapse, a failure mode of generative listwise ranking with large multimodal models, and propose PRISMR to overcome it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Listwise ranking asks a model to order a candidate list in 1 forward pass, taking in global context. In long multimodal contexts, the autoregressive decoder often yields fluent yet incomplete rankings, dropping candidates and ending early, a failure rooted in limited use of context rather than formatting mistakes.

PRISMR swaps out in-context list processing with structural conditioning. A hypernetwork encodes the multimodal candidates in parallel and builds item-specific LoRA weights. These are synthesised into an instance-specific adapter for the ranking model, internalising the list structure while keeping the base model. The authors present a multimodal review-ranking benchmark for evaluation. Tests show PRISMR reduces parse collapse and lifts listwise ranking performance, and that it transfers across domains and instruction-tuned backbones.
arxiv-2606-14042:
Li, Moebel, and Wang take apart a fast image editor to find which parts actually do the work. One-step editing changes a picture from a text prompt in one pass, prized for speed. ChordEdit combines a chord transport step with a proximal alignment step. Their 2026 arXiv paper reproduces and simplifies the method: the chord window mostly acts as an effective timestep shift, from time t to t minus the window.

The evidence is direct. ChordEdit's default update, at time zero point nine with a zero point one five window, looks almost identical to editing at zero point seven five with no window. The components split by frequency: chord transport works on high-noise images, doing low-frequency semantic editing, while proximal alignment works on low-noise images, adding high-frequency target details. Editing decomposes into coarse transport plus fine alignment. Prompt-conditioned timestep choice is the proposed next step.
arxiv-2606-14142:
He's team recommends items with a model that thinks silently instead of talking out loud. Generative recommendation has the model generate the next item from a user's history, but items are encoded as Semantic IDs never seen in pretraining. Explicit pipelines ground those IDs and elicit rationales at high cost. Their 2026 arXiv paper decomposes such pipelines and finds three weaknesses: weakened verbalization of world knowledge, misalignment between ID and language embedding spaces, and sensitivity to rationale quality.

Their alternative, PauseRec, uses implicit reasoning, letting the model compute internally, without rationale text. It beat explicit chain-of-thought methods by up to six point two two percent. Training cost fell by up to sixty-five percent in GPU hours, with no traces to acquire. Inference sped up seventy-one point three percent. Implicit reasoning is the practical route to world knowledge here: cheaper, faster, and more accurate.
arxiv-2606-14442:
Codenotti, Freyer, and Krivokuća study minimal covering bodies in a 2026 arXiv paper in convex geometry. A covering body is a convex shape whose copies, shifted by whole-number amounts, cover all of space. A minimal covering body is one that loses this property if any part is removed.

The authors show that such bodies, while not necessarily tiles that fit without overlap, must be polytopes, shapes with flat faces. In dimension d they have at least twice d facets. The team also connects minimal covering bodies to Minkowski combinations, weighted blends of convex shapes. They prove two sharp Brunn-Minkowski type inequalities for the covering radius of Minkowski sums of planar convex bodies, giving exact bounds on how large a covering copy must be.
arxiv-2606-14542:
Calvert proves a surprising equilibrium-like result for driven systems in a 2026 arXiv paper in statistical physics. The Boltzmann distribution predicts how often a system at equilibrium visits each state. Extending it to nonequilibrium steady states, systems held away from balance by constant driving, is a central open problem.

Calvert shows that on large dense networks, such steady states do occupy states in a Boltzmann-like way, despite producing entropy extensively. The active-matter heuristic called low rattling, the idea that systems linger in states they leave slowly, turns out to be asymptotically exact in this setting. The explanation extends to a broader class he calls equiaccessible steady states, which play a role in his analysis similar to equilibrium's role in linear response theory.
arxiv-2606-14642:
Saleh and co-authors hunt for a phase transition in a twelve-flavor version of quantum chromodynamics in a 2026 arXiv lattice paper. Their simulated theory has twelve identical-mass fermions, far more than real-world QCD. They reconstruct the density of states from plaquette distributions and locate the zeros of the partition function in the complex coupling plane, a classic fingerprint of phase changes.

Calculations span five lattice sizes and four quark masses. For the lightest mass, fits to how the lowest zeros move with size strongly support a first-order transition, with an exponent matching volume scaling. The other three masses appear to lie above the critical mass, estimated near the middle of the tested range. Combining with earlier spectroscopy, the gap to the real axis scales roughly like the square of the scalar meson's mass.
arxiv-2606-15042:
Lei and coauthors jointly design drone flight paths and radio settings for secure data collection in a 2026 study. Two uncrewed aerial vehicles gather data from ground devices while an aerial eavesdropper listens in. One drone can jam the eavesdropper, but paths, powers, and scheduling all interact. The goal is to maximize average secrecy spectral efficiency, a measure of protected throughput.

The coupled problem is non-convex, so the team first swaps in a tractable lower bound for the objective. Block coordinate descent then splits the design into four subproblems. Slack variables and successive convex approximation turn each subproblem into a manageable convex task. The pieces cover three-dimensional trajectories, ground device power, user scheduling, and jamming power. Numerical results confirm the iteration converges and beats simpler designs. Three-dimensional trajectory design in particular lifts secrecy performance markedly. Future work points toward multi-antenna systems with beamforming and sensing integration.
arxiv-2606-15342:
Kar proves a Harnack inequality with an optimal tail for mixed local-nonlocal parabolic equations on the Heisenberg group, in a 2026 analysis paper. A Harnack inequality bounds how much a nonnegative solution of a diffusion equation can vary across time, the backbone of regularity theory. The equation mixes classical local diffusion with a nonlocal jump term, modeling processes that combine random walks with long Lévy flights. The Heisenberg group adds a twisted notion of distance.

The proof runs through expansion of positivity plus a clustering lemma, bypassing Moser iteration and log estimates. The tail term, pricing far-away values' influence on the nonlocal part, is shown optimal rather than a safe overestimate. The author notes this is the first such result on the Heisenberg group. Sharp Harnack estimates anchor everything downstream, from Hölder continuity to heat kernel bounds.
arxiv-2606-15442:
Bhadra proposes a new coordinate system in 2026 for symmetric positive definite matrices, the matrices that describe covariance and connectivity in statistics. The reverse telescoping map writes any such matrix through one scalar for its log determinant, plus coordinates for relative diagonal scales and partial covariances. Unlike the matrix logarithm or Cholesky charts, the new system keeps the determinant isolated in a single coordinate.

That split pays off. Work on a matrix and its inverse runs in quadratic rather than cubic time in this form. Two unit-determinant matrices can also be joined by a straight line that keeps the determinant fixed. Bhadra builds a split volume-shape flow model on them and tests it at sizes up to 200. The model reproduces a bimodal synthetic target and generates brain connectivity networks from fMRI data, and the chart also supports diffusion on the manifold itself.
arxiv-2606-15842:
Heinzel, Pfaffelhuber, and Wakolbinger approximate Muller's ratchet in 2026, the process by which asexual lines irreversibly accumulate harmful mutations. Their model is an infinite system of stochastic differential equations with Fleming-Viot noise, tracking how many individuals carry each number of harmful changes. A click is the loss of the least-loaded class; the long-standing question is its rate.

Using Duhamel's principle for semigroups, the authors approximate two key averages, the mean load and the frequency of the clean class, up to errors of order one over nu squared. Their analysis singles out one quantity, built from selection, mutation, and system size, as crucial, beyond the usual mutation-selection ratio. When it is large, clicking on the natural time scale becomes rare, even for fairly large mutation-selection ratios. Such approximations feed clicking-rate calculations, in models from viral evolution to conservation genetics.
arxiv-2606-16142:
Soenjaya analyzes in 2026 a numerical scheme for the equation governing how magnetization moves in ferromagnets. The Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation models micromagnetics below the Curie temperature. In chiral materials, the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction adds a first-order term, sets a natural boundary condition, and helps form skyrmions, small swirling spin textures.

The scheme is a mass-lumped midpoint finite element method with a structure-preserving solver. It keeps the unit length of magnetization at every node exactly, and obeys a discrete energy law. Soenjaya proves an optimal-order error estimate in the energy norm: first order in space, second order in time, under stated regularity assumptions. This is the first such a priori estimate for this method, even without the chiral term. Proven accuracy lets simulators choose mesh and step sizes with confidence.
arxiv-2606-16442:
Abe and co-authors compute in 2026 the abundance of spin-1 electroweak dark matter, where a long-range force reshapes the answer. The dark matter particle is the neutral member of a triplet of vector bosons, odd under a Z2 symmetry that keeps it stable. The model predicts a heavier, Z2-even vector triplet, the W-prime and Z-prime, whose mass tracks the dark matter mass. Because the dark matter interacts through electroweak forces, slow particles attract each other, the Sommerfeld enhancement, boosting their annihilation.

Including that enhancement in the freeze-out calculation, the observed relic abundance is reproduced for dark matter masses from 3.6 to 9.2 TeV, inside the perturbative regime. Heavier masses are favored as the heavy vector mass approaches the dark matter mass, since annihilation into a heavy vector plus a Standard Model particle strengthens the cross section. That behavior distinguishes spin-1 from spin-0 and spin-1/2 triplet scenarios.
arxiv-2606-16842:
Mashmool and colleagues reflect on teaching software engineering for AI systems in a 2026 education paper. Machine learning courses teach model building, but graduates often lack practice in design, deployment and monitoring of complete AI systems. Evidence about courses that teach the system side is thin.

The paper examines a project-based master's course at the University of Bremen, where students built a movie recommendation system over a semester. Five staged assignments covered requirements, design, trade-off analysis, deployment, monitoring and changing requirements. A mixed-methods study combined student submissions with class questionnaires. Students gained range across tools and stronger system-level reasoning about data-driven practice. Hard points clustered around early design choices, mixing parts of uneven maturity, shifting requirements and data handling. Uneven prior skills in machine learning and software work explained much of the struggle, a lesson for balancing future cohorts.
arxiv-2606-17142:
Do and colleagues measure the bulk motion of nearby galaxies with exploding stars in a 2026 cosmology paper. Galaxies drift with peculiar motions on top of cosmic expansion. Averaged over a volume, that drift should vanish in a uniform universe; its expected size tests the standard model.

The Hawai'i Supernova Flows dataset provides redshifts plus optical and near-infrared distances to Type Ia supernovae, the standardizable candles of cosmology. Two estimators and two distance methods are applied across subsamples in the nearby universe. Inferred flow speeds run from about one hundred to four hundred kilometers per second. Every estimate sits consistent with the standard model's predictions, joining the studies that find no anomalous flow. Adding near-infrared data changes neither accuracy nor precision over optical alone. The exercise also exposes how much method choices move the answer.
arxiv-2606-17342:
Zhao and Simoncelli present a 2026 arXiv paper on modelling visual textures, the repeated patterns in grass, bark, and other surfaces that help people judge materials. Classic texture models match a set of statistics taken from one image, then generate new samples with the same statistics. Those statistics were either hand-designed or borrowed from networks trained for other jobs, and this work learns them from data instead in a principled way.

The method learns a compact set of statistics for a maximum entropy model, the least committed distribution matching those measured values. Training and sampling borrow machinery from diffusion models, an unusual route for this classic problem. With only a few hundred learned statistics, the model matches or beats a leading rival that uses hundreds of thousands. Direct comparison images, tuned to fool one model but not the other, expose each model's strengths and weaknesses.
arxiv-2606-17942:
Sohanpal and colleagues find the most energy-efficient launch power for signals in hollow-core optical fibres, in a 2026 paper. These fibres guide light through air rather than glass, cutting latency and nonlinear distortion and tolerating far higher launch powers than standard fibre. That freedom raises a practical question: run at the power that maximizes throughput, or at the power that minimizes energy spent per bit?

The two optima differ sharply. For a thousand-kilometre link in the C-band, the team shows that tuning launch power for minimum energy per bit cut total power use by more than two fifths. The cost was a throughput penalty of only about two percent against the maximum. The result gives network designers a concrete, numbers-backed case for greener settings in future hollow-core deployments.
arxiv-2606-18142:
Brazilek and colleagues test whether AI travel agents act on the animal welfare values they voice, in a 2026 benchmark paper. Agents now book trips and plan purchases for users, moving from advisors to actors. Existing welfare benchmarks only grade what models say in text answers, not what they do with tools. Their benchmark, TAC, hands an agent thirteen hand-written travel booking scenarios spanning six kinds of animal exploitation, expanded to fifty-two samples that control for price, rating, and position.

Ten frontier models from four labs all scored below the benchmark's chance level for avoiding exploitative options. The best performer landed just under that line. Success on each scenario tracked how publicly criticized the activity is, not any broad welfare prior. Giving the agent an ethical brand identity in its instructions lifted every model's score substantially.
arxiv-2606-18242:
Lu and colleagues put event cameras, sensors that report brightness changes instead of frames, through a full driving exam, in a 2026 paper from the National University of Singapore. Event sensing reacts in microseconds and handles glare and blur that defeat ordinary cameras, which should help self-driving perception. Yet existing event-aware vision-language models were only tested on generic perception, not on the reasoning chain that driving demands.

Their EventDrive suite unifies event streams, RGB frames, and language across perception, understanding, prediction, and planning, with captions, structured questions, grounding, motion-state recognition, forecasting, and planning tasks. A companion model adds a multi-horizon event pyramid and a mixture-of-experts module that fuses the asynchronous event data with frames at several time scales. The benchmark lets researchers see where event sensing truly improves driving decisions.
arxiv-2606-18342:
Ji and colleagues examine one Little Red Dot, a compact red source known as LRD-204851, in a 2026 JWST and VLT study. The galaxy is seen about one billion years after the Big Bang. Little Red Dots look point-like in optical light, yet their ultraviolet shapes often hint at more structure, and their true nature is still debated.

Combining integral-field spectroscopy with emission-line maps at sub-kiloparsec resolution, the team finds a remarkably thin structure running through the galaxy center and stretching several thousand light-years to either side. A bright oxygen clump sits to the southeast, and the double-peaked hydrogen emission leans the same way. Modeling favors a narrow, low-density cone carved through a dense expanding envelope. The system may be a rare case where a central engine's effect on its host galaxy can be seen directly on large scales.
arxiv-2606-18542:
Xie argues that the wrinkling of a soft material under compression is not just mechanical failure but a topological phase transition, in a 2026 paper joining solid mechanics with topological physics. Surface instability in soft solids is usually treated with classical bifurcation theory.

By folding Lie group metric evolution into a general Stroh formalism, Xie maps the nonlinear geometric frustration of a deformed hyperelastic body onto an algebraic surface impedance matrix. For a semi-infinite elastic half-space under finite compression, the system reduces analytically to a one-dimensional Dirac Hamiltonian, with the stretch playing the role of a tunable mass. The onset of wrinkles then marks a transition between topological phases with a quantized jump in winding number, accompanied by a robust localized zero-energy edge state. The author presents the link as a route toward programmable smart soft matter built through topological ideas.
arxiv-2606-19042:
Tërnava asks in 2026 where software variability goes when a language model writes a whole program from a prompt. In classic software work, teams build options into code so one product can fit many uses. A study of ten vibe-coded projects in C and C++ finds near-zero such built-in options. All choices are settled at generation time, the moment the model writes the code.

Rather than call this a flaw, the author proposes Variability by Regeneration. The model acts as the build engine, making a clean, purpose-built binary for each variant from a written spec. A dispatcher then routes each user request to the matching binary. The paper formalizes the idea, contrasts it with classic product-line methods, and demos the full pipeline on a word-count product family. The claim is plain. In AI-made software, variability belongs in the spec, not in the code.
arxiv-2606-19242:
Kahani and colleagues propose C-Trace in 2026, a runtime compliance framework for AI agents handling personal data. Agents using tools and multi-turn dialogue can create duties under the General Data Protection Regulation. Offline red-teaming and static prompt review cannot guarantee lawful behavior at run time. The framework instead checks each action as it happens, against formal rules drawn from consent, purpose limits, data limits, and erasure rights.

Policies are written as formal predicates over execution traces. A runtime monitor intercepts every tool call and model output and rejects non-compliant actions before they take effect. The team tests agents with attack dialogues, including generated prompts and verbatim red-team prompts that try to induce violations. Across four case studies reframed to the regulation, the monitor keeps attack success low under noisy extraction. It reaches zero attack success under perfect extraction. Runtime enforcement moves compliance from audit to prevention.
arxiv-2606-19942:
Zelin Dong and Chenyun Luo prove orbital stability for vortex patches in channel-like domains in 2026. A vortex patch is a region of spinning fluid in the two-dimensional incompressible Euler equations, and orbital stability means nearby flows keep orbiting the patch family rather than drifting away. The domains covered satisfy a weak finite volume condition or form a strip of any width. Neither scaling nor sideways translation symmetry is available to help.

A penalized kinetic energy functional is shown to admit minimizers, each solving an elliptic equation for the vorticity. The full minimizer set is then proven stable under the flow. The proof compares Green's functions with the half-plane case and uses a concentration-compactness argument built on a decay condition. The result extends earlier variational work by Abe and Choi to less symmetric settings.
arxiv-2606-20042:
Jack Hughes, Joudy Jamal Beek, and Fedor Kusmartsev tackle a gap in the Plebanski formulation of general relativity, a version of Einstein's theory built from two-form fields rather than the metric. His team's 2026 paper asks how matter should enter that framework. The energy-momentum tensor records energy and momentum, and it is symmetric. The Plebanski variables instead split into self-dual and anti-self-dual parts, so the two do not fit together directly.

The authors build the missing source by lifting the tensor's trace-free part into curvature space with the Kulkarni-Nomizu product, then reading off its chiral parts. Their construction matches an earlier definition by Krasnov, and the coupled equations still imply the standard conservation law through a Bianchi identity. Applied to a charged spherical source, the equations return the Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter solution, giving a clean recipe for translating matter sources between formulations.
arxiv-2606-20142:
Antón Asla Manzárraga places a reasoning agent in charge of tuning an optimizer's search behavior, rather than replacing the optimizer itself. His 2026 paper introduces RACL, a Reasoning-Agent Control Layer for metaheuristics, the search methods firms use for routing and scheduling. Many firms own a configured optimizer but lack staff who can adapt its internal search as conditions change. RACL learns that job by watching operational memory and testing bounded hypotheses.

The agent observes past runs, proposes small interventions, checks them against guardrails, and keeps policies that work. Vehicle routing serves as the testbed, though the method targets control, not routing. RACL improved or tied a memory-based policy in all twenty-one feasible cases, and beat or tied a stagnation-triggered policy in eighteen. On one sample it cut costs by about eight percent against fixed settings, showing agents can curate algorithmic know-how firms otherwise lose.
arxiv-2606-20342:
Tanmoy Pati and Narayan Rana extend a key renormalization calculation to mixed gauge theories. Their 2026 paper works on the axial anomaly within dimensional regularization, where defining the gamma-five matrix remains a fundamental nuisance. Larin's prescription repairs the chiral Ward identities with extra renormalization constants, known to four loops in pure QCD. Precision phenomenology now needs those constants where strong and electroweak forces mix, in an SU(N) cross U(1) gauge group.

The authors propose a technique based on form factors and the universality of infrared divergences. With it, they present new three-loop results for the constants, plus the pure-singlet parts of the quark axial-vector form factor, in the mixed gauge setting. Such constants are unglamorous but load-bearing: every high-precision prediction involving axial currents depends on them. Extending Larin's scheme beyond pure QCD removes a bottleneck for the precision program.
arxiv-2606-20542:
Ilona Demler and four colleagues release CalTennis, a large multi-view tennis dataset for monocular-to-3D pose estimation. Their 2026 paper benchmarks how well algorithms recover 3D body pose from a single camera in the wild. The dataset holds over 11 million frames, 51 hours, of practice and match play from 40 players.

Two to six synchronized cameras at 60 hertz capture the motion, making the set ten times larger than existing in-the-wild motion datasets and three times larger than mocap-ground-truthed ones. The multi-view setup enables cheap, label-free evaluation of monocular methods against the other views. A simple standardized protocol keeps comparisons honest. Expert athletic motion finally has a benchmark at the scale pose research needs.
arxiv-2606-20742:
Yamil Uchani and three colleagues present a digital twin framework in 2026 for drone pavement monitoring that keeps traffic flowing. Drone inspection can cut the cost and risk of road checks. Real deployment is hard when vehicles and pedestrians block views of defects. Their Unity-based twin, a virtual copy of the road setting, includes generated defects, moving traffic, and autonomous drone navigation.

An embedded perception pipeline works in two stages. A light YOLO detector first locates defects, people, and vehicles. A classifier then separates potholes, single cracks, and crocodile cracks. On the simulator test set, the pipeline reaches 99.26 percent accuracy across five classes. The twin also tests three recovery plans for blocked segments: hover and recheck, small repositioning, and skip and revisit. Testing recovery in simulation lets operators plan for occlusion before risking flights over live traffic.
arxiv-2606-20842:
Junbao Zhou and nine colleagues guide sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting with Fisher information in 2026, aiming for stable and faithful novel views. Gaussian Splatting renders new views from 3D Gaussian primitives. It needs many input views for quality. With few views, it overfits and creates artifacts. Older fixes add depth priors or randomly drop Gaussians. Random choices bring uncertainty and instability.

Fisher information measures how much data informs a parameter. Zhou and colleagues use it to guide two parts of the method. Stereo augmentation selects extra viewpoints on a principled basis. Regularization is also guided rather than random. The result targets uncertainty directly instead of averaging over it. Principled guidance for sparse-view rendering matters for practical capture, where users may photograph a scene only a handful of times yet still expect clean, stable three-dimensional views.
arxiv-2606-20942:
Ulf Danielsson and Suvendu Giri review the dark bubble model in 2026, a proposal that explains the positive cosmological constant through extra dimensions. In the model, our universe is a bubble surface in a higher-dimensional space. Instabilities linked to de Sitter swampland ideas make accelerated expansion inevitable. A distinctive outcome is a hierarchy joining cosmic, gravitational, string, and higher-dimensional scales.

The model predicts a dark dimension of micron size, an idea also argued on other grounds. Gravity should weaken near that scale, matching Sundrum's fat graviton scenario, where gravity stops probing shorter distances. Other predictions include a string scale of tens of tera-electronvolts and measurable positive spatial curvature. Testable numbers matter here. A theory of cosmic acceleration that predicts lab and sky signals can be checked, not only admired for its internal logic.
arxiv-2606-21642:
Lipika Kolay, Soumitra Nandi, Shantanu Sahoo, and Ria Sain ask in 2026 what happens if the invisible particle in B-meson decays is not the neutrino. Analyses of semileptonic B decays into D or D-star mesons assume the missing energy is a massless Standard Model neutrino. If it were instead a massive dark-sector fermion, a sterile neutrino for instance, the decay's kinematics and angular distributions would shift.

Working in a general weak effective theory, they map those shifts. They also trace the fallout for extracting the CKM element Vcb, a cornerstone measurement these decays exist to serve, and discuss the effective and simplified models where such effects arise. The message is double: current Vcb values inherit the massless assumption, and the same distributions offer a systematic hunting ground for dark fermions hiding in well-measured decays.
arxiv-2606-22342:
Muntakim and colleagues build SciTraj in 2026, a claim-grounded typed citation graph for tracing how research evolves across natural language processing, machine learning, and computer vision. Ordinary citation graphs collapse every citation into one edge type, hiding whether a paper extends a method, addresses a limitation, realizes a proposed direction, or disputes a claim. SciTraj instead links each edge to the specific claim sentence motivating it.

The corpus holds 32,559 papers from 2015 to 2024, joined by 573,126 directed edges across six relation types, with claim seeds verified by entailment checking. Analyses reveal field siloing in typed citation flow, with new topics emerging mainly in vision and language-model work. The 287 million typed trajectories of length three or more support forecasting studies. A time-split link-prediction benchmark and a year-shuffle sanity test round out the resource.
arxiv-2606-22442:
Xiangyuan Xue and seven colleagues, including Hong Jia, build a benchmark for medical AI in this 2026 paper. Their focus is pulmonary embolism, a dangerous blockage in the lung arteries that needs fast diagnosis and sound risk assessment. Care for it mixes CT scan images, radiology reports, and long electronic health records, making it a natural test for models that read several kinds of input.

The team uses INSPECT, a dataset of more than twenty-three thousand CT pulmonary angiography studies from over nineteen thousand patients. They frame eight diagnostic and prognostic tasks as structured clinical questions. Compact multimodal models were tested with scans alone, records alone, or both together, under zero-shot and few-shot prompting. Two Gemma4 models performed more strongly when record evidence was available, especially with scans and records combined. Diagnosis tasks scored higher than prognosis tasks, and predicting readmission proved hardest of all.
arxiv-2606-22642:
Priya, Labh Singh, B. C. Chauhan, and Surender Verma connect neutrino masses with cosmic domain walls in this 2026 paper. Their model extends the standard model with a Z3 symmetry, three fermion triplets that generate neutrino masses through the Type-III seesaw, and a scalar singlet which breaks the symmetry.

Breaking Z3 leaves three equivalent vacua, whose boundaries form unstable domain walls that must disappear. Yukawa interactions between the triplets and the singlet generate a Coleman-Weinberg potential that biases one vacuum over the others. That radiative bias lifts the degeneracy and triggers the walls' annihilation. A numerical analysis finds parameter regions matching observed neutrino masses and mixing. The universe's baryon asymmetry arises through thermal leptogenesis, the out-of-equilibrium decay of the lightest triplet at very high mass. Depending on parameters, the predicted gravitational-wave spectrum could reach future detectors, tying neutrino physics to a possible signal.
arxiv-2606-22942:
Xin Liu and colleagues study knowledge distillation during post-training in a 2026 machine learning paper. Distillation trains a small student model using a larger teacher model. Post-training is the stage that turns a raw model into one that follows instructions well. Most earlier distillation studies used small tasks, so the post-training case was poorly understood. The team uses the large Tulu 3 instruction dataset for its tests.

Liu and colleagues find that distillation beats plain supervised fine-tuning when training data is scarce. As data grows, that edge fades away. A stronger teacher that was itself instruction tuned restores large gains even with plenty of data. The lesson is that distillation helps most when the teacher knows things the student cannot learn from the data alone. For low-resource fields, a two-stage plan using teacher-labeled synthetic data, then human-labeled data, improved students steadily.
arxiv-2606-23142:
Madhurendra Mishra and colleagues find a frequency comb hidden in a financial model in a 2026 paper. In physics, a frequency comb is a set of evenly spaced, phase-locked spectral lines born from nonlinear coupling. The team studies a fractional-order economic model whose special derivatives encode long memory in saving, investment, and prices. They ask whether its long-run spectrum shows any such ordered structure. The answer is yes, but only inside specific ranges of the model's saving, cost, and demand parameters.

Mishra and colleagues show the comb survives wide parameter ranges and shrugs off changes in starting interest rate and investment demand. Different starting price levels switch the spectrum between distinct regimes. The comb appears only when the three fractional exponents pass critical thresholds. Push them higher still and the tidy comb dissolves into chaos.
arxiv-2606-23442:
Daham Mustafa and colleagues fix temporal conflict detection in digital rights policies in a 2026 paper. The Open Digital Rights Language, ODRL, writes permissions and duties for digital content. Its temporal constraints mix two sorts of values: instants and durations. The comparison operators do not distinguish them, so one symbol means either earlier instant or shorter duration. That ambiguity makes checking two policies for conflicts unsound. The authors resolve it by sort stratification: every temporal operand is typed as a point in time or an amount of time.

Mustafa and colleagues give each constraint an interval meaning, so conflict reduces to interval comparison. The verdict is three-valued: conflict, compatible, or unknown. They characterize when the check is decidable in static and runtime fragments, and they prove it sound. A benchmark of policy problems, compiled into standard solver formats, accompanies the work as a public artifact.
arxiv-2606-23542:
Prasai and colleagues demonstrate AwakeForest, an interactive platform for analyzing forest imagery at very large scale, in a 2026 paper slated for a major artificial intelligence conference demo track. Forest scientists work with aerial images and stitched orthomosaics, single map-like images that can reach hundreds of gigabytes, and they need detection, outlining, and counting done inside one workflow. General labeling tools handle ordinary photo sets well but struggle with such huge, map-based ecological imagery.

AwakeForest combines model-assisted prediction, automatic annotation, and human checking in a single geospatial workflow, meaning every result stays tied to real map coordinates. Users can plug in pretrained models, review their labels patch by patch, and export analysis-ready outputs for direct use. The team demonstrates the full workflow on the PALMS forest dataset, showing how new scenes can feed fresh annotations back into model improvement for practical forest management.
arxiv-2606-23842:
Učakar shows that wandering domains, the most exotic regions in the dynamics of entire functions, can take almost any unbounded shape one cares to draw, in a 2026 paper on complex dynamics. Iterating an entire function splits the plane into a stable Fatou set and a chaotic Julia set. A Fatou component that never revisits itself under iteration is a wandering domain, possible only for transcendental functions, never for polynomials. What shapes such a domain can take is the newer question.

Using Arakelian approximation, Učakar proves two things. First, components of a uniformly accessible closed set inside a strip arise as escaping or oscillating wandering domains, with the function one to one on each. Second, every simply connected open set admits approximation by such domains. A corollary then yields wandering domains with complements of arbitrarily small area.
arxiv-2606-23942:
Martnishn puts a new neural network regularizer through nine hundred sixty controlled experiments to find when, where, and why it helps, in a 2026 paper on deep learning. Regularizers keep networks from memorizing training data. DREG penalizes each layer's Jacobian, the map of how outputs respond to inputs, weighted by how active that layer's neurons are. Pressure lands where the network bends most, rather than spread uniformly like weight decay. One fixed strength is used everywhere.

Across eight datasets spanning vision, language, tables, and signals, DREG takes the highest overall accuracy, significantly beating the unregularized baseline and weight decay. For noise robustness it comes second, behind only spectral normalization. Under GELU, the standard activation in modern transformers, it is best overall. Its edge grows largest when training data are scarce.
arxiv-2606-24142:
Umetsu and colleagues weigh forty-one galaxy clusters by watching how their gravity bends light. The clusters come from the CHEX-MATE sample, selected through the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect in Planck data. Wide-field imaging from Subaru and the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope feeds an AMALGAM weak-lensing analysis. It measures the subtle averaged distortion of background galaxy shapes around each cluster.

Averaged shear signals register clearly around the X-ray peak of every cluster. A rotated control component stays consistent with zero, as a clean measurement should. Fitting Navarro-Frenk-White profiles, the standard halo shape, yields mass and concentration estimates per cluster. Total systematic uncertainty in the mass calibration is assessed at a modest level. A hierarchical Bayesian framework then converts the sample into scaling relations, calibrated by the lensing masses. The 2026 catalogue gives cluster cosmology a cross-checked mass anchor.
arxiv-2606-24242:
Chen and colleagues track what an experiment does to quantum states, using a quantity entanglement measures cannot see. Two squeezed vacuum states, prepared apart, become entangled when mixed on a balanced beam splitter. Standard inseparability criteria can witness that entanglement. Witnesses, however, cannot separate genuine entanglement from damage done by mode mismatch and detection flaws. The input states start unentangled, so they offer no baseline.

A framework based on quantumness fills the gap. Under ideal mixing, a state's quantumness is conserved by the beam splitter. Comparing values before and after mixing thus benchmarks exactly what the apparatus cost. Chen's team demonstrates the comparison in the lab, on the beam-splitter entanglement setup. The 2026 approach generalises to multi-mode continuous-variable states at any stage of an experiment. It gives the field a conserved currency for auditing where quantumness leaks away, rather than a yes-or-no verdict at the end.
arxiv-2606-24542:
Zhao, Yan, He, and Duan analyse pursuit games where the defenders learn everything late. In reach avoid differential games, attackers race to reach a target while defenders try to capture them first. All move in the plane with bounded speeds. Here every defender observes the other agents' states only after a constant time delay, a realistic handicap from sensing and communication pipelines.

For one attacker and one defender, a description of the attacker's delayed attack region is derived, and proved convex under mild assumptions. When the defender can guarantee capture, a convex program computes the capture point. The resulting strategies form a subgame perfect Nash equilibrium, exploiting the sequential structure the delay itself creates. Extensions cover one attacker against many defenders and the general case, where delay aware pairwise winning relations feed a maximum matching for assigning defenders. Simulations validate the theory.
arxiv-2606-24642:
Cacciapaglia, Del Piano, Sannino, and Vellucci ask when a black hole can split in two, a process whose horizon topology resembles a pair of pants. Classical general relativity forbids it for Schwarzschild black holes, through the area law. Splitting would shrink total horizon area. For spinning Kerr black holes, kinematic constraints block fragmentation even where entropy might allow it. Near extremality, where spin approaches its maximum, is the possible exception.

The hunt therefore turns to escape routes. The Gregory-Laflamme instability fragments extended horizons in higher dimensions. Superradiant instabilities, with non axisymmetric radiation trapping, might pry four-dimensional holes apart. Models modifying the relations among entropy, radius, and mass can also favour splitting. In all these scenarios, emitting small fragments can be entropically favoured, though occurrence still hinges on the initial state's kinematics. The 2026 analysis clarifies the landscape for primordial black holes, and other settings where fragmentation would leave evidence.
arxiv-2606-24942:
Connor Barbaccia, Sudip Vhaduri, and Sayanton Dibbo propose a decentralised AI economy secured against quantum attack. Proof of work blockchains burn energy on hash puzzles that produce nothing of external value. Their design rewards useful machine learning work instead: inference and training done by network nodes. A three layer architecture splits compute, validation, and economic coordination. The token economy is formalised as a closed loop system, and the authors derive the stake condition that suffices for honest participation.

The quantum argument runs on two tracks. Grover's algorithm gives only a quadratic speedup against hash puzzles, and it does not accelerate the linear algebra that machine learning runs on. Shor's algorithm, by contrast, threatens classical blockchain signatures directly. Migrating to lattice based or hash based post quantum standards addresses that layer. Barbaccia and colleagues conclude that useful work consensus offers security advantages, both economic and quantum, over classical proof of work.
arxiv-2606-25242:
Some materials act as if their electrons were far heavier than normal, a state called heavy fermion behaviour. Shunsaku Kitagawa, Kenji Ishida, Yoshihiko Okamoto, and Zenji Hiroi examine two manganese compounds in 2026. Their metal atoms sit on a pyrochlore lattice, a network of corner sharing tetrahedra known for magnetic frustration. Extra manganese atoms muddy the picture, so the team used resonance measurements to separate the true lattice signal from the clutter.

Swapping indium into the structure proved much cleaner than swapping aluminium, which scrambled local sites. Cooling the samples strengthened low energy magnetic excitations tied to heavy fermion formation. Yet the signal stayed about twenty times weaker than in a related compound, because the wider spacing between manganese atoms weakens their interaction.
arxiv-2606-25342:
Agents that run for months should keep learning from experience, but a transformer's memory grows with every token it reads. Luke McDermott, Robert Heath Jr, and Rahul Parhi argue in 2026 that lifelong in context learning demands a different kind of attention. Parametric attention replaces the ever growing store of past keys and values with a small trainable module that absorbs new associations on the fly. Memory then stays constant no matter how long the agent operates, fitting a fixed hardware budget.

Surveying state space models, linear attention, test time training layers, and fast weight programmers, the authors find each current option falls short somewhere, through limited capacity or expensive updates. Rather than proposing one more mechanism, they pose a set of open questions with fresh analysis meant to steer the field. The piece is a position and agenda paper for long horizon agents.
arxiv-2606-25642:
Sound moves faster along the molecular alignment direction in a nematic liquid crystal. Engineers could steer acoustics by steering that alignment with fields. Tim van Beeck takes up the governing model in 2026, the nematic Helmholtz Korteweg equation. It adds two fourth order terms to the classical wave equation. One of them depends on direction. Computing with fourth order equations usually demands very smooth elements. Van Beeck instead proposes a hybrid method whose elements are merely continuous. Penalty terms across element faces repair the gaps.

Stability is proved for every polynomial degree from two upward, in any spatial dimension. One condition is needed: the anisotropy must stay small. Solutions of the scheme converge to the true one under weak smoothness assumptions. Explicit rates follow when the solution is smoother. Tests close the paper, and the analysis sharpens earlier work via the Cordes condition from elliptic theory.
arxiv-2606-25742:
Squeeze a barocaloric material and it warms; release the pressure and it cools, a solid state route to refrigeration without greenhouse gases. Finding good candidates needs atomistic simulation, and machine learned potentials can mimic quantum accuracy if fed enough quantum calculations, which are expensive. Ludwig Hedin and Johan Klarbring ask in 2026 how little training data suffices, using ammonium sulfate, whose temperature driven structural change powers its cooling effect. Three training strategies compete on the MACE architecture across shrinking datasets.

The untuned foundation model failed to reproduce the phase change at all, and models trained from scratch broke down on small datasets. Fine tuned models, by either of two protocols, captured the transformation from as few as five to ten small quantum configurations. A dispersion correction proved necessary for correct phase behaviour, and the data frugality even allows training at a costlier hybrid quantum level.
arxiv-2606-25942:
Long Feng, Le Zhou, and Xiaoyi Wang build a tougher test for high-dimensional location. Hotelling-style tests ask whether a mean vector sits at a claimed value. Modern data break the classic version: dimensions rival sample size, coordinates depend heavily, and tails run heavy. Their test assumes elliptically symmetric data instead of Gaussian data. A sample spatial median anchors the centre. A spatial-sign covariance matrix, centred at that median, supplies the spread estimate.

Ridge regularization needs a tuning choice. The power-optimal ridge depends on the unknown alternative being tested. Their fix aggregates p-values across a fixed grid of ridge values. A Cauchy combination rule merges them into one analytic p-value. No cross-ridge correlation estimates are needed, thanks to a joint Gaussian limit. Null behaviour and local power are both characterized. Simulations and an application show strong performance under heavy tails and dependence.
arxiv-2606-26042:
Souvik Naskar and colleagues compare simulated and observed patterns in Earth's magnetic field. The time-averaged field hints at how the core and mantle interact. Paleomagnetic data and dynamo simulations disagree on its longitudinal structure, though. Many simulations use a generic buoyancy source. That choice may hide separate thermal and chemical effects. The team runs top-heavy thermochemical dynamo simulations instead. Thermal and chemical driving strengths vary across the suite.

No broad morphology measure separates the chemical driving levels reliably. Variability measures fail the same test. One observational demand does discriminate, though. Longitudinal variations in inclination anomaly match only runs with uneven mantle heat flux. Even heat flux runs miss them. Strong chemical driving shrinks the longitudinal structures without erasing them. It also deepens polar minima in the radial field. Both effects likely push Earth's field slightly off the simple axial dipole picture.
arxiv-2606-26242:
Wiesław Laskowski, Tamás Vértesi, and Jan Wójcik find an edge hiding in lopsided entangled states. All maximally entangled two-qubit states break local realism with equal odds under random measurements. Run the test twice, though, with measurement settings swapped between the partners, and states diverge. Permutation-symmetric states give identical nonlocality outcomes in both runs. Asymmetric states can break local realism in one run and not the other.

Two payoffs follow. Joint statistics across the swapped runs can reveal correlations between the partners' measurement choices. In tests with finite setting pools, asymmetric states also raise the odds of spotting nonlocality at all. No extra resources are needed for either gain. Symmetry, usually treated as background tidiness in Bell tests, becomes a working part. Randomized experiments, common in device-independent protocols, are exactly where this asymmetry pays.
arxiv-2606-26342:
Andrew Sabin, Steve Taddei, and Abram Bailey build a hearing-aid metric from the listeners who actually wear the aids. HearAdvisor rates hearing aids for consumers. Its speech metric was built to predict lab intelligibility under simulated distortions. Whether it matches what wearers find easy to understand was unclear. Their study replaces guesswork with scale: visitors with self-reported hearing loss rated recordings blind, on a five-point ease scale.

Ratings top one hundred thousand after quality screening. Recordings span eighty-three commercial products across seventy-two realistic scenes, captured on an acoustic manikin. A learned model compares aided audio against clean speech inside a frozen Whisper encoder and predicts the ratings. On unseen devices it beats the old metric clearly, scene by scene. In loud scenes it reaches the reliability ceiling of the listeners themselves. Consumer judgement, captured at scale, becomes the yardstick.
arxiv-2606-26442:
Jimmy Xin and five colleagues present Axle, a cloud service for automated theorem proving. Lean 4 is a proof assistant. In it, mathematics is written so a computer can verify every step. Modern artificial intelligence provers may need millions of proof checks. Existing tools compile code in parallel. They do not offer scalable verification, proof editing, or isolation between requests. Axle aims to fill that gap.

Axle supplies fourteen tools. They cover strict proof checking and extracting facts about declarations. They also edit proof source in meaning-aware ways. Other tools pull out lemmas and repair or simplify proofs repeatably. The service runs in the cloud with each request isolated. It supports several Lean and Mathlib versions at once. Users reach it through Python, a command line, a web page, and an agent protocol. The authors report more than five hundred million requests served so far.
arxiv-2606-26742:
Haoming Shi and Weijun Fang study convertible codes, storage codes that can change their settings without full rewriting. Data centres store data with erasure codes, which rebuild lost data from surviving pieces. As systems grow or failure rates change, code parameters must change too. Conversion transforms old encoded data into the new code directly. Locally repairable codes also keep single repairs cheap.

The authors focus on the split regime of conversion, for codes with few global parity pieces. They derive lower bounds on the read bandwidth any conversion must pay. The bounds use information theory and assume nothing about linearity of the codes or the conversion. Matching constructions follow, built from array codes with set repair properties. The bounds are thus tight: no method can beat them, and theirs achieves them.
arxiv-2606-26842:
Fumiaki Yamaguchi presents voxmap-studio, an open-source tool for labelling who spoke when in audio recordings. That task, speaker diarization, needs costly hand-labelled training data. Most labelling tools never measure the labour they save. This one records cost directly: counts of typed edit operations and time spent are built-in outputs.

The canvas starts from a fast automatic diarization draft. The annotator corrects the draft instead of drawing every speaker turn from scratch. Export is blocked until a human confirms each segment. Planted phantom checks catch careless confirmation. A pilot study on nine meeting recordings followed. Fully manual labelling was slowest and least accurate. Automatic starting drafts shifted the work from creating to correcting. In the small sample, flagging uncertain segments cost least.
arxiv-2606-26942:
Shuchao Duan and four colleagues present TraMP-LLaMA, a model that grades facial expression quality and explains its grades in words. Parkinson's disease assessment uses facial motion, but existing scoring tools output a bare severity number. Clinicians cannot see what evidence drove the score. Their framework reads both appearance and landmark trajectories, the paths of facial points over time.

Severity prediction and report writing are trained under separate instructions to stop the two tasks interfering. The model thus produces a score plus a structured report of observable motion evidence. The authors extended an existing data set with expert-guided text descriptions of facial motion. On the extended set, the model beat video-language rivals at report generation. It also achieved the best severity prediction under joint training across expressions.
arxiv-2606-27042:
Silva and colleagues address signal damage in analog radio-over-fiber links, which carry wireless signals as light through optical fibre. Power amplifiers in such links bend signals, and that bending must be undone before sending. Undoing it is called digital predistortion, meaning the signal is pre-warped to cancel later damage. The team builds a predistorter from a Kolmogorov-Arnold Network, a network type that uses learnable curves instead of fixed steps. 

Named envelope time-delay KAN, the model is then turned into plain symbolic formulas. That step cuts computing cost sharply and makes the correction easier to read and check. Its error scores match those of standard neural predistorters, while its cost stays near cheap formula-based methods. In a real fibre test setup, the symbolic version cut unwanted side-channel leakage by about four to five decibels.
arxiv-2606-27242:
Sweeney studies how to pick source data for adapting language models that share one vocabulary. In string domains like chemical SMILES, protein, and genome sequences, candidate corpora share a tokenizer but aim at different targets. Similarity of internal features can then go dark, saying nothing about transfer. A key identity shows head Fisher alignment equals a cosine between kernel mean maps in joint activation-error space. That identity exposes activity, error, and coupling factors separately, in a transfer learning paper appearing in 2026.

A streaming estimator, FisherSketch, computes that cosine in one pass. Task signatures stay tiny, small enough to store beside a model hash. Experiments with shared-parameter and layer checks, plus verbalizer-shift tests on a Llama model, keep the score informative. Representation similarity fails to separate tasks in those same tests. Update geometry, not feature resemblance, carries the transfer signal. Source selection for huge vocabularies becomes practical.
arxiv-2606-27342:
Pulsone, Goren, and Shraga probe how a leading low-resource entity matching system behaves when budgets and domains shift. It decides whether records from different sources name the same real-world thing. The BEACON method borrows labelled data across domains under a fixed annotation budget, aligning distributions as it goes. Strong headline results left open how design choices and data scarcity drive them. Targeted experiments vary those choices and availability conditions in this data management study from 2026, an extended version of a workshop paper.

Distribution alignment, the method's core trick, is isolated and stress-tested across settings. Performance shifts trace back to specific choices rather than the whole package. Supervision level interacts with domain gaps in ways headline numbers hid. Practitioners gain a clearer map of when cross-domain borrowing pays. Low-resource matching claims become easier to audit and reproduce. The study favours careful ablation over leaderboard faith.
arxiv-2606-27542:
Dash and colleagues run distributed power-flow optimisation on real hardware, where a live 5G network carries the control messages. The alternating direction method of multipliers splits grid optimisation across local controllers, but communication delays can stall its convergence. Their testbed divides a standard one hundred twenty-three-bus feeder into five areas, each run by a small single-board computer, with commercial 5G connectivity between them. In the 2026 smart grid study, a delay threshold mechanism decides when controllers proceed without waiting for stragglers.

The threshold alone cuts convergence time by seven point seven five percent against a no-threshold baseline in the reported experiments. A policy that updates the threshold dynamically from communication and computation conditions does better, cutting convergence time by twenty-six point four two percent against the best static threshold in the same tests. Communication-aware control proves its worth outside simulation.
arxiv-2606-27642:
Smart grids need fast, reliable communication for live monitoring and control. Fifth-generation mobile networks promise low delay and high reliability. Most earlier studies of 5G for grids relied on simulation, though. Biswajit Kumar Dash, Luis Herrera, and Filippo Malandra instead validate with real hardware in 2026. Their testbed uses Raspberry Pi grid nodes and a Typhoon hardware-in-the-loop simulator.

The team first measured 5G performance under varied reporting rates and settings. Delay, jitter, and frame loss were the key measures. Worst-case mean delay came out about six and a half times lower than in their earlier LTE study. Real measurements then streamed from an IEEE four-node feeder model. Voltage, current, and phase angle went to a remote data concentrator. State estimation stayed accurate under steady and changing loads. Fault detection was reliable and prompt. The fastest detection delays were about eight tenths of a second.
arxiv-2606-27942:
Rebuilding the proteins of extinct organisms is a powerful tool in evolution research. Most methods assume each site in a protein evolves on its own. Real proteins break it, because their parts interact. Alya Zeinaty and five colleagues build a framework in 2026 that respects those interactions. Standard family-tree inference is combined with Direct Coupling Analysis. Uncertainty at each site is kept, and constraints between paired residues, learned from living families, are enforced.

A controlled test checks the method. A simulator evolves proteins forward under realistic rules, so the true ancestors are known. Two protein families serve as applications, beta-lactamases and DNA-binding domains. The approach, in turn, improves reconstruction when ancestral states are interaction-constrained. It gives ensembles of candidate ancestors rather than one answer. The candidates fit both the family tree and the statistics of natural families. The point is to respect how proteins really evolve.
arxiv-2606-28042:
Vilem Liepelt, Danielle Marshall, and Dominic Orchard work on graded types. These are a way for programming languages to track extra information in types, such as how a program uses resources or depends on its context. Two families of such systems grew up separately over the last decade, and nobody knew exactly how they related.

Liepelt and colleagues build translations between example languages of both families and prove the translations preserve types, grades, and program behavior. One family sprinkles annotations through every function type. The other layers a single graded operator on top of linear types, an older discipline from logic. Because the same context effects can be written either way, results can now travel between the two traditions, guiding future language design.
arxiv-2606-28142:
Deployed models face distribution shift, and test-time adaptation adjusts them on the fly. Standard methods tweak only the per-channel scale and shift of normalisation layers. Mansoo Jung, Youngwook Kim, and Jungwoo Lee argue in 2026 that such axis-aligned updates cannot fix cross-channel structural changes. Their module, MixTTA, adds a low-rank cross-channel transformation to normalisation layers. Two projections keep the branch well-behaved.

A decoupling projection keeps the branch strictly separate from the diagonal affine path. A spectral projection prevents rank-one collapse under non-stationary test streams. MixTTA plugs into any existing normalisation-based adaptation method. Experiments in standard and wild settings show consistent improvements over strong baselines. Adaptation failure under challenging conditions is mitigated. Shift disrupts inter-channel correlations most severely in earlier layers, the conclusion adds. Adaptive rank selection is future work, and overhead stays minimal.
arxiv-2606-29042:
Wu, Tong, Mao and Zhang report that a quantum system watched continuously can settle into an exactly ergodic state, exploring its whole state space evenly. Ergodicity in Hilbert space is usually assumed for generic quantum dynamics, justified by the idea that evolving states sample the space uniformly subject to constraints. Making that idea rigorous means the ensemble of states must match the Haar-random ensemble, or its structured cousin, the Scrooge ensemble.

For any chosen target density matrix, the team construct a monitored system whose late-time distribution of trajectories is exactly that target's Scrooge ensemble. They prove it is the unique such equilibrium. Remarkably, the monitoring's jump operators need only form a deformed unitary 1-design, a condition much weaker than full ergodicity. Simulations with thermal equilibrium states confirm the predictions. The result offers a rigorous mechanism for ergodicity's emergence, and a practical route to study it on quantum devices.
arxiv-2606-29842:
Gelman and three colleagues introduce the Squealer, a tool that adds sound to the job of checking how well a statistical model fits data. A user starts from the best-fitting curve and drags it to a new position.

As the curve moves away from the data, the computer emits a squeal that grows louder and more unpleasant the worse the mismatch gets. The aim is to let researchers feel where a model fits, where it misses, and which data points block a better fit, without watching the screen constantly. The authors demonstrate the method on four examples: golf putting data, dilution assays in the laboratory, cosmological data tied to Big Bang parameters, and a flexible curve fit to temperature readings.
arxiv-2606-30042:
Michal Ajdarów, A. Balasubramanian, and Łukasz Orlikowski classify the difficulty of reachability in continuous counter systems. Vector addition systems model machines with non-negative counters. For the classic version, this question is famously Ackermann-complete, an extreme complexity. Continuous versions let counters hold rational values and scale updates. That change drops the question to NP-complete in general.

The authors fix the number of counters and study eight problem variants. The variants mix reachability and coverability, unary and binary encodings, and two semantics. For rational update vectors, a clean split emerges. With one counter, all eight sit inside polynomial time. With two or more counters, all eight become NP-complete. Hardness holds even when the machine has no cycles. A new Egyptian prime fractions technique drives the proofs. Integer transition vectors are classified for most dimensions too.
arxiv-2606-30142:
Hoang Phi Dung and Duong Khanh Ly seek to cut total infections in an epidemic by deleting network links. Their model is the discrete SIS model on a network. In SIS dynamics, recovered people become susceptible again. Removing edges slows spread, but choosing which edges matters. The authors extend an existing edge deletion algorithm to this setting in 2026.

A mean-field approximation first linearizes the network dynamics. The result is a deterministic version of the SIS model. They prove total infections are bounded by a supermodular function. Supermodularity is what makes greedy edge deletion efficient here. Experiments run on synthetic Erdős–Rényi networks first. A real dataset from the BBC Pandemic Haslemere app follows. Simulations confirm the theory in both configurations tested. Both setups converge to the stable, disease-free equilibrium.
arxiv-2606-30442:
Nikolai Rozanov, Subhabrata Dutta, Preslav Nakov, and Iryna Gurevych argue that AI's famous Bitter Lesson misses a hidden cost: slow feedback. The lesson says general methods scaling with data beat built-in knowledge. Historic AI wins enjoyed near-instant verification of predictions.
