Twenty labs took part in a blind comparison. Each measured the same dye-labeled DNA samples with its own setup. With a unified method, results agreed closely across labs. The team suggests steps for turning transfer values into accurate distances. They also discuss the sources of uncertainty. The study gives the field a reference point for more reliable measurements.
europmc-pmc6156142:
Herbet and co-authors wrote a review in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy on a major white matter pathway of the brain. The inferior longitudinal fasciculus links the back of the brain, where vision is processed, to the front of the temporal lobe. Its connections suggest a role in many brain functions. Until recently, hard evidence was scarce.

The review gathers recent anatomy, brain stimulation, and neuropsychology studies. They show a layered, two-way tract that processes visual cues and guides decisions based on them. Damage to it appears in a wide range of disorders, from mental illness to epilepsy. Readers get the historical reports and the current hypotheses in one account.
europmc-pmc6164842:
Salehi and co-authors wrote a review in Biomedicines on resveratrol, a plant polyphenol found in grapes and red wine. It occurs in more than 70 plant species, mostly in grape skin and seeds. Plants make it to fight bacteria and fungi. Studies credit it with strong antioxidant power.

The review sums up evidence for antitumor activity and other health effects. Lab and animal studies support a role in preventing and treating several cancers. Yet the title calls it a double-edged sword. Dose and context can change what it does in the body. The authors weigh the promise against those limits, giving readers both edges of the evidence.
europmc-pmc6279042:
Mehling and co-authors present a revised survey for measuring inner body awareness. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE. The trait is called interoceptive awareness. It covers how people sense and read signals from inside the body. The survey has eight scales and was first published in 2012. Two scales proved weak in repeated use.

Six new items were written to fix those scales. Over a thousand museum visitors in London completed the survey. Half the sample guided item choices by factor analysis. Five of the six new items were kept. The other half confirmed the eight scale structure of the new 37 item version. Internal consistency improved as hoped. The new survey, MAIA-2, is free for public use. It serves research on mind and body therapies.
europmc-pmc6357742:
Dominy and co-authors present a research article in Science Advances linking a gum bacterium to Alzheimer's disease. The team studied Porphyromonas gingivalis, the main pathogen in chronic gum disease. They asked whether its toxic enzymes, called gingipains, appear in Alzheimer's brains and help drive the illness.

They found gingipain proteins in Alzheimer's brains at far higher levels than in control brains. Bacterial DNA also appeared in patient brains and in spinal fluid from living subjects. In tests, new small-molecule blockers stopped gingipain activity in animals. The authors argue the findings support a causal role for the bacterium. They also point to gingipain blockers as a possible treatment path.
europmc-pmc6361242:
Langmead and co-authors present a methods article in Bioinformatics on making genome software use modern processors well. Chips now run hundreds of threads at once, but read aligners often slow down as threads multiply. The team studied why, and tested fixes in the Bowtie, Bowtie 2, and HISAT aligners.

They trace much of the slowdown to locks that guard shared input and output files. Some lock types scale badly, while queueing and standard locks hold up far better. They also show that the FASTQ file format hinders scaling, and they suggest format changes that keep file sizes about the same. Their updated tools scale far better on many-core machines.
europmc-pmc6387042:
Tian and co-authors review mTOR signaling in cancer, in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. The mTOR pathway controls cell growth, survival, and protein making. It is switched on too strongly in many cancers.

Faults at many points in the chain can cause that overdrive. The review maps the chain's main upstream and downstream parts. It covers mTOR-blocking drugs tested in eight solid tumor types. Single-drug and paired-drug trials both get attention. The authors weigh why results have been mixed and where the drugs still promise gains.
europmc-pmc6403142:
Zhen and Zhang review the NLRP3 inflammasome in inflammatory bowel disease, in Frontiers in Immunology. This protein complex sits in gut lining and immune cells. It senses alarms from germs and from the body's own damaged tissue.

Once active, it releases signals such as IL-1 beta. Those signals can protect the gut lining or drive its inflammation. Studies point in both directions for bowel disease, the authors note. The review gathers what is known about its build and triggers. It closes with the control points that drugs might target. Blocking it may calm bowel inflammation.
europmc-pmc6413442:
Guo and co-authors review exosomes and pre-metastatic niches in Molecular Cancer. Before cancer spreads, its home tumor prepares distant organs for arrival. Those prepared spots are called pre-metastatic niches.

Exosomes, tiny vesicles shed by tumors, do much of the preparing. They stir inflammation, grow blood vessels, and weaken immune guard at the target organ. They also carry PD-L1, which helps tumor cells escape immunity. The review sorts these effects and their order. Exosome signals in blood may one day warn where a cancer plans to spread.
europmc-pmc6415442:
Zhao and co-authors review chitosan nanoparticles in medicine, in Polymers. Chitosan is a natural polymer that is safe in the body and breaks down over time. As a drug carrier it holds great promise, the authors say.

Its main flaw is that it barely dissolves in plain water. Chemists modify it by many routes to fix that and add new traits. Nanoparticles made from the altered forms are stable and body-friendly. The review covers drug, gene, and protein delivery uses. It also covers wider medical uses, from wound care to imaging.
europmc-pmc6481742:
Li and co-authors take stock of exosome research from three directions at once, biology, engineering, and cancer therapy. These lipid parcels, roughly 30 to 140 nanometers across and shed by most cell types, ferry proteins, lipids, and RNAs between cells. That makes their cargo a tempting source of diagnostic clues, and the vesicles themselves candidate drug couriers.

Progress lags the promise because the basics are hard: separating exosomes cleanly from look-alike vesicles, describing them reliably, and finding markers specific enough to trust. Cup-shaped images from electron microscopy, long treated as canonical, are now suspected artifacts. The review lists established and emerging tools for isolating and measuring them, and points the field at its bottlenecks.
europmc-pmc6532842:
Vincent and co-authors revisit Leptospira taxonomy through genomics. Their study appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases. Leptospira bacteria cause leptospirosis, a zoonotic disease found worldwide. Spread often runs through soil or water fouled by animal urine. The genus was then split into 35 species in three clusters.

The team sequenced 90 strains from sites across the world. Comparing average nucleotide identity revealed 30 new species. The data support two clades and four subclades. The authors name them P1, P2, S1 and S2. One subclade, near the saprophytes, had not been described. Pangenome work then flagged genes that mark each group. Health risks of the new species remain open.
europmc-pmc6629542:
Choi and O'Reilly present PRSice-2, software for polygenic risk score analysis. Their article appears in GigaScience. A polygenic risk score sums many small genetic effects on a trait. Such scores now serve research on shared causes and causal inference. Biobank data sets have grown too large for older tools.

The rewrite in C++ runs the whole pipeline without intermediate files. It handles genotyped and imputed data alike. Users can test many traits, both continuous and binary, at once. The program gives empirical p-values that guard against overfitting. It supports additive, dominant, recessive, and heterozygous models. Benchmarks show it far faster and lighter than rival tools. Predictive power stays on par with those rivals.
europmc-pmc6646942:
Brysbaert and Stevens give a tutorial on power and effect size in mixed effects models. Their paper appears in the Journal of Cognition. Psychology replications succeed far less often than expected. One cause is chronically underpowered designs. Cognitive studies sample both participants and stimuli. Most textbook power formulas ignore that double sampling. The authors review the literature on the problem. They test recent software on two high-power priming studies.

Their benchmark for reaction time work is concrete. A repeated measures experiment needs about 1,600 word observations per condition. Forty participants with forty stimuli meets that bar. Reported effect sizes also shift with stimulus counts. Meta-analyses must therefore record observations, they argue.
europmc-pmc6681642:
Lattie and co-authors review digital mental health programs for college students. Their review appears in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. Students report rising depression and anxiety levels. Barriers block many from standard campus care. Web and app programs promise wider access. The team searched five major databases. Eighty-nine studies met the entry rules. Most programs were delivered through websites. Web-based cognitive therapy was commonest. A third of programs included human coaching.

Nearly half the programs proved effective outright. Another third were partly effective. Half the studies reported no usability outcomes. Broad campus roll-out was rarely examined. Bias risk ran moderate to severe. Work on holding user interest is the authors' priority.
europmc-pmc6722042:
De Boer and co-authors report updated results from the PORTEC-3 trial in high-risk endometrial cancer. Women with this womb cancer were assigned at random to radiation alone or radiation plus chemotherapy. The trial ran at many centers. In all, 660 women were eligible, split evenly between the two arms.

At a median follow-up of 72.6 months, five-year survival was 81.4% with combined treatment versus 76.1% with radiation alone. Failure-free survival was 76.5% versus 69.1%. Distant spread was the most common first recurrence in both groups, but less frequent with added chemotherapy. Severe side effects stayed uncommon. Adding chemotherapy improved outcomes for these women.
europmc-pmc6734942:
Sanderson and co-authors clarify multivariable Mendelian randomization, a method for estimating causal effects. The method uses genetic variants as instruments to separate cause from mere correlation. Its multivariable form handles two or more exposures at once. Questions remained about what its estimates mean under different setups.

Using simulations and theory, the authors sort out the interpretation. They show how results read when a second exposure confounds, mediates, or distorts the first. They also give tests for instrument strength and validity in one-sample and two-sample data. An example uses UK Biobank data on education, cognitive ability, and body mass index. The method estimates direct causal effects throughout.
europmc-pmc6748942:
Zeng and co-authors hunted gut microbe markers that separate obesity types. Gut microbes link to obesity and metabolic disease. The team sequenced gut bacteria genes in 1,914 Chinese adults. They compared healthy people, obese people without metabolic disease, and obese people with such disease. Computer classifiers searched for telling microbe patterns.

The classifiers told obese groups from healthy ones fairly well. Six microbe genera marked obesity across its metabolic forms. Telling the two obese groups apart proved much harder, though. Specific problems such as high uric acid or high blood pressure had their own shared markers. Twenty genera tied to several clinical measures at once.
europmc-pmc6767042:
Dąbrowska reviews what shapes phage pharmacokinetics and availability in the body. Bacteriophages are viruses that infect bacteria. Once dismissed, they are now studied as medicines, carriers, and microbiome members. How a phage travels, penetrates tissue, and gets cleared decides whether it can treat anything. The review gathers experiments from 1924 to 2016, including non-English reports.

Delivery route mattered greatly. Injections into muscle, vein, or body cavity beat oral dosing by a wide margin. Active phages appeared in blood within minutes of injection. Gut survival and tissue entry were analyzed in a systematic way. Phage shape and special features also steer the course through the body.
europmc-pmc6789542:
Khan and co-authors ask whether altered gut microbiota cause inflammatory bowel disease or result from it. IBD, including Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, is a chronic gut inflammation of unknown origin. A disturbed gut flora, called dysbiosis, is now a leading suspect. The gut community acts like a metabolic organ, so its disruption reaches far.

Studies clearly show perturbed flora in patients and in mouse colitis models. A clean causal chain, though, has not been proven. Microbiome-based treatments have eased colitis in animals and shown promise in patients. Prebiotic results are inconsistent, and guidelines remain cautious. The flora still looks like a promising treatment target, pending deeper work.
europmc-pmc6837442:
Vabalas and co-authors study a trap in machine learning research, in PLOS ONE. Modern studies of the brain and body collect rich data but few subjects, since human data are costly. With many measures and small samples, learning algorithms can seem better than they are. The authors noticed this pattern in papers that claimed to detect autism from such data.

Small studies reported the highest accuracy. Simulations then showed why. Common validation schemes that select features outside the test loop leak information and inflate scores. The effect was worst at small sample sizes. Nested validation, which keeps selection fully inside the check, removed the bias. The authors urge that standard on small-sample studies.
europmc-pmc6921542:
Lan and co-authors study the protein KIAA1429 in liver cancer. Their research article appeared in Molecular Cancer. KIAA1429 is the largest part of the m6A writer complex. That complex marks RNA with a chemical tag. Its role in hepatocellular carcinoma was poorly defined.

The team found KIAA1429 strongly raised in tumour tissue. High levels were linked to poor patient prognosis. Silencing it curbed cell growth and spread. Tests covered lab cultures and animal models. Its direct target proved to be GATA3 pre-mRNA. Tagging its tail region drove its decay. A long noncoding RNA, GATA3-AS, guided that pairing. Growth and spread driven by either molecule ran through GATA3.
europmc-pmc6969442:
Zhu and co-authors review progress on the gut-brain link in brain disorders. Their review appeared in the Journal of Neuroinflammation. Thinking was once seen as the brain's private business. Growing evidence shows gut microbes sway brain function and behaviour.

Diet and other factors reshape the gut community. Microbes release molecules that stir immune signals reaching the brain. Those signals feed into pain, depression, anxiety, and autism. They also play into Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases and stroke. The authors describe the study methods of the field, then microbe-made metabolites and immune routes. Damage to the blood-brain barrier and to brain blood flow gets close attention. Their map ties gut change to downstream nerve dysfunction.
europmc-pmc7024142:
Bauersachs and co-authors review the burden of coronary and peripheral artery disease in Cardiovascular Therapeutics. Both conditions stem from atherothrombosis, fatty blockage of arteries, and both can lead to heart attack, stroke, limb ischemia, heart failure, and cardiovascular death. The team set out to measure the human and economic cost and to find unmet needs.

Their search covered studies published between January 2010 and August 2017, plus guidelines. Worldwide, about 5 to 8 percent of people had coronary disease and 10 to 20 percent had peripheral disease, depending on the population studied. Registry data showed many patients had disease in more than one vascular bed. Survival has improved, the authors note, but disability, quality of life, and costs still weigh heavily.
europmc-pmc7061942:
Luo and co-authors report upgrades to the ENCODE data portal in Nucleic Acids Research. The Encyclopedia of DNA Elements project aims to identify every functional element in the human and mouse genomes. Its consortium data are free to all through a portal run by the Data Coordinating Center, first released in 2013. Keeping such a resource findable and usable takes constant work.

Recent updates add new data and assay types, uniform processing pipelines so experiments are analysed the same way, and fresh visualisation tools. A dataset cart lets users gather files across pages. The full collection is now openly available on the Amazon Web Services open data registry, removing access friction for cloud computing. Tutorials and documentation were expanded as well. The authors frame the changes around making ENCODE data findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable for any researcher.
europmc-pmc7072842:
Choi, Doss, and Kim review the many faces of adiponectin in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Adiponectin is the most abundant fat hormone in human blood. White fat makes it, and it moves through blood in three weight classes of assemblies. It is famed for good effects: it sharpens insulin action, guards arteries, and calms inflammation. Low levels go with type 2 diabetes, obesity, and atherosclerosis.

Newer studies muddy that portrait. In autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, chronic kidney disease, and inflammatory bowel disease, high adiponectin tracks with worse inflammation and faster disease progress. The clash likely resolves at the level of forms and targets: each assembly acts in its own way in each tissue. The review sums up what adiponectin does across metabolic and autoimmune disease. Knowing each isoform's job, the authors argue, could let drug designers aim at one form while sparing the rest.
europmc-pmc7146642:
Kraemer and co-authors measure how human movement and control measures shaped COVID-19's spread across China, in Science. They combined real-time mobility data from Wuhan with detailed case records, including travel histories. Early on, where cases appeared in China was explained well by how people moved.

After restrictions began, including the Wuhan cordon of 23 January and limits in 14 other Hubei cities, that link weakened and growth rates turned negative in most places. Case patterns still showed local transmission chains outside Wuhan. The authors conclude the drastic controls substantially slowed the epidemic's spread. The study is an early demonstration of phone mobility data as an epidemic tracking tool.
europmc-pmc7237642:
Cano-Gamez and Trynka review how functional genomics turns genome-wide association findings into disease mechanisms. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Genetics. Such studies have mapped thousands of spots linked to common diseases. Most of those spots sit outside genes, in control regions. Which gene they affect, and in which cells, is usually unclear.

That gap blocks the path from statistics to new drugs. The review covers a decade of methods built to close it. Layering gene activity data onto association results is a central trick. Statistical approaches use variants as levers to estimate a gene's true effect. Cell type and context decide when a control region acts. The authors show how these layers name the genes behind the signals. Drug hunters gain a route from risk maps to targets.
europmc-pmc7276742:
Juan and co-authors review what was known early on about COVID-19 in pregnancy. Their systematic review appeared in Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology. They searched medical databases up to April 20, 2020 for reports with confirmed infection and at least one outcome for mother or baby.

Only 24 studies, covering 324 pregnant women, met their criteria. Most of the literature was single case reports and small series. The review gathers maternal illness patterns, delivery outcomes, and newborn results from that early evidence. It also asks whether the virus can pass from mother to baby before birth. Given the thin base, the authors treat their summary as a starting point that larger studies would need to confirm.
europmc-pmc7283042:
Moss, Maghini and Bhatt show how to recover complete bacterial genomes from mixed microbial communities using nanopore sequencing. Their methods paper appeared in Nature Biotechnology. Short-read sequencing leaves genome assemblies in fragments, because repeated stretches cannot be placed correctly. Finished genomes matter for understanding what those repeats do.

Their workflow, called Lathe, combines long nanopore reads with short-read error correction. On a test mixture of 12 bacterial species, seven genomes closed into single pieces and three more into four or fewer pieces. Applied to 13 human stool samples, the method produced 20 circular genomes, including one for Prevotella copri. The trade-off is lower letter-by-letter accuracy, repaid by far better completeness for studying microbial function.
europmc-pmc7325942:
Maruyama and co-authors review bone healing in Frontiers in Endocrinology, focusing on the role of inflammation. About 5 to 10 percent of fractures fail to heal, and the first, inflamed phase of repair helps decide the outcome. Immune cells and stem-like stromal cells trade signals throughout that phase.

The authors explain how a short burst of acute inflammation supports repair, while blocked or lasting inflammation can stall it. They then review cell treatments that calm immune responses, such as preparing stromal cells before use so they suppress harmful inflammation. Gene and drug approaches get attention too. Readers get a plain account of why healing bone needs the right amount of inflammation, not none.
europmc-pmc7426442:
Shah and co-authors review the immune response to SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19. They draw lessons from past coronaviruses such as SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV. The virus attacks the airways and can cause pneumonia and low lymphocyte counts.

The review traces how B cells and T cells react to spike and nucleocapsid proteins. It covers antibody output, cytokine release, and cell killing in the acute phase. Gene variants in the MHC system shape how well viral pieces are shown to T cells. Memory T cells from past infections may protect, yet cross-reaction can also harm tissue. The authors survey drug trials and convalescent plasma use. Work on neutralizing antibodies and cytokine control closes the review.
europmc-pmc7432042:
Nadarajah reviews how plants control reactive oxygen species under abiotic stress. Such stress, driven by climate change, cuts crop growth and yield. Stress makes reactive oxygen species build up in cell parts, where they can damage cells.

Plants balance these molecules with enzyme and non-enzyme defenses that clear them. At low levels the same molecules act as signals. They switch on local and whole-plant defense responses. The review covers how plants sense and signal with these molecules and which genes switch on under stress. Knowing these genes and pathways can guide breeding of crops that stand up to harsh conditions. That need grows as farm climates shift.
europmc-pmc7447642:
Jin and Jin review the tumor microenvironment and how old drugs might gain new uses against it. Cells and materials around a tumor can steer its start, growth, spread, and drug response. Cancer care has shifted from a tumor-only view to this wider one.

The review maps niches within the setting: low-oxygen, immune, metabolic, acidic, nerve-linked, and mechanical. It then surveys common drugs with anti-tumor promise. Aspirin, celecoxib, beta blockers, metformin, and statins all appear. These drugs are cheap, well known, and already used in clinics, which suits pairing with other therapy. Yet targeted attacks on this setting still work poorly in patients. The authors close with open questions and future paths for the field.
europmc-pmc7449042:
Chandra and co-authors review microbial lipases and their industrial uses. Lipases are enzymes that break down fats, and microbes make many versatile forms. Sources include bacteria such as Bacillus and fungi such as Aspergillus.

Microbial lipases drive hydrolysis, ester formation, and alcoholysis reactions. Fixing them onto carriers, called immobilization, boosts their performance and reuse. The review covers sources, purification, substrates, and assay methods. It then maps uses across biodiesel, food and drink, leather, textiles, detergents, drugs, and medicine. Carrier choice shapes stability, safety, and cost. The authors argue these enzymes give industry a greener, flexible catalyst. Demand for them keeps growing across many sectors.
europmc-pmc7542442:
Douangamath and co-authors screen fragments against the SARS-CoV-2 main protease. This protease is vital for viral replication. No proven drugs existed for related coronaviruses at the time.

The team combined mass spectrometry with X-ray methods. They screened electrophile and non-covalent fragments at scale. Crystal work found 71 hits across the active site. Three more hits sat at the dimer interface. Some low-reactivity fragments were improved into stronger binders. Merging covalent and non-covalent hits offers a design route. The structures give rich data for drug design. Readers can see starting points for protease inhibitors in detail.
europmc-pmc7610742:
Smith and co-authors expand genome-wide association studies of brain imaging traits in UK Biobank. The resource links brain scans, genetics and health outcomes. A prior release covered fewer people and traits.

The new release almost triples the discovery sample. It uses the 2020 data release from the study. New trait classes include subcortical volumes and tissue contrast. The X chromosome is included for the first time. Replicated association clusters rose from 148 to 692. Twelve of those sit on the X chromosome. New links point to rare syndromes and Alzheimer disease. Mitochondrial disorders also appear among the signals. Summary statistics are shared as an open resource for researchers.
europmc-pmc7616842:
NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC) estimates diabetes prevalence and treatment trends in 200 countries from 1990 to 2022. Diabetes can be found at primary care level. Good treatment lowers the risk of complications.

The pool held 1108 population studies in total. Participants numbered 141 million adults across those studies. In 2022 an estimated 828 million adults had diabetes. That is a rise of 630 million since 1990. Age-standardised rates rose in 131 countries for women. They rose in 155 countries for men in that span. Big rises hit parts of Asia and the Middle East. Treatment coverage data were pooled with prevalence. Gaps in care remain wide in many low-income settings.
europmc-pmc7846842:
Lyu and co-authors review painful disc degeneration and the role of inflammation. Low back pain is a leading cause of disability. Worn spinal discs drive much of that pain. Inflammation now looks central to disc breakdown.

Inflammatory signals both damage discs and spark pain. The authors trace the pathways that carry those signals. Animal models of painful discs get a full hearing. Puncture, load-based, and natural models each have strengths. Drug candidates that calm disc inflammation are surveyed next. Some sit in labs, and others are in trials. The team hopes to pull more research toward pain itself, not just disc structure.
europmc-pmc7884042:
Ogrodnik and co-authors report a mouse study on clearing senescent cells from the ageing brain. Senescent cells have stopped dividing but stay active, releasing inflammatory signals. Their build-up is tied to ageing and age-related disease. The team asked whether removing them protects thinking skills.

The researchers first mapped senescent cells in the hippocampus of young and aged mice. Such cells rose with age, most of all in microglia. They then cleared the cells in two ways: with a drug switch in engineered mice, and with a senolytic drug pair. Both routes cut microglial activation and inflammatory signals. Both also improved cognitive function in the aged mice. The authors present the work as proof of concept for senolytic treatment of age-linked decline.
europmc-pmc7916842:
De Pessemier and co-authors present a review of the gut-skin axis. Skin diseases often come with changes in microbes, and not only on the skin. Many skin conditions pair with an altered gut microbiome too. The microbes help run the immune system by talking with tissues across the body. When that balance slips, skin disease can follow.

The review lists common conditions tied to such imbalance. They include atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, acne, dandruff, and even skin cancer. Diet and the chemicals microbes produce form part of the link. The authors gather the evidence on gut changes seen in each skin condition. They explain how these shifts may steer immune responses in the skin. The goal is a firmer base for new treatments that work through the microbiome.
europmc-pmc7946142:
Cowdry presents a study of Taoist ideas of human anatomy, based on books held in Peking. The White Cloud Temple, outside the city gate, holds the fullest library of Taoist medical and literary works. Studying them is no easy matter, he writes. A friend of the High Priest must smooth the way. Cowdry recounts the delays and courtesies of his visits in warm detail.

A gift book honouring the temple's first High Priest won the present holder over. Tea with the junior priests followed, and access at last. The paper then turns to the content of the Taoist texts. Their picture of the body's structure differs sharply from Western anatomy. The account mixes travel writing with close study. It introduces readers to a medical tradition held inside a living temple library.
europmc-pmc8044242:
Feng and co-authors build a flat nanoenzyme sheet that copies six natural antioxidant enzymes at once. Reactive oxygen species drive inflammation and nerve cell loss when they run too high. The natural enzymes that tame them are fragile proteins. They fail in sick tissue, where they are needed most. The team's sheet is made of vanadium carbide, a 2D MXene. They call the construct a MXenzyme.

The sheet mimics superoxide dismutase, catalase, and peroxidase. It also copies glutathione peroxidase, thiol peroxidase, and haloperoxidase. In cell tests, it shielded cells from oxidative stress. It reset the redox balance without weakening the cells' own guard systems. Animal models of inflammation and neurodegeneration both did better on it. No harsh side effects appeared in the reported tests. The work opens a path to treat diseases fed by reactive oxygen.
europmc-pmc8068842:
Siracusa and co-authors update the picture of fibromyalgia, from its roots to its treatment options. The syndrome brings chronic, widespread muscle pain. Fatigue, gut trouble, and broken sleep and mood ride along. Between two and eight percent of the world population is affected. Women develop it more often than men. No organ damage explains the pain.

The review centers on central sensitization as the core fault. The brain's pain circuits gain too much volume on incoming signals. Genes, hormones, immune factors, and life stress feed into it. Diagnosis leans on pain in all body quadrants for three months. Tender points under finger pressure still guide many clinicians. The authors survey biomarker hunts, from genes to blood tests. Standard drugs give only limited relief. Ninety percent of patients also try complementary care.
europmc-pmc8111542:
Sousa and co-authors review how cells swallow nanoparticles, and how medicine can use that knowledge. Nanoparticles serve in cosmetics, food, and a fast-growing nanomedicine. Drug carriers must enter the right cells to work. They must also dodge immune cells that clear them. Entry happens through several endocytic pathways, not one door. Particle size, shape, charge, and surface all pick the route.

The review first maps each uptake pathway in turn. It then warns how messy the study tools can be. Chemical blockers, marker proteins, and gene tricks each carry flaws. Counting uptake fairly gets its own hard look. The second half turns to control of the process. Natural and synthetic compounds can raise uptake where wanted. Others can lower it where uptake harms. Smarter targeting follows from that two-way control. Getting in, the authors stress, is half the therapy.
europmc-pmc8140142:
Shi and co-authors show that the support beneath single platinum atoms tunes their hydrogen-making power. Splitting water for hydrogen needs catalysts that waste little energy. Platinum works best but costs the most per atom. Single-atom designs stretch every atom to its limit. The puzzle is what sets each atom's activity. Electronic talks between metal and support are the lever here.

The team dialed platinum's oxidation state through that interaction. Spectroscopy and electrochemistry tracked the changes atom by atom. Activity in acid tracked the average oxidation state closely. Alkaline performance followed the same electronic logic. Bonds to hydrogen and hydroxide intermediates explained the trend. A clear structure–activity rule emerged from the data. Catalyst designers can now aim at an oxidation window. Guesswork gives way to a tunable dial. The rule should travel to other single-atom systems. Green hydrogen gets a sharper design manual.
europmc-pmc8226842:
Jennings and co-authors find that trust and conspiracy beliefs predict COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy. They surveyed 1,476 adults in the United Kingdom in December 2020. Five focus groups added depth in the same period.

Distrust in vaccines in general raised hesitancy. So did mistrust in government and belief in conspiracies. Trust in health bodies and experts pulled the other way. Feeling personal threat from the virus also mattered. Focus groups exposed a false belief that herd immunity protects the unvaccinated. The work shows where honest messaging must aim. Heavy social media use also tracked with hesitancy in the data.
europmc-pmc8342542:
Cho and co-authors improve human brain organoid culture with a brain matrix and a microfluidic chip. Organoids model brain development and disease in a dish. Standard culture gives uneven, fragile results.

The team added human brain extracellular matrix for brain-like cues. A chip with periodic flow fed the organoids steadily. The matrix boosted neurogenesis in the growing tissue. Flow improved survival and cut variability between organoids. Together, the two changes raised organoid quality. More reliable organoids should sharpen disease studies. The setup points toward standardised production for drug testing. Brain-specific cues were the missing piece they supplied.
europmc-pmc8443442:
Dai and co-authors test whether text message nudges raise COVID-19 vaccination rates. Getting people to act on vaccine plans is a core public health task. The team built reminders that make vaccination stand out and feel easy.

Two randomized trials ran inside one health care system. The first trial, with 93,354 people, sent a text one day after an eligibility notice. It lifted appointment and vaccination rates by clear margins. A second trial with 67,092 people, reminded eight days later, helped less. Wording that made people feel the dose was theirs worked best. A video add-on aimed at hesitancy gave no extra lift.
europmc-pmc8494642:
Ziffra and co-authors use single-cell epigenomics to reveal how the human cortex develops. As brain cells mature, their chromatin state shifts with them. Those shifts mirror changes in the gene control landscape. Cell fate and place identity form in this window.

The team used a single-cell chromatin access assay on human forebrain tissue. They found spots in the genome whose access changes by cell type and region. From those patterns they predicted candidate control elements for each type. Brain organoids copied most of those patterns but missed many found in real tissue. Progenitor cells varied by region more than expected. Retinoic acid signaling helped set neuron lineage identity.
europmc-pmc8596342:
Lan, Luo, and Wei review mesenchymal stem and stromal cells as a tool in cancer care. These cells can form bone, cartilage, and fat cells. They can also calm immune responses and home in on tumors. Those traits make them a draw for cell-based cancer treatment.

The review covers how these cells might fight tumors and the signals they use. It weighs the mixed roles the cells play in tumor growth. Some effects help, while others may aid the cancer. The authors also assess trials that test safety and benefit in patients. Readers get a clear view of a field with promise but real gaps in knowledge.
europmc-pmc8603942:
Lee and co-authors describe a protein complex that drives a fiery form of cell death during infection. Inflammasomes sense germs and trigger death in infected cells. Each known sensor was thought to act on its own signal. Live germs, though, release many signals at once.

The team found that the sensor AIM2 controls two other sensors, pyrin and ZBP1. All three join a large complex with cell death proteins. This complex drives PANoptosis, a mix of death paths, and helps the host fight infection. Tests used herpes simplex virus 1 and a Francisella species. The work offers new targets for drugs that tune harmful inflammation.
europmc-pmc8825842:
Fagiani and co-authors review how the body's daily clock is run at the molecular level. Circadian rhythms are internal cycles of about 24 hours. A set of transcription factors drives them through feedback loops. The clock does far more than set sleep timing. It shapes work in nearly every tissue and organ.

The review traces links between the clock and key cell pathways. Those paths govern cell growth, DNA repair, blood vessel growth, and energy balance. They also govern inflammation and immune response. The authors then ask what happens when rhythms break down. Misaligned clocks show up in cancer and inflammatory disease. They close by urging medicine that respects time. Such circadian precision care is their stated goal.
europmc-pmc8924142:
Yu, Zhu, and Chen review type I interferons as engines of tumor immunity. Checkpoint blockade helps many cancer patients. Most, though, fail to gain lasting benefit from it alone. Type I interferons can attack tumors two ways. They harm tumor cells directly. They also rally immune cells against the tumor. Boosting these interferons may deepen checkpoint responses. Trials testing that pairing are now running.

The review maps where type I interferons arise in tumors. Dendritic cells, tumor cells, and vessel cells all produce them. Macrophages and fibroblasts add their share. The authors then trace effects cell by cell. Natural killer cells and neutrophils feature. Regulatory T cells get a careful look. Combination strategies close the survey. Inducers range from radiation to oncolytic viruses. The STING pathway recurs as a lever. The piece links basic signaling to trial design.
europmc-pmc9287542:
Antonelli and co-authors report the Medical Segmentation Decathlon, a contest to test if one algorithm can segment many medical image types. Past contests each covered a single clinical task. This one set ten tasks across organs and scan types. Seven tasks were open for training; three stayed secret until the final round.

The results backed the core idea. Top algorithms did well on the hidden tasks without redesign. Steady results across many tasks proved a strong sign of general skill. The winning method kept doing well on new problems for two years. The authors conclude that training good segmentation models is now routine. That opens computer-aided diagnosis and surgery planning to more teams. The data remain a benchmark for the field.
europmc-pmc9289742:
Dai and Shen survey the state of omics technology and where it is heading. Omics means measuring a whole class of molecules in a cell at once. The field began with DNA microarrays and grew with fast sequencing and mass spectrometry. New molecule types keep expanding what counts as an omics layer.

The review focuses on the four big omics: genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics. It adds their epi-levels and the webs of molecular interaction. Single-cell methods give finer detail, and multi-omics merges layers into one picture. The goal is using this knowledge against disease with minimal cell disturbance. The authors predict redoxomics, the study of redox balance, as a rising layer. Cell fate, they argue, turns on that balance.
fielding-joseph-andrews-1742:
Fielding's Joseph Andrews, from 1742, began as a joke at Samuel Richardson's Pamela. Richardson's heroine resisted her master; Fielding gives her a brother, Joseph, who must resist his widowed mistress. The parody quickly grew into Fielding's first true novel.

Joseph and his friend Parson Adams walk the roads of England, meeting cheats, snobs, and kind hearts. Adams, absent-minded, brave, and good, steals the book from its hero. Fielding's preface sets out his theory of the comic epic in prose. What started as mockery became a founding work of the English novel, warmer and funnier than its target.
frus-1861-d142:
William Dayton sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 2 August 1861. It is document 142 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

By August, Paris had the news of the Union defeat and was weighing it. Dayton's report told Washington how deep the damage ran in French esteem. Such candor was the chief worth of an envoy in a hard season. Candor from Paris let the cabinet weigh its next steps on fact, not hope. Fact, not hope, was the diet on which the cabinet learned to live that year.
frus-1861-d242:
A letter home from James Shepherd Pike, dated 4 July 1861, landed on Seward's desk. It was printed as Document 242 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d42:
George Dallas sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 April 1861. It is document 42 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Three days later, guns opened on Fort Sumter and the war began. Dallas could not know that as he wrote, and the letter keeps the calm of the old world. It stands in the record as one of the last London reports of a still whole, if shaking, Union. The Sumter news reached London near the end of April and changed the tone of every talk. Stances set that month in London guided talks for the rest of the year.
frus-1862-d142:
In a letter dated 15 September 1862, William H. Seward gave Charles Francis Adams his latest word from Washington. It was printed as Document 142 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d242:
On 3 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William Stuart in a letter printed as Document 242 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart was still acting head of the British legation in Washington.

Early October found Britain still debating its course, with Gladstone soon to speak warmly of Southern nationhood at Newcastle. Seward's correspondence with the legation kept the Union's objections and claims in formal view. A letter from this date is one more entry in the long written contest that ran beside the war itself. Cases under such notes were often small: one ship, one prisoner, one point of form.
frus-1862-d342:
Document 342 is the second Seward dispatch to William L. Dayton dated 4 November 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Secretary of State William H. Seward sent the whole set to the Paris legation together.

The middle letter of a same-day set often held the working detail: figures, copies, or points the envoy should raise in order. Election day in the North fell on this date, adding political noise to the channel. Seward's steady output that day shows a department refusing to let a foreign crisis wait on domestic politics. The Paris mail sailed from Le Havre and took about two weeks to reach Washington.
frus-1862-d42:
In a report dated 3 April 1862, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 42 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The letter comes from the spring of 1862, a year into the war, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d442:
The Prussian file opens on 8 January 1862 with this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Norman B. Judd, the American minister in Berlin. It is Document 442 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Prussia was rising in Europe and broadly friendly to the Union, and Judd, a Chicago lawyer close to Lincoln, held the Berlin post. German opinion mattered: German immigrants filled Union regiments, and Berlin's stance weighed in the balance of European courts. Seward's early order set out the case Judd was to make. The letter begins a correspondence that shows the Union cultivating the one great power whose sympathy it could mostly count on.
frus-1862-d542:
On 25 August 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this note to Roest van Limburg at the Netherlands legation. It is Document 542 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

Seward wrote in the week of the second Bull Run campaign, when Washington itself felt exposed. Even so, the Dutch correspondence kept its even pace, one more proof that the Department's foreign business never paused for battle news. The questions at issue were the durable ones of neutral commerce under blockade. A reader following the Van Limburg file through August watches two governments maintain a working relationship. They do it by a simple means. They answer each other's letters, fully and on time.
frus-1862-d642:
On 14 October 1861 Townsend Harris wrote from Japan to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 642 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record laid before Congress.

By October, Harris had received the first news of the war at home, months old on arrival. His letter belongs to the season in which the distant posts learned, one ship at a time, that the republic was fighting for its life. His own report stuck to Japan: the treaty, the ports, and the legation's affairs. The restraint is characteristic of the file. At the far end of the world, the war changed the meaning of the mission without changing its daily work. Harris's letters show both truths at once.
frus-1863p1-d142:
Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 3 April 1863. Three Adams letters in the volume bear the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 142 in part one of the 1863 volume.

A three-letter day in April matched the pace of the ship fight then at its height. Adams split his news across the sheets: talks, facts from the yards, and the temper of the town. This one opens the set of 3 April. In the run of the volume, the day stands as a peak of the legation's spring work.
frus-1863p1-d242: Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Charles Francis Adams, his minister in London, on 20 July 1863. It is document 242 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, within the orders that steered American policy toward Britain during the Civil War. Through such letters Washington told its man in London what to press, protest, or let pass.
frus-1863p1-d342:
One of Lord Lyons's regular notes to the State Department, this paper to Secretary of State William H. Seward is dated 20 December 1862. It appears as document 342 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Taken as a run, these notes chart Britain slowly accepting that the Union would not collapse. That judgment, formed in Washington, helped keep Britain out of the war. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d42: Signed with the initial E., this paper is dated 18 October 1862. It is printed as document 42 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It sits among the Confederate papers in that part. The evidence gives a date and a lone initial but no full name and no one addressed, so this note stays at that level.
frus-1863p1-d442:
The letter printed as document 442 was written on 3 April 1863 by William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d542:
The date 29 May 1863 heads a letter from Assistant Secretary of State F. W. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d642:
Dated 20 October 1863, document 642 is a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. Adams in London was the Union's front line in Britain, pressing its case with the British government week after week. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?

Adams's task was to make the Union's case where it counted, inside the British capital, while Seward set the line from Washington. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d142: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on November 19, 1943, three days before the Cairo Conference opened. The message is Document 142 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. By then both leaders were in the Mediterranean world, and their letters crossed shorter distances than at any time in the series. The record gives the date and the two names and no subject. It survives in the Foreign Relations volume's arrival papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d242:
Assistant Secretary of War John McCloy wrote a secret memorandum at Cairo, dated about 21 November 1943, recording a dinner talk with Ambassador Harriman at Ambassador Kirk's house. Harriman, fresh from Moscow, shared his chief impressions of the Soviet mood, stressing that he spoke as a reporter, not an advocate.

The Soviets, he said, long passionately to end the war. Strained and tiring, they believe a prompt push with all forces at hand would make Germany crumble, and they hold Overlord as settled while still demanding more action this winter. Above all, they want real pressure on Turkey to join the war, which might by itself satisfy them. McCloy pressed for specifics and got none, since neither side knew the planners' facts well enough.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d342:
James Moose, the American minister resident in Saudi Arabia, was temporarily at Cairo. On 30 November 1943 he wrote a memorandum commenting on the British minister's telegram of 15 November. That telegram concerned arms for Saudi Arabia. That telegram, printed earlier in the volume, had complained of American questioning of King Ibn Saud.

Moose answers point by point. One of the seven questions listed was never asked, though the king's messenger supplied the answer anyway. What the British telegram left out, he says, is twofold. The king was told beforehand that Washington was consulting London on Saudi arms. And the American minister did discuss the inquiry with his British colleague within days. Moose also notes dryly that the British minister never checked his facts with that colleague before reporting to the Foreign Office.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d42: Roosevelt wrote to Stalin on October 14, 1943, one of several letters he sent that day. It is Document 42 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The Moscow meeting of foreign ministers was five days off, and the leaders were setting the frame their ministers would work in. The catalog record names no subject for the letter. Its text appears in the Foreign Relations volume among the mid-October summit papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d442: Number 442 is one of the editorial notes written by the volume's historians. Foreign Relations volumes use such notes where the papers leave a gap. A note may summarize missing context or direct readers to another file. Here the setting is the Cairo-Tehran record from late 1943. Roosevelt and Churchill met in Cairo, then joined Stalin in Tehran. The note keeps that fast-moving sequence readable for later readers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d542:
President Roosevelt answered Prime Minister Churchill on January 8, 1944, the day after Churchill's message to him. The quick exchange was typical of their wartime correspondence at full flow. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

By January 1944 the questions before the two leaders ran from invasion planning to the shape of the postwar world promised in the Tehran Declaration. Roosevelt's replies to Churchill balanced agreement with the claims of his other partners, above all Stalin and Chiang. For readers, this message is one turn in the central conversation of the Western alliance, conducted when the war's outcome was turning in their favor.
frus-1944-quebec-d142:
The United States Chiefs of Staff replied to the British amendments on September 8, 1944, in C.C.S. 654/5. Two of the three British changes were accepted, each with American rewording. The third, on assisting other co-belligerents, Washington preferred to handle case by case, and it supplied its own text instead.

The agreed lines pledged measures to aid Russia, including coordinating the action of forces. Help for other co-belligerents was limited to available resources and to what they could effectively use against the Axis. On shifting forces to the Pacific, the Americans accepted a caution but wrote "agreed commitments" where the British had said "inescapable." Quebec would take up the settled text.
frus-1944-quebec-d242:
Churchill wrote to Roosevelt from Quebec on September 14, 1944, about the vacant chief commissionership of the Allied Control Commission for Italy. The post was a British appointment, empty since General MacFarlane's departure. To bring political knowledge to work so full of economic and political issues, Churchill proposed Harold Macmillan, who would keep his duties as resident minister and political adviser.

Day-to-day management would rest with the American deputy, Mr. Stone, in whom Churchill expressed great confidence. The appointment was urgent: the post had stood vacant two months. Churchill also hoped to discuss having Mayor La Guardia visit Italy as Roosevelt's representative and attend commission meetings, and to run through other proposals helpful to the Italians once Eden arrived.
frus-1944-quebec-d42:
On August 31, 1944, Roosevelt replied to Churchill. It was the last exchange before both men traveled to Quebec. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Roosevelt's late August letters had a host's purpose. He meant to welcome his guest. He meant to frame the agenda. He also held American positions firm where argument was likely. The conference at Quebec City would open on September 12. For readers, this reply closes the written preparation. It hands the story to the conference itself. The whole volume has been building toward that meeting.
frus-1945-50-intel-d142:
"National Intelligence Authority Directive No. 2" bears the date 8 February 1946. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 142 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. Washington was still building a peace-time spy service, run for the moment by the National Intelligence Authority and the Central Intelligence Group.

A directive is not advice: it is an order that offices below must follow until it is changed or replaced. Staff could be held to each line, which is why the words were fought over before issue. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d242:
The Secretary of the State–Army–Navy–Air Force Coordinating Committee (Moseley) addressed a memorandum to the Under Secretary of State (Lovett) on 15 October 1947. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 242 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The National Security Act had just taken effect. The CIA had replaced the old group, and the Council had just begun to meet.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d342:
On 12 March 1948, Secretary of State Marshall sent a memorandum to the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers). The Office of the Historian kept it as document 342 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. With the Soviet threat in mind, the Council was deciding what secret work the United States should do abroad.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d42:
The Lovett Committee sent its memorandum to Secretary of War Patterson on 3 November 1945. The committee, headed by Robert Lovett, had been asked to study how intelligence should be organized in peace. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Committee reports are where scattered views get hammered into a program. The Lovett group's paper gave the War Department a worked-out position in the contest with State and the Budget Bureau. Readers should treat it as a landmark in the run: after it, the argument had full plans on every side. The committee's name recurs through the autumn papers as its members carried their study into the wider fight.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d142:
Cabinet seats were the currency in Churchill's Moscow report of 22 October 1944. This excerpt of his message number 801 to Roosevelt is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It tells what happened on the last day of the Moscow talks on Poland.

Mikolajczyk met Bierut, the Lublin leader. Bierut admitted his troubles freely: fifty of his men shot in a month. Many Poles were taking to the woods rather than join his forces. Bierut still demanded three-quarters of the cabinet if Mikolajczyk became premier. Mikolajczyk countered with seats for each of the five Polish parties. Stalin then saw him for over an hour, in a friendly talk, but held firm that the Lublin Poles must have the majority.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d242:
Ambassador Patrick Hurley summed up the Chungking–Communist talks for the President on 14 January 1945. His top secret cable from Chungking, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, is for the President's eyes alone. It traces his own shuttle between the two Chinese camps.

After fruitless talks at Sian and Chungking, Hurley went to Yenan and came back with a five-point proposal signed by Mao Tse-tung. Chou En-lai returned with him and stayed a month. The National Government countered with three points, which the Communists refused. Chou's talks looked promising until his final meeting with the Generalissimo, at which Hurley was not present. Chiang, Hurley reports, is now ready to grant all the five points but one: he will not have a coalition government or a coalition military council.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d342:
Fuel, landing craft, and dates for the war's end fill this Combined Chiefs session at Alupka on February 6, 1945. The chiefs first checked the supply of petroleum products in Britain and northwest Europe. They then set planning dates for the end of the war against Germany. The earliest date was July 1, 1945. The date past which the war was unlikely to run was December 31, 1945.

Landing vehicles for the Mediterranean also came up, and then the zones of occupation in Germany. The minutes mix the grand and the plain. Wars at this level were run as much on oil stocks and calendars as on battle maps.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d42: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on 5 January 1945, as both capitals counted down to departure. The message is document 42 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences. January letters between the two men carried the last written exchanges before they could simply talk in person, first at Malta and then alongside Stalin at Yalta.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d442:
Britain's answer on reparations, dated February 10, 1945, starts from fairness among the claimants. Shares allotted to each country, London proposed, should be set by two measures. The first was each country's contribution to winning the war. The second was the degree of material loss it had suffered. Deliveries from other enemy countries would also count.

Payment would come in three forms. The first was removals within two years of Germany's surrender, drawn from German wealth at home and abroad. These removals aimed chiefly at destroying Germany's war potential. The paper avoids the Soviet fixed sum. It offers principles where Moscow offered a number — the core of the reparations dispute.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d142:
President Truman backed Churchill's handling of the German fleet question in a telegram dated May 28, 1945. The printed message, partly cut, is document 142 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Churchill had told Stalin that the fate of the surrendered German naval and merchant ships belonged on the summit agenda.

Truman says he is in general agreement with Churchill's reply to Stalin about the ships, and that he will send Stalin a similar message of his own. The rest of the telegram is not printed here; a note points readers to another document for its final paragraph. The brief cable aligned Washington with London before Truman wrote to Moscow, an early case of the two Western leaders coordinating their lines to Stalin.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d242:
Acting Secretary Grew told London the Italy announcement would go ahead in an urgent telegram dated July 14, 1945. The message to Ambassador Winant is document 242 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Italy had now declared war on Japan, with the declaration to be made public on July 15.

The Department therefore proposes to announce on July 17 its intention to support officially Italy's admission in due course to the world security organization, Grew writes. Winant is to inform the Foreign Office urgently and express the hope that the British government will support the American position. The date chosen, July 17, was the day the Potsdam Conference opened, which soon put the announcement on a collision course with the British.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d342:
Secretary of War Stimson took up the German import fight in a letter to the Secretary of State dated July 4, 1945. He had weighed Clayton's letter of June 18 about who in Washington should pay for imports into Germany. Stimson pointed back to his own letter of June 14 on the same problem.

No money, he stressed, had been voted to finance supplies for Germany and Austria beyond the War Department's narrow military duty. With no funds in hand, the question could not be settled between departments. Stimson closed by backing a small group, McCloy and Judge Rosenman among them, to draft recommendations for the President.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d42:
On May 30, 1945, Soviet leader Joseph Stalin sent President Harry Truman a short secret message from Moscow. It is document 42 in the first volume of the Foreign Relations of the United States papers on the Potsdam Conference. Germany had just surrendered, and the three Allied leaders were fixing a date to meet and settle the peace.

Stalin's whole message takes two lines. He says that Harry Hopkins, Truman's envoy, had passed on the President's proposal about the meeting of the three, and that he had no objection to the suggested date of July 15. The note is a small but real step toward the Potsdam Conference, which opened near Berlin two days later than planned.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d442:
Greece opens the briefing book's country papers with an appeal for an active, benevolent American interest. To take such an interest now, the paper argues, offers a most practical way to show American resolve. The United States, it says, means to play a world role that matches its strength and its public pledges. Greece has traditionally stood closer to Britain than to any other great power.

Yet a friendly bond between America and Greece runs deep, the paper says. Greece is the ancient home of democratic ideals. Classical learning, reaching America through Rome, helped shape the republican ideas of the young United States. The American example in turn stirred Greece's own fight for freedom from the Ottoman Empire.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d542:
President Harry Truman wrote to the Secretary of State on July 5, 1945, from Washington. His short secret memo is document 542 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It deals with lend-lease arms now that the war in Europe has ended.

Truman says he has that day sent an order to the Joint Chiefs of Staff. The order lets lend-lease arms and gear go to allied states only for use in the war against Japan, and for no other end. It grew out of a June 28 memo on lifting a ban on supplies to French troops. The note shows how fast aid rules were tightened once Europe was at peace.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d642:
Minister Wadsworth sent Washington the text of a French statement on the Levant forces late on July 8, 1945. His wire, marked restricted, is document 642 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Copies of the French text were mailed to Arab capitals.

The statement comes from the French Provisional Government. It declares that the locally raised troops are transferred to the Syrian and Lebanese governments. The terms of the transfer will be defined within a maximum delay of 45 days. Paris frames the move as good will toward two states now holding full sovereignty. With the war in Europe over, it says, there is no bar left to Syria and Lebanon forming their own national armies.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1042:
Thomas Blaisdell, chief of the American economic mission in London, cabled a confidential report on British coal on July 21, 1945. A British working party had surveyed the country's large coal position. The War Cabinet was weighing its findings, and Blaisdell shares the likely outcome. The report signals the stand Britain will take at Potsdam.

The findings are stark. Britain cannot export large coal after August, nor any coal usable at home after September deliveries. London will ask America to keep supplying bunker coal, about 100,000 tons a month. That need lasts until captured ships can be fueled from Polish and Silesian sources instead. Only very low grade fuel, unusable in Britain, could be spared later.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1142:
Charles Yost of the Central Secretariat wrote this memorandum on 8 August 1945, his second in the closing series. A week after the summit ended, the American team's paperwork chief was still at work. The delegations had gone home; the files had not.

Closing out a summit means fixing the record: what was agreed, in what words, and where each paper belongs. Yost's notes did that work for the American side. The famous part of Potsdam is the leaders' talk. The lasting part is the archive, and notes like this one built it. They show the summit's long tail of plain, careful labor.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1242:
The Secretary of State wrote to the Acting Secretary of State on 21 July 1945. The direction ran from Potsdam home: Byrnes reporting and directing from the talks, Grew holding the department in Washington. The pair exchanged word through the whole summit.

A secretary's cable home could carry the talks' drift, fresh orders for the desks, or word the president wanted spread. The home office then acted on it within the day. This message is the summit end of the circuit at work. It shows the chief abroad running his department at a distance, by cable, in the talks' first week.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1342:
George Allen of the Near Eastern and African affairs office wrote once more to Assistant Secretary James Dunn on 25 July 1945. The two men exchanged several papers during the Potsdam weeks. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Repeated notes between the same pair of officials show a working tie, not a one-off message. Allen's desk spoke for a region where oil, bases, and new states were all in play in the summer of 1945. Readers following the Allen and Dunn papers through the volume can watch a policy line form in real time, one short paper at a time.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-142:
Arthur Bliss Lane, newly appointed as ambassador to Poland, wrote to the Acting Secretary of State on July 31, 1945. Poland sat at the heart of the Potsdam dispute. Its borders and its government had strained the alliance for months. Lane was preparing to take up the Warsaw post as the conference closed. His letter entered the second Potsdam volume.

An incoming ambassador's letter carries a field view. Lane wrote about the post he was to fill and the country he would face. Readers see the human end of a headline issue: one envoy getting ready to work inside a hard settlement. The letter links the conference table to the embassy desk.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-42:
A United States delegation working paper lists the agenda for the heads of government meeting of July 20, 1945. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The paper, from the Truman Papers, was apparently before the President during the session.

Six items are listed for the 4 p.m. meeting. They are the Council of Ministers, Italy in the United Nations with a reference to Spain, and Austria, with a paper from Churchill. The western frontiers of Poland and trusteeship follow, both on Soviet papers of that morning. Turkey closes the list, on a paper Churchill was to present. Truman's own hand adds the session's fate in the margins. He marked the council disposed of, the Italy item referred to the foreign secretaries, and the Austria item settled. The last three items he marked postponed.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d742:
The Secretary of State answered Gerig on August 8, 1945, in document 742. The reply came a week after Potsdam closed. Business about the United Nations' first steps did not pause for the summit's end. Byrnes wrote from a Washington resetting itself for peace. The letter entered the second Potsdam volume.

A secretary's reply closes a loop opened by a field report. Readers can pair this letter with Gerig's July notes. The exchange shows guidance flowing back down the line. It also marks a shift in the volume's mood: from dividing a beaten continent to staffing the body meant to keep the peace.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d842:
The United States delegation tabled this proposal on July 25, 1945, as document 842. It belongs to the conference's second week. American texts by then were written against a clear map of resistance. The proposal joined the second Potsdam volume beside rival drafts.

A July 25 American proposal shows the endgame being prepared early. Its writers aimed at lines the final protocol could hold. Readers can test how many of those lines survived. The document also shows the delegation's drafting depth. Fresh texts kept coming while older ones were still being fought over in committee. That depth was itself a form of strength.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d942:
Edwin Pauley sent the Secretary of State a draft letter to Soviet negotiator Ivan Maisky on July 28, 1945. A twin letter to President Truman goes with it. Pauley asks both men to review the draft before he sends it. He says the pair of letters gives a brief history of the reparations talks and America's present attitude.

The Maisky draft recalls twenty-two days in Moscow with no Soviet plan presented. It presses the need to define reparations, restitution, and war booty as a first step. Pauley also argues that a written record matters. Public interest in America will be high, and spoken words are easily misquoted.
frus-1952-54v13p2-d842: Chargé McClintock cabled from Saigon on May 10, 1954, with late word from Dien Bien Phu. The central redoubt had fallen, DeJean told him at 8:30 p.m. local time. There was no surrender, and men fought on alone. The Isabelle post still held out. De Castries was alive and fighting at his last report. McClintock asked that his salute to the garrison's gallantry be passed to the commander in chief.
frus-1964-68v23-d42: A short memorandum for the record gives the minutes of a Special Group meeting held on November 10, 1960. It is document 42 in Volume XXIII of the 1964-1968 Foreign Relations series. Those present were Merchant, Douglas, Gray, Dulles, and Bissell. The one item kept here concerns the Congo. Bissell said brief plans were being made in case a pro-Soviet Lumumba government took hold, or in case Katanga's drive for independence caused trouble. The State Department's African bureau backed the general approach.
frus-1969-76v17-d142:
A memorandum of conversation records the working session in Beijing on the night of July 10-11, 1971, during Kissinger's secret trip. It is document 142 in Volume XVII of the 1969-1976 series. Kissinger met Huang Hua and Chang Wen-chin, with Marshal Yeh Chien-ying joining the second session. Both sides brought draft texts of the announcement of Nixon's visit. They haggled over who had asked for the meeting.

The Chinese side sought wording that stressed normal ties as the summit's aim. Kissinger pressed for a broader scope, and won a phrase on exchanging views. The two sides settled the date as before May 1972. The agreed text followed the next day.
frus-1969-76v42:
Volume XLII of Foreign Relations of the United States, 1969-1976, prints the Kissinger-Le Duc Tho negotiations from August 1969 to December 1973. Chapter heads tell the arc: Attempting the Impossible, then Discovering the Possible. A chapter on the October 1972 settlement follows the stall of May 1972. Breakdown and then settlement fill the next chapters. The last covers the hard work of carrying out the accords through 1973.

The records are full talk transcripts, with asides and laughter marked. Kissinger and Le Duc Tho haggle over maps, troop terms, and single words. Three appendixes print key texts. The volume is the fullest print record of the Paris talks.
gao-gaoreports-b-295742:
On April 4, 2005, GAO issued its ruling in file B-295742, the protest of United Enterprise and Associates. The firm had missed a noncompetitive contract under the Small Business Administration's section 8(a) program. The work was facilities support at the AmeriCorp facility in Charleston, South Carolina. GAO denied the protest. The SBA's process on the chosen vendor's fitness had flaws under its own rules. But the SBA agreed with the buying agency that the vendor was not responsible. It would not have appealed, the only step open to it.

With no appeal in prospect and no bad faith shown, the flaw caused no prejudice. The protest therefore failed.
gao-gaoreports-b-297342:
Alion Science protested a Defense Information Systems Agency award in GAO decision B-297342, dated January 9, 2006. The winner was a unit of ITT Industries. The work was spectrum design support. The winner makes goods that use spectrum bands. Its work would shape rules and plans for such goods. Those rules could sway sales for it, its rivals, and its buyers.

GAO sustained the protest. The record did not back the view that clash risk was small. Work grade harm was also not shown to be small. The winner would use its own calls on rules that touch its goods. That clash went deep. A thin clash check cannot back an award in such a case.
gao-gaoreports-b-297742:
Trailboss Enterprises protested an Air Force award for transient alert work in GAO decision B-297742, dated March 20, 2006. The winner was GCH Services. The site was Andersen Air Force Base in Guam.
