Plant fibers promise greener, lighter panels than glass fiber, but the right fiber share is a balancing act. The team hand-laid epoxy laminates carrying hemp at twenty-five to forty-five percent by weight, then measured stretching, bending, and impact performance for each blend.

The thirty-five percent blend won across the board. It reached the best tensile strength and stiffness while keeping useful stretch before breaking, plus the highest bending strength and the strongest impact absorption. The authors credit tight fiber-to-resin contact and efficient stress transfer at that loading. Beyond it, fibers clump and the resin network breaks up. They propose the blend for car body panels, light construction, and other low-load structures.
pmc-13235942:
Karoline Horgmo Jæger, Aslak Tveito, and Alain Nogaret modeled in 2026 ion motion inside the tiny gap where one brain cell signals to the next. Textbooks often treat that motion as pure diffusion, ignoring the electrical pull on charged carriers. Their 3D model solved the full physics equations for five ion types at nanometre scale. Results were matched against the simpler diffusion-only model under many settings.

The two models produced clearly unlike ion amount maps across the modeled cleft. Electrical and diffusive flows proved similar in size for every ion species tracked. Gaps grew when more receptors or more transmitter were present, or when the cleft narrowed. Competing effects kept the electrical current gap modest despite the amount gaps. The authors conclude that exact ion amounts in the cleft need the full equation set, not the diffusion shortcut.
pmc-13237342:
Safaa S Hassan and co-authors synthesized a new palladium complex in 2026 from a fused sulfur- and nitrogen-rich ring system, then tested it against microbes and cancer cells. Spectroscopy and diffraction pinned down the ligand's structure, and computer modeling supported a flat, square arrangement around the palladium center. Docking simulations probed how the molecules might fit two target proteins.

The palladium complex outperformed the free ligand against the tested bacteria and fungi, most strikingly against Klebsiella pneumoniae, where the authors see a possible route around gentamicin resistance. Both compounds showed similar power against a human liver cancer cell line. Their anti-inflammatory effect on a test protein was moderate. The work adds one more candidate scaffold to metal-based drug research.
pmc-13238242:
Kakeshita and colleagues report a rare cancer arising in a repaired aorta in a kidney transplant patient. The patient had earlier received a stent graft for an abdominal aortic aneurysm, then a successful living-donor kidney transplant. Graft function stayed stable on immune-suppressing drugs, the normal bargain that keeps a donated kidney alive.

Within the old aneurysm, doctors later found a spindle cell sarcoma, an uncommon cancer of spindle-shaped cells. Whether the stent, the immune suppression, or chance played a part is an open question. Single cases cannot answer it, but they put transplant and vascular teams on notice to watch repaired aortas for late, strange growths.
pmc-13239142:
Satoshi Kambayashi and colleagues reported in 2026 a healthy one-year-old castrated male cat whose blood creatine kinase, a muscle injury marker, stayed above two thousand units for no visible reason. The cat showed no signs, and examination, X-rays, and ultrasound found nothing wrong. Isoenzyme testing showed an odd pattern: almost all the activity sat in the band usually tied to heart muscle, yet a specific assay for that band read nearly zero.

The contradiction pointed to macro-creatine kinase type 1, a bulky complex of the enzyme with an antibody that inflates readings and confuses standard tests. The condition is recognized in human medicine but barely reported in veterinary practice. The authors urge clinicians to include it when a healthy cat shows persistent unexplained enzyme elevation. More work is needed to make the diagnosis firm in cats.
pmc-13239442:
Wei Dong and co-authors present a 2026 laboratory study of mouth cancer linked to betel nut chewing, a habit practised by hundreds of millions of people. The team mapped individual cells and their positions in tumours from six patients with oral squamous cell carcinoma.

Single-cell sequencing and spatial mapping revealed a scarred, immune-suppressed tumour environment rich in fibroblasts and poor in killer immune cells. One malignant cell group, marked by the protein LAMC2, showed strong programmes for spread and blood vessel growth. Treating cancer cells with arecoline, a betel nut chemical, raised LAMC2 and made cells move and invade more readily. The findings suggest targets for interrupting tumour support.
pmc-13239942:
Shreyashi Bista and colleagues study living alongside Asiatic black bears in Nepal's Gaurishankar Conservation Area in a 2026 paper. Clashes between people and bears are rising as habitats overlap, and the team combined habitat modelling with household interviews to see both sides of the problem.

A model built from 173 bear records rated about a third of the area as suitable habitat, mostly mid-elevation forest away from roads. Among 188 households surveyed, most said conflict is increasing. Indigenous residents and women reported the sharpest conflict, reflecting forest-edge work such as collecting fuelwood and fodder. People who valued bears ecologically showed greater tolerance.
pmc-13240142:
Sailan Liu and co-authors sequence the genome of a commercially valued sea bream along the Chinese coast in a 2026 study. Earlier work using small marker sets disagreed about how the threadfin porgy, Evynnis cardinalis, relates to relatives and whether its coastal groups differ genetically.

The team built a chromosome-level genome with long-read and chromosome capture methods, confirming a close kinship with red sea bream. Reading millions of DNA variants in fish from Shantou, Zhuhai, and Hainan showed almost no separation between the groups, consistent with free mixing in coastal waters. One chromosome carried the most differing genes, hinting at local adaptation worth future study for conservation and fishery management.
pmc-13240442:
Shang Li and co-authors follow children's eyes through three years of overnight lens wear in a 2026 retrospective study. Orthokeratology lenses reshape the cornea during sleep to correct short sight by day, and parents need long-term evidence on both safety and the quality of vision the lenses deliver.

Records covered 130 children aged eight to eighteen wearing the lenses from 2021 onward. Eyes lengthened modestly and prescriptions drifted slightly more short-sighted, in line with earlier reports. Overall optical quality measures improved, and internal eye aberrations fell, even though the cornea's own surface irregularities rose. No serious infections or vision-threatening events occurred, and the cells lining the cornea stayed stable.
pmc-13240842:
Bufan Li and co-authors report a 2026 study of a two-layer scaffold for repairing large skull bone defects in rats. Autografts remain the usual choice for big defects, yet donor sites are limited. The scaffold pairs an electrospun fiber membrane with a gel layer carrying mineral particles and a plant compound.

Lab tests showed the scaffolds held water well and had sound mechanical behavior. The loaded version encouraged bone formation and blood vessel growth while discouraging bone-eating cells. In rats, the fully loaded scaffold nearly closed large skull defects within eight weeks. The authors present the layered design as a strong candidate for regenerating bone where injury size rules out simple healing.
pmc-13241442:
Santana and colleagues in São Paulo pooled trials of curcumin for prostate swelling in a meta-analysis. Six studies covered six hundred ninety-seven men already taking standard prostate drugs. Symptom scores led the list, with prostate size and urine flow alongside. Random-effects models pooled the comparisons against placebo.

Curcumin users beat placebo groups by about four points on symptom scores. Prostate volume, residual urine, and a blood marker all shrank modestly while flow grew stronger. Benefit ran larger alongside alpha-blockers alone than with combination therapy. Santana urges bigger trials, citing wide variation between studies.
pmc-13241642:
Yunlu Liu and co-authors present a 2026 case of a chlamydia infection that looked like ovarian cancer. The patient was a 32-year-old woman with nearly three months of abdominal pain. Scans showed masses near the ovaries plus a large amount of abdominal fluid.

Initial tests found no cancer cells and no clear infection, and advanced cancer could not be ruled out. A broad genetic sequencing test on the abdominal fluid detected Chlamydia trachomatis, a common sexually transmitted bacterium. Treatment with doxycycline brought satisfying improvement. The authors advise considering this infection in young women with unexplained fluid and pelvic masses once cancer and tuberculosis are excluded. Modern sequencing can settle difficult cases.
pmc-13241842:
Paula P. Schnurr and co-authors publish a 2026 analysis of what counts as real improvement for veterans treated for posttraumatic stress disorder. Data came from a trial comparing two trauma-focused talk therapies. Symptom change was sorted into four levels, from no change through response and loss of diagnosis to full remission.

Simple response was linked to improvement on most measures, yet it delivered a good overall outcome on only one. Losing the diagnosis added little beyond response. Remission stood apart, raising the odds of meaningful gains and good endpoints on every measure. The authors argue that treatment goals should aim past symptom reduction alone. Recovery in daily life, they say, needs the deeper benchmark of remission.
pmc-13242342:
Liu and colleagues at Qingdao Agricultural University correct a figure in their 2023 study of pig skin progenitor cells. The paper mapped gene activity in multipotent dermal fibroblast progenitors with germline potential. One fluorescence image in Figure 6 was the wrong one. The panel showed PRDM1 staining in lab-grown germ cell-like cells.

A correct PRDM1 image now replaces the misused panel. The figure tests whether SOX17 appears in mouse primordial germ cell-like cells; it did not. Flow cytometry backed the staining verdict. The original article has been corrected in place.
pmc-13242742:
Qiuchen Ge and co-authors report a 2026 retrospective study of lymph node removal near the voice-box nerve in early esophageal cancer surgery. Removing these nodes may help staging, yet it risks nerve injury and voice problems. The value in early, node-negative disease was disputed.

Patients with at least one such node retrieved lived longer and stayed disease-free longer than those without retrieval, even after statistical balancing of the groups. Full dissection beat simple sampling for disease-free survival, while taking nodes from both sides added nothing. Nerve palsy was more common with retrieval. The authors weigh a survival association against a real complication trade-off.
pmc-13242842:
Mohammad Alaa Aldakak and co-authors present a 2026 case of a chest wall sarcoma that was misread as a nerve sheath tumor. A 62-year-old carpenter arrived with persistent chest pain and a firm mass fixed deep in the chest wall. A needle biopsy suggested one tumor type, which guided initial thinking.

Surgeons removed the mass in one block with parts of three ribs and involved muscle, then rebuilt the wall with mesh and metal plates. Full tissue analysis told a different story: an undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma carrying an epithelial marker that widened the diagnostic confusion. One margin still held tumor, while others were clear. The authors highlight the limits of core biopsy and the need for team discussion on added local therapy.
pmc-13243442:
Kun Yang and Jitao Chen built a self-supervised AI that listens to piano practice and pinpoints specific mistakes. Their paper appeared in Scientific Reports in 2026. Teacher feedback is slow and subjective, which limits large-scale music education. Their transformer learns from three streams at once: the sound spectrum, the symbolic MIDI score data, and a movement proxy computed from that MIDI. The proxy stands in for hand video, which the dataset lacks.

Then fine-tuning aims it at five error types: pitch, timing, dynamics, touch, and pedal. Tests used the public MAESTRO collection of virtuoso recordings with controlled errors introduced. The authors say fusing sound, symbols, and motion detects fine-grained faults with far fewer labeled examples. The setup is a proof of concept, not yet a classroom tool.
pmc-13244242:
Palakdeep Kaur and colleagues write a 2026 letter raising questions about a small trial of aerobic exercise after brain injury. The trial tested whether exercise lifts memory, attention, and fatigue in people with acquired brain injury. The letter praises the topic while probing how firm the results can be.

Only 12 people took part, far below the planned number, so the trial lacked power to spot real effects. Many thinking tests were run without correction for repeated testing, which clouds the one clear gain in working memory. Mixing stroke and trauma patients adds further blur, since recovery paths differ. The writers ask the trial team to clarify these points for readers.
pmc-13244342:
Justin Cordova offers a 2026 poem about a doctor who longs not to know his patients are dying. The speaker spends days wishing for a veil of blissful ignorance to hide pain and grim forecasts. Knowing each patient's family and hopes makes every loss cut deeper.

The verses list small details that stay with him, like a toddler the same age as his own child. He calls these memories echoes carved into his heart after each death. Yet he refuses to let grief rule him and casts the memories as light against the dark. The poem ends with a vow to let the veil tear daily and keep seeing clearly.
pmc-13244942:
Wei Sun and colleagues used machine learning to hunt the genes that make cabbages fold their leaves into a head. Their study appeared in Molecular Horticulture in 2026. Heading is the defining trait of Chinese cabbage and cabbage, and its gene list is still incomplete. A random forest model was trained on forty-seven known heading genes. It was then set loose on both species' genomes, with gene networks built alongside to show how candidates connect.

The models scored with high accuracy in both crops. Filtering their predictions left eleven genes flagged with high confidence in both species, a cross-check that strengthens belief in them. Network analysis grouped the genes into clusters whose hubs include known growth regulators such as ANT and the GRF factors. The same genes and similar wiring in two species support the approach. Breeders gain a shortlist for heading experiments.
pmc-13245442:
Khadeejeh Yousef Aldasoqi and colleagues map birth care for women with multiple sclerosis in a 2026 scoping review. More women of childbearing age live with the disease, yet labor care for them varies widely. Needless surgery is one worry when guidance stays scattered.

Following Joanna Briggs methods, the team gathered studies from 2020 to 2025 and kept eleven. Cesarean rates ran higher than in the general population, though the disease alone does not require surgery. Spinal pain relief proved safe, with no rise in relapse after birth. Fatigue and mobility limits marked labor for many women. Relapse after birth tied mostly to disease activity before pregnancy.
pmc-13246342:
Junhe Cui and co-authors test how athletic identity feeds wellbeing among elite college team athletes in 2026. A strong athlete identity can anchor a young player's life, for better or worse. The team asked whether felt support from teammates and belief in one's skill carry that link.

Valid surveys came from 309 athletes at six Chinese universities. Stronger identity went with higher wellbeing in the final model. Felt team support and self-belief each carried part of the effect on their own. The two also worked in sequence, with support feeding self-belief. The authors advise coaches to build warm team climates that grow both supports.
pmc-13246442:
Philip Sulewski and co-authors ask why our eyes linger longer on some spots than others in a 2026 brain study. Each day we make about 200,000 eye movements, pausing from a blink to half a second. Long pauses were assumed to mean hard visual work.

Five people viewed more than 4,000 natural scenes while brain waves and gaze were tracked. Brain pattern timing did not explain the longer pauses. In fact, spots that models found easy to classify drew longer looks. Pauses instead tracked how memorable a spot was and whether people later named it. Brain rhythms linked to memory rose during long pauses. Memory writing, not visual strain, seems to set the dwell time.
pmc-13246542:
Rybak, Ely, and Gustafson designed a future satellite network for Mars in this 2026 Journal of the Astronautical Sciences paper. Explorers and robots on Mars will need both communications and GPS-like positioning. A previously proposed three-satellite equatorial system, ideal for data links, proved poor at pinpointing surface locations because of bad viewing geometry.

The team tested alternatives in simulation. Tilting the orbits helped only over long tracking times, while a six-satellite inclined constellation delivered much better fixes within shorter spans, with the best results at a fifty-degree tilt. A seven-satellite design added uniform polar coverage. The paper weighs those trade-offs to guide how a combined navigation and relay network for human Mars missions might be built.
pmc-13247042:
Shen, Lin, Lin, and co-authors created an exotic state of matter inside a quantum computer, in this 2026 Nature Communications paper. The fermionic Laughlin state is a cornerstone of topological physics, in which electrons collectively behave as if carrying fractional charge, but it had never been demonstrated for fermions on a quantum processor. The team used IonQ's trapped-ion machine, running a sixteen-qubit circuit built from hundreds of two-qubit gates.

With error-mitigation tricks, they measured the state's signature features: a correlation hole showing particles avoid each other, matching patterns at the bulk and edge, and the topological entanglement entropy expected from theory. Values agreed strongly with exact calculations. The authors present the work as an end-to-end recipe for simulating topological matter digitally.
pmc-13247242:
Khan and co-authors comment on a striking anti-aging experiment in this 2026 brief report in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. With age the thymus shrinks, fresh T-cell output fades, and vaccine responses and cancer immunity weaken. A recent Nature study they discuss delivered messenger RNA to the liver of old mice, turning it into a temporary factory for three thymus-supporting factors the body stops making.

The treated mice expanded young immune-cell precursors, produced fresh T cells again, and answered vaccines and cancer immunotherapy better, teaming well with checkpoint-blocking drugs. Because messenger RNA fades, the effect was reversible, and, unlike harsh cytokine treatments, it caused no autoimmunity in the study. Khan and colleagues frame the approach as a safe, transient way to rewind immune aging, pending human evidence.
pmc-13247642:
Yoo, Suh, and Kwon examined blood transfusion practice in septic shock across Korean hospitals, in this 2026 Journal of Korean Medical Science study. Guidelines advise transfusing red cells only below a hemoglobin threshold, yet clinicians often transfuse earlier when lactate, a marker of tissue oxygen debt, runs high. Using a national shock registry of more than eight thousand patients from 2015 to 2022, the team compared transfused and untransfused patients within hemoglobin bands.

About one patient in ten was transfused within six hours, and well over half of those transfusions happened above the restrictive threshold, especially where lactate was elevated. Transfused patients were sicker, with faster heart rates and higher lactate. After adjustment, transfusion showed no association with lower hospital mortality in any band, including the high-lactate group. The authors question lactate-driven transfusion habits.
pmc-13247742:
Dandan Wang and co-authors study what makes heart patients feel ready to leave hospital in a 2026 survey. Readiness for discharge shapes how well patients manage drugs and warning signs at home. Support from others may build that readiness through confidence.

The survey gathered 463 coronary heart disease patients at a hospital in Wuhu in 2025. Support, confidence, and drug adherence each rose with readiness scores. Careful modeling showed support lifted readiness mainly by raising confidence first. Adherence also helped readiness directly, though it did not change the confidence path. The authors advise nurses to build patient confidence and family support before discharge day.
pmc-13248842:
Pharit Gridtayawong and a large team design a greenhouse film that cools crops while letting growth light through in 2026 work. Tropical greenhouses overheat under strong sun, and standard covers trap that heat inside. Their layered film sorts sunlight by wavelength instead of blocking it wholesale.

One layer scatters light, while partner films block ultraviolet and near-infrared rays. Two versions trade light share against heat rejection for crops with unlike needs. The films shed heat to the sky through a clear atmospheric window with near-perfect efficiency. Rooftop trials in tropical sun ran three to five degrees cooler than commercial covers. The laminate also proved strong under pulling tests.
pmc-13248942:
Nguyen and colleagues recount a misleading aneurysm case in a 2026 surgical report. A forty-eight-year-old man arrived after blunt trauma, and his swollen abdominal aorta was first read as a traumatic injury. A stent graft was placed, but the vessel then decayed rapidly, revealing the true problem: an infected, or mycotic, aneurysm.

Surgeons removed the infected graft and rebuilt the aorta with a cryopreserved donor vessel, which resists infection better in a contaminated field. Sixteen months later the man remained stable with the graft open and working. The authors use the case to show how infection can hide behind a trauma story, and why graft choice matters.
pmc-13249542:
Walker, Meeuwig, and Thompson counted the small fish and animals that ride along with sharks, in a 2026 Ecology and Evolution study. These companions gain protection, food scraps, or free transport from their hosts, and losing a host can drag its companions down too. Using records from baited underwater cameras across three ocean basins, the team examined seven shark species.

Almost half of the individual sharks carried at least one companion. Australian blacktip sharks hosted companions most often, and scalloped hammerheads least. Warmth, salinity, wind, and distance from shore predicted companion presence best. Partly protected waters raised the odds of companions, while the strictest reserves held more companions per shark when they appeared.
pmc-13250842:
Xiaowei Sun and co-authors target the fat that hugs arteries in this 2026 study of abdominal aortic aneurysm, a dangerous ballooning of the main belly artery. No drug treatment exists for it, only surgery once it grows large.

Scans and animal work showed that the fat layer around the aorta helps drive the disease. One of its proteins pushes white blood cells to cast out sticky DNA webs, which harm the artery wall. Tiny parcels released by stem cells, given into the belly, cut fat build-up, lowered that protein, and slowed aneurysm growth in animals. The team proposes them as a preventive approach worth further study.
pmc-13251642:
Clotilde Rouxel and a large European team add twelve new genomes of the tick-borne bacterium Anaplasma phagocytophilum, reporting in 2026. The bacterium causes tick-borne fever in cattle and sheep and a flu-like illness called anaplasmosis in people. Its pattern differs sharply between the United States, where human cases climb, and Europe, where livestock losses dominate.

Four of the new genomes came from human patients and eight from cattle, doubling the public European collection. The team used a capture-based method that fishes bacterial DNA out of blood samples from naturally infected hosts. Quality checks also exposed incomplete and contaminated assemblies already sitting in public databases. Cleaned comparisons confirmed a marked genetic split between European and American strains. The authors offer new genetic markers that may flag lineages able to jump from animals to people.
pmc-13253142:
Qing Deng and a large team design a light-activated nanoparticle to wake up the immune system against osteosarcoma in a 2026 study. This bone cancer, commonest in teenagers, shrugs off immunotherapy because its tumors suppress immune attack. Light-based treatment can kill cancer cells in a way that alerts immunity, but damaged mitochondria get recycled too quickly, muting the alarm.

The other blocks mitochondrial splitting, which indirectly stalls the recycling process. A glutathione-responsive shell releases the cargo where that molecule runs high, as it does in tumors. In cell and animal tests the treatment triggered immunogenic cell death, reshaped the tumor's immune environment, and roused strong anti-tumor responses. The authors offer the design as a way past immunotherapy resistance.
pmc-13253642:
Timothy Paul Hickling and colleagues review how machine learning is reshaping preclinical immunogenicity risk assessment in a 2026 article. Such predictions now guide candidate selection and protein redesign toward lower risk. They are candid about the bottleneck: inconsistent assays and measurements across companies make training data hard to merge. Modeling that links immune mechanisms to trial simulations partly bridges the gap. The review closes with the data standards the field needs next.
pmc-13254442:
Obeidat and a large team survey how clinicians worldwide handle acute upper gut bleeding before the emergency endoscopy. Their 2026 Therapeutic Advances in Gastroenterology study collected five hundred thirty-three responses between April and November 2023. Death rates from this emergency have barely improved despite clear guidelines.

Fluid choices split evenly, and blood transfusion practice loosened sharply for unstable patients. A third never used stomach-emptying drugs routinely, while most gave acid blockers and, for suspected variceal bleeding, vessel drugs and antibiotics. Younger clinicians followed recent guidelines more closely than veterans, and the authors flag wide practice variation.
pmc-13254942:
Taku Yamamichi and colleagues describe a two-step imaging strategy that located a lymph leak in an infant in a 2026 case report. Their patient, a four-month-old girl, developed a swelling abdomen and feeding failure from chylous ascites, milky lymph fluid pooling in the belly. Drainage removed nearly a liter of fluid rich in triglycerides and lymphocytes, and the leak still ran at about half a liter a day.

The next day, surgeons used near-infrared fluorescence with indocyanine green dye during the operation itself, watching the leak glow in real time. Guided to the exact spot, they sealed it with electrocautery and fibrin glue, and the fluorescence visibly faded. The baby progressed to full oral feeding. Two years later the ascites had not returned.
pmc-13255742:
Dana Franklin and co-authors wrote a 2026 review of racial disparities in ductal carcinoma in situ, an early breast lesion confined to the milk ducts. Many such lesions never turn invasive, yet some do, and doctors cannot reliably tell which. Black women face higher risks of progression, recurrence, aggressive disease, and death than other groups.

Candidate markers such as KIFC1 and ACKR1 may help flag dangerous lesions earlier. The authors call for risk tools that combine tumor biology, the surrounding tissue, and population context, so treatment intensity matches real risk and care becomes more equitable.
pmc-13256642:
Yanlin Wu and co-authors report in 2026 a binder-free copper nanoparticle electrode grown directly on nickel foam for measuring glucose in beverages without enzymes. Food producers need fast sugar checks, yet conventional coated electrodes bury their active sites under polymer binders and slow the measurement down.

Their one-step hydrothermal method produced a self-supporting electrode with fast charge transfer and a large active surface. The sensor responded within three seconds across a wide concentration range, with high sensitivity and a detection limit of 0.32 μM. It stayed selective against common food interferents and worked in real beverage samples, suggesting a practical route to portable glucose testing in food quality control.
pmc-13257342:
Yura Choi and colleagues review in 2026 how eye surface inflammation destroys the stem cells that renew the cornea. pmc-13258242:
Paola Pavačić and co-authors explore gut microbes, metabolism, and inflammation in young women with rosacea in a 2026 study. Stool gene sequencing, blood tests, body measures, and questionnaires were combined.

pmc-13258742:
Jonin Serafin Zumsteg and coauthors analyze which injury region drives death risk by age in a 2026 trauma registry study. Nearly one hundred thousand severely injured adults from Swiss, German, and Austrian centers met the study criteria. Leading injuries were grouped as head, chest, abdomen, or limb.

Death rates climbed steeply with age across all groups. Head injury carried high risk at every age. Chest, abdomen, and limb injuries showed far steeper age related risk jumps than head injury. The oldest group faced the highest relative risks for non head injuries. Authors suggest standard severity scores may miss age related differences in injury impact.
pmc-13259242:
Sirachat Nongsok, Chutima Vanichvattanadecha, and Penwisa Pisitsak dye cotton with lignin and silver using two chitosan pretreatments in a 2026 textile study. Lignin colors fabric while also forming germ fighting silver particles. Two natural forms of chitosan were compared as the base layer.

The alpha form held nearly triple the silver of the beta form. Particles grew larger on alpha treated fabric and smaller on beta treated fabric. Despite lower silver, beta treated fabric killed more staph bacteria in tests. Sun protection, strength, and color depth all improved with coating. Finish designers learn that particle placement can beat particle amount.
pmc-13260042:
Mykyta Fomin and colleagues wrote a 2026 review of how excess fat in the body can break down autophagy, the cell's system for clearing damaged parts and surplus lipids. Cholesterol-rich particles such as LDL, often called bad cholesterol, can stress the cell's recycling compartments. By contrast, HDL, often called good cholesterol, helps move cholesterol out of cells. The review covers heart vessel disease, fatty liver disease, and disorders of thinking and memory.

Fat droplets then build up, energy-producing structures falter, and inflammation stays switched on. The authors propose treatments that combine lowering body fat load, lipid-lowering drugs, and tuning the recycling system. They frame autophagy failure as one shared mechanism linking metabolic stress to chronic inflammation.
pmc-13260542:
Eunseuk Lee and co-authors wrote a 2026 review of infection problems after CAR T-cell therapy, a treatment that engineers a patient's immune cells to attack B-cell cancers. pmc-13260942: Piotr Długosz and Liudmyla Yuzva published a 2026 correction notice for their Scientific Reports article on mental health disorders and stress coping among forced migrants from Ukraine and Russia. The original article contained errors in its abstract about who was sampled and where they lived. The corrected text says people were gathered through invites on Telegram and Facebook. It states the sample as two hundred Ukrainian forced migrants living in Poland, and 164 Russian forced migrants living mainly in Serbia and other countries. The article has been corrected.
pmc-13262642:

pmc-13263042:

The team reviewed biopsy records for patients aged 60 and older, collecting sex, age, site, and diagnosis data across the full period.

Of 21,367 lesions diagnosed from 1978 to 2023, about one in eight came from older patients, mostly aged 60 to 79 and slightly more often women. Reactive lesions, growths from irritation, were the largest group. Fibrous hyperplasia was the most common single diagnosis, followed by oral squamous cell carcinoma, a mouth cancer. The authors call for stronger prevention and long-term oral care.
pmc-13263142:

It also caught lopsided parental effects, where a mother's or father's score for body mass or cognition shifted the child's risk unevenly. A smaller cleft study showed the method handling gene-environment interplay with maternal factors. The authors pitch the tool for transcriptome-wide scans as well.
pmc-13263342:

Radar imagery exposed surface cracks and lineaments, and the area split into three promising zones for exploration. Fluorite sat in pegmatite veins crossing older rocks. pmc-13263642:
Cherie Wan-Yin Wong and co-authors report a 2026 journal article comparing two speech therapy models for aphasia, the language loss that often follows stroke. Interviews added patient views on each model's benefits, informing future service design.
pmc-13263742:

Their map aims at the bottlenecks choking modern immunotherapy.
pmc-13263942:
Tobias A. M. Niehoff and co-authors present a 2026 simulation study on mating choices in commercial animal breeding programs. pmc-13264042:
Onur Baser wrote a 2026 validation study of MELD, a large health data set that joins Medicare claims with medical records, lab results, and patient surveys. The data cover 2020 to 2024 and hold about 60 million patients. Before such data can guide strong claims, its quality must be checked.

Checks showed high inner consistency, and illness rates matched official counts with a mean error of 3.1 percent. Record linking matched 94.7 percent of cases. The data also predicted death and return to hospital fairly well. The author judges the set sound for real-world studies.
pmc-13264442:
Karoline B Bräuner, Hjalte L Berthelsen, and Anne G Vedel wrote a 2026 case report on a rare harm from a common bowel treatment. A phosphate enema, a fluid given through the rectum to clear the bowel, raised blood phosphate to a severe level. That surge then drove blood calcium down.

The patient was a 77-year-old man healing from pelvic surgery after a major injury and long bed rest. He came back with belly pain, sickness, and swelling from severe constipation. After the enema he developed the phosphate surge and low calcium. The authors note the risk is higher when kidneys work poorly. They stress fast spotting of the signs and prompt care for this rare event.
pmc-13264942:
Yacoub Abuzied and colleagues present a 2026 interview study on living with intermittent catheterisation after spinal cord injury in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. These patients cannot empty the bladder on their own and pass a thin tube several times a day. The study explored daily challenges and coping in Arab men at a large rehabilitation hospital.

The third covered body image and sexuality. The authors stress that local norms of modesty and privacy shape how patients manage and cope, and care should respect that.
pmc-13265842:
Izzet Turker and Hilal Isleroglu wrote a 2026 food science study on extracting protein from fennel seeds with help from enzymes and ultrasound. Adding just ten minutes of ultrasound after enzyme treatment reached about 93 percent. The treated protein dissolved, foamed, and held water and oil better than the control. Heat tests showed it also withstood higher temperatures before unfolding, and its amino acid mix was balanced. The authors back the pairing for food use.
pmc-13267342:

pmc-13267542:
James E Ip and colleagues report a 2026 analysis of blood pressure effects of a nose-spray heart drug. Etripamil is a self-given spray for sudden fast heart rhythms, the first of its kind approved in the United States. Other calcium channel blockers, given by vein or mouth, can drop blood pressure or cause fainting. The team asked whether the spray does the same.

The analysis pooled over 1,600 people treated across the drug's phase 3 trials from 2018 to 2023. Low blood pressure occurred in only about 0.4 percent of participants, and fainting in about 0.2 percent. Test doses given while the heart beat normally let the team watch pressure closely. The authors conclude the spray has minimal effects on blood pressure.
pmc-13268142:
Luiz Henrique Santos Cambrussi and colleagues report a 2026 study of wrist fracture repair with a locking plate. Breaks of the far radius bone are among the most common adult fractures. A plate fixed from the palm side locks bone angles and allows early movement. The team reviewed 135 fractures treated between January 2023 and August 2024, measuring three alignment angles on X-rays at three points.

All three measures improved strongly from before surgery to right after, and held to clinic discharge. The small drift after surgery was not significant. The same held in the hardest fracture types under three different classification systems. Two blinded raters did the measuring and grading. The authors conclude the plate gives firm first correction and keeps it, even in complex breaks. They class the evidence as a case series.
pmc-13268642:
Yahya Shahsavari and colleagues present a 2026 tutorial on joining federated learning and blockchain for health care data. Hospitals want to train shared AI models without pooling raw patient data. Federated learning does that, training locally and sharing only model updates, but it can be poisoned or leak information. Blockchain, a tamper-proof shared ledger, can add trust and audit trails.

The tutorial maps medical data types and their learning needs. It compares three ways to couple the two technologies, from tightly fused to loosely linked, weighing security, scale, and rule compliance. It reviews attacks specific to health care and defenses such as zero-knowledge proofs and privacy noise. A compliance framework covers US and European privacy law and device rules. Uses range from disease prediction to drug discovery.
pmc-13269742:
Nan Feng and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on cell recycling receptors in papillary thyroid cancer, the rising form of thyroid cancer. The receptors govern a process that eats worn parts of the cell's protein factory. Public cancer data were mined, then cell experiments tested three candidate receptors.

All three receptors, RTN3, SEC62, and ATL3, were lowered in thyroid cancer, and lower levels meant poorer survival. Their levels also tracked closely with immune cell entry into tumors. Silencing any of the three in cancer cells made the cells grow and spread faster in the lab. A shape-shifting program in the cells seemed to drive that change. The authors propose the receptors as diagnostic markers and brakes on this cancer.
pmc-13269842:
Yuhui Yu, Mengya Wang, and Bin Zhao published a journal article in 2026 building a four-gene risk score for uveal melanoma, a highly malignant eye tumor. Immune cells called macrophages and monocytes in the tumor's surroundings help it escape and spread. Cancer atlas data and single-cell profiles were used to find their key genes.

Six cell groups were mapped in tumor samples, with macrophage and monocyte cells prominent. The risk score combined BTBD6, C2CD4B, CCL24, and S100A4. Patients with high scores had poorer survival, more monocyte-lineage and T-cell entry, and higher immune checkpoint gene activity. High scores also went with stronger sensitivity to eight chemotherapy drugs in the analysis. The authors offer the score for prognosis work.
pmc-13270242:
Britney Sekulovski, Noam Miller, and Rachael Shaw published a journal article in 2026 on zebrafish raised for three months in unpredictable tanks. Temperature, feeding times, habitat complexity, and group membership kept changing for one group, while the other group lived in stable conditions. Six behavior tests then compared how the fish sought and used information.

Fish from unpredictable tanks sought more information, watched social cues more closely, and reacted more strongly to them. Their shoals swam closer together but less in coordination. When their own learned information clashed with fresh social information, they chose the social side more often. The authors say unpredictability makes stored information lose value faster, pushing animals toward quick social updates.
pmc-13270642:
Valentin V Veselinov and co-authors present in 2026 a scalable way to decorate housanes, tiny cage-like hydrocarbons proposed as stand-ins for benzene rings in drug design. Housanes drew little attention because adding groups late, and in the right places, was hard. Their method uses a directing group to guide metalation first at the bridgehead, then along the fused three-membered ring.

The sequence gave two- and three-substituted housanes with excellent control of position and shape. Crystal structures and calculations checked how well the products mimic ortho-substituted benzene geometry. A boron-mediated rearrangement turned one housane into a crowded cyclopentane boronic ester, and a mirror-selective variant gave a single handed form. The work opens housanes to the late-stage variety that drug chemists expect.
pmc-13270842:
Rebecca A Stone and co-authors report in 2026 how staff experience England's pilot specialist services for children and young people living with severe obesity. Thirty-eight Complications of Excess Weight services were launched to offer holistic, person-centered care through multidisciplinary teams. As part of a national evaluation, the researchers interviewed twenty-eight team members across seven services about barriers, demand, and fit with wider care.

Three themes emerged: achieving person-centered care, navigating a complex patient journey, and the strain of delivering a pilot. Staff described children needing innovative, whole-family support, but faced heavy demand, no step-down services for graduates, and missing transition paths into adult care at sixteen to eighteen. Pilot funding uncertainty threatened staffing and continuity. The authors call for a long-term commissioning plan so gains made in these services are not lost.
pmc-13271042:
Sitota Gebremelak and Tefera Darge Delbiso report a 2026 cross-sectional survey on maternal depression and child undernutrition in poor urban areas of Ethiopia. They studied children aged 12 to 36 months in Adama, Addis Ababa, and Debre Birhan, measuring mothers' mood with a standard nine-question scale and children's growth by body measurements.

Among 627 mother-child pairs, 16.0 percent of mothers showed depression, and 52.7 percent of children were stunted, meaning too short for their age. After accounting for other factors, children of depressed mothers had 2.21 times the odds of stunting. No clear link appeared with wasting or underweight. The authors call for nutrition programmes that also support mothers' mental health.
pmc-13271142:
Ruohao Wu is lead author of a 2026 multi-centre study building a prediction chart, called a nomogram, for genetic test results in children with syndromic neurodevelopmental disorders. The test, trio whole-exome sequencing, reads the protein-coding DNA of a child and both parents, but its success rate for unexplained cases is unsatisfying.

Training data came from 265 children at one hospital, with checks in 38 and 97 children at two other centres. Three features independently predicted a positive genetic result: severity of developmental delay, abnormal head size, and the complexity of linked developmental conditions. The combined chart performed well in training and even better in outside checks, the authors report.
pmc-13271242:
Sina Fadaei and colleagues report in 2026 on how rheumatology staff in the Netherlands view prediction models for rheumatoid arthritis care. Such models are built often, yet none has entered treatment guidelines so far. The team asked clinicians what would make these tools welcome or unwelcome in daily practice.

Fifteen rheumatologists and nurse practitioners took part in semi-structured interviews, which the researchers analyzed for shared themes. Staff said models need trust, clear inputs, and proof of benefit before adoption. They also wanted tools built into health records, with little extra work, that support judgment rather than replace it. Protecting professional choice and patient contact mattered throughout.
pmc-13271342:
Wiwiek Harsonowati is lead author of a 2026 review on endophytes, microbes that live inside plants, as helpers for crops under climate stress. Crops now face heat, drought, and disease together, and while endophytes can raise stress tolerance, their benefits vary unpredictably between settings, which this review aims to explain.

The authors build a framework across molecular, metabolic, and ecological levels, covering stress signalling, carbon trade-offs, microbiome interactions, and host genetics. Helpful effects hold, they argue, only while stress chemistry, energy balance, and ecological fit stay within workable limits. Under severe or long stress, those supports break down. They propose measurable markers, such as stress chemical thresholds and photosynthetic stability, to predict when partnerships will last.
pmc-13271442:
Masresha Derese Tegegne is lead author of a 2026 registered report protocol, a pre-registered study plan, on mapping emergency rescue terms to ICD-11, the World Health Organization's disease classification. The early rescue chain coordinates automated alerting, responders, and clinical systems after emergencies, but it still relies on spoken language without standard terms.

The project will map the rescue chain terminology, the minimum concept set for automated information exchange, onto the ICD-11 Foundation, the detailed terminology behind the classification. Aims are to assess how the two sets of terms relate, judge mapping quality, and find missing concepts and meaning gaps. The protocol sets criteria and steps for judging each match in advance.
pmc-13271742:
Annika Massenberg is lead author of a 2026 journal article on an early step in human papillomavirus infection. These viruses cause several cancers, most famously cervical cancer. They reach target cells through breaks in the skin-like barrier. First they bind to heparan sulfate, a sugar chain in the material around cells.

Using skin cells that build a strong surrounding matrix, the team blocked the virus's active recruitment to the cell surface, released the block, and watched under a microscope. Within fifteen minutes, virus particles coated in heparan sulfate moved to the entry factor CD151 at the cell edge or on thin cell fingers. They shed the sugar coating over the next few hours, likely before entering the cell.
pmc-13272142:
Julia Chan and coauthors update in 2026 a systematic review of treatments for serious sleep disturbance in people with cancer. Poor sleep is a frequent after-effect of cancer and its treatment, yet trials often count any sleep complaint rather than clinically meaningful disturbance. The review asks what works for that harder outcome.

Forty-two randomized trials with 3,844 participants, published up to mid-2025, met the criteria. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia improved sleep quality with a moderate effect and cut insomnia severity with a large effect. Complementary and alternative approaches also showed a large effect on sleep quality. The authors grade how certain each piece of evidence is.
pmc-13272242: Oliver W. A. Wilson is first named author on a 2026 correction notice for an article in Supportive Care in Cancer. That article covered breast cancer survivors' views of a clinical decision tool for personalised exercise plans. The correction states that typesetting errors in the Results section printed extra numbers next to the upper limit of each confidence interval. It lists the affected percentages in the Tool Usefulness and Tool Uses passages. It gives each figure as published and as corrected. It says the publisher regrets the error.
pmc-13272342:
Miao Yan and coauthors test in 2026 how deep slow-release fertilizer should be placed in melon fields in Xinjiang, China. Melon growers want simpler feeding methods, yet the best depth for this fertilizer type was not known in the region. Depth can change nutrient timing, yield, profit, and soil microbes all at once.

Field plots compared depths of fifteen, twenty-five, and thirty-five centimeters with standard feeding and no feeding. The deepest placement raised soil nitrogen and phosphorus in the middle and late season and boosted microbes that cycle those nutrients. Standard feeding instead favored potassium and carbon-cycling microbes. Yield and profit figures rounded out the advice for growers.
pmc-13272442:
Kexin Liu and coauthors test in 2026 whether adjusting fertilizer carbon-to-nitrogen ratios can repair soil water and salt balance under plastic mulch in arid cotton fields. Years of mulch use leave residue that disrupts soil structure and salt movement, dragging yields down. The trial ran two years in Xinjiang with three irrigation levels and four ratio treatments.

Raising the ratio improved soil water holding, cut salt accumulation, and evened out water and salt distribution across irrigation levels. The six-to-one ratio produced the best cotton yield, averaging about eight percent above the other treatments. The authors propose ratio tuning as a practical counterweight to mulch residue damage.
pmc-13272542:
Raise Ahmad and a large team studied social isolation during adolescence in rats for a 2026 report. Being cut off from peers in the teen years is a known risk for anxiety and depression. The team asked whether isolation also alters memory, gene activity in brain and gut, and gut microbes, and whether effects differ by sex.

Young rats spent four weeks alone or housed in pairs. Against the team's expectation, isolated females did better on a novel object memory test, and no added anxiety behavior appeared in either sex. Isolated females showed shifts in brain genes tied to memory and myelin. Males showed no behavior change but had altered activity genes in brain and immune genes in the colon. Gut microbe variety trended lower in isolated females.
pmc-13273142:
Yimeng Mei and colleagues hunted for antioxidant peptides in silver carp bone collagen in a 2026 study. Fish bones are a cheap by-product, and short protein pieces from them might fight oxidative damage in the body. The team combined computer, lab, and cell methods to find and test candidates.

Three peptides stood out for scavenging free radicals and binding iron, and they survived simulated digestion well. Modeling showed they latch onto a sensor protein that switches on the cell's own antioxidant defenses. In cell tests, treated cells raised their protective enzyme activity, lowered a damage marker, and survived peroxide exposure better. The authors present fish bone collagen as a low cost source of natural antioxidants worth developing further.
pmc-13273242:
Jiahui Zhang leads a 2026 study identifying a protein pair that controls protein synthesis in lung adenocarcinoma, a lethal lung cancer subtype with few treatment options. The team screened gene, RNA, and clinical data to find ubiquitin ligases, enzymes that tag proteins, acting as tumor suppressors. One ligase, SPOP, stood out.

SPOP tags the cancer-promoting protein PABPC1 in a way that holds it in the nucleus and blocks global protein synthesis, slowing tumor growth. A second enzyme, HAUSP, reverses that tag and fosters cancer. The authors present this axis as a key regulator and offer their screening framework as a model for finding other treatment targets.
pmc-13273842:
Liu and colleagues report the TESS phase II trial of a sandwich treatment plan for rectal cancer. Their 2026 journal article covers low-risk, locally advanced cancer of the lower rectum. The plan gives chemotherapy and radiation before surgery, in a layered sequence.

The trial enrolled 98 patients. Total neoadjuvant therapy means all drug and radiation treatment comes first. A clinical complete response was seen in 46.9 percent of patients. That means no tumor could be found on checks. Sphincter preservation reached 79.6 percent. Overall survival was 96.9 percent. Keeping the sphincter lets patients avoid a permanent stoma. The authors present the regimen as a strong option for this group.
pmc-13274142:
Shahin Gavanji and colleagues wrote a 2026 review article on the human microbiome and its shifting role in health and disease. Trillions of bacteria, viruses, and fungi live in the gut, skin, mouth, and airways. Far from passive passengers, they aid digestion, make vitamins, train the immune system, and steer metabolism.

The review gathers evidence on what shapes these communities, including diet, geography, and medicines. It then surveys harm from imbalance, called dysbiosis, across gut, metabolic, brain, heart, autoimmune, and cancer disorders. Microbes also change how drugs work in each person. Treatments covered include probiotics, prebiotics, stool transplants, and engineered microbes meant to restore balance.
pmc-13275242:
Mengshi Tang, Yingxu Ma, and Yating Wang ranked drug treatments for fatty liver disease with scarring risk in a 2026 network meta-analysis. This condition, called MASH, can be attacked through several hormone and metabolic pathways, and many drug classes show promise. Recent trials of an oral diabetes class had not yet been placed in the ranking.

They gathered thirty-four phase two and three trials in adults with biopsy proven disease. For shrinking liver scarring, FGF21 analogs and the SGLT2 inhibitor class ranked at the top, ahead of the one approved drug and GLP-1 drugs. For clearing the disease itself, dual hormone agonists and FGF21 analogs led. A balance chart put SGLT2 inhibitors in the best zone of effect and tolerability, though their tissue data rest on a single pivotal trial.
pmc-13275442:
Xinqiang Chen and a large team report a 2026 cross-sectional study of heart-health habits and gallstone disease in China. They used baseline data from the China Multi-Ethnic Cohort. The study asks whether a higher Life's Essential 8 score, a measure of healthy habits, matches lower gallstone risk.

Records from 85,302 adults were analysed, and gallstones affected about seven in every hundred people. Each ten-point rise in the score matched a clearly lower risk, with a curved rather than straight pattern. Part of the link ran through lower inflammation and oxidative stress in the body. The protective pattern looked strongest in women, younger adults, and Han participants.
pmc-13275742:
İlker Kurt and co-authors report a 2026 study on monitoring vancomycin, a strong antibiotic used against hard-to-treat germs. Dosing is tricky because too much can injure the kidneys. Newer guidance favors a measure of total drug exposure over a day, rather than the lowest blood level alone.

The team followed thirty-six adults who got the drug by vein for at least three days. They compared the older lowest-level method with two ways of estimating daily exposure. The methods often disagreed on whether a patient was in the safe range, agreeing only about two thirds of the time. Higher drug levels were linked to kidney injury, which hit nearly four in ten patients. A gene variant also tracked with higher levels and slower drug removal.
pmc-13276342:
Eric Cramer and co-authors present a 2026 protocol article for filming how three-dimensional cell balls invade their surroundings. Spheroids, small balls of cells grown in gel, mimic tumors and let researchers watch invasion over time. A nagging problem is that the gel shifts between imaging sessions, scrambling positions.

The protocol walks through making spheroids, embedding them in collagen plugs, and recording image details. A software pipeline called TRACEQC then realigns each spheroid's position across time points and flags poor matches. The method works with any spheroid type, cell mix, or formation technique. The authors developed it with fibroblast and cancer cell lines. They present it as a quality control standard so that changes seen over time reflect biology, not camera drift.
pmc-13276842:
Dou Lu and a large team use laser light tests to read tumour signals in glioblastoma, in a 2026 study. Response to the standard drug temozolomide hinges on whether a gene called MGMT is silenced by methylation. Current tests reveal methylation but give no clues for drug design.

Gene-edited cell models with set methylation states gave clean reference patterns. Methylated cells showed more saturated fat signal, while unmethylated cells showed stronger DNA, amino acid, and unsaturated fat signals. Chemical analysis confirmed the light-based findings before the team built a sorting model. On sixty-two patient samples the model separated methylation states well, suggesting metabolic routes against drug resistance.
pmc-13277242:
Katica Cvitkusic Lukenda leads a 2026 trial of a diabetes drug given once before a heart artery imaging test. The test uses dye and radiation that can cause oxidative stress, meaning damage from reactive oxygen. Sixty patients without diabetes were assigned to standard care or to empagliflozin two hours before the planned procedure.

Blood tests over the next day showed less oxidative DNA damage in the drug group and steadier antioxidant defenses. Sugar patterns on immune proteins also shifted toward a less inflammatory profile, though some changes were not firm after strict checks. A single dose may protect vessels during the test, the authors say, while calling for larger trials to confirm it.
pmc-13277542:
Progna Banerjee leads a 2026 study of how the solvent around tiny semiconductor plates changes whether they stack or float free. The plates, made of cadmium selenide, are flat crystals used in light devices. In toluene they joined into long ribbons, while in a second solvent they stayed well dispersed, the team found using electron imaging and X-ray scattering.

Computer simulations traced the split to the solvent's shape flexibility, which subtly changed the oily coating on each plate and even the plate's twist. Broken-up ribbons also gave strong amplified light emission at low energy input. Solvent choice, often treated as a background detail, can steer how these particles assemble for devices.
pmc-13277642:
Pei Jing leads a 2026 study of a tiny cancer treatment particle that can be seen on MRI scans. Effective immune therapy needs killer T cells to enter tumors and keep working. The particle is built with manganese and plant polyphenols, compounds that help generate reactive oxygen inside tumor cells.

That chemistry triggers an inflammatory form of cell death and frees cell DNA that switches on an immune alarm pathway, producing a signal protein that matures other immune cells. The death and alarm steps reinforce each other in a loop. In animals, T cells entered tumors and immune memory formed, while MRI tracked the particle. Imaging and treatment in one agent is the design's appeal.
pmc-13278242:
Ahmet Murat Bayraktar leads a 2026 letter about how studies should judge AI tools that read bladder scope images. The letter responds to a study that tested four large language models on 401 cystoscopy images across forty finding types. Its reference standard was agreement between two urologists looking at the images, with no tissue confirmation.

That visual standard carries real uncertainty, the letter argues. Even expert urologists often mismatch tissue results when grading bladder tumors by sight, and flat lesions called carcinoma in situ are easily missed under white light. Leading studies in the field require tissue-based confirmation. The title proposes a tiered reference framework as the way forward for such AI studies.
pmc-13278742:
Michela Russo and colleagues read Parkinson disease mental symptoms from walking patterns in a 2026 study. Depression, anxiety, and psychosis are common in Parkinson disease and erode quality of life. Gait analysis is cheap and non-invasive, so a walking signature could flag patients carrying that burden.

One hundred four patients walked under camera-based motion capture in single and dual-task conditions. Patients with neuropsychiatric symptoms walked more slowly, with greater instability and poorer movement control. Machine learning classifiers separated the groups with promising accuracy, best on detailed movement and force features. The features driving the models matched the statistical findings. The authors propose gait testing as an early marker tool.
pmc-13278842:
Carmen Dobszewicz leads a 2026 review arguing that the epaulette shark is an ideal model species for climate-ready shark conservation. Sharks and rays are highly threatened, yet data on how they respond to climate change are sparse. This small, bottom-dwelling shark abounds on Great Barrier Reef flats, tolerates low oxygen and acidified water, and breeds well in captivity.

Experiments across life stages show adults and juveniles keep routine behavior under raised carbon dioxide. Warming is the sharper threat: embryos hatch earlier and smaller, energy costs rise, and death risk climbs at high temperatures. The authors propose using this tractable species to set temperature and oxygen safety margins for reef habitats and nursery areas.
pmc-13280342:
Mohamed S. Elbelkasi and colleagues present a 2026 study of a fast, image free method to spot electric arcs on railways. Pantograph catenary systems carry the arm that draws power from overhead rail wires. Arc faults threaten safety, reliability and efficiency on electric lines. Image based checks lag too much for real time use, past the arc time scale. Their method reads traction current signals direct, with no cameras.

A wavelet transform, which splits signals in short bursts, feeds features to a small neural network. Many mother wavelet families were tested for which detail levels best catch arc transients, or brief spikes. Daubechies db9 and Symlet sym8 wavelets discriminated best. The compact network, trained on normalized features, hit a high regression score that marks excellent classification accuracy. Direct signal reads could guard trains in real time at low cost.
pmc-13280442:
Gisele Sampaio Silva and colleagues published a 2026 narrative review of stroke epidemiology and risk factors across the Americas, synthesizing Global Burden of Disease estimates and national data. The region recorded 1.2 million new strokes and 15.7 million people living with stroke's effects in the cited 2023 estimates. Age-adjusted rates fell after 1990, yet recent analyses show a worrying rebound, particularly among younger adults.

Patterns differ between countries. Incidence runs higher in Latin America and the Caribbean, while prevalence runs lower than in wealthier settings, a combination reflecting weaker acute care and higher death rates after stroke. Social and racial inequities delay treatment and worsen recovery. More than 75 percent of the stroke burden traces to modifiable risk factors in the cited analyses, which the authors use to argue the epidemic is largely preventable. Their conclusion is a call for system-level action rather than new knowledge, since the main risk factors are well identified.
pmc-13280542:
Ieva Lase and team report a 2026 study of hormone secretion as a prognosis sign in lung neuroendocrine neoplasms. These lung tumours can secrete hormones, though ectopic secretion is rare and poorly explored. New evidence hints that secreting tumours carry a worse prognosis. A look back cohort of one hundred sixty seven patients, without small cell lung cancer, was checked for clinical and biochemical data and outcome. Tumour tissue was checked for serotonin and calcitonin levels.

Among one hundred twenty seven patients with hormone measures, fifty two had raised levels. The serotonin metabolite 5-HIAA led, then calcitonin. High calcitonin levels strongly correlated with calcitonin in tumour tissue. Serotonin in tissue did not correlate with metabolite levels. Diffuse calcitonin staining went with shorter overall survival. Secreting tumours had shorter survival than non secreting ones, about sixty two versus one hundred twenty four months.
pmc-13280642:
Maria F Sanes Guevara and colleagues published a 2026 analysis of hepatitis B prevalence among people with and at risk for HIV in a cohort spanning thirteen sites between 2018 and 2024. The study covered 5,238 participants in the MACS and WIHS cohort programs. Blood markers sorted each person into chronic infection, recovered past infection, or never infected. The team compared rates across risk groups under modern HIV treatment.

Chronic hepatitis B affected 2.4 percent of the cohort, and coinfection stood at 3.0 percent among people with HIV. Past infection was commoner in men and rose with age. People carrying both viruses had lower immune cell counts and lower HIV suppression rates than comparison groups. Among participants with HIV who had never encountered hepatitis B, 40.6 percent lacked antibodies, leaving them vulnerable despite vaccines. The authors call for tighter screening and immunization in HIV care, since a preventable second virus is compounding risk for this population.
pmc-13280742:
Thanika Ketpueak and colleagues studied gut germs as a clue to survival in a 2026 report on bile duct cancer. This cancer is rare in most places but common in parts of Asia. The team ran a forward-looking study at their center. Stool samples came from patients before drug care began. Germ profiles were read from gene traces in the stool. Outcomes tracked response to care and length of life.

In thirty patients with advanced cancer on drug care, gut germ mixes split by outcome. Some germ types were higher in patients who fared poorly, and others were lower. One germ type went with slower growth in the first six months. Tissue germ mixes did not split two cancer types apart. The authors say stool tests might one day help doctors guess how care will go.
pmc-13282042:
Charlotte Henningsen Hansen and co-authors offer a 2026 protocol for a scoping review on treating a severe form of dehydration in hospital patients. In hyperosmolar dehydration, the body lacks water and blood salts become too concentrated. It affects a large share of admitted adults and raises the risk of illness and death. Current guidance often fails to separate it from low blood volume, so patients may get the wrong type of fluid.

As a protocol, the work reports no treatment results yet. It sets out searches of major medical databases, plus checks of reference lists and trial records. Studies will be kept only if adults had proven dehydration of this type and were treated in hospital. The planned map of what fluid treatments have been tried should show gaps and guide later trials on safer, better-matched care.
pmc-13282442:
Lewis J C Grant and colleagues published a 2026 study using computer vision to stretch a handful of laboratory measurements across a hundred meters of drilled ocean crust. Geologists normally describe core visually and sample sparsely, because no expert can annotate every centimeter. Working on a carbonate-cemented breccia core from beneath the seafloor, the team trained deep learning classifiers on the core imagery to label rock types. They then projected measured bulk density and carbon content onto the whole core at quarter-square-centimeter resolution.

The density record improved on the instrument measurement it was checked against. The carbon estimate underlined how much carbon this broken, cemented seafloor rock locks away, which matters for global carbon accounting. The authors pitch the framework as scalable to the world's existing core repositories: archives of already-drilled material could be re-audited automatically, turning stored imagery into continuous quantitative records.
pmc-13282742:
HaoQi Huang and a large team offered a 2026 framework joining two forms of cell death that depend on metals. Cuproptosis is driven by copper and harms cell powerhouses, while ferroptosis is driven by iron and damages cell fats. The two were often treated as separate paths.

The authors instead place both on one scale set by metal balance, energy use, and redox state, which is the balance between oxidising and protective chemistry in a cell. Where a cell sits on that scale shapes which death form it takes and whether it can switch. The paper sets out testable predictions and suggests that combined data methods could forecast cell fate under metal stress.
pmc-13282842:
Kaori Inoue and co-authors present a 2026 study testing a novel internet advertising approach to raise awareness of fatty liver disease tied to metabolic problems. The disease, shortened to MASLD, can progress to cirrhosis and liver cancer yet remains little known. The team first analysed what people search alongside the term fatty liver, then ran banner adverts. One group saw the advert after searching key terms; a control group saw it regardless.

Searches clustered on treatment and lifestyle, with diet, blood sugar, cholesterol, and visceral fat among the key terms. The targeted banners earned a higher click rate than untargeted ones, and far more survey responses. Targeted viewers also more often said they intended to seek medical care early, about sixty percent against about forty-two percent. The authors conclude that search-term based advertising may raise disease awareness and prompt earlier consultation.
pmc-13283442:
Shanthan R Ramidi authored a 2026 case of stubborn low oxygen from a heart flap opening, with breathlessness when upright. The opening, called a patent foramen ovale, occurs in about a fifth to a quarter of adults. It is usually silent, but rare shunting can starve blood of oxygen.

The patient was a 59-year-old woman with chronic low-oxygen breathing failure. Full checks ruled out main lung, vessel, and tissue causes of her problem. A bubble heart scan showed early right-to-left shunting through the opening. A catheter procedure closed the opening without open surgery for her. Oxygen rose at once and stayed better, freeing her from added oxygen. Position-linked symptoms are a key clue.
pmc-13283942:
Vincy Nelson and co-authors reviewed in 2026 whether lifestyle programmes beat usual care for blood pressure in Indian adults. Heart disease is a top killer, and high blood pressure is a main driver, yet care access in India is uneven. The team searched three databases for studies from 2000 to 2025 on adults with high or borderline pressure, following standard review rules.

Fourteen studies with 1,547 people qualified, testing yoga, aerobic exercise, salt reduction, and mixed programmes. Pooling seven trials showed lifestyle care cut systolic pressure by about five points and diastolic by about two points against usual care. Yoga and meditation approaches showed the largest drops, and results were fairly consistent across studies. The authors pitch such low-cost programmes as add-ons for national disease control.
pmc-13284042:
Evyatar Hubara and colleagues tested in 2026 whether a brain injury protein in blood can predict new nerve deficits after infant heart surgery. Brain injury during congenital heart surgery can leave lasting development problems, and early warning would help doctors act. The protein S100B was measured before surgery and six hours after in 130 infants, while a standard stroke outcome scale was scored before surgery and at discharge.

The six-hour value, adjusted for age, predicted new deficits best. It caught 93 percent of affected infants and correctly cleared 85 percent of unaffected ones, with a rule-out strength the authors highlight. A cut-off at two standard deviations gave the best balance. In combined models the six-hour score stayed the strongest independent predictor. The team supports its use in post-surgery decisions.
pmc-13284542:
Jing Li and co-authors report a 2026 clinical study of combined care for young and middle-aged adults with hypertension. One group got standard care, while the other added mindfulness-based stress reduction plus ear triple therapy for eight weeks. Each group had 115 patients treated at Jiangsu Provincial Hospital of Chinese Medicine.

After eight weeks, the added-care group did better on treatment effect, quick blood pressure lowering, symptom scores, anxiety scores, and mindfulness scores than the control group. Baseline traits and drug use were alike at the start. The authors conclude the combined approach eased symptoms and negative feelings, and may help patients manage their condition and stick with medication.
pmc-13284742:
European Food Safety Authority authors deliver a 2026 statement on a United States toxicology profile for mercury. The European Commission asked EFSA to judge whether the 2024 ATSDR profile should change EFSA advice from 2012. The statement was backed by the CONTAM Panel before approval.

EFSA found no need to update its weekly intake limits for either inorganic mercury or methylmercury based on the new profile. A new 28-day rat study was judged unfit to set a dietary reference point. Gaps in how ATSDR reported some methods were noted, but no major missed studies were likely. EFSA adds that newer methods and evidence since 2012 might still merit a fresh review in time.
pmc-13285542:
What do top heart-muscle centers in the United States do well, and where do they strain? Martin Maron, Barbara Steeves, and Andrew Wang survey staff, patients, and advocates in a 2026 study of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy centers. Chosen sites all offer septal surgery, defibrillator implants, and transplants.

Care teams and diagnosis steps looked much alike across centers, with shared habits for imaging and treatment picks. Teaching patients and staff about new drug classes, such as cardiac myosin blockers, proved key for smart choices and smooth flow. Gaps in funding and in dedicated staff, from office help to skilled scan readers, topped the strain list. The authors share habits that general heart clinics could adopt.
pmc-13285742:
Shuaiwei Song leads a 2026 multicenter cohort study on uric acid and new diabetes in people with coronary heart disease. High uric acid is best known for gout, but it also tracks with wider metabolic trouble. The study asks whether uric acid levels predict who goes on to develop diabetes, and whether inflammation carries part of that effect.

Patients were followed at five centers in China, and higher uric acid came with higher diabetes risk in a curved, dose-linked pattern. Risk rose past set levels that differed slightly for women and men. Adding uric acid to standard factors sharpened risk prediction a little. Blood markers of inflammation carried part of the link between uric acid and diabetes. The team suggests watching uric acid as one more warning sign in heart patients.
pmc-13286142:
Teresa Chen and co-authors scope smart software for finding deep vein clots in a 2026 review of imaging studies. Clots in deep veins demand fast answers, since delays raise the risk of a lung blockage or lasting leg damage. Reading scans takes scarce expert time, so the review asked how well computer models spot clots on ultrasound, CT, and MRI.

Seven databases yielded eleven studies from 2021 to 2025 that fit the rules, most of them built on ultrasound. Scores for catching clots and clearing healthy veins ranged widely on ultrasound, while the lone MRI model scored high on both counts. Models tested across mixed scan sets reached the strongest marks of the group. The authors place the tools as helpers beside experts, not stand-ins, and call for shared trials across hospitals plus proof the systems save time and money.
pmc-13286442:
Shuai Wang and co-authors review the gene BUB1 and its roles in cancer, in a 2026 article. BUB1 helps run the checkpoint that makes sure chromosomes split evenly when cells divide. Many tumors produce too much of it, and high levels often track with worse features and poorer survival, though the pattern varies by cancer type.

Beyond division, BUB1 touches DNA repair, cell movement, a form of iron-driven cell death, stem-like behavior, and immune escape. Early laboratory studies show that blocking it can slow tumors, especially alongside radiation or several standard drugs. Open problems include separating its enzyme work from its scaffolding work, sparing healthy dividing tissue, and choosing patients by biomarkers.
pmc-13287142:
Wen-Zhuan Huang and colleagues describe a new moss species and a new moss family from Motuo County in the eastern Himalayas, a region where plant diversity remains under-collected. The 2026 study began with an odd moss resembling the genus Scabridens but with a shorter double midrib on its leaves. The team assembled twenty complete chloroplast genomes to place it.

Family trees built from those genomes put the new moss as sister to a known Scabridens species with strong support. Leaf margin curling and longer stalks added physical distinctions. Despite the close relationship to another family, the genus's distinct form justified a family of its own, named Scabridentaceae. The find underlines the eastern Himalayas as a priority for moss exploration.
pmc-13287242:
Liuyi Luo and colleagues applied explainable computer vision in 2026 to face and skull images from 130 adults, half with sleep apnoea confirmed by overnight testing and half matched controls. Their goal was to find shape traits linked to the condition without starting from a fixed list of expected features.

The model separated the groups well, with an accuracy measure the authors report as 0.87. Highlight maps pointed to the jaw and chin, as expected, but also to the forehead, brows, and upper eyelids. Direct measures then confirmed narrower brow spacing and greater forehead projection in patients. The authors say larger groups must confirm the upper-face traits.
pmc-13287542:
Daiki Nakajima and co-authors describe in 2026 a man aged 84 with a stiffened spine condition who fell two metres and broke a lower chest vertebra. Scans also showed blood filling the right chest, yet no ribs were broken and lungs looked unbruised.

Chest drainage rose past 2400 millilitres within ten hours, forcing emergency camera surgery. The main injury site was not bleeding. Blood came instead from a hidden break in a bony spur several levels higher. Heat sealing and clotting agents stopped it, and spine fusion followed later. The authors urge teams to hunt for distant spur breaks when chest bleeding keeps growing in such patients.
pmc-13287842:
Do Young Shin and co-authors reviewed records in 2026 for 113 Korean children treated for Graves disease, an overactive thyroid condition, between 2004 and 2023. They hunted early signs that predict who will settle off drugs, who will relapse, and who will need lasting high doses of the standard tablet.

About four in ten children reached remission, on average after roughly three years. Lower hormone and antibody levels at diagnosis, and faster antibody falls, marked the remission group.
