Framing the disease as a joint glomerular tubular failure opens fresh treatment angles. The review maps those signals for researchers hunting the next kidney protective therapy.
pmc-13338942: Adriana Oliveira Manfiolli and colleagues issued a 2026 correction for a study of stress kinases in the fungus Aspergillus fumigatus. Only Figure 4A was wrong: matching images were used by accident for two strains under Congo Red, the test was repeated, and the corrected panel now shows the true growth results.
pmc-13339642:
Hélio M. T. Albuquerque and colleagues settle a fifty-year-old structure dispute in a 2026 chemistry study. Burning of 3-amino-1H-indazole with oxygen was reported by Hünig and Pozharskii as an azo product, but proof was thin. Repeating the work in basic conditions gave two products.

Which product formed depended on how much tert-butyllithium was used as reported. Magnetic resonance and X-ray methods pinned both structures. The deep-red Hünig compound is an imine form. The orange Pozharskii compound is truly an azoazole, with bond layout opposite to the 1977 claim. One framework now reconciles both old reports.
pmc-13340542:
P. Singh and colleagues commented in 2026 on whether charge transfer across hydrogen bonds can stabilise oil droplets in water. Stable oil nanodroplets carry a negative surface charge, attributed either to hydroxide adsorption or to charge transfer across improper C-H···O hydrogen bonds. Zhao and colleagues had questioned charge transfer based on simulations of hexane in water.

Singh and colleagues argue hexane is a poor model, since it dissolves nine orders of magnitude more readily than hexadecane and does not form kinetically stable droplets. They also correct a misconception about a blue shift in earlier scattering work and note no molecular level proof for hydroxide adsorption either. The comment sharpens a live debate on oil water interfaces.
pmc-13342242:
Haobin Peng and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a rare crisis during kidney stone surgery. A 63-year-old woman having percutaneous nephrolithotomy for several right kidney stones suddenly bled into both chest cavities and her abdomen while the operation was under way.

Airway pressure spiked, oxygen fell, and blood pressure dropped before bedside ultrasound revealed fluid around both lungs and inside the abdomen. Doctors drained both sides of the chest and the abdomen, gave fluids, blood, and pressure-raising drugs, and the patient steadied. She went home after 10 days and was well at three months. The authors urge quick ultrasound checks when breathing trouble strikes during such surgery.
pmc-13344042:
Keke Wu and colleagues sequenced armoured ciliates in 2026 to uncover the gene basis of mineralised outer structures. Within Ciliophora, this trait is found only in the family Colepidae. High quality genomes for three Colepidae species, Coleps hirtus, Levicoleps biwae, and Coleps viridis, showed marked growth of gene families for calcium carbonate biomineralisation.

Tree analysis showed a novel aldo keto reductase domain moved sideways from bacteria to the Colepidae line. That domain joined a carbonic anhydrase domain in a novel fusion protein found only in Colepidae. The work shows how sideways gene transfer plus gene family growth built a mineral armour in single celled eukaryotes.
pmc-13344242:
In a 2026 study, Itai Atar and co-authors asked which birth events raise the risk of a blood pool in the vaginal or vulvar tissues after birth. They also asked which of these cases end up needing surgery. Such blood pools are rare. Yet they can cause sharp pain, heavy bleeding, and sudden low blood pressure. Early warning signs thus matter for care on the ward.

The team matched 57 sick women with 170 controls from over 147,000 births at one teaching hospital from 2012 to 2024. Vacuum birth, a cut to widen the opening, and a second-degree tear each raised risk a lot. Higher body weight and epidural pain relief were linked with lower risk. A score built from these factors helped rule out danger. About one in four sick women needed surgery, most often after a long second stage of labour.
pmc-13344542:
Cecilia Taverna and colleagues described in 2026 two new setups for studying tiny samples at very high and very low temperatures on the AILES beamline at Synchrotron SOLEIL in France. Infrared and terahertz light can reveal how materials and molecules behave, but only if temperature and pressure are held under tight control.

One setup reaches down to 10 kelvin and the other up to 600 kelvin, with pressures from vacuum to 100 gigapascals, using liquid cells, diamond anvil cells, and strain devices as needed. The bright synchrotron beam lets researchers probe samples smaller than a millimetre across a wide range of light energies. The paper gives other beamline users a tested route to extreme-condition measurements that were hard to arrange before.
pmc-13347942:
Katherine W Eyring and co-authors map DNA methylation cell by cell. Their study was published in 2026. It covers autism brain tissue. A paired method read two signals at once. One signal was methylation. The other was gene activity. Over 60,000 nuclei were read in total. All came from the front brain cortex. The donors numbered 49 in all.

Over 30,000 regions differed in methylation. They clustered at promoters and control sites. Those sites stay active across life. Shifts were small beside ageing effects. They barely tracked gene activity levels. Age marks centred on excitatory neurons. Age-varying autism marks pointed elsewhere. They flagged growth of neuron projections as a disturbed path. Autism effects thus shift across the lifespan.
pmc-13348142:
Pragadeesh Ayyamuthu Rajarathinam Uma and colleagues report the complete genome of a leaf bacterium that helps tomato plants grow, in an announcement from 2026. Strain MtTm-13 was picked from tomato leaves in Coimbatore, India, where a pink colony grew on methanol feed. The strain is known to bear stress while aiding plants through hormones, mineral freeing, and protective compounds.

The genome spans 5,231,310 base pairs with a G plus C share of 69 percent and 4,660 protein-coding genes in the reported assembly. A full gene set lets researchers find the exact paths behind growth help and stress cover, guiding use as a living farm aid.
pmc-13348242:
Hongran Moon and colleagues test whether kidney stones speed decline in polycystic kidney disease, in a prospective cohort study published in 2026. A total of 410 patients had entry scans within a year that separated true collecting-system stones from cyst wall crusts, then were followed for a median of 5.18 years toward dialysis start and a wider decline marker set.

Dialysis start hit 51 patients and the wider marker hit 96 in the reported counts. Stone carriers faced a hazard ratio of 2.84 for dialysis after full adjustment, with a smaller lift for the wider marker. Links looked stronger in men, giving stone checks a sharper role in watching this inherited disease.
pmc-13349342:
Federica Borghi and co-authors wrote in 2026 about purine and pyrrolo ring scaffolds as multi-target drugs. This design path has drawn less focus than single-target work, despite its promise. These ring systems show up in drugs that act on kinases, folate enzymes, histone deacetylases, bromodomains, transporters, phosphodiesterases, ion channels, and toll-like receptors.

Surveying two decades of drug chemistry, the write-up weighs design rules and structure-activity links for compounds that hit several targets at once. It flags build traits that give balanced multi-target action. It also flags pitfalls, such as off-target harm. For drug makers, the synthesis gives a road map for single drugs that hit linked paths in complex ills.
pmc-13349842:
Shaoqiu Chen wrote a 2026 editorial introducing a collection on finding biomarkers and drug targets with both traditional methods and artificial intelligence. Careful lab work built on clear hypotheses has produced many markers now used in precision medicine.

Modern biomedical data, though, are now too large and mixed for older analysis pipelines to handle comfortably, leaving gaps in repeatability and in joining different data types. AI tools can pull compact signatures from such data and carry lessons across diseases. The editorial frames the two approaches as partners: machine methods can rank candidates fast, while classic experiments supply the depth needed before a target reaches patients.
pmc-13349942:
Muhammad Wasif Saif and colleagues commented in 2026 on a network meta-analysis ranking targeted drug combinations for advanced pancreatic cancer. The work they discuss pooled 13 phase III trials with 5,759 patients, comparing gemcitabine-based combinations against gemcitabine alone.

Network methods compare many treatments at once by mixing direct trial results with indirect links, useful when head-to-head trials are missing. The commentators value that reach for guidelines and policy, but warn that indirect comparisons rest on shaky ground when trials differ in patients or design, a common problem in cancer research. Their piece weighs what such rankings can and cannot tell doctors choosing therapy.
pmc-13350542:
Hongjiang Zhang and co-authors tested in 2026 a distributed-parameter model using quantitative dynamic contrast MRI. It aims to split clinically significant prostate cancer from insignificant disease. This split guides whether to treat or watch. Multiparametric MRI is key for spotting. Yet contrast imaging remains largely qualitative in current reporting rules.

Patients with suspected prostate cancer were enrolled prospectively. Pharmacokinetic maths was applied to contrast uptake curves. Traits that mirror blood flow and permeability were derived. The model was weighed against standard checks. If validated, quantitative contrast work could sharpen biopsy picks. It could cut both missed fierce cancers and overtreatment of indolent ones.
pmc-13351642:
Jennifer J Salinas and colleagues report beta testing in 2026 of the 50K4Life phone app, built to run walking challenges. Health apps often fail because people find them hard to use, so early testing matters. Twelve public school office staff in El Paso County, Texas used the app, built on the Pathverse platform, for a 2-week challenge.

All 12 finished the challenge, and ratings were high for design, layout, and battery use. Problems still appeared: over half struggled with navigation and slow step-count updates, and some could not find all features. Every user opened the leaderboard and challenge pages. The results guide fixes before wider rollout to school staff.
pmc-13352142:
Kwon and colleagues build a tool that picks out peptides able to cross cell walls. These short chains can carry drugs into cells. Yet no one can spot good ones by eye. The team fed a data set of known chains into a group of learning models. A method called SHAP ranked which traits mattered most. Five traits rose to the top. They cover shape, charge, and how atoms link.

The tool was right in just over four cases out of five on test data. It beat older tools on the same test. Since the five key traits are clear, chemists can use them to design new chains. The same method may suit other peptide types.
pmc-13354442:
Asra Amjad and colleagues reframe late breast cancer relapse as a problem of aging immunity, in a 2026 narrative review. Estrogen receptor-positive disease can return years later, yet the biology that keeps tumor cells dormant and then wakes them stays poorly mapped. Standard follow-up also lacks the sensitivity to foresee relapse with confidence.

The review joins geroscience with cancer biology, drawing on work from 2015 to 2025 on immune senescence, chronic inflammation, and dormancy. It weighs liquid biopsy tools and experimental therapies, and it flags methods and translation gaps for future study. The authors offer clinicians and researchers a unified lens on why aging tissue may shelter sleeping cancer cells.
pmc-13354842:
Kosuke Sasaki and others told of a case of postherpetic belly pseudohernia diagnosed with standing sound scan, in 2026. Pseudohernia means the belly wall bulges without any built defect, and it can follow shingles when nerve damage weakens belly muscles. The illness is easily mistaken for a true hernia.

A sixty-year-old woman built right flank pain and blisters, treated with valacyclovir, and later noticed new bulging on the right side of her abdomen. Standing sound scan showed relaxation of the right rectus muscle with no fascial defect, confirming pseudohernia, and later scans showed gain as bulging faded. The case shows how bedside sound scan, performed standing, can settle the finding without unnecessary surgery.
pmc-13358342:
Amene Ghaderi and co-authors present a 2026 study of electronic prescribing in Iran. The program lets doctors send prescriptions to pharmacies by computer instead of on paper. The team asked doctors, pharmacists, nurses, and office staff what helps the program work and what holds it back.

Through interviews sorted into strengths, weaknesses, chances, and threats, the study maps the program's real state on the ground. The findings can guide health leaders who want to fix weak spots, train staff well, and spread the system more widely. Clear evidence like this matters as more countries move prescribing online.
pmc-13358542:
Huanhuan Yang and co-authors pool past research on a simple blood score in esophageal cancer in a 2026 review. The score, called HALP, joins four routine measures: hemoglobin, albumin, and counts of lymphocytes and platelets. Together they reflect blood health, nutrition, and immune strength. The team asked whether a low score warns of worse outcomes.

They combined 11 studies and compared survival across score levels. Patients with low scores died sooner and saw their cancer return earlier than those with high scores. Because the score comes from cheap, standard blood tests, it could help doctors spot patients who need stronger support and closer follow-up.
pmc-13358842:
Gilson Gabriel Viana Veloso and co-authors question a key lung cancer test in a 2026 commentary. For most patients with non-small cell lung cancer, treatment hinges on a score called PD-L1, which gauges a protein tumors use to hide from the immune system. High scores favor immune drugs. Yet the score is an imperfect hero, the authors argue.

About a fifth to a third of patients score negative, and they tend to respond less well, but some still benefit. The authors discuss new ways to read the marker, including blood-based tests. Their piece urges doctors not to let one score alone decide who receives immune therapy.
pmc-13359942:
Xiaomeng Hu and co-authors build a simple survival model for advanced liver cancer in a 2026 study. Patients at middle to late stages now often receive a triple mix: targeted drugs, immune therapy, and procedures that block the tumor's blood supply. Results still vary widely between patients. The team sought a forecast from facts already in the chart.

Using data from 184 patients, they built a model on three items: sex, a liver function grade called ALBI, and a blood ratio called ALR. The model split patients into clearly different outlook groups. A tool this simple could help doctors stratify risk and tailor how aggressively each patient is treated.
pmc-13361842:
M Alfawaz and co-authors tested a plant compound in tiny carriers against colon cancer in rats in a 2026 study. Paeonol, from peony root, fights oxidative stress and inflammation, two drivers of colorectal cancer. The team loaded it into biodegradable nanoparticles to help it reach tissue. Sixty male rats were split into six groups, including healthy controls and groups given a cancer-triggering chemical for ten weeks.

Some triggered rats got plain paeonol, others the nanoparticle form. Blood markers of tumors, stress, and inflammation were measured, along with gene activity for cell death and clean-up paths. Tissue from colon, liver, and kidney was examined closely. The focus was a protective pathway called NRF2/HO-1. Better delivery could turn a promising plant compound into a real shield.
pmc-13362342:
Mukhlid Alshammari explored nurses' views on medication safety in Saudi hospitals in a 2026 qualitative study. Medication errors remain a major threat to patients. Nurses, who give most medicines, see the system up close. Alshammari found they frame safety as a shared process built on communication, workload, staff skill, and teamwork with technology, not as lone personal slips.

Barcode scanners and electronic records did improve safety in the nurses' eyes. But their value depended on nurse vigilance, good training, and teamwork, above all under heavy workload. The study urges bundled fixes: standard communication habits, enough staff, ongoing training, and reporting cultures that do not punish honesty. Technology should support clinical judgment, the nurses insist, never replace it.
pmc-13364042:
Nayanne Lima Dos Santos Ferreira and a large team present a 2026 study on food packaging films made from okra mucilage and corn starch, strengthened with liquid smoke. The smoky liquid, rich in phenolic compounds, was cast into the films at up to three percent. The team tracked thickness behavior, water traits, strength, structure, antioxidant power, and how fast the films rot in soil.

Liquid smoke thickened the casting mix, made the film surface more water-shy, and cut vapor passage, while the film dissolved a bit more readily in water. Stretch strength rose by over half at the top dose, with a small loss of stretch. The smoke supplied nearly all the antioxidant action. Soil burial ate most of each film, backing their use as active, compostable packaging.
pmc-13364742:
Jeong Lee and co-workers report in 2026 the first case set of a rare drug side mark: seed fluid that turns blue or green on a gut drug named upadacitinib. Six men with gut swell disease at four Korea care sites noted the change a mid span of two months into high dose care.

No man had pain, germ signs, or odd lab tests of the seed fluid. The tint faded when the dose fell and cleared when the drug stopped for some. The team casts it as a rare, dose tied, soft harm that fades, and asks for more study.
pmc-13365342:
Jie Li and co-workers check in 2026 if soft glass micro grains, prized as drug ships, harm mice when fed by mouth. The team made three grain types, with pure glass frames and two that break down more fast. Mice got high doses, up to a top dose, with repeat feeds.

No mice died, and blood, chem, and flesh checks showed no clear harm. The fast break type left liver, spleen, and kidney more quick than its kin. Immune cell counts held calm for all types. The work guides safe grain design for mouth drug ships.
pmc-13369742: Gebreyohannes and colleagues published a correction in 2026 to their 2024 study of anticholinergic burden, the cumulative effect of drugs that block a key nerve signal. Quality of life in a resource-limited setting. The counts of medicines by burden score were wrong: sixteen, not fifteen, medicines scored one point, and five, not four, scored three points, with trihexyphenidyl added to the top group. Furosemide, warfarin, and morphine remain the most used one-point medicines, and a corrected first figure replaces the original in the journal record.
pmc-13371142:
Ben Bepouka and colleagues follow HIV prevention pill use among female sex workers in Kinshasa in a 2026 study. Daily oral PrEP works well against HIV, but only if taken steadily, and evidence from the Democratic Republic of the Congo has been thin. The team tracked 120 women receiving PrEP at four friendly clinics over six months in 2024, checking pill counts and self-reported missed doses.

Pill-count adherence rose from 80 percent at entry to about 95 percent by month six, while self-reported adherence moved the other way. Clinic site was linked to adherence at entry, pointing to service differences that matter early. The study suggests that supportive clinic care can lift steady use, and it flags the need to reconcile pill counts with self-reports when judging prevention programmes.
pmc-13371242:
Marja Leonhardt and colleagues ask clinicians what heroin-assisted treatment should look like in Norway in a 2026 study. The programme, launched in 2022, offers prescribed heroin to people with opioid use disorder who have not been helped enough by methadone or similar drugs. Past work links it to less crime and better health and work outcomes.

Twenty-one semi-structured interviews with programme clinicians were analysed for themes. Four broad themes emerged, the first three closely linked, centred on individualised, patient-centred care as the ideal philosophy. Clinicians also flagged practical hurdles to putting that ideal into practice. The study gives policymakers a clinician-grounded view of how to shape the programme so it serves its most marginalised patients.
pmc-13371542:
Huili Qian and others study how weight before pregnancy shapes newborn results after assisted reproduction in a 2026 paper. The team reviewed 994 mothers who had single babies through assisted reproductive technology and delivered between mid 2020 and mid 2024. Mothers were grouped as thin, normal weight, heavy, or obese by pre-pregnancy body mass index.

Thin mothers faced about four times the adjusted odds of a small-for-gestational-age baby compared with normal-weight mothers. Heavy and obese mothers faced sharply higher odds of large babies and macrosomia. When pregnancy weight gain was adequate, the thin link to small babies persisted, while heavy links faded. The work supports weight counselling before fertility treatment.
pmc-13371642:
Masanori Oshi and colleagues test whether TP53 mutations change how long breast cancer treatments last in a 2026 study. The focus is hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer, using real-world data from Japan's C-CAT cohort alongside the METABRIC cohort for survival analysis. Treatment duration served as a real-world proxy for benefit.

TP53-mutated tumours carried a poorer prognosis in METABRIC. In the real-world cohort, TP53 mutation was linked to shorter time on CDK4/6 inhibitors, but not clearly to shorter time on immune checkpoint inhibitors. Age groups from young adults to older patients were compared. The split suggests that TP53 status may help predict which drug class will hold longer for a given patient.
pmc-13374242:
Bo Wang and colleagues trace a feedback loop linking mitochondrial damage to nerve pain in mice in a 2026 study. Nerve injury drives spinal cord inflammation, yet how mitochondrial failure sustains that inflammation was unclear. A peripheral nerve injury model was used, with mitochondrial integrity, DNA release, and cGAS-STING-IRF3 signalling examined by imaging, molecular work, and single-cell sequencing.

Injury damaged spinal mitochondria, spilling mitochondrial DNA into the cell interior and switching on the cGAS-STING-IRF3 pathway. IRF3 bound the CMPK2 promoter and raised CMPK2 expression, suggesting a loop that keeps inflammation going. Silencing CMPK2 and blocking the pathway with NDGA were tested for pain relief. The loop offers a new target for neuropathic pain that persists long after injury.
pmc-13377842:
Ekin Yiğit Köroğlu and others test whether surgery extent, tumour size, and that hormone predict results in that type thyroid cancer in a 2026 study. Rules base surgery mainly on that hormone levels, yet the cost of straying from rules was not fully known. Ninety-one patients with proved medullary thyroid cancer treated at a large centre from 2019 to 2025 were reviewed.

Operations were classed as concordant, less wide, or more extensive against ATA, ESMO, and NCCN guidelines. Outcomes included persistent disease within six months, recurrence after excellent response, reoperation, and problems. The study weighs tumour size, calcitonin, and surgical extent together, asking whether individualised surgery compromises results or whether guideline follow-through matters less than tumour biology.
pmc-13378342:
Miguel E Domínguez-Romero and colleagues published a 2026 study on spinal cord injury in frogs that can no longer regrow the cord. Young frog larvae can repair such injuries, but after they change into adult form they lose that ability, much like mammals. The team looked at energy systems inside the injured cord.

Using imaging, energy measurements, and gene activity tests, they found that mitochondria, the cell parts that make energy, became fewer, larger, and abnormal after injury. Even so, energy levels rose, because the cord switched on sugar-burning pathways and used stored fats instead. That switch may help cells survive when their normal energy system is damaged.
pmc-13382042:
Roscoe Lim and colleagues present a 2026 study testing whether ultrasound signs of a stiff heart can flag early disease in a transplanted heart's arteries. That artery disease develops early after transplant and causes much later harm. The team reviewed 136 heart transplant recipients treated between 2018 and 2023.

Heart ultrasounds provided several measures of how the heart relaxes. The outcome was artery disease seen on imaging one year after transplant, found in about fifteen percent of recipients. Only one measure, a short relaxation timing value, was clearly linked with the disease. A model combining that measure with age and sex separated patients fairly well, suggesting a non-invasive early warning sign.
pmc-13384042:
Lauren De Bruyn and colleagues test cholesterol top-ups during long sepsis in mouse studies in 2026 work. Blood cholesterol falls sharply in sepsis and low levels track with worse outcomes, but cause and effect were unclear. Septic mice received five days of infusions rich in LDL or HDL cholesterol, or a placebo.

Infusions raised the targeted blood fractions and eased cholesterol loss in the adrenal glands. Muscle mass, force, and fiber cholesterol did not improve, though, and adrenal structure and hormone response stayed impaired. The authors conclude that repletion alone does not fix the adrenal and muscle problems of prolonged sepsis.
pmc-13384242:
Sumit Kumar and colleagues review why guideline-based care for esophageal cancer often falls short in North East India in 2026 work. The region carries one of the country's heaviest loads of this deadly cancer. Modern care calls for staging, nutrition checks, combined drug and radiation steps, surgery, and steady follow-up.

The review traces gaps along the whole care path, from late arrival to loss during follow-up. Distance, weak transport, language range, money strain, and scarce specialist centers all push patients off the guideline path. The authors argue that fixing delivery systems matters as much as new drugs for closing the outcome gap.
pmc-13384542:
Xinguang Liu's team covers China's 2025 guideline for adult primary immune thrombocytopenia, in a 2026 synopsis. ITP is an autoimmune condition marked by isolated low platelets. New therapies and fresh evidence prompted the Thrombosis and Hemostasis Group of the Chinese Society of Hematology to issue an updated guideline.

The update gives new roles to TPO receptor agonists and adds spleen kinase blockers, Bruton's kinase blockers, and neonatal Fc blockers. Advice shifts toward tailored, goal-directed therapy aimed at lasting drug-free breaks. Spotting ITP remains a matter of ruling out other causes, needing repeat low platelet counts with a normal blood smear.
pmc-13385442:
Bowen Zhang and colleagues find surface markers that can isolate platelet-biased blood stem cells in 2026 work. Such stem cells favor platelet output and matter in aging and blood cancer, yet no markers could pick them out alive. The team combined gene, chromatin, and surface protein data from single mouse stem cells.

Machine learning settled on a four-marker pattern that isolates the biased cells to high purity, proven by single-cell transplants. A compact gene panel also split biased from balanced stem cells in a chip-based test. Both tools tracked the known rise of biased cells with age and their selective wake-up after platelet loss.
pmc-13390442:
Lu Liang's team scoped how machine intelligence is used in teen mental health support and therapy, searching four data banks plus grey writings from 2015 to July 2025 under scoping-review guidance. Teens face high mental-health risk, while usual talk therapy may miss their evolving needs.

Twenty-four studies made the cut, all from 2020 to 2025 and led by the United States and China, mostly tackling depression, anxiety, stress, and suicide thoughts. AI showed promise for risk guess, self-management, tailored care, wider access, and stigma reduction, but missed-call errors, secrecy, and moral gaps persisted, cooling enthusiasm for unwatched rollout.
pmc-13390642:
Friedrich Krohn leads a 2026 imaging study asking whether a small midbrain region degenerates in Alzheimer's disease and tracks thinking ability. Post-mortem work shows varied damage in the substantia nigra alongside classic Alzheimer's pathology, but its link to symptoms during life was unclear.

Using a prospective German study of cognitive impairment and dementia, the team tested whether magnetic resonance measures of this region differ in Alzheimer's patients and relate to general cognition. The region's markers were lower in Alzheimer's disease and linked to cognitive function. Dementia researchers gain a candidate imaging signal outside the usual memory circuits, suggesting that Alzheimer's decline involves more brain systems than the classic ones.
pmc-13390742:
Maria Paniagua-Garcia leads a multi-country 2026 cohort study of Campylobacter bacteria found in the bloodstream, comparing patients with intact and weakened immunity. Bloodstream infection with this gut bacterium is uncommon, and its course across immune states has been hard to summarise from single hospitals.

Cases collected from 2009 to 2024 across many centres let the team compare presentation, treatment, and outcomes between immunocompetent and immunodeficient patients. Doctors who treat such infections gain a fifteen-year, multi-country picture. It shows who gets this bloodstream infection. It shows how hard it hits when immunity is low. It also shows where care should differ. The scale also helps separate consistent patterns from local quirks. Most past work came from one site at a time, so this shared pool counts for much.
pmc-13391442:
Akam Ramezani's team studied pain and mental damage in 1,343 older Iran adults from the Birjand Longitudinal Aging Study, separating pain strength from pain meddling. Chronic pain is common in later life, but which dimension tracks cognition was unclear.

Nearly sixty percent were cognitively impaired by joint test criteria. After controls, both strength and meddling linked clearly to damage, with each point of meddling carrying a larger chance increase than strength. The findings suggest pain clinics and memory services should assess meddling, not just strength, in older adults. The study drew on the Birjand Longitudinal Aging Study.
pmc-13392342:
Haiyan Yu and colleagues show, in 2026, that gut bacteria-derived compounds can inflame and kill bile duct cells, a finding relevant to an autoimmune liver disease. Primary biliary cholangitis destroys small bile ducts, but the effects of p-cresyl sulfate and p-cresyl glucuronide in it were unclear.

Human bile duct cells treated with either compound showed increased cell death by flow measurement. Mice given the compounds developed portal inflammation with lymphocyte infiltration, alongside changes in death-related proteins and inflammatory signals in blood. Liver researchers gain a mechanistic link between microbial waste products and bile duct injury that may help explain disease triggers.
pmc-13392642:
Pramono and co-authors report a 2026 genetics study of 710 Indonesian Friesian Holstein cows on a commercial farm in West Java. They examined four single-letter DNA variants in two genes: leptin, a hormone gene tied to fertility, and IGF-1, a growth-factor gene. Each cow's variants were matched against milk records, such as 305-day yield, and reproductive records, such as calving interval and days open.

One leptin variant, g.820 C>T, showed moderate diversity and real associations with days in milk, calving interval, first insemination after calving, days open, and conception rate. Cows carrying the CC type reproduced better than TT carriers, marking the variant as a candidate for marker-assisted selection, where breeders use DNA tests to choose animals. The second leptin variant showed little variation and no associations. One IGF-1 variant was identical in every cow tested, so it cannot guide breeding here.
pmc-13393142:
Takayuki Gyoten and Akihiro Yoshitake report a giant clot floating in the aortic arch. It was traced to a deep vein thrombosis that crossed into the arterial side through a hole between the heart's upper chambers. Scans suggested clot fragments had already reached the brain, and ultrasound confirmed the opening, a patent foramen ovale, with flow in both directions. The heart team judged the picture a paradoxical embolism alongside a lung clot.

Because the arch clot resisted heparin and threatened further strokes, surgeons removed it urgently under circulatory arrest. They pulled out a fresh cast thirty centimetres long, then cleared the lung arteries and closed the hole directly. Later testing pointed to protein C deficiency as an underlying driver. Six months on, scans showed no remaining clot and the patient stayed free of nerve complications on blood thinners.
pmc-13393842:
Emrah Aslan and Yıldırım Özüpak build a deep learning tool for cotton leaf disease in a 2026 study. Foliar disease and pest damage cut cotton yield and fiber quality, so fast, reliable, automated diagnosis matters for sustainable farming.

The hybrid model pairs a ResNet50 backbone with squeeze-and-excitation attention modules, trained on six disease classes with weighted loss and adaptive scheduling. It reached 99.72 percent training accuracy and 99.31 percent validation accuracy, converging by the fourteenth epoch. Heatmaps showed the model focusing on true symptom regions, aiding expert trust in field use.
pmc-13394342:
Gabriela Arenas and co-authors offer a 2026 first look at fat-carrying proteins in human breast milk. Milk from 22 healthy women was spun at very high speed to pull out these particles. The team measured their density, fat content, and marker proteins, and watched how they moved in a gel. The work asks whether milk carries the same kinds of particles that move fat through blood.

The particles matched the density of the lighter blood lipoproteins, but not the high-density kind. They held far less fat than whole milk and moved much like blood particles. The authors present this as early evidence that milk fat transport is wider than once thought.
pmc-13394642:
Saara Otonkoski and co-authors report, in 2026, a year of follow-up after sound-wave treatment for uterine fibroids. Fibroids are benign growths that cause heavy bleeding or a sense of pressure. Guided by magnetic scans, focused sound heats and kills fibroid tissue with no cuts. The study enrolled 163 women picked as fit for the treatment at one centre.

Women with bleeding and women with pressure both felt much better by three months. Gains held at twelve months, and quality of life scores rose in both groups. About three fifths of each fibroid lost its blood supply. The authors call the method a fast, knife-free relief when it works.
pmc-13395242:
Fabian Patauner and co-authors review, in 2026, trials of drugs for Gram-negative bacterial infections since 2000. These germs cause many grave hospital and community infections. The team gathered 68 trials in adults covering belly, lung, urinary, and blood infections. They read each trial's design, aims, and patient mix.

Belly and urinary infections drew the most trials. Most studies tested whether a new drug was no worse than standard care, and few aimed to prove better. New drugs featured often, yet resistant germs were rare in the patient pools. That gap weakens use of results in real wards. The authors call for more funding and rule changes to aid real-world trials.
pmc-13395342:
Belle Tamir Brahms and co-authors compare, in 2026, two blood pressure drug families for long-term cancer risk. Both families are widely used and guard heart and kidneys well. Records from Israel's largest health fund covered hundreds of thousands of adults who stayed on one family only. Follow-up ran from 2002 to 2024.

Overall cancer odds came out lower for the ACE inhibitor group than for the blocker group. The gap varied by cancer type, with lower odds for several common cancers. Leukaemia showed no real gap. Age at diagnosis and time to diagnosis also differed. The authors stress that records alone cannot prove cause. They call for forward studies and lab work.
pmc-13395442:
Kaoru Okano and colleagues scan, in 2026, the knee cushions of young rugby players for early wear signs. A cushion that slips outward, called extrusion, tracks with later knee arthritis. The team used ultrasound on 94 college rugby men with no past knee harm and 42 student controls. Both knees were checked lying, bent, and standing on one leg.

Rugby players showed more cushion slip in every pose. The gap held after body size was weighed in. No player had clear knee injury, so the shift looks like an early change from hard play. Ultrasound proved handy for checks under load. The authors urge longer studies and early guard steps for contact athletes.
pmc-13396342:
Kavya Raveendran and co-authors uncovered how a guardian protein reaches unsynapsed chromosomes during meiosis, the cell division that makes eggs and sperm. Their 2026 study focuses on HORMAD2, a checkpoint protein that flags chromosome sections that have failed to pair, and SYCP2, a scaffold protein of the chromosome axis.

Deleting a short binding motif in SYCP2 broke its grip on HORMAD2 and kept HORMAD2 off the axes, while the axes themselves still formed and pairing machinery stayed intact. Without that recruitment, the silencing of unpaired chromatin and the alarm signal to the cell weaken. The result clarifies a surveillance step that guards fertility and genome quality.
pmc-13396542:
Yiying Gao and co-authors rebuilt the radiation dose from a lab accident after the fact, using small dosimeter chips read minute by minute. Their 2026 study reconstructs an incident with a wavelength-dispersive X-ray fluorescence spectrometer, a machine that identifies elements in samples, where no personal dose records existed.

The team replayed the event: dosimeters were placed at seven spots matching head and hand positions, and the machine ran at its recorded settings of 40 kilovolts and 7 milliamps. Minute-level dose rates at each spot were combined with estimates of how long each body part stayed there. The method offers a template for the many accidents where nobody wore a meter.
pmc-13396642:
Madeleine Bloomfield and co-authors explored how people feel about taking low-dose lithium as a daily supplement, in a 2026 qualitative study. Lithium is a proven drug for mood disorders at full doses, and small doses have been sold as supplements for decades, yet research on the supplement form is nearly absent.

The team ran a focus group with people who had never taken it but worried about their own or a relative's mood, and a second study with current users. Conversations covered willingness, hopes, and worries. With hints that micro-doses might help mood and thinking at lower risk, the authors argue that user attitudes should shape the trials now being planned.
pmc-13397342:
Adam Yasgar and co-authors paired mass screening with computer learning to find chemical probes for an enzyme that manages the cell's inositol phosphate signals, in a 2026 study. The enzyme, ITPK1, keeps the balance among those signal molecules, and its pathway is tied to human disease.

First the team shrank the enzyme's test to plates with 1,536 wells and screened about 19,000 known and varied compounds. That haul of real results then trained a machine learning model to predict which further compounds would block the enzyme, raising the hit rate beyond blind screening. Good probes for ITPK1 would let biologists switch the pathway off cleanly and watch what happens.
pmc-13397742:
Esther Moraleda-Sepúlveda and others compare language skills in children with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome and Down syndrome in a 2026 study. Gene-based syndromes offer a frame for language limits, and syndrome patterns can steer help.

Forty children with each syndrome, matched for age and nonverbal ability and aged 6 to 16, took stock understanding and speaking language tests. The deletion group showed stronger listening vocabulary and syntax but weaker morphosyntax and practical use, with word stock rising with age. The Down syndrome group scored lower overall, chiefly in morphosyntax, with scant age gains. Teachers gain distinct patterns for fitted language support.
pmc-13399342:
Bianca Lopes Cunha and colleagues comment on a three-year comparison of pacemaker patients, in a 2026 editorial written in Portuguese. The study under discussion followed people who received pacemakers for one of two rhythm problems. Cunha's group argues the results point beyond the pacing wire itself to the health of the atria, the heart's upper chambers.

Serial ultrasound scans showed that sinus syndrome patients developed progressive enlargement of the left atrium and left ventricle plus worsening mitral valve leakage. Block patients stayed comparatively stable, even though their ventricles were paced more than 90 percent of the time. The editorial notes the study's limits: it was retrospective, single-center, and small, with no detailed data on lead position or atrial strain. Even so, the authors float the idea that sick sinus syndrome itself marks an underlying atrial muscle disease.
pmc-13399542:
Schwarzmüller and co-authors show, in 2026, that the kinase PAK1 drives resistance to two hormone therapies in estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer, but through different wiring. Up to 40 percent of late-stage patients resist endocrine therapy and relapse. Using MCF7 cell models made resistant to tamoxifen or to estrogen loss, the stand-in for aromatase inhibitors, they found PAK1 levels high and hyper-responsive to growth factors.

Blocking PAK1 cut proliferation in both resistant models, yet the mechanisms split. In tamoxifen-resistant cells, inhibition switched on the pro-death protein BAD and triggered apoptosis. In estrogen-deprived cells it suppressed growth-related kinases instead. Proteomic profiling mapped the substrate networks behind the split response. Earlier data found high PAK1 levels in 19 percent of premenopausal ER+ patients. The authors propose blocking PAK1 to outflank endocrine resistance in luminal breast cancer.
pmc-13400342:
Ethan P Rogers, Parker D Sperstad and Erik D Holmstrom study, in 2026, how two parts of the hepatitis C virus genome bind each other. One part, called 3 prime X, sits at the genome end and is needed for the virus to copy itself. It pairs with a second conserved part inside the coding region.

The team watched single molecules using a light-based method that reports when RNA parts come close. They measured binding strength across many conditions. The partner part bound the two shapes of the first 55 letters of 3 prime X unevenly, favoring one shape. That bias may help the virus switch between making proteins and copying its genome.
pmc-13400442:
Proczka, Zagzoog, and Haulon describe, in 2026, a move to stop endografts from being squeezed during endovascular repair of the aortic arch in chronic dissections. Retrograde branches can compress the graft's lumen in the tight true channel of a dissected arch, creating a pseudocoarctation that risks cardiac failure. Their example patient got an arch endograft with three branches, placed for an anastomotic false aneurysm with dissection reaching the supra-aortic trunks.

Preoperative imaging showed distal arch narrowing with a true lumen of 21 millimeters against a false lumen of 25 millimeters in the affected zones. After wiring the left subclavian artery, they performed kissing angioplasty, inflating balloons simultaneously in the endograft and the left common carotid branch. That branch carried a 9 by 75 millimeter bridging stent. The maneuver disrupted the dissection flap. By postoperative day three, imaging showed the true lumen expanded and the graft at its 28-millimeter nominal diameter.
pmc-13400542:
Yaojun Peng and team show, in 2026, that an enzyme called MMP8 helps sepsis pry open lung blood vessels. Sepsis can wreck the vessel lining, letting fluid leak into the lungs and other organs, a major driver of death. The enzyme was known to rise in sepsis, but its role at the barrier was unclear.

MMP8 rose in treated vessel cells and in lungs of septic mice. Raising or lowering it in cells changed how leaky the lining became under inflammatory attack. Blocking it in mice eased lung leakage, organ injury and death. Mechanistic work traced a chain: the enzyme activated a signaling protein, which freed cutting enzymes that destroyed a key cell-to-cell anchor. Patient blood levels also ran high, especially with chest fluid.
pmc-13401242:
Panhui Yu, Kang Liu, and Fang Chen describe a 2026 case of MOG antibody-associated disease, an immune attack on the nervous system, that looked like a brain infection in a teenager. The patient was a previously healthy 13-year-old boy with headache, fever, vomiting, and double vision.

His spinal fluid showed inflammation, and brain MRI scans revealed patchy lesions across the right temporal lobe, basal ganglia, and other areas that changed over time. Extensive microbe testing found nothing. Blood tests repeatedly showed MOG antibodies by a live cell-based assay, while aquaporin-4 and autoimmune encephalitis antibodies were negative. He improved during overlapping treatment that included intravenous immunoglobulin. The case warns that MOG disease can closely imitate central nervous system infection in children.
pmc-13401342:
Jean Jacques Nenba Sambo and colleagues report a 2026 cross-sectional study of tuberculosis lesions in cattle slaughtered for food in Ngaoundéré, Cameroon. Bovine tuberculosis can pass to people, and control measures in Cameroon are weak, raising the stakes for meat inspection.

Between April and October 2024, veterinary inspectors examined 1,256 slaughtered cattle at two slaughterhouses for tuberculosis-like lesions, and lesion samples were stained by the Ziehl-Neelsen method to look for acid-fast bacilli. A structured questionnaire gathered information on possible risk factors, and the team analysed links with lesion prevalence using logistic regression. The study gives an estimate of how common such lesions are in cattle entering the local food supply, and which animal or management factors travel with them.
pmc-13401542:
Dai Maruyama and co-authors report a 2026 Japan subgroup analysis of the phase III SUNMO trial in relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma. The trial tested subcutaneous mosunetuzumab, a T-cell-engaging bispecific antibody, plus polatuzumab vedotin, an antibody-drug conjugate, against a standard rituximab chemotherapy pairing.

In the full trial, 208 patients were randomized two to one, 138 to the new pairing and 70 to rituximab with gemcitabine and oxaliplatin. Sixteen patients came from Japan, nine on the new pairing and seven on the standard arm. Every Japanese patient on the new pairing responded, a 100 percent response rate, against about 57 percent on standard treatment. Progression-free survival was strongly prolonged as well. The authors frame the fixed-duration outpatient regimen as a new option that is easy to reach for this hard-to-treat lymphoma.
pmc-13401942:
Benster and team compare, in 2026, how quickly two approved treatments work in treatment-resistant depression, using UC San Diego Health records from 2017 to 2025. Adults received either repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, 279 patients, or intranasal esketamine, 93 patients. Response meant at least a 50 percent drop on the PHQ-9 depression scale, with weighting to balance the groups on age, trauma, anxiety, drug use, and baseline severity.

Esketamine acted faster: median time to response was 36 days against 49 days for magnetic stimulation, with a hazard ratio of 1.62 for response speed in the weighted model. Suicidal ideation improved faster too, at a median of 9 days versus 26 days for the stimulation group. Final response and remission rates also favored esketamine, 68.8 and 45.2 percent against 59.4 and 40.1 percent, converging by about 90 days. In the stimulation cohort, anxiety and benzodiazepine use predicted slower response.
pmc-13402442:
Farah Ismail leads a team that pooled every published case of neurobrucellosis, infection of the nervous system by Brucella bacteria, into one patient-level picture. Searching PubMed Central and Google Scholar through November 2025, they kept 23 articles covering 34 confirmed patients with brain involvement. Average age was 35.7 years, and about two in three patients were male.

Headache led the symptoms at 67.64 percent, ahead of fever and vomiting. Weakness, seizures, and hearing loss each appeared in roughly a quarter of patients. MRI was the favored scan, most often showing frontal lobe lesions, and blood antibody testing confirmed most diagnoses, while spinal fluid culture rarely grew the germ. Diagnosis took 8.83 months on average, a delay the authors blame on vague early signs. Most patients recovered on medicines alone; about a third also needed surgery. Brucella melitensis was the species named most often.
pmc-13402642:
Jones, Lilly, and Cole explore, in 2026, how Australian health promotion practitioners use theories of the policy process, the frameworks for understanding how policy gets made and changed. Influencing policy is a core professional function, yet engagement with the theory behind it was unstudied. They interviewed practitioners working in Queensland online, using semi-structured conversations analyzed by reflexive thematic analysis.

Ten practitioners took part, eight recruited purposively and two by snowball sampling, with a median of 18 years of industry experience spanning one to 24 years across the group. Four themes emerged. Practitioners grasp policy complexity but barely know the theories by name; they nonetheless apply the theories' constructs implicitly in daily work. Organizational context decides how far they can engage policy, and industry-level factors gate their involvement. A cited United States study echoes the gap, with 78 percent of students valuing policy action but 76 percent lacking understanding of the process.
pmc-13403642:
Tatiane Cristina da Silva and colleagues asked in 2026 how people without homes reach mental health care in a São Paulo state town. They spoke with 21 people living without housing in July 2024. Care runs through a local network of linked services.

People moved between care points when blocks in one place pushed them onward. A street outreach clinic stood out as a bridge that eased entry into care. Some felt welcomed, while others met bias that cut care short. Their hopes were plain: equal access for all. The authors urge warmer welcome, better training, and steadier support.
pmc-13404242:
Ravindra S Bohra and co-authors compared two ways in 2026 to find germs behind ventilator lung infections in intensive care. Their North Indian center enrolled 106 patients with the infection. One group got a rapid gene panel plus standard culture, while the other group got culture alone.

Patients tied to the rapid panel left intensive care sooner, with a median stay of nine days against thirteen for culture finds. Breathing tubes also came out within a week more often in the panel group. Death at 28 days ran lower with the panel, though not by a firm margin. Odd, test-negative panel patients fared worse than test-negative culture patients.
pmc-13404842:
Wonjeong Yoon and co-authors trace smoke-free rules and smoking behaviour in South Korea from 2005 to 2020, in a 2026 report. The country tightened bans over two decades, but links between wider bans and everyday behaviour were rarely tracked together. Five national survey waves supply the data.

The analysis covers 10,028 adults who smoked at least weekly. Restrictions in bars, restaurants and workplaces grew sharply across the period. Seeing smoking in those venues fell from very high levels to between 5.8 and 12.4 percent in the reported figures, while support for bans climbed. Voluntary smoke-free homes and quit motivation were tracked alongside, using weighted models that account for repeat respondents.
pmc-13405342:
Yingcui Li and colleagues delete a cartilage gene in mice to learn what keeps joints healthy, reporting in 2026. Hyaluronan, a slippery matrix sugar, fills cartilage and joint fluid. The enzyme Has2 makes most of it in skeletal tissue, but its adult role was undefined.

Twenty male mice carried a switchable Has2 deletion in cartilage cells, triggered by tamoxifen at three weeks of age. Within a week, hyaluronan had nearly vanished from joint cartilage and growth plates, confirmed by specific staining. Later tissue checks trace how cartilage and joints cope without their main lubricant and scaffold. The model isolates adult maintenance roles that embryo studies could not separate.
pmc-13406942:
Dong Hoon Suh and Dong Soo Han, in a 2026 perspective piece, consider how researchers should use generative artificial intelligence when writing scholarly papers. Surveys show many academics already lean on such tools for drafting help and error checking, yet rules for proper use remain unsettled.

Submission records from large journal groups show far fewer authors declaring AI help than survey figures would predict. That gap suggests confusion about what must be reported, or quiet underreporting. Views also differ on AI help with drafting itself and with peer review. The authors argue for shared, explicit disclosure rules so readers can trust how a paper was produced and judge the work fairly.
pmc-13408342:
Ritchel Gannaban and colleagues report in 2026 that fatty sugar-coated lipids act as organisers of a key membrane supply route. The cancer protein KRAS must sit in the cell's outer membrane to signal, and that seat depends on a lipid called phosphatidylserine delivered to the membrane's inner face. Two transport proteins ferry it there from the endoplasmic reticulum at contact points between the organelles.

High-resolution imaging showed that blocking production of certain glycosphingolipids scattered the transport proteins, displaced a kinase needed to prime the exchange, and cut membrane phosphatidylserine sharply. Other machinery stationed at the same contact sites, including calcium channels, also failed. The findings recast these lipids as structural organisers of membrane contact sites and suggest a fresh angle on controlling KRAS in cancer.
pmc-13409042:
Erika Maharani and co-authors pool the published trials in 2026 on whether a standard heart tracing can separate a dangerous inherited heart muscle disease from a benign rhythm nuisance. Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy can kill suddenly, while outflow tract arrhythmias with a similar tracing pattern are usually harmless, and advanced imaging is not available everywhere. Ten studies covering over seven hundred patients were combined.

Inverted T waves across the right chest leads were the most studied sign, catching just over half of true cases while rarely appearing in the benign condition. The rare epsilon wave almost never appeared in benign cases but missed most disease. Measures of signal width across the chest leads performed strongly, one ratio approaching excellent discrimination. The authors offer the pooled figures to help clinicians decide who needs referral for definitive imaging.
pmc-13411842:
Merve Tok and colleagues measured egg output and hatch success for Caucasian pheasants raised away from their wild habitat in Turkiye in 2026. The subspecies matters for both wild conservation and game farming, yet breeders need hard numbers on how it performs in pens.

Forty hens and four cocks in open pens laid about 91 eggs per hen over 140 days, with fertility at 90 percent and overall hatchability near 66 percent in this pen trial. The paper backs pen-raised Caucasian pheasants as a workable breeding option, giving farms a baseline for feed, housing, and hatch planning.
pmc-13412142:
Ghyslaine Giselle Ramírez and colleagues review in 2026 how heat stress damages cattle eggs and early embryos down to the molecular level. Hot seasons already cut fertility on farms, and warming climates widen the risk. The review gathers studies done in living animals and in laboratory dishes, tracing effects from the ovary through fertilization to the first days of embryonic life.

Heat disrupts follicle growth and hormone output in the ovary, leaving eggs in a poorer setting. Inside eggs it stirs oxidative stress, strains mitochondria, tangles the division spindle, and leaves lasting epigenetic marks. Embryos then cleave and implant less reliably, and effects may reach offspring. The authors map these weak points as targets for protective interventions.
pmc-13412542:
Matiullah Alimzai and colleagues run a 2026 case-control study of scabies risk among dermatology patients in Kabul province, Afghanistan. Scabies, a contagious mite infestation, burdens poor communities heavily, and Afghan data on its drivers were scarce. Clinics enrolled 410 participants between March 2024 and May 2025: 210 confirmed cases and 200 controls, compared on housing, hygiene, and sharing habits.

Bathing only two or three times a week carried the strongest link, with odds over twenty times those of frequent bathers in adjusted models. Sharing blankets or clothes, weaker personal hygiene, and living in a mud house each raised risk several-fold. Brick housing, employment, female sex, and older age appeared protective. The authors urge control programs that pair treatment with better water and housing.
pmc-13412642:

pmc-13418142:

pmc-13418842:

pmc-13419442:

pmc-13433842:

pmc-13433942:

pmc-13437242:

pmc-13437442:

pmc-13438142:

pmc-13439242:
Che and colleagues trace how sleep quality, psychological distress, and thinking ability influence one another over time in rural older adults, in 2026 aging research from China. The team followed 2,196 rural residents across 4 years and applied cross-lagged panel network analysis, a method that maps which symptoms predict which later symptoms. Untangling that web matters because the three problems usually arrive together and reinforce each other in later life, especially where healthcare is scarce.

Subjective sleep quality, how rested people felt their sleep was, emerged as the most influential predictor node in both time intervals studied. Cognitive components proved the most vulnerable targets, especially orientation, attention and calculation, and language. Networks for men and women stayed moderately similar in structure across the periods. Che argues that improving perceived sleep quality is the most central, modifiable lever available, with potential knock-on benefits for both mood and cognition in rural aging programs.
pmc-13439442:
Qiaodong Li and a large team tackle a battery bottleneck: solid electrolytes that break down against high-voltage electrodes, reporting a fluorine-rich fix in 2026. All-solid-state lithium batteries promise more stored energy, yet their solid electrolytes oxidise at the voltages rich cathodes need. Adding fluorine should help, but older routes added too little and hurt ion flow. The team swapped anions in a precursor to make core-shell particles rich in lithium fluoride.

Those precursors yielded halide and sulfide electrolytes loaded with fluorine while keeping ions moving well. At the cathode, a sturdy fluoride-rich skin formed and limited further decay. A test cell with a lithium-rich oxide cathode kept over three quarters of its capacity after two thousand fast cycles at a five-volt cutoff. The authors offer the exchange route as a general platform for fluorinated battery materials.
pmc-13439642:
Mauricio Benetti and colleagues present a stroke case where an eye-movement syndrome pointed to hidden brainstem ischemia, reporting in 2026. Parinaud's syndrome paralyses upward gaze and brings a set of eyelid and pupil signs. Tumours near the pineal gland cause most cases, while stroke accounts for roughly a quarter. A 66-year-old man arrived with sudden double vision on vertical gaze, slurred speech, and unsteady walking.

Examination showed the full classic pattern of the syndrome. Brain scans and vessel imaging, though, showed no fresh lesion or blockage. Treating the picture as a likely back-of-brain stroke, the team gave clot-busting medicine within three and a half hours of onset. Recovery was complete within a day, and later scans confirmed no lasting damage. The authors urge clinicians to trust the eye signs when imaging stays silent.
pmc-13439742:
Arora and colleagues built new porous crystals in 2026 by copying a pattern found in proteins. The crystals, called covalent organic frameworks, are ordered networks of small carbon-based units with many tiny holes. This team added amide side chains, which form hydrogen bonds like those in protein beta sheets, forcing the layers to stack in opposite directions.

Their two materials, named aCOFamide-1 and aCOFamide-2, trapped large amounts of iodine from vapour. They also pulled iodide, a charged form of iodine, out of water, which is a hard task in molecular capture. Computer maps showed positive electric patches near the amide groups that attract the negative iodide ions. pmc-13441042:
Sharare Rahnama and Nazem Ghasemi combine human fat-derived stem cells with a pineapple enzyme to repair myelin in a mouse model of multiple sclerosis, reporting in 2026. The disease strips the fatty insulation from nerve fibres, slowing signals and movement. Mice with induced disease were split into untreated, enzyme-only, stem-cell-only, and combined groups, beside healthy controls. Behaviour tests graded motor recovery, tissue stains counted myelin-making cell markers, and blood tests measured immune signals.

Treated groups all beat untreated disease on myelin density and on counts of cells bearing Olig2 and Mog, two myelin-lineage markers. Calming signals IL-10 and TGF-beta ran higher, while inflammatory IL-17, interferon gamma, and antibody IgG ran lower in treated blood. Balance and motor function improved alongside the tissue gains. The authors present the pairing as a candidate step toward regenerative care for demyelinating disease.
pmc-13442042:
Claire S. Goul's team identified LASER in 2026, a protein assembly that couples lysosome damage sensing to repair. Lysosome membrane breaks threaten cell survival, and ESCRT machinery patches them, yet how ESCRT-I recognizes damaged lysosomes was unclear. Genome-wide CRISPR interference screens in damage-sensitive cells found LASER, centered on TFG, which moves to damaged lysosomes upon calcium release by binding ATG8 proteins on lysosomal lipids.

Cell biologists get a complete sensing-to-repair circuit with a neurodegeneration link. The work reframes faulty lysosome repair as a driver of TFG-linked disease.
pmc-13442442:
Holly Aitken and colleagues survey bone and joint patients about phone-based motion capture in a 2026 study at a rural referral center. The tool, OpenCap, reads 3D joint motion from videos shot on two iOS devices. Three groups took part, with 200 child patients, 200 sports patients, and 200 joint replacement patients in the pool.

Each person filled a survey on access to a computer, the internet, and Apple devices, plus comfort with a home motion test. Shares with the needed gear ran from 65.5 percent to 83.5 percent across the groups. Home place, town or country, did not shift access in a clear way. The team reads the rates as a green light for remote motion checks, which could spare long trips. Gaps in gear still bar a sizable share of patients.
pmc-13442542:
Xuelian Wang and colleagues review how smart computer models merge life exposure and gene-scale data to find liver cancer marks in a 2026 paper. Liver cancer kills many people worldwide, and the cell type called HCC leads the count. Known drivers span virus liver illness, drink-linked liver harm, and fat-linked liver disease, each shaped by life exposures.

The review weighs mark hunts that join exposure records with gene, protein, and fuel data, plus maps of where cells sit in tissue. Clear models that show their logic get praise for early catch, outlook sorting, and care choice. Gaps get blunt talk: exposure records stay thin, data tools vary, most work looks back, and few models face outside tests. New layers such as single-cell reads may sharpen marks, the authors say, if checks grow stricter.
pmc-13442642:
Wenjing Wu and colleagues track United States lung illness deaths across 1999 to 2024 in a 2026 study. Death records came from the CDC WONDER system, with rates checked by sex, age, race, and region. Raw death counts rose from 227,985 in the first year to 263,209 in the last, a gain of 15.5 percent across the span.

Age-adjusted rates told the twin tale, since they fell from 129.37 deaths per 100,000 people to a mark of 91.70 per 100,000 by 2024. Men carried higher rates than women, though male rates fell faster. The West cut rates most, while the South logged the largest rise in raw counts. Older adults bore the heaviest load, and adults aged 25 to 34 years saw a slight rate rise. The authors urge plans aimed at those groups.
pmc-13443042:
Todo Bom Luís and colleagues grade infection risk in hospital adults across Portugal in a 2026 study. Germs caught in care raise harm, cost, and stay length, yet risk checks stay loose in many wards. Their team scored 1,092 adults in wards across local health units during 2025 with a structured scale called RAC.

The scale weighs body-born risks, such as age and illness, beside care-born risks, such as tubes and wounds. Percentile splits put 53.6 percent of adults in the mid risk band. A high band held 11.4 percent of adults in the same count. Curve tests helped set the split marks. The authors say a shared scale can steer wards to guard the highest-risk beds first, a step many sites still skip in daily care.
pmc-13443542:
Yuchen Yang and colleagues spin layered fiber mats that guard lungs while they spare plastic in a 2026 paper. Throwaway filter media strain to catch the finest dust, and their waste piles up in landfills. Their multi-level splitting spin method weaves three fiber scales, from ultrafine threads to submicron strands, in one mat.

The woven maze traps dust through twisty paths while air slips through open channels. Mats held top-grade capture of PM0.3 dust, the hardest size class, with low breath drag in their tests. Polymer use fell by 99 percent next to market N95 masks in their count. The fibers also break down after use, unlike standard mask plastics. The authors pitch the mats for masks and vents that must protect without waste.
pmc-13443842:
Minoru Terashima and colleagues identify a 2026 mechanism by which the transcription factor C/EBPγ pushes lung adenocarcinoma cells toward a mobile, invasive state while also boosting DNA repair. The team mapped broad histone marks tied to cell identity, then tested the factor by adding it, silencing it, and tracing its protein partners.

Adding C/EBPγ produced mesenchymal shapes and gene patterns, while silencing it blunted the transition. Its leucine zipper domain, not its DNA-binding domain, proved essential, and partners included C/EBPβ plus the repair factors XRCC5 and XRCC6. By blocking a suppressive partner and recruiting repair proteins to breaks, the factor may foster drug resistance, a link worth pursuing for therapy.
pmc-13444142:
Zhe Xian Koong and colleagues gain clean control of quantum-dot spins while keeping their light links pure in a 2026 paper. Dot spins can hold quantum data and spit single photons, a dream pair for quantum nets. The snag: spin control and one-shot reads once fought each other in the same dot.

A light-hole mix trick builds a lopsided ladder in a charged dot, which splits the two jobs. Stark shift fixes and nuclear spin cooling set the stage. A flip pulse hit a contrast mark of 97.4 percent, while light loops kept a cyclicity mark of 471 in the runs. Both GaAs and InGaAs dots took the scheme. The authors show the setup can pair with a nuclear memory for repeater nodes.
pmc-13444242:
Zhuo-Yu Ren and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of whether constipation raises depression risk in the general population, a gut-brain question with mixed prior evidence. The team pooled 18 observational studies covering 730,263 participants, using random-effects models with heterogeneity, subgroup, sensitivity, and bias checks.

Constipation linked to more than double the odds of depression, an association that survived sensitivity checks despite high heterogeneity. Stronger links appeared in adolescents, in Asian and North American studies, in smaller studies, and where depression was self-reported. The authors call for joined gut and mental health care plus prospective studies of the gut-brain pathway.
pmc-13446042:
Codey E. Dueck and colleagues set out a method to grade how well a solids-based extraction pulls viral material from wastewater, in a 2026 paper for surveillance labs. Wastewater tracking of disease leans on extraction, yet each lab needs a yardstick for its own losses. A cattle coronavirus, spiked into samples on purpose, serves as the stand-in.

Heat-based release measured the starting stock more truly than a machine method. The team also found the cattle virus already present in wastewater at low levels, a background any grade must subtract. Sixteen hours of soaking gave the best recovery in their runs. A paired test that reads the cattle virus and a pepper virus at once matched the single tests, which saves time in routine checks.
pmc-13446342:
Hongtu Cui and colleagues build a platform that forecasts cancer drug response from which genes a tumor cannot live without, in a 2026 study. Matching drugs to tumors is the heart of precision oncology, yet standard molecular reads predict response unevenly. Their system, DrGee, reads gene activity and infers sensitivity through gene essentiality instead.

The built-in model weds gene activity, gene essentiality, drug-protein grip, and drug-gene links to call the dose that halves cell growth. It beat fresh rival methods on held-out cell lines. Four drugs flagged for one lung cancer line were tested in dishes and mouse grafts, and two held up, with a like check in ovarian cells. Patient groups split by its calls also split in survival.
pmc-13447342:
M K Yildirak and M T Demırpolat compare a 2026 retrospective study of laser closure versus crystallized phenol for pilonidal sinus disease in young adults. The team analyzed 230 patients treated at a tertiary center from 2023 to 2024, tracking satisfaction, quality of life, symptoms, pain, and return to work at one week and one month.

At one week, laser patients reported less itching, burning, discharge, and pain, with higher physical, social, and pain quality-of-life scores and faster return to daily activities. By one month most outcomes converged, though discharge stayed higher after phenol. Complications ran low and similar in both groups, supporting laser closure for early recovery.
pmc-13447742:
An, Lee, and Kim published a 2026 study on how young children judge their own eating. Most past work asked parents, not children, about daily food habits. The team surveyed 243 preschoolers and their parents at daycare centers in Cheonan. Both sides filled out the same healthy eating practice questionnaire.

Children rated their eating habits higher than their parents rated them. The gap ran wider for nutrition than for hygiene habits like hand washing. Hygiene ratings matched more closely between children and parents across the board. Boys showed a bigger gap with parents than girls did in scores. The authors say diet checks should ask both children and parents. Daycare meal programs could use both views to plan better lessons.
pmc-13448042:
Nazar and colleagues used Sweden's nationwide spine registry in 2026 to compare long-term reoperation risk after two neck operations for worn discs. One, fusion, welds vertebrae together; the other, disc replacement, preserves motion. Fusion may shift load onto neighboring levels and wear them out, a problem called adjacent segment disease. Earlier trials disagreed on whether implants prevent it.

The analysis covered 9,338 patients, most fused and a few hundred with disc replacements, followed for up to about nineteen years. About one in ten patients needed another operation at a neighboring level by ten years, with 509 such reoperations in all. After adjustment, disc replacement carried a lower risk, but the gap vanished in a matched comparison. Younger patients and single-level surgery carried higher risk, and the authors counsel caution in claiming a protective effect.
pmc-13448642:
Samuel Wright and a large team profile blood proteins and immune cells across melanoma treatment to explain immunotherapy resistance in 2026 work. Many patients gain no lasting benefit from checkpoint blockade, and blood markers that flag early resistance could spare toxicity and redirect care sooner. Serial sampling during treatment, rarely combined with matched tumour tissue at scale, was the study's distinctive asset.

Over twenty-nine hundred plasma proteins and deep immune cell profiling tracked two hundred fifty patients with metastatic melanoma, alongside ninety-two matched tumours. Proteins rising after treatment in responders tied to effector immune activation, while non-responder proteins traced to suppressive myeloid cells and tumour cells themselves. Proteins linked to side effects in responders appeared to come from damaged healthy tissue. The dataset maps how tumours and the wider immune system interact under therapy.
pmc-13449042:
Yuk Kam Yau and colleagues study in 2026 whether the pandemic-era breakup of regular primary care harmed Hong Kong patients with diabetes. Their cohort held 123,403 adults whose continuity was scored by how consistently they saw their usual clinic before the outbreak, from 2017 to 2019, and during it, from 2020 to 2022. Outcomes were then followed from June 2022 to June 2024.

Patients whose continuity score fell by twenty to thirty percent faced a 33 percent higher risk of cardiovascular disease than those whose score fell least. The largest drops carried similar excess risk, and the same pattern showed for coronary disease and heart failure separately. Kidney failure risk also rose once continuity fell by more than a fifth. The authors urge health systems to build contingency plans that keep chronic care continuous through future public health crises.
pmc-13449342:
Pasko and colleagues compared in 2026 how exactly knee replacement surgery hits its planned plastic insert thickness.  They reviewed 815 patients of one surgeon treated between 2018 and 2022. About half had robotic help and half had the standard method, with a nine-millimetre insert planned for all.

About 72 in 100 robotic patients got exactly the planned thickness, against only 16 in 100 standard patients. Spread around the target was also much smaller with robotic help. The authors say robotic tools execute the plan more faithfully and balance knee gaps more evenly.
pmc-13450542:
Varalika Jain and colleagues tested whether ravens follow weekday-weekend routines or react to daily visitor changes in 2026, using GPS data from a wildlife park. Human rhythms create cycles of opportunity and disturbance for wildlife, and the weekend effect hypothesis predicts animals anticipate weekday-weekend patterns. Raven foraging probability and space use tracked day-to-day visitor changes more closely than the calendar pattern. The findings suggest ravens read actual human presence, not the weekday label. pmc-13452142:

One test was validated backward in time, not forward as rules require. Only 36 of 100 babies were rechecked, and half had surgery between checks. pmc-13453742:
Jaime A Teixeira da Silva writes a letter urging journals to face how generative AI is slipping into peer review and editing. His 2026 letter notes that some editors still dismiss AI's role, while AI written work already circulates and risks being cited as if human checked. Cheap AI review could ease the reviewer shortage, he allows, but its biases must be weighed first. The deeper crack, he argues, is hidden use: authors quietly polish with AI and reviewers cannot spot it, a failure already surfacing in post publication retractions. pmc-13453842:
Mahmoud Alshneikat and others told of a one-surgeon scope harvest of the small leg vein in 2026, with a retractor to hold the leg up. pmc-13454142:

pmc-13454342:

The authors offer the method as a green route to better aqueous batteries.
pmc-13455042:

The authors propose the gene pair as a diagnostic signature worth testing in clinics.
pmc-13455342:

pmc-13457042:

Its hit rate climbed steeply with certainty, from none in unlikely cases to about 73 percent in definite ones. Overall sensitivity was modest, near 41 percent, while every positive call was correct. pmc-13457742:
Noura Bin Hussain and colleagues check the teeth and brushing habits of preschool children attending dental clinics in Dubai. pmc-13458042:

pmc-13458242:

pmc-13458342:
Qianmei Wang and colleagues track the price bacteria pay for polymyxin resistance in a 2026 study. pmc-13458442:

Yields rose by 3.44 to 18.21 percent, field preparation costs fell by 62.15 percent, and net profit rose by 13.91 to 31.62 percent, with amino acids and phenolics up in grain. pmc-13458642:

Short dye strands were built from those spans, in two grades of build.

The probes caught real swaps: one whole swap line in rape seed, and a bit of one chromosome tucked in a mate in a six set cross. Breeders can now watch swaps plant by plant, the team says. pmc-13458742: Abad Alzuman and colleagues correct their article on the organizational health behavior index, an instrument for measuring organizational health. It also repairs author affiliations. Zaiba Ali and Lina Ibrahim Bakadam sit in the university's Department of Management in Riyadh, and Rahila Ali in the Faculty of Management at Jagran Lakecity University in Bhopal, India. The original article has been updated.
pmc-13458842:

During microsurgery, ultrasound helped locate fragments that had migrated inside the membrane, and these were removed. A tear in the membrane front was sealed with an absorbable collagen pad, not stitches. At seven weeks and at 18 months, she was pain-free, with no new nerve problems and no spinal fluid leak. The authors suggest ultrasound guidance and collagen repair as useful options.
pmc-13459242:

pmc-13459342:

The index ran far higher in patients, with a median of 3.31 versus 0.91, and discriminated modestly with an area under the curve of 0.754 and a best cut-off of 3.785. pmc-13459442:
