The authors offer the buckyball case as a guide to designing odd magnetic textures in other curved 3D tiny-magnet systems. Readers get a full heat tour of a curved spin lattice.
pmc-13551542:
Gilberto Sánchez-González, Luz del C Hernández-Hernández and Elaine Gallagher published this 2026 systematic review of what dengue fever costs Mexico. Dengue, a mosquito-borne viral disease, is entrenched in Mexico and strains public budgets through treatment, prevention and lost productivity. In the first review of its kind for the country, the authors gathered cost studies from 2010 to 2020, in English and Spanish, including ministry reports and grey literature.

Seven articles met the inclusion criteria, all reporting national costs and three focusing on particular states. The burden peaked in 2013, when annual costs reached 176.82 million dollars as reported, or 281.60 million in present value. Studies counted direct care, prevention and surveillance spending plus indirect losses such as missed work. The authors warn that methods differed so much between studies that comparisons are shaky. They conclude dengue's economic burden in Mexico is high and swells further in outbreak years.
pmc-13551942:
A 2026 study by Daniel Egger and five colleagues followed a drug switch in a serious eye disease. The disease is wet age-related macular degeneration. Some eyes stay active despite standard injections. Clinics switched 43 eyes from 38 patients to a newer drug, faricimab. All had failed to stretch visit gaps beyond eight weeks on older drugs. The team tracked vision, retinal thickness, and fluid for up to two years.

Vision held steady through follow-up, with no firm change at any visit. Retinal thickness fell and stayed lower. A pigment layer swelling also shrank over time. Fluid under the retina dropped at every check. The share of dry maculas rose from zero to about a quarter. Visit gaps lengthened from under six weeks before the switch.
pmc-13555642:
Young-Min Kim and three colleagues watch a memory switch change at the nanoscale after its first firing in a 2026 study. These threshold switches select cells in dense three-dimensional memory stacks. What physically changes during first firing has stayed murky. A sharp microscope tip applied voltage to tiny targeted spots, confining the action.

After local switching, electron microscopy revealed tiny crystals forming where the top contact meets the switching layer. That crystal growth thinned the glassy layer, easing later switching. The voltage needed for repeat firing dropped well below the first-firing level. The authors show the crystal-glass boundary carries the local current, clarifying a mechanism long argued from indirect evidence alone.
pmc-13556042:
Yuchen Cui and six colleagues built in 2026 a deep learning system that reads pathology images to diagnose oral squamous cell carcinoma, a common mouth cancer. Diagnosis today leans on a pathologist's eye, which takes time and varies between observers. Their network, PGMA-Net, was designed to work across microscope magnifications, to cope with images from different hospitals, and to explain its decisions.

Guide maps drawn from pathology knowledge steer the model's attention to the tissue features that matter. Extra modules align features across magnifications, rebalance rare classes during training, and adapt the model to new centres. On an internal test set the system scored high on both discrimination and accuracy, and it held up well on an outside set after adaptation. Visualisations show which regions drove each call, a step toward tools clinicians can trust.
pmc-13556342:
Yuwei He and eight colleagues track the ECSA-MAL lineage of chikungunya virus in the 2025 Guangdong outbreak. Guangdong reported over 20,000 cases by November 2025, the largest outbreak in the region's history. The strain carries the E1-A226V envelope change, known for boosting replication in Aedes albopictus, the dominant local vector. Their 2026 letter follows viral kinetics in human hosts at high resolution.

The lineage replicates robustly and clears rapidly. Peak venous viremia arrives on day 1 of symptoms. Older age links to higher peak viral loads. Capillary blood monitoring shows clearance by day 6. The findings fill a gap in human-host kinetics for this lineage, whose vector competence was already well documented.
pmc-13558542:
Lana Salloum and nine colleagues widened in 2026 the picture of dissecting cellulitis of the scalp, a scarring inflammatory disease usually described as a condition of young Black men. Their retrospective cohort covered 29 patients across a large Boston-area health network over ten years. A parallel scoping review gathered seventeen published cohorts holding 710 patients. Records supplied background details and histories of metabolic, psychiatric, and autoimmune conditions, plus smoking.

The local group was mostly male with an average age in the mid thirties, yet racially mixed. Nearly half had another disease from the same follicle-blocking family, over eight in ten carried a metabolic condition, and about four in ten had a psychiatric diagnosis. Published cohorts agreed on male predominance and metabolic company while under-reporting mental health. The authors argue the disease is global and tied to metabolism, not confined to one population.
pmc-13559342:
Stasiak and colleagues review what happened when patients taking oral or targeted drugs for blood cancers underwent major lung surgery, in a 2026 retrospective case series. Anatomical lung resection, removing a lobe or more, is standard for early lung cancer but carries a bleeding risk. Blood cancer patients face extra danger because both their disease and their medicines disturb clotting. The series examines postoperative hemorrhagic complications in this small, specific group treated at one center.

Median operative blood loss was 100 milliliters, yet median drainage on the first postoperative day reached 1,040 milliliters, signaling substantial bleeding after surgery in these patients. The authors describe the incidence of hemorrhagic complications as unexpectedly high for lung resection. Notably, the two patients who had stopped oral chemotherapy before surgery did not bleed afterward. Stasiak stresses causality cannot be proven from so few cases, and urges multidisciplinary planning plus larger studies of perioperative drug management.
pmc-13560042:
Rahmadi Budiman and colleagues surveyed members of an Indonesian hydrogen and fuel cell association on how energy knowledge links to saving behaviour. The study asked whether personal values and attitudes carry part of that link.

Data came from 195 members, split into three kinds of saving: cutting use, buying efficient gear, and acts that help others save. Energy literacy predicted saving behaviour directly and also through values and attitudes, with a strong total effect in the model. The indirect routes worked better for cutting use and helping others than for efficiency buying, which costs money upfront. Budiman suggests literacy campaigns should build values and attitudes, while efficiency gains may need price or policy help too.
pmc-13560142:
Haixia Wang and three colleagues review neutrophil extracellular traps in diseases of the central nervous system. Their 2026 article explains these web-like structures of DNA, histones, and antimicrobial proteins that neutrophils cast out to snare pathogens. Helpful in infection, the traps turn harmful when they form excessively or clear too slowly inside the brain.

The review covers how neutrophils cross the blood-brain barrier, what triggers trap release there. The webs then contribute to stroke, traumatic brain injury, bleeding around the brain, Alzheimer's disease, and multiple sclerosis. Oxidative stress and inflammatory mediators feature among the triggers discussed. Emerging treatments aim either to stop traps forming or to dissolve them faster, and the authors survey that neuroprotective pipeline. They frame the synthesis as a guide for researchers hunting new targets in neurological disorders.
pmc-13560242:
Huaxing Zhao and colleagues identify interleukin 17D as a follicular fluid protein that helps eggs acquire developmental competence during maturation. Their 2026 study begins with proteomic comparison of pig follicular fluid, then tests the protein across roughly twenty thousand pig and mouse oocytes and over thirteen thousand embryos. Failed maturation underlies much subfertility in animals and humans.

IL17D rose sharply in follicular fluid as maturation proceeded. Adding it strengthened the two-way communication between egg and surrounding cumulus cells by raising the junction protein CX43 and the projections linking them. Treated eggs kept better redox balance and tighter synchrony between nucleus and cytoplasm. Embryos from treated eggs developed better in dishes and to full term in animals, aided by shifts in fat metabolism and histone marks. The protein works through the receptor CD93, and relatives IL17A and IL17F helped as well.
pmc-13560342:
Yulu Qiu and colleagues build a mouse model of how autoimmunity against TRIM21, the target of anti-Ro52 antibodies, can seed interstitial lung disease. Their 2026 in vivo study immunizes mice with the full protein, then challenges them with a viral mimic to imitate infection triggers. Anti-Ro52 antibodies are the commonest marker tied to lung involvement across connective tissue diseases.

Immunized mice produced systemic autoantibodies and activated B cells, with inflammation that oddly concentrated in the lungs and IgG deposited there. The viral mimic then sharply worsened matters, drawing in CD8 T cells and myeloid cells and switching on chemokine pathways. Gene sequencing flagged Ccl6 as a top-rising gene, and its protein was confirmed in the inflamed tissue. The authors conclude TRIM21 autoimmunity primes the lung for CD8-driven inflammation, offering targets for anti-Ro52 positive disease.
pmc-13560542:
Sham Mohamad Farouq Alkhateeb and colleagues test whether a carbon dioxide laser boosts fluoride uptake into tooth enamel beyond varnish alone. Their 2026 in vitro split-tooth study uses six human upper premolars extracted for orthodontic reasons, each crown halved so one side serves as its own control. Every specimen received five percent sodium fluoride varnish; experimental halves then got fifteen seconds of one-watt laser light.

Under the electron microscope, varnish-only enamel kept its etched, microporous look. Laser-treated enamel melted and fused into a smoother, recrystallized surface. Elemental analysis showed significantly more fluoride locked into the laser side, with the paired comparison favoring the combined treatment. The authors read the laser as a genuine adjunct that drives fluoride deeper into enamel structure. The work is bench science on extracted teeth, a proof of mechanism ahead of any clinical testing.
pmc-13560742:
Stephen P. Becker, Alison E. Pritchard, and Jessica R. Lunsford-Avery review behavioral sleep treatment for children and teenagers with ADHD, a group where sleep problems may reach seventy percent yet long went untreated. Their 2026 review organizes recent findings by developmental stage, from early childhood through adolescence. Sleep is framed as a twenty-four-hour dimension of a disorder usually treated as a daytime problem.

Across age bands, behavioral sleep interventions proved feasible and improved parent- and self-reported sleep in the studies surveyed. Evidence on weaving sleep strategies into standard ADHD behavioral care remains thin, and the authors map both the opportunities and the friction there. They call for treatments tailored to development and to mechanism, with new attention to circadian rhythm and sleep regularity. Digital and integrated care delivery could widen reach for families.
pmc-13562342:
ABDULZAHRA Hussain and four colleagues look back at what happened over many years to patients who received a one-anastomosis gastric bypass with a fixed 250 cm bypassed limb. Several centres took part in the 2026 review of records. Of 892 bypass operations done between 2010 and 2020, 97 used the long limb. Full follow-up, averaging eleven years, was available for 78 of those patients.

Nearly one in four of the followed patients, 19 people, developed severe problems that forced another operation. The causes included protein malnutrition, stubborn bile or acid reflux, severe diarrhoea, liver failure, and a twisted join between stomach and bowel. Revisions converted the bypass to a sleeve, to a different bypass layout, or back to normal anatomy. The authors warn against routinely choosing such a long limb.
pmc-13562542:
Sohag Ahmed and seventeen colleagues search, entirely by computer, for new blockers of a DNA-repair enzyme that ovarian and prostate cancers depend on. Approved drugs against PARP-1 exist, but resistance and side effects push the search for fresh chemical shapes. The 2026 team started from emodin, a plant pigment, and screened its anthraquinone relatives. Prediction tools first judged likely activity, drug-likeness, and safety traits. Survivors were docked into the enzyme's active pocket in a molecular model.

The most stable pairings went through 500-nanosecond simulations that tracked how the complex flexed and held together. One compound, catalogued as CID-10425624, bound steadily, kept the complex compact, and held its hydrogen bonds throughout. Its predicted behaviour matched or beat the reference drug. The authors offer the anthraquinone frame as a starting scaffold. Bench experiments must now test whether the computer's promise survives contact with real cells.
pmc-13563742:
Wei Li and five colleagues document how a flesh-destroying infection travelled from a chest drain site down to a man's back and killed him. Necrotising fasciitis usually starts at a wound; spread along tissue planes from chest to pelvis is rare. The patient, 61, had alcoholic cirrhosis and a smoking and drinking history. A drain placed for infected fluid around his lung drew off foul pus, yet the infection kept moving under his skin.

Serial scans, surgical exploration, and microbe cultures let the team trace the route through the loose tissue layers, a fascial highway from thorax to lumbosacral region. Despite care the case proved fatal. The authors publish the chain because this path is so poorly documented that diagnosis often comes late. Their warning is aimed at clinicians caring for immune-weakened patients with chest drains: watch the skin far from the tube, not only at it.
pmc-13563842:
Sisi Tao and Gustavo Carlo interview university students about doing good online, a behaviour research has mostly borrowed offline labels for. Likes and shares are the visible tip; the study wanted the fuller repertoire, the motives, and the emotional cost. Their 2026 team ran in-depth group interviews with twenty students picked for demographic variety, then read the transcripts through a theory-guided thematic lens.

Five kinds of online kindness emerged: emotional social support, practical instrumental help, online donations, stepping in against cyberbullying, and digital allyship. That last one, the siding with vulnerable groups, has no offline twin. Students explained their acts by values, empathy, morals, and duty, never by pressure or hunger for applause. Helping lifted mood yet also brought backlash and silence. The team names the sustaining skill digital prosocial resilience: continuing to help, fed by the private satisfaction of acting on one's values when no thanks arrive.
pmc-13563942:
Shengwei Du and colleagues test, in a 2026 laboratory study, whether blocking an enzyme called TrxR1 makes liver cancer cells more sensitive to the drug motesanib. They paired motesanib with auranofin, a drug that inhibits that enzyme, across several experimental models of hepatocellular carcinoma.

The pair killed cancer cells far more strongly together than either approach suggested alone. Blocking TrxR1 let harmful oxygen molecules build up through a self-digestion process in the cells, triggering stress responses that damaged DNA and slowed growth. Removing a key self-digestion gene reduced that damage, supporting the proposed chain. The work points drug developers toward a paired strategy for advanced liver cancer.
pmc-13569542:
Agnès Aubry and co-authors examine, in a 2026 biographical study, how legal guardians in Switzerland cope with work the authors frame as dirty work. Their clients are vulnerable adults who often refuse the imposed help, and the tasks can be coercive. Life-history interviews reveal two broad coping styles shaped by class and gender upbringing.

One style leans into care, recasting guardianship as noble work, at the cost of heavy emotional labor. The other leans on law and administration, treating coercion as legitimate and keeping emotional distance. Social work researchers get a lens on how personal history quietly organizes professional survival.
pmc-13572342:
Yi Dong and colleagues traced how a circular RNA drives papillary thyroid cancer, publishing the study in 2026. Papillary carcinoma is the most common thyroid malignancy, and its spread, especially in young patients, needs better targets. The team compared circular RNA profiles in tumour and neighbouring tissue, finding circ-MAP4K3 markedly raised in cancers and cell lines.

Silencing the circular RNA slowed cancer-cell growth and movement and shrank tumours in mice. Experiments showed it acts as a sponge for miR-758-3p, freeing the RRM2 gene, and restoring either partner reversed the silencing effect. The circ-MAP4K3, miR-758-3p, and RRM2 chain offers a candidate axis for future thyroid-cancer therapy.
pmc-13572542:
S Anandaraj, with seven colleagues, presents a 2026 study that predicts the strength of green concrete with a neural network. The mix swaps part of the fine aggregate for marble dust and adds luffa, a plant fibre, as reinforcement. Lab tests alone cannot cover every blend, so a model that learns from past mixes can guide new ones.

Marble dust ran from 0 to 40 percent and luffa fibre from 0 to 2 percent across the test mixes. The best blend, 20 percent dust with 1 percent fibre, hit 34.5 megapascals in compression. It also reached 6.2 in bending and 4.25 in split tension. The authors credit tight particle packing from the dust and crack bridging by the treated fibre. A two-layer network then learned to predict all three strengths at once.
pmc-13573442:
Nisa Nur Ayhanci, with five colleagues, reports a 2026 study that brings a child migraine disability questionnaire into Turkish. The PedMIDAS form asks how much migraine cuts into school, home, and play life for children and teens. A sound Turkish version lets local clinics and studies gauge that burden the same way others do.

Sixty young patients with migraine took part. The form was translated forward and back to guard meaning. In a first session, children gave background and migraine details and filled in the form plus a quality-of-life scale. Fifteen days later, they filled in the migraine form again. Scores held steady across the gap, with a repeat correlation near the top of the scale. Internal consistency reached an acceptable level, and scores tied to migraine traits and quality of life as expected. The authors deem the version fit for use.
pmc-13574742:
Daniel A Ermann, with 12 colleagues, reports a 2026 real-world study of a drug class for chronic lymphocytic leukaemia in older Americans. The drugs block Bruton tyrosine kinase, a signal the cancer needs, and several near twins compete with no head-to-head trial between them. Routine care data can fill that gap for patients who start treatment.

The team used a de-identified Medicare fee-for-service database, which covers most Americans over 65. Patients who began one of the rival drugs as first treatment were compared on outcomes that matter in practice, such as survival and staying on therapy. Trial patients skew younger and fitter than Medicare patients, so real-world gaps may emerge that trials miss. The comparison aims to guide first picks for a cancer of older age. The authors frame the data as a partner to trial results, not a swap.
pmc-13575142:
Sagar Changela and four colleagues ask whether COVID-19 raises the later risk of obstructive sleep apnoea in a 2026 records study. Sleep apnoea, where the airway repeatedly closes during sleep, links to heart, metabolic, and thinking problems. Whether infection triggers new cases was unclear.

Health records came from the Montefiore system in the Bronx, covering adults tested between March 2020 and August 2024. Among 910,393 eligible patients, those hospitalised with COVID-19 had a 41 percent higher adjusted risk of new sleep apnoea than test-negative controls. Non-hospitalised cases also carried higher risk, at 33 percent. Findings held against a pre-pandemic comparison group. The authors support targeted screening after infection for people at high risk.
pmc-13576342:
Joung Min Choi, Yat Fei Cheung, and Liqing Zhang present CancerSubtyper, a 2026 deep learning framework that sorts tumours into subtypes using DNA methylation data. Methylation, a chemical tagging of DNA, carries rich signals about a tumour's type. Yet the data are vast, noisy across batches, and hard for non-specialists to handle.

Their system runs the whole pipeline automatically: cleaning, feature picking, batch correction, and subtype calling. Two models cover two jobs, one sorting cancers with known subtypes under light supervision, the other mixing supervised and unsupervised learning to hunt for new subtypes. An interactive web interface lets users explore and check results visually. Code is freely shared. The authors aim to lower the entry bar for large-scale methylation analysis in precision cancer research.
pmc-13578342:
Mohammad Javad Zarei and Somayeh Davoodabadi Farahani test plasma devices as a way to lift the output of straight bladed wind turbines, in a 2026 computer study. Such turbines spin around an upright shaft and work at any wind direction, yet their blades stall easily at low spin rates. Plasma actuators are strips that push air along the blade surface with an electric field, with no moving parts.

The team varied voltage, strip length, and placement on the blade in fluid flow models. Under the best settings a three blade rotor nearly doubled its average power score, and gains were largest at slow spin where stall bites hardest. Output also swung less across the working range, which steadies the machine. Rotors with two to five blades were checked under the same best setup.
pmc-13578542:
Maren Friederike Balks and colleagues ask whether a meal changes blood flow in the chest aorta enough to skew scan studies, in a 2026 study. Twenty young healthy adults, half of them women, had flow scans of the aorta after fasting and again after eating. The scanner tracks flow in three directions over time, giving beat by beat measures of volume, speed, and peak flow.

Eating nudged every measure up by a small but real margin. Peak flow rose in about three quarters of the group, and the top speed climbed the most of the set. The shifts were modest next to person to person spread. Still, the authors warn that mixed fasting states across visits or sites could tilt study results, so meal timing deserves a note in scan protocols.
pmc-13578742:
Cheikhouna Gaye and colleagues map the chemistry of three mangrove species in Senegal's Sine Saloum Delta, in a 2026 study. West African mangroves are little studied for their drug like compounds, despite harsh coastal lives that push plants to make strong defenses. Leaves were extracted in water and in alcohol mixes, then read by a high precision mass tool that groups related compounds into families.

The scan named about one hundred fifty compounds, led by plant acids, pigment flavonoids, and tannins. Two of the three species carried the richest phenolic loads and the strongest power against damaging oxygen forms. A live test during the scan pinned the main protective compounds, among them ellagic acid and two flavonoid families. The third species leaned on a different compound class and scavenged weakly.
pmc-13579742:
Yonas Wondie and colleagues ask how many medical students in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, have tested themselves for HIV, in a 2026 survey dated to 2024 fieldwork. Self testing is a core route to early detection, yet students face exposure risks at work and in private life with little targeted support. A questionnaire went to 375 students at a government medical college, and every form came back.

About one in five had used an oral self test. Students who had joined HIV programs were far more likely to have tested, as were men, students with a recent risk exposure, and those with a past sexually transmitted infection. The authors say the rate is low for a group this exposed, and they urge campuses to fold self testing into program work and counseling access.
pmc-13580042:
Truong and Tran describe in 2026 a survey dataset on Vietnam's local civil servants. It was collected just after the country's July 2025 administrative amalgamation, which merged units and pushed digital transformation. The dataset links digital skills to motivation and performance in this reshaped workforce.

The online questionnaire drew 380 responses from local government staff spread across Vietnam's six socio-economic regions. It measures digital literacy, digital competence, public service motivation, satisfaction with the job, and intention to leave, using scales the authors show to be reliable and valid. Because the survey ran right after the restructuring, it captures the workforce at a moment of unusual change. The authors offer the data to practitioners managing the digitalization drive and to scholars studying how digital skill and public service motivation shape performance outcomes.
pmc-13581442:
Viktor J Oláh and a large team of co-authors locate a little studied receptor at the release sites of calming brain cells, in a 2026 study. The receptor variant, built with a part called GluN2D, sits on the sending tips of a key interneuron type in the hippocampus. Its tail carries the address label that parks it there. Background glutamate levels switch it on, and it then dials the release of the calming signal GABA up or down.

Drugs that tune this receptor family, plus low dose ketamine, lost their grip on GABA release in mice missing the part in those cells. One selective blocker copied ketamine's lasting gains: stronger memory wiring and restored reward drive in a depression model, without ketamine's side effects. The authors nominate the receptor as a drug target.
pmc-13583342:
Şeyda Kaya, Zeliha Selamoglu, Sevgi Durna Daştan, and three co-authors turn to Kazakhstan's beekeeping sector and ask what its hive products might offer drug research. Bee products carry plant compounds called flavonoids, and the team picked four of them: myricetin, galangin, kaempferol, and quercetin. Using a web tool named SwissADME, they predicted how each compound would behave inside the body.

All four scored alike for likely uptake, and none was expected to reach the brain. Galangin, kaempferol, and quercetin were predicted to absorb well from the gut and passed every common drug-likeness rule the team applied. Myricetin lagged on gut uptake, which the authors link to its more polar shape. Galangin came out as the most balanced candidate for later lab work.
pmc-13583542:
Brison A Shira, Alana K E Thomas, and R Graham Cooks study a curious cluster of the amino acid serine. Eight serine units can lock together into a charged cluster that strongly favors partners of the same handedness, left or right. Such clusters interest chemists who probe how life's molecules came to favor one handedness over the other.

Using an ion trap mass spectrometer, the team swapped single amino acids into the cluster and watched which swaps it accepted. Swaps kept the same-handed preference in most cases, though two swaps at once, or swaps with less common amino acid forms, weakened or even flipped that preference. Their reading is that the cluster forms first, then trades units one at a time, guided by weak forces that can sense handedness.
pmc-13584342:
Zhou and colleagues reported in 2026 that gut microbes of plateau pikas, small herbivores of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, can break down PVC plastic. PVC microplastics have reached even this remote region, and microbes that digest plant fibre often carry tools that attack plastics too. The team fed pikas PVC particles, then enriched the gut microbes that responded, and studied the mix with multi-layer molecular methods.

Zhou isolated a microbial group that split PVC into long-chain alkanes, with Rhodococcus acting as a specialist responder and Leifsonia as a generalist. Two enzymes did key work: a dehalogenase from Rhodococcus freed chloride from PVC film, and a peroxidase from Leifsonia produced breakdown intermediates. A scan of 39 wild pika gut data sets confirmed both enzyme types are widespread there. The findings widen the enzyme toolkit for plastic cleanup in harsh settings.
pmc-13585842:
Melissa M Rangel and colleagues reflect on leave policy for breast surgical oncology fellows in this 2026 piece. Fellows in this one-year training path face births, deaths, illness, and caregiving like anyone else, yet their specialty has no shared leave standard. The linked study was the first national check of policy and practice across accredited programs in the United States.

Survey answers came back from program directors at a strong response rate, and meeting records were reviewed too. A third of programs had no formal leave policy, and allowed time ranged from none to twelve weeks, with a middle value of four. Leave for new non-birthing parents and for bereavement ran shorter than for birth or illness. The authors urge a shared framework that sets minimum leave and keeps graduation rules clear.
pmc-13586042:
Hugo Perazzo and colleagues road-test hepatitis C self-testing kits with men who have sex with men and transgender women in Rio de Janeiro. All 250 who took part were on PrEP, the preventive HIV medicine, and each person tried both a blood-based kit and a mouth-fluid kit on the same day under watch. Their 2026 study logged where people stumbled, what they got wrong, and which kit they liked.

The blood kit tripped more people up: close to two thirds needed help at some step, most often adding the buffer or drawing blood with the dropper. The mouth kit's main slip was a wrong fluid collection. Readings agreed well when kits were re-read or repeated, and nearly everyone said they felt safe and would test again. Mouth fluid was the slight favorite overall.
pmc-13588542:
Downing and colleagues describe in 2026 the CHSTRONG KIDS project, a survey effort tracking the long-term outcomes of American children born with congenital heart defects. Clinic-based studies miss children who drift away from specialist care, so this project starts from population records.

Birth defect surveillance systems in Atlanta, Massachusetts, and Minnesota identified 7,239 children born between 2006 and 2021 with heart defects, of whom 6,240 were eligible for recruitment. Caregivers of 1,841 children, thirty percent, returned survey data in 2024 and 2025. Response differed by state, defect severity, and family background, so the team built statistical weights to correct the picture. After weighting, about one in five children was not up to date with the cardiology visits guidelines recommend for their defect. The authors note this group is invisible in ordinary clinic data.
pmc-13588642: The European Heart Journal - Cardiovascular Pharmacotherapy issues a short correction to a review of urate-lowering therapy in heart, kidney, and metabolic care. The review, by Claudio Borghi, Federica Fogacci, and Arrigo F G Cicero, appeared in the August 2026 issue. The notice changes one sentence: the last in the abstract's conclusion. Where the sentence once spoke of identifying patients most likely to benefit, it now names patients with asymptomatic hyperuricemia, the group with high uric acid but no symptoms. No data, figures, or other conclusions are altered.
pmc-13589142:
Chunlin Yu and colleagues compare the flavor chemistry of breast meat from a fast commercial broiler and five local Chinese chicken breeds. Meat flavor rides on small molecules, amino acids, fats, and their breakdown products, and breeds differ sharply. Their 2026 study first measured carcass and meat traits, then profiled breast muscle chemistry with headspace gas chromatography and mass spectrometry.

Local breeds yielded less breast meat with less drip and cooking loss, but tougher texture, more fat, and brighter, redder color than the Cobb broiler. Their chemistry separated cleanly from the commercial bird's, with each local breed differing in a dozen to nearly thirty compounds, mostly amino acids and fatty acids. Those compounds clustered in pathways for fat building, ketone handling, and flavor development. The authors frame the maps as guidance for breeding and quality control.
pmc-13589542:
Beizhuo Li and colleagues built GENIUS-LLM, a framework that turns plant multi-omics data into traceable gene-function hypotheses. Gene-function analysis guides crop breeding, but integrating scattered omics datasets is labour-intensive, deep-learning predictions are opaque, and database queries demand exact identifiers. Their 2026 letter describes a language-model workflow that organises seven categories of gene-centred evidence across cotton, rice, and Arabidopsis into auditable reports.

For each queried gene, the system retrieves records, rewrites them as standardised natural-language blocks, and reasons through a fixed scaffold in GPT-4o, weighting direct functional cues above expression and co-expression evidence. The authors present traceable reasoning, not just prediction, as the advance, lowering the barrier to usable biological insight for breeders and researchers.
pmc-13591342:
Hanqing Shi and eight colleagues show how to write and rewrite magnetic patterns in a flat crystal that stays magnetic above room temperature. The patterns, called skyrmion bags, are swirls of magnetism whose winding count marks their type. That count normally resists change, which guards stored data yet blocks reuse. The crystal, Fe3GaTe2, has quirks that split surface behavior from the interior, the team found.

By pulsing current, they set bags with chosen winding counts and reshaped surface branches while the core pattern held. Such control could store more than simple binary data in one spot, using higher counting bases. Shi and the team frame the work as a step toward programmable spin based electronics that run warm, without deep cooling.
pmc-13593542:
Jad A Ballout and co-authors examine steam pops, small explosive bursts of heated tissue. The pops occurred while they used a dual-energy lattice-tip catheter to ablate the cavotricuspid isthmus, a strip of tissue in the right atrium. Their 2026 report pairs the cases with a review of device problem reports filed in the federal MAUDE database.

Even though the catheter controls its own temperature, pops still happened when lesions were stacked on top of each other or placed inside tissue pouches. The system gives no feedback on impedance or other usual ablation measures, so the events were hard to predict. The authors note that the pulsed field mode might avoid pops, though near this site it must be used with care because of the risk of coronary artery spasm.
pmc-13593742:
Sara Rodriguez-Mena and co-authors report the first systematic test of how grass pea stands up to Aphanomyces euteiches. Grass pea is a hardy legume crop, and the water mold rots the roots of peas and lentils. The team inoculated 169 grass pea accessions from a worldwide collection with a single strain of the pathogen and scored leaf and root symptoms twenty days later.

Responses ranged widely, from fully susceptible plants to some with partial or even complete resistance. Scanning nearly thirteen thousand DNA markers across the collection tied resistance to twenty markers spread over five of the seven chromosomes, a pattern pointing to many genes each contributing a little. Seven nearby candidate genes touch on transport, signaling, cell wall building, and fat and hormone pathways. The authors offer the resistant lines and markers as starting material for breeding tougher grass pea varieties.
pmc-13594342:
Edgar Petrosyan and colleagues review how the endoplasmic reticulum stress response shapes cancer's spread to the brain. The endoplasmic reticulum folds proteins inside cells. When conditions such as low oxygen or high secretory load overwhelm it, stress pathways fire. Their 2026 review follows tumor cells through each step of reaching and colonizing the brain.

Leaving the original tumor, surviving in the bloodstream, crossing the blood-brain barrier, and settling into brain tissue each impose distinct stresses. Only a small minority of cells adapt well enough to finish the journey. Because surviving cells lean chronically on these stress pathways, that dependence may itself be a weakness worth drugging. The authors frame the stress response as a kind of compass steering adaptation, and they argue it deserves attention in the search for better control of brain metastases.
pmc-13597542:
D. Wouters and co-authors listened to what women with vulvar cancer and its precursor condition actually ask online, mining public forums in the Netherlands, Britain, and the United States. From nearly five thousand posts spanning 2008 onward, 619 questions were coded into themes in their social listening study.

Seven themes covered causes, early signs, diagnosis, treatment, the period after treatment, long-term worries, and emotional impact. Early signs and life after treatment tied as the biggest themes. Standing above all of them was one crosscutting need. The authors call it recognition uncertainty. It means not knowing whether a bodily change is normal, abnormal, or a sign of recurrence. It made up a fifth of everything coded. Questions after treatment clustered on wound problems and what recovery should feel like. The authors recommend communication that starts before diagnosis and honest preoperative guidance on wounds.
pmc-13598142:
Yasmine Taki and co-authors present FloraLebanon, a field image dataset of Lebanon's native Mediterranean plants built for machine learning and biodiversity monitoring. University volunteers photographed plants across the Al Shouf Biosphere Reserve during 2024 expeditions, following a set protocol that captured whole plants plus leaves, stems, flowers, fruits, and habitats.

The curated release holds 24,944 images covering 102 species. Every identification was checked against pressed voucher specimens and confirmed by two independent taxonomists, and poor or duplicate images were removed by hand in two cleaning passes. The open dataset ships with naming metadata and specimen scans. Field images, cluttered and variable unlike laboratory portraits, should train hardier identification models, the authors argue. Their stated ambition is to grow the collection toward Lebanon's full flora of roughly twenty-six hundred species.
pmc-13599642:
Liyun Yue, Hao Li, and Songtao Zhou report a 2026 method to make drug-producing cells yield more antibody medicine. Antibodies are grown in hamster ovary cells, and fixing the antibody gene at a known spot in the cell's DNA gives steady production. That fixed-spot method's weakness is low output. Strong promoters, the DNA switches that turn genes on, are one route to higher yields.

The team combined potent switch elements at the landing site into synthetic promoters one-third the length of the standard CMV promoter. Some matched or beat CMV by up to 20 percent on a test gene. In fed-batch production, titers rose as much as 45 percent above CMV for a standard antibody. A two-armed bispecific reached about 2.7 grams per liter, below CMV's 3.8 grams. Promoters tuned to their landing site, the authors conclude, can make fixed-spot cell lines far more useful.
pmc-13608542:
Rasha Aziz Attia Salama leads a twelve-author team pooling trial results for one breast cancer regimen question. Triple-negative breast cancer is aggressive and short on targeted drugs, so chemotherapy before surgery is standard. Complete disappearance of the tumor, called pathological complete response, predicts better survival. The team gathered studies of pre-surgery treatment built on nab-paclitaxel, a packaged form of paclitaxel, with platinum drugs and/or checkpoint inhibitors.

Twenty-one studies qualified. Four randomized trials of checkpoint inhibitor addition, covering 1,228 patients, pooled to a risk ratio of 1.25 for complete response, favoring the added immune drug. Fourteen single-arm datasets covering 539 patients pooled to a complete response rate of 59.8 percent. This second figure only describes those cohorts and cannot rank treatments, the authors warn. Their conclusion stays narrow: adding checkpoint blockade improved complete response in the randomized comparisons.
pmc-13612242:
Alison E Meyer leads a fourteen-author team reporting a surprise cooperation between two leukemia defects in 2026. Core binding factor leukemias carry chromosome rearrangements such as inv(16). Cohesin mutations, which loosen chromosome organization, appear less often with inv(16) than with its sister rearrangement, so the team expected them to hinder it. Mice engineered with inv(16) plus half-dose cohesin subunit Smc3 did the opposite: leukemia arrived sooner.

Before any leukemia appeared, double-mutant blood stem cells already showed more open chromatin, studded with binding motifs for the transcription factor Fli1. Single-cell sequencing confirmed higher Fli1 levels and stronger target-gene activity in short-term stem cells. Established leukemia from these mice then proved dependent on Fli1 to persist. The authors reframe cohesin loss as an aggressiveness booster for inv(16) disease rather than a brake. They nominate Fli1 as a new therapeutic vulnerability in cohesin-mutated acute myeloid leukemia.
pmc-13616342:
Ilaria Incaviglia and colleagues build a microscope-stage balance that weighs single living cells and small cell balls while also feeling their stiffness, all in real time under normal culture conditions. Cell mass, growth, and mechanics are tightly linked, yet no tool read all three together fast enough to follow quick changes. Their device uses tiny diving-board sensors, set vibrating by light heat, paired with a microscope camera.

The sensor's quality factor, a measure of how cleanly it rings, mirrored the cell's mechanical character while its frequency shift tracked mass. Readings came at millisecond resolution, quick enough to catch subcellular events. Watching weight and springiness change together through growth, specialisation, or disease could reveal which shift comes first, a clue to how cells decide their fate.
pmc-13617142:
Muhammad Tayyab Arshad and seven colleagues review the medicinal and industrial value of Thai legumes, the pea and bean family plants woven into Thai food and folk medicine. Soybean, mung bean, pigeon pea, butterfly pea, and cowpea anchor the review. These plants supply protein, fiber, and a store of active compounds, and farmers value them for enriching soil with nitrogen.

The plants carry phenolics, flavonoids, saponins, and active peptides tied in earlier studies to antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, plus protection for the heart and nerves. Industry uses range from functional foods, plant proteins, and fermented products to drug ingredients, cosmetics, and materials that break down on their own. The authors flag weak clinical validation, variable chemistry between harvests, and processing scale-up as the main obstacles, and they call for combined research methods to unlock the full potential.
pmc-13617242:
Md Lemon Hasan and seven colleagues review how researchers are upgrading hydrogel dressings for burn wounds. Hydrogels already keep burns moist, cool the tissue, and ease pain, yet plain versions do little to actively regrow skin, which slows healing of deep burns. Recent work loads these water-rich gels with living or active ingredients to make them true treatment platforms.

The review covers added proteins, peptides, antimicrobial compounds, drugs, metal nanoparticles, cell-derived vesicles, and extracellular matrix, the natural scaffold between cells. It explains how such gels are made, how each addition fights infection or speeds tissue repair, and what evidence supports the designs. Because burns cause deep, extensive damage and carry high death rates, the authors argue faster, biologically active dressings could improve survival and reduce scarring, especially where hospital resources are scarce.
pmc-13619642:
Márcio Oliveira Alves, Felipe Silva Carvalho, and João Pedro Braga present a steadier way to recover adsorption potential energy from measured isotherm data. Adsorption, where molecules collect on a surface, matters for cleaning water, yet working backward from uptake curves to the energy landscape is an inverse problem prone to instability. The usual route first estimates an intermediate coefficient and then inverts it, which lets errors grow at each step.

Their method skips the middle step by writing the problem as a tensor contraction, a structured multiplication drawn from statistical physics. Tested on both water-based and gas-phase datasets, the direct approach matched the data almost perfectly. The authors argue that removing the fragile intermediate step gives researchers a cleaner physical picture of how surfaces bind molecules, with far less error carried along.
pmc-13619742:
Taylor Probst, Cameron D Siler, and Drew R Davis produced the first genomic survey of the lined snake, a secretive burrowing species spread across the Great Plains. Four subspecies had been named from body features, yet almost no genetic samples existed to test them. The team sequenced genome-wide markers from snakes across the range and mapped how populations relate.

Genes flowed broadly across the plains, which undercuts the case for separate subspecies. Snakes at the northern edge in South Dakota stood apart a little, forming a fairly uniform group that may have been isolated recently or shrunk by drift in fringe habitat. That northern population is listed as endangered in the state. The authors say range-edge snakes deserve conservation attention, and they call for denser sampling in regions that might hold other isolated pockets.
pmc-13620442:
Theodora Zouvani and ten colleagues asked what finding cytomegalovirus in lung wash fluid means for patients with weakened immune systems. This common herpesvirus sleeps quietly in healthy people but can turn dangerous after transplants or blood cancers. The team analyzed more than two thousand six hundred bronchoscopy visits involving 1,301 immunocompromised patients with suspected lung infection between 2009 and 2017.

Two hundred thirty-five samples from 157 patients tested positive. Most positive cases carried another infection alongside the virus, and those mixed cases showed a fluid profile heavy in neutrophils, while virus-only cases held more macrophages. Findings changed treatment in well over half the positive cases. Positive patients were hospitalized more often and died within thirty days at higher rates than negative patients. The authors urge preventive and early antiviral strategies, stressing that one virus found never rules out others hiding with it.
pmc-13621642:
Paul Kaufmann and eight colleagues linked a sluggish blood enzyme to later Alzheimer's disease, using the Malmö preventive project cohort in Sweden. The enzyme, PAM, finishes many hormone-like peptides, among them adrenomedullin, which guards blood vessel walls and the blood-brain barrier. The team measured PAM activity and adrenomedullin forms in 4,543 adults free of dementia and tracked new cases in national records.

Over roughly five years, 205 people developed Alzheimer's and ninety-three got vascular dementia. Lower PAM activity more than doubled Alzheimer's risk per standard step down. Lower levels of the active, finished adrenomedullin form also predicted the disease. A shrunken ratio of finished to raw peptide pointed to molecules piling up half-built. The signals held regardless of APOE risk status and ran stronger in non-obese people, while vascular dementia showed no steady link. The authors float weak amidation as an early blood sign of neurovascular vulnerability.
pmc-13623142:
Anne L Buffardi and three co-authors survey the world's policy tools for improving health through better housing. Poor housing harms health, that much is well documented, but evidence on which fixes work is thin and scattered. Their scoping review hunts for real programmes in practice, including reports outside academic journals, and records each one's aims, costs, actors, and results.

Drawing on thirty-seven reviews and reports, the team catalogued 327 distinct interventions. Rules that shape markets, such as rent regulation and planning changes, plus direct building or upgrading of social housing, appeared far more often than information campaigns or tax tools. Evidence of benefit was strongest for physical home improvements and some economic rules, and weakest for health outcomes measured along a full chain of change. Costs were rarely stated, and the people who pay often differ from those who save. The authors urge building evaluation into running programmes.
pmc-13624042:
Federico Emanuele Pozzi leads a report from a Brain Health Service in Monza, Italy, which sees people worried about memory slips despite normal test results, a state called subjective cognitive decline. Up to forty-five percent of dementia may be preventable through lifestyle factors, so services like this aim to find and shrink risk early. The team profiled their first attendees and tested a blood marker of Alzheimer's change.

Baseline data covered 186 people, 132 of them with subjective decline. The commonest fixable risks in that group were poor sleep, smoking, inactivity, and high blood pressure. About a third carried a positive blood marker result; they were older, scored worse on screening tests, and showed more brain degeneration on scans. Grouping analysis split attendees into a low-risk, sharp group and a high-risk, weaker group. Telling people their marker result was well accepted, with no extra anxiety in the positive group.
pmc-13630442:
Chunlian Jin and four colleagues write, in a 2026 letter, about building a gene editing system for one flower. The plant is Eustoma grandiflorum, the prickle-less rose. It ranks among the world's top cut flowers. Breeding progress has been slow. Transforming this plant is famously hard. Earlier leaf-based and flower-dipping methods yielded very few edited plants.

The letter reviews the obstacles. They include weak tissue regrowth and the challenge of editing a plant with a complex genome. It then describes the team's approach, built on growing embryos from ordinary body cells. Earlier editing in this plant had been shown only in loose cells. It had never been shown in a whole regrown plant. The authors frame their system as the missing bridge. It links cell-level proof to practical trait work. Targets include colour, shape, scent, and stress resistance.
pmc-13631542:
L Hardefeldt and colleagues test a workaround for a common gap in veterinary records. Dog weight, needed to judge whether an antibiotic dose is right, is missing in well over half of electronic records. The team turned to VetCompass Australia, building average weights by breed, age, and sex from 72,089 dogs among the ten most common breeds. They then applied those averages to a second group of 69,683 dogs over one year old that had weights recorded and had received antibiotics.

Against Australian veterinary prescribing guidance, 66 percent of doses were appropriate on true weights. Using breed, sex, and age averages instead, the method correctly flagged appropriate doses 82 percent of the time and inappropriate doses 78 percent of the time. Stewardship researchers get a reasonably accurate population-level fix for missing weights, useful for audits and feedback, though not a substitute for weighing an individual dog.
pmc-13635042:
Dyes that make near-invisible eye structures visible during retinal surgery are surveyed by Giannuzzi and colleagues. Chromovitrectomy, the use of vital dyes during vitrectomy, lets surgeons see the vitreous gel, the thin internal limiting membrane, and scar-like membranes that would otherwise blend into view. The review weighs the main dyes, including brilliant blue G, trypan blue, indocyanine green, and triamcinolone, for how strongly they stain each tissue and how safely they behave.

Newer high-density and multi-component dye preparations improve selectivity and handling, while three-dimensional heads-up displays and adjustable spectral filters sharpen contrast and ease the surgeon's posture. The authors also discuss hidden retinal breaks, sequential staining, and the dangers of light-related toxicity and macular injury. Giannuzzi and colleagues argue that pairing gentler dyes with digital visualisation and, later, intraoperative imaging and artificial intelligence should keep improving surgical precision.
pmc-13637342:
Khalil Hamadeh and six colleagues published this 2026 survey of what Lebanese parents know and do about unhealthy blood fats in children. Childhood dyslipidemia seeds later heart disease, and parents control screening and habits. Nearly nine hundred fifty parents of schoolchildren in Greater Beirut and Mount Lebanon answered an online questionnaire in 2025. Most respondents were mothers, and nearly all held university degrees. The team scored their knowledge and linked it to practices.

Fewer than half had even heard of the condition in children, learning of it mostly from media or clinicians. Average knowledge landed mid-scale. Only a tiny share had ever had their child's lipids tested. Being female, university educated, or a health professional each predicted stronger knowledge, as did having heard of the condition. Knowledge tracked with healthier eating at home and with getting children screened. The authors back education campaigns aimed at parents and frontline clinicians.
pmc-13639042:
Andrea Gardoni and eleven colleagues report a 2026 brain imaging study of how sound cues improve hand movement in early Parkinson's disease. Slowness of movement, called bradykinesia, is a core symptom, and rhythmic cues are known to help some patients move better.

Twenty-six patients and twenty healthy volunteers tapped their right hand during scans, sometimes following a beat and sometimes at their own pace. Without cues, patients showed shrinking tap size across repetitions, while cueing reduced that decline. Brain activity in the pallidum rose with cueing and tracked better performance. The results suggest cues work partly by engaging deep brain movement circuits.
pmc-13642542:
Amir Targholizadeh and two colleagues present a 2026 device study that pairs a cryogenic metalens with a superconducting nanowire single-photon detector. Such detectors lead the field, but one element faces a trade-off: a large area catches more light, while a small area keeps counts fast and clean.

Their dielectric lens, working at cryogenic temperatures, focused light onto a tiny five-micrometer-square active area and boosted detection efficiency about seventy-seven-fold over an identical bare detector. Design work also showed polarization-resolved detection at telecom wavelengths with very low cross-talk. The authors aim at smaller, cheaper quantum sensing hardware.
pmc-13645242:
S. Kamaludeen and four colleagues present a 2026 study comparing two ways to predict a difficult airway view before anesthesia. Seeing the vocal cords poorly during tube placement is a leading cause of anesthesia harm, and standard bedside checks predict it weakly.

In one hundred adults having elective surgery, the team measured jaw-to-neck distance by hand and the soft tissue thickness in front of the windpipe by ultrasound. The ultrasound measure was clearly thicker in patients whose laryngoscopy proved difficult, and it outperformed the distance measure. The authors recommend adding the quick scan to routine airway checks.
pmc-13645542:
Shijun Tan and Caifeng Li report a cross-sectional study of college students in Chongqing, China, linking fitness scores with stress, anxiety, and low mood. The pair tested 2,190 students drawn from 73 universities. Fitness was scored from lung capacity, sprint and distance runs, flexibility, and strength tasks. Mood symptoms were measured with a standard twenty-one item scale.

Students with moderate or high fitness scores had lower odds of stress, anxiety, and depression symptoms than less fit students. The pattern held for both male and female students, though some links were weaker in split analyses. Because all data came from one point in time, the study cannot prove that fitness protects mood. Still, it gives schools a practical, fitness-based lead for student mental health work.
pmc-13646142:
Bakytzhan Alibekov, Alina Gutoreva, and Elisa Raffaella Ferrè build a computing framework to predict how people adapt to gravity levels unlike Earth's. The brain keeps an inner model of gravity, and spaceflight bends it. Two model parts were trained on open data from altered-gravity studies such as parabolic flights. One predicts brain wave patterns under different loads, while the other models heart, skin, and movement responses.

A large language model then turned those body predictions into written scenes of alertness and bodily awareness for weightlessness, Moon and Mars gravity, and overload. The authors offer the combined tool as a way to forecast performance and resilience before missions fly. It could help planners design training and countermeasures for crews. The work also gives researchers a test bed for questions that are costly to probe in real altered-gravity settings.
pmc-13647042:
Rebekah P Horner, Eloise A Marais, and Lee T Murray calculate how much nitrogen oxide pollution each lightning flash produces, using flash energy measured by satellite sensors. Lightning is a major natural source of these gases high in the atmosphere, where they steer ozone and other climate-relevant chemistry. Earlier models used one fixed value per flash everywhere. The trio instead let production vary by place and hour over the years 2015 to 2019.

Ocean flashes proved more productive than land flashes, a pattern the fixed models missed, though land still emitted more overall because flashes are more frequent there. The global total fell by nearly two units of nitrogen against the old inventory. Feeding the new rates into a chemistry model lowered several key gases and eased known model overestimates. The authors call for independent checks of the rates, since much rides on them for methane and ozone accounting.
pmc-13647642:
Eun-Mi Seol and Soo-Hyun Nam analyze a national survey to find why South Korean adults with disabilities still miss needed health care despite near-universal insurance, in a 2026 paper. The 2023 survey supplied 6,772 adults with registered disabilities. A classic behavioral model sorted the influences into predisposing traits, enabling resources, and vulnerability factors. Reports of care missed in the past year formed the outcome.

About seventeen percent had unmet needs. Transport difficulty and cost together explained nearly two thirds of the stated barriers. Lacking insurance was the strongest single predictor, and physical disability plus poor self-rated health also raised the odds sharply. Curiously, severe disability came with lower odds than mild disability, hinting that support systems overlook people whose limits look smaller. Women with physical disabilities stood out as a high-risk pocket. The authors prescribe paratransit expansion, lower out-of-pocket costs, and enrollment help as first moves.
pmc-13648842:
Monica M. Diaz and fourteen colleagues develop and validate a brief tablet-based cognitive screening battery for HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder in Lima, Peru. The condition stays common despite treatment, and underserved clinics need Spanish-language tools that are quick yet accurate.

Eleven candidate tablet tests were tried in a development group, and four were kept, giving a battery of about fourteen minutes covering several thinking domains. Against a full paper-and-pencil reference battery, the short version discriminated well in both development and validation samples, with validation sensitivity above eighty percent. The authors caution that the battery screens rather than diagnoses, and that thresholds, low-literacy users, and rural settings still need study.
pmc-13649442:
Abdul Ali Peer-Zada and six colleagues report a 13-year-old girl with acute myeloid leukaemia whose cancer carried a rare change in the FLT3 gene. Changes in this gene drive about a quarter of such cancers, but hers was a new insertion of extra code in a spot where few changes are seen.

Her disease resisted standard strong chemotherapy yet shrank fast on a drug that blocks FLT3. When heart harm forced a pause, the cancer came back. She then had a stem cell transplant from a donor while the disease was still active, plus two more years of the blocker drug. She stayed free of disease for 63 months after the transplant. The authors urge more study of these rare gene changes.
pmc-13649642:
Aryel C. Goes and four colleagues offer a new frame for studying social immunity in termites, the colony defences that insects mount against germs. In ants and bees, strict roles make clear guesses about who does the costly cleaning and grooming tasks. Termites break that mould, since their workers keep a flexible chance to breed later in life.

The authors map what is known about germ defence in termites onto a frame built on growth stage and future breeding odds. Wide gaps appear at once: few studies use germs the insects meet in the wild, and hygiene traits have rarely been compared across termite kinds. Their frame sets up sharper tests of why selfless defence evolves.
pmc-13651242:
Karl Friston and one colleague review the long arc of predictive processing, the theory that the brain is a fantastic organ in the old sense. It builds an inner fantasy, a model of the world. It perceives by testing that model against the senses. The review opens with Newton's musings on colors and Helmholtz's idea of perception as unconscious inference.

From those roots the authors trace predictive coding through its generalizations into the Bayesian brain and the free energy principle. Organisms act to sample the world in ways that confirm or refine their predictions. The framework spans synaptic self-organization, structure learning, anatomy, and physiology, offering one language for many levels of brain function. That breadth is the opportunity and the challenge, since each discipline hears the term differently. The authors aim to keep theory and experiment in contact by spelling out hypotheses that data can judge.
pmc-13652542:
Kai Zhang and five colleagues add the missing physics of water removal to computer models of biomolecular phase separation. Inside cells, proteins and RNA gather into droplets called condensates, and forming them requires chains to shed their water shells while sticking to one another. Popular coarse-grained models skip the water entirely, which limits their accuracy. Guided by detailed atomic simulations and lab measurements, the team built drying costs directly into a simpler model's energy rules.

Applied to disordered proteins that form droplets, the corrected model matched experiments more closely and showed how desolvation steers both the stability and the motion of condensates. The work matters beyond modeling technique, since faulty condensates are tied to disease. A model that respects the water step gives researchers a sharper tool for predicting when droplets form, dissolve, or harden into harmful aggregates.
pmc-3516142:
Fu, Niu, Zhu, and co-authors present a faster version of CD-HIT for clustering next-generation sequencing data. CD-HIT is a widely used program that groups similar sequences, cutting repeats and improving the speed of later analyses. Sequencing output was rising rapidly when they wrote.

The update keeps clustering practical as datasets swell by orders of magnitude. Removing near-repeat sequences shrinks databases without losing real diversity. Faster grouping matters for community DNA work and protein family studies, where raw sequence sets can reach hundreds of millions of entries.  Protein databases use clustering to offer non-redundant sets for search services online.
pmc-3974642:
McMurdie and Holmes argued in 2014 that a common step in microbiome work should be dropped. Studies of microbe communities produce count data, and labs must adjust those counts before they compare samples. Many labs thin counts down to an equal size, a step called rarefying.

The authors show that rarefying wastes data and is weak in a strict statistical sense. Simple proportions also fail, since they do not deal with uneven spread in the counts. Better models keep all the data and handle that spread head on. The paper pushed many labs to change how they treat microbe counts before testing for real differences.
pmc-3998142:
Jones, Binns, Chang, and their colleagues described InterProScan five in 2014. The software sorts proteins by function, a basic need when a genome yields millions of new sequences. The update was rebuilt in Java to cope with work at genome scale.

InterProScan checks a protein against many member databases at once and combines the matches into one report. That gives users a quick view of likely families, domains, and roles for each sequence. The new design runs faster and is easier to install and link with other tools. Genome centers rely on it as a first pass to make sense of fresh sequence data.
pmc-5310842:
Skene and Henikoff presented CUT&RUN in 2017, a strategy for mapping where proteins bind DNA. Chromatin profiling shows which parts of the genome a protein touches, which reveals how genes are controlled. Standard methods needed many cells and gave noisy background signals.

CUT&RUN stands for Cleavage Under Targets and Release Using Nuclease. An antibody guides a nuclease to cut DNA only at the target protein's sites, releasing those complexes for sequencing. The method gives high-resolution maps with far fewer cells than older approaches. It quickly became a favored tool for studying transcription factors and chromatin marks in small or precious samples.
pmc-5899442:
Eili Klein, Thomas Van Boeckel, Elena Martinez, and colleagues tracked antibiotic use across many countries in 2018. Use of these drugs drives resistance, a growing threat to health worldwide. Their report covers sixteen years of sales data at the start of this century.

Total use rose worldwide, with the fastest growth in low and middle income countries. Use rates began to converge as poorer countries gained access while rich ones cut back. The authors warn that rising use without stewardship will speed resistance. The figures give global health groups a baseline for judging control efforts.
pmc-6119242:
Valeska Ormazabal, Soumyalekshmi Nair, Omar Elfeky, and coauthors reviewed insulin resistance and heart disease in 2018. Heart and vessel disease has long been the leading cause of death worldwide. It often travels with obesity, abnormal blood fats, and insulin resistance.

The review traces how poor insulin response harms blood vessels over time. High sugar, pressure, and fats injure vessel walls and favor clots and plaque. The authors connect cell-level changes to the heart attacks patients actually suffer. Their account helps explain why diabetes care puts so much weight on early metabolic control.
pmc-6357742:
Stephen Dominy and colleagues reported evidence linking a gum bacterium to Alzheimer disease in 2019. The bacterium, Porphyromonas gingivalis, causes chronic gum disease. The team looked for its traces in the brains of Alzheimer patients.

They found bacterial toxins called gingipains in patient brains, at levels tied to disease markers. In mice, blocking those toxins with small-molecule drugs cut brain infection and amyloid build-up. The work raised a striking claim: that an oral infection may help drive dementia. It spurred trials of gingipain blockers, though the idea remains debated. The authors also reported similar toxin signals in a large share of the patient brains examined.
pmc-6629542:
Seunggeun Choi and Paul O'Reilly presented PRSice-2, software for polygenic risk scores, in 2019. A polygenic score sums many tiny genetic effects into one risk number. Such scores now serve research on shared causes and causal tests.

PRSice-2 is built for the biobank era, handling hundreds of thousands of people quickly. It automates threshold tuning, where scores are built at many cutoffs and the best is kept. Careful handling of related variants reduces double counting. Genetics teams adopted it as a standard workhorse for score building and testing. The software is freely available and runs on ordinary desktop machines as well as clusters.
pmc-7146642:
Moritz Kraemer, Chia-Hung Yang, Bernardo Gutierrez, and coauthors studied mobility and control measures in China's COVID-19 epidemic in 2020. The outbreak expanded fast across China in its first weeks. Travel limits, case isolation, and distancing were deployed at huge scale.

Using phone-based movement data, the team shows spread tracked travel out of Wuhan early on. After controls tightened, local transmission fell and the link to travel weakened. Their analysis suggested aggressive measures bent the curve inside China. It offered other countries an early, data-based look at what mobility control can achieve.
smith-antiquities-1842:
William Smith published his Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities in 1842, the first of his great classical reference works. Smith was a schoolmaster turned publisher's editor with a genius for organizing knowledge. The dictionary was built for students and teachers who needed the ancient world explained in English.

Entries cover the laws, gods, games, dress, houses, and daily tools of Greece and Rome, all in alphabetical order. Smith gathered a team of scholars and illustrated the articles with images of real objects. Victorian schoolboys learned their antiquity from these pages, and the book set the standard for a generation. It was the great dictionary-maker's first triumph. Later editions grew still larger, but the 1842 volume shows the moment when classical reference in English came of age.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5042:
Lyndon B. Johnson gives six yearly addresses, from January 8, 1964, to January 14, 1969, parted by three stars. The first pledges brevity, since time is short and the agenda long. Last year's session was the longest in peacetime, Johnson notes, and on that base he calls the house to make this year's the best in the nation's past.

Let this session be known, he urges, as the one that did more for civil rights than the last hundred sessions joined. As the one that passed the widest tax cut of the age, declared all-out war on poverty and want of work, and at last owned the health needs of all older citizens. As the one that mended tangled transport plans, made foreign aid work at its best, and helped build more homes, schools, libraries, and hospitals than any one session before it.
stephanos-alexandria-magna-arte-ideler-1:
Stephanos of Alexandria lectured at Constantinople in the early seventh century, under the emperor Heraclius. His nine lectures On the Great and Sacred Art are the last great statement of Greek alchemy. J. L. Ideler printed the Greek text in his 1842 edition of the medical and physical writers. No English version in the public domain exists.

Stephanos blends the furnace with the stars, teaching that the work on metals mirrors the order of the heavens. He addresses the emperor as a pupil and calls alchemy a sacred, God-given science. His lectures carried the Alexandrian art into Byzantium whole. From there it passed, in time, to the Islamic world and back to Europe.
teste-transactions-magnetisme-1842:
Alphonse Teste edited the Transactions of Animal Magnetism in French, and its first year ran in 1842. The journal gave French magnetizers a place to print their work. Cases, debates, and reports of trials filled its pages through that opening year.

Readers find healers testing trance, sleep, and claimed cures in public view. Supporters and critics argue over what the facts really prove. The tone is earnest, hopeful, and often combative. As a record, the volume reads like a lab notebook for a movement. It shows mesmerism in France while its leaders still thought proof was near.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: Vol. 1, No. 42 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is dated August 26, 1897. The paper is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and a premium offer. The premium is a Scientific Box Kite, for any one who sends one new subscriber. The kite is the invention of H. H. Clayton, of Blue Hill Observatory, near Boston. Kites of this type have reached 9,200 feet, nearly two miles.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2-part:
The Ormsby Don Quixote, Cervantes' tale in English, opens Volume 2, Part 42 here. Chapter seventy-three tells of the omens Don Quixote had as he entered his own village, and other incidents that give a colour to this great history. At the village entrance, so says Cide Hamete, two boys quarrel on the threshing-floor.

One boy tells the other to take it easy, for he shall never see it again as long as he lives. Don Quixote seizes on the words and turns to Sancho to mark them. A child's taunt becomes an omen in the knight's ear, as the long road ends where it began and the history nears its close.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
The Mirror's number for Saturday, January 17, 1829, No. 352, illustrates Prince Rupert's palace in the Barbican. Rupert lodged in a Beech Lane house under Charles II, and the king once visited him there; Cripplegate's ringers earned a guinea for their merry peal. The article predicts Rupert will be remembered in the useful and fine arts when his military fame is forgotten. He was among the most ingenious men of his time.

His inventions and improvements include Prince's metal, locks for firearms, and better gunpowder. After the Restoration he joined the Privy Council and the new Royal Society, and helped establish the Hudson's Bay Company as its first governor. Vertue and others credit him with mezzotint engraving, though the article thinks that claim disputed and disproved. A second feature, on the Colosseum in Regent's Park, follows. Readers meet the cavalier prince reclassified as a scientist with a City address.

For Saturday, April 25, 1829, the Mirror's No. 367 illustrates Sussex Place in Regent's Park, then prints a correspondent's translation of an Irish deed of gift. Sussex Place, among the park's earliest terraces, is said to be Nash's design and one of his least successful. Its whimsical contrast with chaster neighbors drew critical pasquinade. A centre with pediment, two octagonal towers, and four more towers to each wing carry cupola tops and minarets.

The article calls the attempt at magnificence on so small a scale unjustifiable on grounds of beauty or taste. Yet the landscape painter's eye may enjoy its picturesque outlines grouped with the scenery. Before the facade the park's lake reflects the oriental cupolas with charming effect. Gardens are tastefully disposed, and the prospects rank among the park's most fascinating. Readers get an architect scolded and forgiven in a single view.

The Mirror's No. 405, dated Saturday, December 19, 1829, illustrates new buildings in the Inner Temple. The Temple ranges from Fleet Street to the Thames, once the Knights Templars' principal establishment. Henry III, papal nuncios, and ambassadors were entertained there in the thirteenth century. The king's treasure was kept in the part now called the Middle Temple, and the Temple Church's chief minister is still styled Master of the Temple.

After the order's suppression, the professors of the common law bought the buildings. They became the Inns of Court called Inner and Middle Temple, from their relation to the Outer Temple by Temple Bar. A footnote points readers to the magazine's own Temple Church description in No. 274. The Inner Temple's nucleus, its hall and chapel, was substantially repaired in 1819. Unsightly brick ranges beyond it give the number its subject. Readers watch crusader headquarters persist as lawyers' chambers.

A Swiss cottage at the Colosseum in Regent's Park leads volume 19, No. 544, dated April 28, 1832. The Colosseum's great attraction was its Panorama of London, a painted view covering 40,000 square feet, nearly an acre. The magazine had toured the unfinished building with its projector, Mr. Horner, three years earlier.

That earlier visit, made amid scaffolding and workmen, still shapes the account. The Panorama is called a pictorial history of London, showing the vastness, wealth, and commerce of the city at a single glance. The present piece turns to the principal apartment of the Swiss Cottage within the grounds, promising further views of the Colosseum's embellishments as sketches allow.
the-reciprocal-influence-of-body-and-min: The Reciprocal Influence of Body and Mind, 1842. The body-mind influence. This book preserves that work. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it. Those who study the era will use it in their work.
the-two-noble-kinsmen-pg1542: A second record of The Two Noble Kinsmen, by John Fletcher and William Shakespeare, adds a note on its text: this edition follows C. F. Tucker Brooke's 1908 Shakespeare Apocrypha, with italics mostly removed. The original 1634 title page follows, printed by Thomas Cotes for John Waterson, boasting the play was presented at Blackfriars by the King's servants with great applause. A persons list names Theseus, Hippolita, Emilia, the jailer and his daughter. The cousins' story begins beyond these leaves, as in its sibling record.
tob-0042:
Donald N. Wilber, the CIA officer-scholar who helped plan the 1953 coup in Iran, wrote the agency's internal history of the operation soon after it succeeded. Operation Ajax overthrew Premier Mohammad Mossadeq and restored the Shah's power. The history stayed secret until it reached The New York Times in 2000.

Wilber describes the planning, the propaganda and street action, the near failure, and the final success, as an insider's after-action report. It is both a spy's manual and a confession, written for the agency itself. Declassified, it remains the core document of the coup that shaped Iran's view of America for generations.
tob-0142:
Seven days at a royal wedding frame the Chymical Wedding of Christian Rosenkreutz, printed in 1616. The aged Rosenkreutz, founder in legend of the Rosicrucian order, receives a strange invitation and travels to a castle of wonders. Tests, riddles, and marvels meet him at every door.
